What this curriculum is for:
The first lesson is about the route itself, because this one has an unusual end point and knowing it changes how you read everything after it.

**The finish line is code you already own.** `the-world-of-terrath/products/` holds three working Godot projects:

| Project | Scripts | Lines of GDScript | Scenes | Shaders |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **shepherds-we-shall-be** | 535 | 114,394 | 82 | 10 |
| **cultus-botanicus** | 68 | 29,000 | 3 | 0 |
| **the-lost-sheep** | 69 | 20,139 | 3 | 2 |
| | **672** | **163,533** | **88** | **12** |

All three run on **Godot 4.7** with the **GL Compatibility** renderer.

**And you wrote none of it. I did.** That is the fact this curriculum is built on. It means the obvious shape — *skip the basics, go straight to the gaps* — is wrong, because there is no evidence of which basics you have. So this is an ordinary beginner's route with an unusually distant end: **by the end there should be nothing those 163,533 lines do that you have not met deliberately.**

**What that buys you.** Not the ability to write a game from nothing, though you will have it. The ability to **open a file in your own repository and know what it says** — to read a bug report, change a number, follow a signal, and judge whether a thing I tell you is true.

**The shape, thirteen stages:**

| # | Stage | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | The editor | The tool itself, before any code |
| **2** | Scenes and nodes | The one idea the whole engine is built on |
| **3** | GDScript | The language, with static typing from the first lesson |
| **4** | 2D and movement | Bodies, shapes, areas, input, and movement that feels right |
| **5** | Signals and structure | How two objects talk, and the rule that keeps it sane |
| **6** | Animation | `AnimationPlayer` to `AnimationTree` to `Tween` |
| **7** | Data and resources | Where the numbers live |
| **8** | Worlds | Tilemaps, terrains and navigation |
| **9** | Interface and camera | `Control`, containers, and the stretch problem in full |
| **10** | Looking good, shipping, testing | Shaders, audio, profiling, export, and a test suite |
| **11** | 3D, from zero | The half of the engine your projects do not use |
| **12** | Multiplayer | Likewise |
| **13** | C# and .NET | Likewise, and the door past it |

**Stages 11 to 13 are there because you asked for everything.** None of your three projects needs any of them, and they are last for that reason. They are not optional, they are simply not urgent.

**Three things about how the lessons are written.**

**1. Every lesson teaches its point in full.** You should not have to open the documentation to follow a lesson. The exact property name, the menu path, the number and the trap are all here. The docs are listed as sources for going further, not for filling gaps.

**2. Every lesson ends in practice.** A line telling you what to do in the editor. Reading about `move_and_slide()` teaches you nothing; moving a square across a screen teaches you most of it.

**3. The worked examples are your own code.** Where a lesson needs a real example it names the project, the path and the symbol — never a line number, so a function that moves is still findable. Those citations are illustrations of a point already made in full, so a stale one costs you thirty seconds rather than the lesson.

**There is no card deck**, alone among your curriculums, and that was your call. **F1** opens the class reference inside the editor, and the practice is building things.

**What is assumed.** Nothing about Godot. You can type, you can use a terminal, and you have used the Odin Project's JavaScript, so a function, a variable and a loop are not new. Everything specific to this engine starts here.

**Practice.** Open `the-world-of-terrath/products/the-lost-sheep/` in a file manager and look at the folder tree. Do not open Godot yet. Just notice that `project.godot` is at the root, that there are `.gd` and `.tscn` files, and that you cannot currently read either. That is the gap this route closes.
Install Godot 4.7: the standard build, n:
Godot ships as a **single executable with no installer**, which is unlike almost every other tool you have installed and is the first thing to understand about it.

**Which build to download.** Two are offered for every platform:

| Build | What it is | Take it? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Godot Engine** | the standard build. GDScript only. ~50 MB. | **Yes** |
| **Godot Engine — .NET** | adds C# support. Larger, needs the .NET SDK. | Not yet — stage 13 |

**This curriculum is GDScript throughout**, so take the standard build. Stage 13 covers the .NET build when you get there, and you can have both on disk at once — they are just two executables.

**The current version is 4.7.2**, released 18 August 2026. Take the latest 4.7.x stable, not a 4.8 dev or beta.

**Installing it, on Omarchy:**

```bash
# Download from godotengine.org/download/linux, then:
mv ~/Downloads/Godot_v4.7.2-stable_linux.x86_64 ~/.local/bin/godot
chmod +x ~/.local/bin/godot
godot --version
```

**Put it somewhere permanent and put it on `PATH`.** Both matter:

- **Permanent**, because a project remembers nothing about where the editor lives, but *you* will be typing the path for the rest of this curriculum.
- **On `PATH` as `godot`**, because your own projects already assume it. `shepherds-we-shall-be/tools/run_tests.sh` opens with `GODOT="${GODOT:-godot}"` — it looks for `godot` on the path and lets you override it with an environment variable, precisely so no machine-specific path is written into the repository. Matching that convention now means the test suite runs later without argument.

**Check the version and write it down.** `Help > About` inside the editor, or `godot --version` outside it.

**The reason to care is one-way and permanent:** a project opened in a newer editor is **silently upgraded and cannot go back**. If you open your `shepherds-we-shall-be` in a 4.8 editor, the project files are rewritten and the only way back is git. All three of your projects declare their version in `project.godot`:

```
config/features=PackedStringArray("4.7", "GL Compatibility")
```

**So the rule is: match the editor to the project.** 4.7 editor, 4.7 projects.

**What a flatpak or a package manager gives you instead.** Both work and both are fine; the reason this lesson hands you a raw binary is that it makes the version explicit and lets you keep several side by side, which you will want the first time 4.8 arrives.

**Practice.** Download the standard 4.7.x build, put it on your `PATH` as `godot`, and run `godot --version` in a terminal. Then run `godot` with no arguments and confirm the Project Manager opens. Then check `grep config/features ~/Work/"Master Roachi"/the-world-of-terrath/products/the-lost-sheep/project.godot` and satisfy yourself the versions match.
The export templates, and getting them n:
A separate download from the editor, about a gigabyte, version-locked, and **nothing exports without them.** Getting them on day one means stage 10 is not a download.

**What they are.** The editor is the tool you build *with*. The export templates are the **engine binaries your game gets bundled with** — one per target platform. When you export a Windows `.exe`, Godot takes the Windows template and packs your project into it. No template, no export.

**Where they come from:**

> **Editor > Manage Export Templates… > Download and Install**

It fetches the set matching your exact editor version and unpacks it to the editor data directory. On Linux that is `~/.local/share/godot/export_templates/4.7.2.stable/`.

**The three things worth knowing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Size** | roughly 1 GB for the full set — every platform, debug and release |
| **Version-locked** | templates for 4.7.2 will not serve a 4.7.1 editor. Upgrade the editor, download again. |
| **Not in your project** | they live with the editor, so they are not in git and a fresh machine needs them again |

**Why now rather than at stage 10.** Because it is a gigabyte over whatever connection you have, and because the first time you try to export is exactly the moment you do not want a download. It also means every later lesson can say *export it and run it* without a caveat.

**Debug against release templates**, which is the distinction that confuses people:

- A **debug** export keeps the debugger, `print()` output and assertions. It can connect back to the editor.
- A **release** export strips them. Smaller, faster, and silent when it breaks.

Both are in the set you just downloaded; which one you get is a checkbox at export time, and stage 10 returns to it.

**If the download fails** — and it does, because it is a large file from a mirror — the templates can be downloaded manually from the same page you got the editor from (`Godot_v4.7.2-stable_export_templates.tpz`) and installed with **Manage Export Templates > Install from File**. The `.tpz` is just a zip.

**One honest note about web export.** The web template needs the GL Compatibility renderer, which is what all three of your projects already use. That is not a coincidence — it is one of the reasons `godot.md` lists Compatibility as a standing decision, and stage 10 makes the case properly.

**Practice.** Open **Editor > Manage Export Templates…** and download the set. While it runs, read the dialog: it names the exact version it is fetching. When it finishes, confirm `ls ~/.local/share/godot/export_templates/` shows a `4.7.2.stable` directory, and notice how large it is.
Make a project: the renderer choice:
Creating a project takes four decisions, and one of them has consequences you will live with.

**The dialog**, from the Project Manager's **+ Create** button:

| Field | What to put |
| --- | --- |
| **Project Name** | anything. It becomes the window title and the default export name. |
| **Project Path** | an **empty folder**. Godot will refuse a non-empty one unless you tick *Create folder*. |
| **Renderer** | the decision. See below. |
| **Version Control Metadata** | **Git**, which writes a sensible `.gitignore` |

**Take the Git option.** It writes a `.gitignore` that excludes `.godot/`, which is the editor's cache directory and must never be committed — it is large, machine-specific and regenerated on open.

**The renderer, which is the real choice.** Three options:

| Renderer | What it is for |
| --- | --- |
| **Forward+** | the desktop default. Every modern feature, Vulkan, heavy. Wrong for 2D pixel art and will not export to the web. |
| **Mobile** | a cut-down Vulkan renderer for phones and tablets. |
| **Compatibility** | OpenGL / WebGL. Fewer features, runs on almost anything, **exports to the web**. |

**Take Compatibility.** The reasons, in order:

1. **It is what your three projects use.** `renderer/rendering_method="gl_compatibility"` in all three. Matching them means every lesson here transfers directly.
2. **2D does not need Forward+.** The features Forward+ adds — volumetric fog, SDFGI, real-time global illumination — are 3D features. A 2D pixel-art game uses none of them.
3. **It runs anywhere**, including old laptops and integrated graphics.
4. **It is the only one that exports to the web.** If a game should be playable in a browser, this is not a preference.

**It can be changed later**, and the documentation says so plainly — Project Settings > Rendering > Renderer > Rendering Method. But it is not free: a project built against Forward+ may use nodes and material features Compatibility does not support, and those break on the switch. **Choosing right at creation costs nothing; switching later costs an audit.**

**What stage 11 will say about this.** When you reach 3D, Compatibility becomes a real limitation and the lesson says so. For now, and for everything your projects do, it is the right answer.

**What you get.** An almost empty folder:

```
my-project/
├── project.godot      # the project file — the next lesson
├── icon.svg           # the default Godot icon
├── .gitignore         # excludes .godot/
└── .godot/            # the editor's cache. Not yours. Not in git.
```

**No `src/`, no `assets/`, no structure at all.** Godot has no opinion about your folder layout, which is freedom and a trap: three of your own projects impose a layout deliberately, and stage 2 looks at how.

**Practice.** Create a project called `godot-practice` in an empty folder, with the **Compatibility** renderer and **Git** version control metadata. Let it open. Then close it and look at the folder in a terminal — `ls -a` — and confirm you can account for all five entries above.
The project folder, and what project.god:
`project.godot` is the file that makes a folder a Godot project, and it is a plain text file you can read. Knowing what is in it makes the whole Project Settings dialog legible.

**Open it.** It is INI-like:

```ini
config_version=5

[application]

config/name="The Lost Sheep"
run/main_scene="res://game/scenes/app/game.tscn"
config/features=PackedStringArray("4.7", "GL Compatibility")

[display]

window/size/viewport_width=960
window/size/viewport_height=540
window/stretch/mode="viewport"

[rendering]

renderer/rendering_method="gl_compatibility"
```

**Every setting in Project Settings is a line in this file.** The dialog is an editor for it, which is worth knowing for three reasons: you can diff it in git, you can grep it, and you can fix a project that will not open.

**The sections you will meet most:**

| Section | What is in it |
| --- | --- |
| `[application]` | the name, the main scene, the icon, the engine version |
| `[display]` | window size, stretch mode, scale mode, fullscreen |
| `[rendering]` | the renderer, and quality settings |
| `[input]` | your input actions — stage 4 |
| `[autoload]` | the singletons — stage 2 |
| `[layer_names]` | names for physics and render layers — stage 4 |
| `[importer_defaults]` | defaults for importing textures and audio |
| `[gui]` | theme, font, and interface defaults |

**The three lines worth being able to read on sight:**

**`run/main_scene`** — the scene that runs when you press **F5**. If it is unset, F5 asks you to pick one and then writes your answer here.

**`config/features`** — the engine version and renderer the project declares. This is the line that decides whether an editor offers to upgrade your project:

```
config/features=PackedStringArray("4.7", "GL Compatibility")
```

**`config_version`** — the format version of this file. 5 for Godot 4.x. You do not touch it.

**What `res://` means**, since every path in the file uses it: **`res://` is the project root** — this folder. It is how Godot refers to anything inside the project, and it is the same path in the editor and in an exported game, which is the whole point. The next lesson takes it properly, along with its writable twin.

**Reading a real one.** Your `shepherds-we-shall-be/project.godot` is a good deal longer and worth a look even now. Two things in it that this curriculum returns to:

```ini
window/size/viewport_width=960
window/size/viewport_height=540
window/size/window_width_override=1920
window/size/window_height_override=1080
window/stretch/mode="viewport"
window/stretch/scale_mode="integer"
```

**A 960×540 game drawn into a 1920×1080 window at exactly 2×.** That is the pixel-art answer and stage 9 spends several lessons on it.

```ini
[autoload]

ViewportSizer="*res://game/scripts/presentation/pixel_perfect_viewport.gd"
HitStopController="*res://game/scripts/presentation/combat/hit_stop_service.gd"
```

**Two autoloads**, which are global singletons. The leading `*` means *enabled*. Stage 2 explains them and stage 9 reads `ViewportSizer` in full.

**What `.godot/` is**, since it sits beside the project file: the editor's cache — imported textures, the script index, the UID map. It is machine-specific, it is regenerated, it is large, and the `.gitignore` you took at creation excludes it. **If a project behaves strangely, deleting `.godot/` and reopening is a legitimate first move.**

**Practice.** Open your `godot-practice/project.godot` in a text editor and read all of it. Then change `config/name` by hand, save, and reopen the project in Godot to see the window title change. Then open `shepherds-we-shall-be/project.godot` and find `run/main_scene`, the two autoloads, and the stretch settings.
The interface: the docks, and what each:
The editor is five regions, and most confusion in the first week is not knowing which one answers a given question.

**The layout:**

| Region | Where | What it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Scene dock** | top left | *what is in this scene?* The node tree. |
| **FileSystem dock** | bottom left | *what is in this project?* The files on disk. |
| **Viewport** | centre | *what does it look like?* 2D, 3D, Script and AssetLib tabs across the top. |
| **Inspector** | right | *what are this node's properties?* |
| **Node dock** | right, tabbed with Inspector | *what signals and groups does this node have?* |
| **Bottom panel** | bottom | Output, Debugger, Animation, Audio, Shader Editor — opens as needed |

**The four workspace tabs at the top centre** switch what the viewport shows: **2D**, **3D**, **Script**, **AssetLib**. They are not different modes for your project — the same scene is open in all of them. 2D and 3D are two views of one tree, and **Script** is a full code editor with the scene still loaded.

**The two docks on the right are tabbed together**, which is the single most missed thing in the editor. Select a node and the right panel shows **Inspector**; click the **Node** tab beside it and the same node shows its **signals** and **groups**. People spend weeks not knowing signals are there.

**What each dock is actually for, in order of how often you use it:**

**Inspector.** Every property of the selected node, grouped by the class that declares it. A `Sprite2D` shows `Sprite2D` properties, then `Node2D`'s (position, rotation, scale), then `CanvasItem`'s (visibility, modulate), then `Node`'s. **Reading that stack top to bottom tells you the inheritance chain**, which is a free lesson in how the engine is built.

**Scene dock.** The tree. Nodes are added here (**+**, or Ctrl-A), renamed (double-click, or F2), reordered (drag), and reparented (drag onto another node). The icons are the node types, and stage 2 teaches reading them.

**FileSystem dock.** Your project's files. Dragging a `.png` from here into the viewport creates a `Sprite2D` with it. Dragging a `.tscn` in instances it. **Right-click > Show in FileSystem** on anything is how you find where a thing lives.

**Output.** `print()` goes here, and so do the engine's own warnings. Lesson 13.

**Debugger.** Errors with a stack trace, breakpoints, and the remote tree. Lessons 14 and 15.

**Moving and resetting them.** Any dock can be dragged to another edge or floated. **Editor > Editor Layout > Default Layout** puts everything back, which you will want at least once.

**The one change worth making immediately.** The bottom panel is short by default. Drag its top edge up so Output shows about ten lines — you will be reading it constantly and a two-line Output is how people miss errors.

**Practice.** Open `godot-practice`, add a `Sprite2D` (Scene dock **+**, type `Sprite2D`), and then: find its `position` in the Inspector; click the **Node** tab and read its signal list; find `icon.svg` in the FileSystem dock and drag it onto the sprite's `texture` property. Then open **Editor > Editor Layout** and look at what is on offer without changing anything.
The Scene dock: the tree and its icons:
The Scene dock is where you will spend more time than anywhere else, and it rewards knowing its small set of operations cold.

**What the tree is.** A scene is a tree of nodes with exactly one root. The dock shows that tree. Indentation is parenthood, and parenthood means three things that stage 2 takes properly:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Transform** | a child's position is relative to its parent |
| **Lifetime** | deleting a parent deletes its children |
| **Visibility** | hiding a parent hides its children |

**The operations, with their shortcuts:**

| Action | How |
| --- | --- |
| **Add a child node** | **Ctrl-A**, or the **+** button. Type to filter. |
| **Rename** | **F2**, or double-click |
| **Delete** | **Delete**. Children go too. |
| **Duplicate** | **Ctrl-D** |
| **Reparent** | drag onto the new parent — or **Ctrl-drag** to keep the global position |
| **Reorder** | drag between siblings. Order matters for drawing and for input. |
| **Change type** | right-click > **Change Type**, which keeps the shared properties |
| **Save as its own scene** | right-click > **Save Branch as Scene** |
| **Open the script** | the script icon on the right of the row |

**Ctrl-drag to reparent is the one to remember.** A plain drag moves the node into the new parent and keeps its *local* position, so it jumps. Ctrl-drag keeps it where it looks like it is.

**The icons on the right of each row**, which are easy to miss and all mean something:

| Icon | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Script** | the node has a script. Click to open it. |
| **Chain link** | the node is an **instanced scene** — stage 2 |
| **Eye** | visibility. Click to toggle; it edits the `visible` property. |
| **Signal** | the node has at least one connected signal — stage 5 |
| **Lock** | the node cannot be selected in the viewport |
| **Group icon** | the node's children cannot be selected individually |
| **Warning triangle** | a configuration warning. **Hover it and read it.** |

**The warning triangle is the editor telling you something is wrong before you run.** *"This node has no shape, so it can't collide"*, *"CharacterBody2D must have a CollisionShape2D"*. It is almost always right and it is the cheapest debugging in the engine.

**The node-type icons on the left** are worth learning by sight because they tell you the category at a glance: blue-ish for 2D nodes, red for 3D, green for `Control` (interface), and distinct shapes for the common ones. You will know `Sprite2D`, `CharacterBody2D`, `Area2D` and `Label` by their icons within a week without trying.

**The search box.** With a large tree, typing filters it. Your `shepherds-we-shall-be/game/scenes/app/game.tscn` is a tree you cannot read top to bottom, and filtering is how you find a thing in it.

**The two tabs at the top of the dock: Local and Remote.** Local is the scene as saved. **Remote** is the live tree while the game runs, and it is the most underused feature in the editor — lesson 15.

**Practice.** In `godot-practice`: build a tree of `Node2D` → `Sprite2D` + `Label`, with the sprite and label as siblings. Rename all three with F2. Move the `Sprite2D` by dragging in the viewport, then Ctrl-drag it onto the `Label` to reparent it and notice it stays put. Then plain-drag it back out and notice it jumps. Then add a `CharacterBody2D` and hover the warning triangle it gives you.
The FileSystem dock, res:// and user://:
Where your project's files are, and the two path schemes Godot uses instead of absolute paths — which is the single most practical thing in stage 1.

**The dock** mirrors the project folder on disk. It shows only what Godot cares about: `.gd`, `.tscn`, `.tres`, imported images and audio. It hides `.godot/` and the import metadata.

**The operations:**

| Action | How |
| --- | --- |
| **Open** | double-click. A `.tscn` opens as a scene, a `.gd` in the script editor. |
| **Instance a scene** | drag a `.tscn` into the viewport or onto a node |
| **Use a texture** | drag a `.png` into the viewport — it creates a `Sprite2D` |
| **Rename or move** | **F2**, or drag. **Godot rewrites every reference**, which is the point. |
| **Find references** | right-click > **View Owners…** — what uses this file |
| **Copy the path** | right-click > **Copy Path** — gives you the `res://` form |
| **Reveal on disk** | right-click > **Show in File Manager** |

**Rename and move inside the dock, never in a terminal.** Godot rewrites the references; `mv` does not, and you get a scene full of broken paths. This is the rule that saves the most time in week one.

**The two path schemes.**

**`res://` — the project, read-only at runtime.**

```gdscript
var tex := load("res://media/sprites/sheep.png")
var scene := load("res://game/scenes/actors/sheep.tscn")
```

`res://` is the project root. In the editor it is a real folder; **in an exported game it is inside the package and cannot be written to.** That is the part that catches people: code that saves to `res://` works perfectly while you develop and fails silently or loudly the moment you export.

**`user://` — the writable one, per user, per machine.**

```gdscript
var f := FileAccess.open("user://save.json", FileAccess.WRITE)
```

Where it actually lands:

| Platform | Path |
| --- | --- |
| **Linux** | `~/.local/share/godot/app_userdata/<project name>/` |
| **Windows** | `%APPDATA%\Godot\app_userdata\<project name>\` |
| **macOS** | `~/Library/Application Support/Godot/app_userdata/<project name>/` |

**The rule, stated once and assumed from here on: read from `res://`, write to `user://`.** Saves, settings, logs and screenshots are `user://`. Everything you shipped is `res://`.

**Project > Open User Data Folder** opens it, which is how you find a save file to delete when testing.

**`uid://`, which is new and you will see it.** Godot 4.4 added stable unique IDs for resources, so a `.tscn` may reference a script as `uid://ckx8m1n0p2q3` rather than by path. Each file gets a `.uid` sidecar. The point is that moving a file outside Godot no longer breaks everything — the UID still resolves. **You do not write these by hand; you just stop being surprised by them in a diff.**

**One thing your own projects do that is worth copying.** `shepherds-we-shall-be` keeps code, scenes and data strictly apart — `game/scripts/`, `game/scenes/`, `game/resources/` — and its `REPOSITORY_STRUCTURE.md` states the rule: *"Code stays in `game/scripts/`; scenes in `game/scenes/`; data in `game/resources/`."* Godot imposes no layout at all, so a project either has a rule like that or becomes unnavigable at about two hundred files.

**Practice.** In `godot-practice`: make folders `scenes/`, `scripts/` and `art/`. Move `icon.svg` into `art/` **using the dock**, and watch the reference in your scene survive. Then right-click it and **Copy Path** to see the `res://` form. Then run **Project > Open User Data Folder** and see where `user://` is on your machine — it will be empty, which is correct.
The Inspector, and where a property is a:
The Inspector shows a node's properties, and understanding *where those values live* explains a great deal of later confusion about scenes, instances and defaults.

**The layout.** Properties are grouped by the class that declares them, most-derived first. A `Sprite2D` reads:

| Group | Properties |
| --- | --- |
| **Sprite2D** | `texture`, `centered`, `offset`, `flip_h`, `flip_v`, `hframes`, `vframes`, `frame`, `region_*` |
| **Node2D** | `position`, `rotation`, `scale`, `skew`, `z_index`, `z_as_relative` |
| **CanvasItem** | `visible`, `modulate`, `self_modulate`, `material`, `light_mask` |
| **Node** | `name`, `process_mode`, `process_priority`, `unique_name_in_owner` |

**Reading that stack top to bottom is reading the inheritance chain**: `Sprite2D` extends `Node2D` extends `CanvasItem` extends `Node`. Every 2D visible thing has `modulate` because `CanvasItem` has it.

**The revert arrow is the important part.** A property shown with a small **revert arrow** beside it has been **changed from its default**. No arrow means it still holds the class default.

**And that is not cosmetic — it is what gets saved.** A `.tscn` stores **only the changed properties.** This is why:

- A scene file is short and readable, even for a complex node.
- A default that changes in a new Godot version changes in your scene too, silently, if you never set it.
- An instanced scene's overrides are stored as a small list of differences — stage 2's whole subject.

**So the revert arrow answers "is this value mine or the engine's?"**, and clicking it hands the property back to the engine.

**The three controls at the top:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Search box** | filter by name. With fifty properties this is faster than scrolling. |
| **The three-dots menu** | **Expand All**, **Collapse All**, and **Copy / Paste Properties** between nodes |
| **The pin** | keeps this node in the Inspector while you select others |

**The toggle next to the search box** switches between showing only common properties and **showing everything**, including the ones Godot normally hides. Worth knowing exists, rarely worth turning on.

**Editing a property three ways.** Any value in the Inspector can be set:

1. **In the Inspector**, by hand. Saved into the scene.
2. **In code**, at runtime: `sprite.modulate = Color.RED`.
3. **By an `@export` annotation**, which is how your *own* variables appear in the Inspector — stage 3 teaches it, and stage 7 builds a whole data layer on it.

**The standing decision this leads to**, stated here and assumed throughout: **numbers live in `@export` or a `Resource`, never buried in a script body.** A speed of `220.0` written inline is a number only you can change; the same value `@export`ed is a number in the Inspector that a designer, a `.tres` file or a test can change. Your own projects follow this — `game/resources/definitions/` is a whole folder of `.tres` data files holding hero kits, skills and items precisely so the numbers are not in the code.

**The trap worth naming now.** Setting a property in the Inspector on an **instanced** scene changes only that instance; setting it in the **source** scene changes every instance that has not overridden it. That is the right behaviour and it surprises everyone once. Stage 2, lesson by lesson.

**Practice.** Select your `Sprite2D` and set `modulate` to red; notice the revert arrow appear. Save the scene, open the `.tscn` in a text editor, and find the single line that records it — then click the revert arrow, save again, and watch the line disappear from the file. That is the whole mental model of Godot's scene format in one exercise.
The Node dock: signals and groups:
The second tab on the right, tabbed behind the Inspector, holding two things that most beginners do not find for months.

**Click the Node tab** beside Inspector with any node selected. Two sub-tabs:

| Tab | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Signals** | every signal this node can emit, and what is connected to each |
| **Groups** | the named sets this node belongs to |

**Signals, in one paragraph** — stage 5 takes them properly. A signal is an announcement a node makes: *I was pressed*, *a body entered me*, *my animation finished*. Other nodes connect to it and get called. The Signals tab lists every signal the node's class declares, grouped by declaring class, exactly like the Inspector:

| Node | Signals it declares |
| --- | --- |
| **Button** | `pressed`, `button_down`, `button_up`, `toggled` |
| **Area2D** | `body_entered`, `body_exited`, `area_entered`, `area_exited` |
| **AnimationPlayer** | `animation_finished`, `animation_changed` |
| **Timer** | `timeout` |
| **Node** (all of them) | `ready`, `renamed`, `tree_entered`, `tree_exited` |

**Connecting one from the dock:** double-click the signal, pick the node that should receive it, and Godot writes the receiving function into that node's script for you:

```gdscript
func _on_button_pressed() -> void:
	pass # Replace with function body.
```

**A connected signal shows a green icon** in the dock, and the node gets the signal icon in the Scene dock. Clicking the connection shows you where it goes; right-click **Disconnect** removes it.

**Connecting in code instead**, which is what your projects do almost everywhere:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	button.pressed.connect(_on_button_pressed)
```

**Both are correct and the choice matters**, which is why stage 5 spends a lesson on it. Briefly: editor connections are visible in the scene and invisible in the code; code connections are the reverse. A large project usually picks one. Yours picks code.

**Groups, which are simpler and more useful than they look.** A group is just a name a node claims. Any node can be in any number of them.

```gdscript
add_to_group("enemies")
get_tree().call_group("enemies", "take_damage", 10)
var all := get_tree().get_nodes_in_group("enemies")
var one := get_tree().get_first_node_in_group("enemies")
```

**What they are for: finding nodes without knowing where they are.** No path, no reference, no coupling — just a name.

**Your own code uses this for exactly that.** `shepherds-we-shall-be/game/scripts/presentation/pixel_perfect_viewport.gd` declares:

```gdscript
const SHELL_GROUP: StringName = &"presentation_shell"
```

and then asks the tree whether such a thing exists at all:

```gdscript
if get_tree().get_first_node_in_group(SHELL_GROUP) != null:
```

**The autoload has no idea where the shell is, or whether there is one.** It asks a question about the whole tree and behaves differently depending on the answer. That is what groups are for, and it is a pattern worth recognising now because you will meet it repeatedly.

**Note the `&"..."` prefix** — that is a `StringName`, an interned string that compares by pointer rather than by characters. Group names, signal names and node paths are all `StringName` under the hood, and stage 3 explains why you write them that way.

**Practice.** Add a `Button` to your scene, open the **Node** tab, and connect its `pressed` signal to your root node from the dock. Let Godot write the function, and put `print("pressed")` in it. Run it (**F5**) and click the button. Then add the root to a group called `test` in the Groups tab, and notice the Scene dock icon change.
The 2D viewport: pan, zoom, select, and:
Moving around the 2D view, and the snapping that makes pixel art possible — which is most of the editor skill you need before stage 2.

**Navigation:**

| Action | How |
| --- | --- |
| **Pan** | **middle-drag**, or **space-drag**, or scroll with the bars |
| **Zoom** | **scroll wheel**, or **Ctrl -** / **Ctrl +** |
| **Zoom to 100%** | **Ctrl-0** — the *real* pixel size, which matters enormously for pixel art |
| **Frame selection** | **F** — centre the view on what is selected |
| **Frame everything** | **Shift-F** |
| **Centre the view** | **Ctrl-Shift-F** |

**Ctrl-0 is the one to use constantly.** At any other zoom, Godot is interpolating the view and your 16×16 sprite does not look like it will in the game. 100% is the truth.

**Selecting and moving:**

| Action | How |
| --- | --- |
| **Select** | click. Click again on overlapping nodes to cycle down the stack. |
| **Select the parent instead** | **Alt-click** moves up the tree |
| **Rubber-band select** | drag on empty space |
| **Move** | drag, or **W** then drag |
| **Rotate** | **E** |
| **Scale** | **R** |
| **Move only on one axis** | drag the red or green handle |
| **Lock a node** | the lock icon — stops it being selected by accident |

**The toolbar modes — Q W E R** — are select, move, rotate, scale. Coming from any other editor these will feel familiar.

**Snapping, which is the part that matters for your games.** The toolbar's magnet icon and its dropdown:

| Setting | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Use Grid Snap** (`Ctrl-G`) | positions land on the grid |
| **Use Rotation Snap** | rotation lands on a step |
| **Use Scale Snap** | likewise |
| **Snap to Parent / Node Anchor / Node Sides / Node Centre** | snap relative to other nodes |
| **Configure Snap…** | the grid step, the rotation step, the offset |

**Set the grid step to your tile size.** For a 16×16 pixel-art game, **Configure Snap > Grid Step = 16, 16** and then grid snap places things on tile boundaries by construction. For the half-pixel work, 8.

**Smart snapping** is the second magnet icon: it snaps to other nodes' edges and centres as you drag, with guides appearing. Good for interface work, usually noise for tiles.

**The rulers and the grid.** The rulers along the top and left read in pixels, and **View > Show Grid** draws it. Both are view-only and neither affects the game.

**What the red and blue lines mean.** The **red** line is the X axis, **green** is Y, and the **blue rectangle** is the game's viewport — the 960×540 your project declares in `project.godot`. **Anything outside the blue rectangle is off-screen at the default camera position.** It is the single most useful reference in the viewport and people routinely do not notice it is there.

**One pixel-art truth worth stating now.** Your games run at 960×540 scaled up to 1920×1080 at exactly 2×. That means **one game pixel is two screen pixels**, and a sprite placed at a fractional position lands between pixels and shimmers when it moves. Grid snap at integer steps is the editor half of the answer; stage 4 handles the runtime half, and stage 9 explains the whole scaling arrangement including why your projects do it with a viewport rather than with filtering settings.

**Practice.** In `godot-practice`: press **Ctrl-0** and find the blue viewport rectangle. Open **Configure Snap…**, set the grid step to 16×16, turn on grid snap with **Ctrl-G**, and drag a sprite around — it should land on multiples of 16. Then turn snapping off and drag it to a fractional position; note the `position` in the Inspector showing something like `(37.5, 112.5)`. That value is a bug waiting to happen.
Running: F5, F6, F7, F8:
Four keys, and knowing which one you want saves a great deal of time — because running the whole project to test one scene is the commonest waste in Godot.

**The four:**

| Key | Action | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **F5** | **Play** | runs the project from `run/main_scene` |
| **F6** | **Play Scene** | runs **the scene you are editing**, on its own |
| **F7** | **Pause Scene** | pauses the running game, leaving it inspectable |
| **F8** | **Stop** | stops it |

All four are remappable at **Editor > Editor Settings > Shortcuts**.

**F6 is the one to use most.** You are building a sheep; you want to run the sheep, not the whole game from the title screen. **F6 runs the current scene as though it were the main scene**, which means it must be able to stand on its own — and that constraint is a design discipline rather than an inconvenience.

**Scenes that can run alone are better scenes.** A scene that only works when some manager three levels up has already initialised it cannot be tested, cannot be opened in isolation, and cannot be reasoned about. Your own projects take this seriously enough to have a test fixture for it — `shepherds-we-shall-be/game/tests/fixtures/foundation_lab/` exists so scenes can be exercised without the real game around them.

**F7, which almost nobody uses and should.** Pause freezes the game **and leaves everything inspectable**: the remote tree is live, every property is readable, and you can see exactly what state the game is in at the moment it went wrong. It is the cheapest debugging in the engine after the warning triangle.

**What `run/main_scene` is.** The scene F5 runs, set in `project.godot`:

```ini
run/main_scene="res://game/scenes/app/game.tscn"
```

If it is unset, F5 asks you to choose and writes your answer there. Set it explicitly once; **Project > Project Settings > Application > Run > Main Scene**, or right-click a scene in the FileSystem dock > **Set as Main Scene**.

**Running a specific scene that is not the current one:** the dropdown beside the play buttons, **Play Custom Scene** (**Ctrl-Shift-F5**).

**What happens when you press play.** Godot launches a **separate process** — a new window running the game. The editor is still there, and the two are connected over a local debug channel. That connection is what gives you:

- `print()` output in the editor's Output panel
- errors with a stack trace in the Debugger
- the **remote** scene tree, live
- the profiler

**Lose the connection and you lose all four**, which is what happens in an exported build and why stage 10 distinguishes debug from release exports.

**The window appears somewhere unhelpful**, usually on top of the editor. Two fixes worth knowing: **Editor Settings > Run > Window Placement > Rect** can pin it, and on a multi-monitor setup **Screen** puts it on the other one. With one monitor, move it manually and Godot remembers.

**Running from a terminal, which stage 10 needs and your test suite depends on:**

```bash
godot                          # the project in this folder
godot --path /path/to/project  # a project elsewhere
godot res://scenes/thing.tscn  # one scene
godot --headless --script res://tests/a_test.gd   # no window at all
```

**That last form is how your 145-odd tests run.** `tools/run_tests.sh` boots one headless Godot per test file, eight at a time — stage 10 reads it properly.

**Practice.** In `godot-practice`: press **F6** to run your current scene and watch a window open. **F8** to stop. Set a main scene, press **F5**, and see the difference. Then press **F5** again and this time press **F7** while it runs — then look at the Scene dock's **Remote** tab, which is the next-but-one lesson.
The Output panel: print, push_warning, p:
Where the game talks to you, and the four ways to make it talk — which is the whole of debugging until lesson 14.

**The Output panel** is in the bottom panel, and it carries everything the running game prints plus everything the engine wants to tell you.

**The four printing functions, and they are not interchangeable:**

| Function | Where it goes | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `print()` | Output, plain | ordinary tracing |
| `print_rich()` | Output, with BBCode colour | tracing you want to scan quickly |
| `push_warning()` | Output **and** the Debugger's warnings, with a stack trace | something is wrong but survivable |
| `push_error()` | Output **and** the Debugger's errors, with a stack trace | something is wrong and should not be |

**The difference that matters: `push_warning` and `push_error` carry a stack trace and show up in the Debugger.** `print()` tells you a thing happened; `push_error()` tells you where from. Using `print()` for a real problem is how a bug stays mysterious.

```gdscript
print("velocity is ", velocity)
print_rich("[color=yellow]state:[/color] ", state)
push_warning("No texture set; using placeholder.")
push_error("Hero kit resource failed to load: %s" % path)
```

**`print()` takes any number of arguments and concatenates them** with no separator, which is why `print("velocity is ", velocity)` has a trailing space inside the string. There is also `prints()`, which inserts spaces, and `printt()`, which inserts tabs.

**Formatting, because you will want it immediately.** The `%` operator:

```gdscript
print("hp %d of %d" % [hp, max_hp])
print("%.2f seconds" % elapsed)
print("%s entered %s" % [body.name, name])
```

| Spec | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `%d` | integer |
| `%f` / `%.2f` | float / to two places |
| `%s` | anything, via its string form |
| `%v` | a vector |
| `%x` | hex |

**A worked example from your own code.** `shepherds-we-shall-be/game/scripts/presentation/pixel_perfect_viewport.gd` prints one line every time the window changes size:

```gdscript
print(
	"[presentation] window %dx%d | viewport %dx%d at %dx = %dx%d | %s"
	% [ … ]
)
```

and the comment beside it explains why it is unconditional rather than behind a debug flag:

> *Logged every time, not behind a debug flag. Whether the picture fills the screen is the kind of thing that is argued about from memory otherwise … One line at startup settles it.*

**That is the best argument for logging there is**, and it is worth taking as a principle: log the thing that gets argued about. A prefix like `[presentation]` makes it greppable and makes it obvious which system spoke.

**Reading the engine's own output.** Godot writes its own warnings here too, and they are usually precise and worth believing:

> `Node not found: "Sprite2D" (relative to "/root/Game/Player").`
> `Attempt to call function 'take_damage' in base 'null instance' on a null instance.`

**That second one is the error you will see most in your first month**, and it almost always means a `$Path` resolved to nothing — usually because the node was renamed, or because the lookup ran before the tree was ready. Stage 2's lifecycle lesson and stage 3's `@onready` lesson are both about preventing exactly it.

**Clearing and filtering.** The Output panel has a clear button, and a filter box worth using when a game prints every frame. **Printing every frame is itself a mistake** — `_process` runs 60 times a second, so `print()` in it produces 3,600 lines a minute and slows the game measurably.

**The log on disk.** Godot also writes `user://logs/godot.log`. Your own test runner cares about this: it gives every parallel Godot process its own temporary data root specifically so they do not *"fight over `user://logs/godot.log`"*.

**Practice.** Put all four functions in a script's `_ready()` and run it. Notice that the two `push_*` calls also appear in the **Debugger** tab with a stack trace, and the `print()` calls do not. Then write one line using `%` formatting with three values. Then deliberately call a method on a node that does not exist, and read the error carefully — you will see it many more times.
The Debugger: breakpoints, the stack, an:
The bottom panel's Debugger tab, which turns *"it does not work"* into *"this variable is null on line 42"*.

**Six sub-tabs.** The ones that matter now:

| Tab | What it gives you |
| --- | --- |
| **Stack Trace** | where execution is, and how it got there |
| **Errors** | every error and warning, with a traceable stack |
| **Profiler** | frame timings — stage 10 |
| **Visual Profiler** | where GPU time goes — stage 10 |
| **Network Profiler** | stage 12 |
| **Monitors** | live graphs of memory, draw calls, objects |

**Breakpoints.** In the script editor, **click the gutter** left of a line number, or put the cursor on the line and press **F9**. A red dot appears. When the game reaches it, **it stops** and the editor comes forward with the game frozen.

**What you get while stopped:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The stack** | the call chain, innermost first. Click any frame to jump to that line. |
| **The variable list** | every local, member and constant in scope, with its current value |
| **The remote tree** | live, in the Scene dock — next lesson |
| **The ability to continue** | and to step |

**The stepping controls**, on the Debugger's toolbar:

| Control | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Step Into** (**F11**) | run one line; descend into a function call |
| **Step Over** (**F10**) | run one line; treat a call as one step |
| **Continue** | run until the next breakpoint |
| **Break** | stop wherever it currently is |

**The variable list is the whole point.** Most bugs are a value being something you did not expect, and this is the thing that shows you the value rather than making you guess it. `print()` is a worse version of this.

**`breakpoint`, the keyword.** You can also break from code:

```gdscript
if hp < 0:
	breakpoint
```

**Which is better than a gutter breakpoint when the condition is rare** — you do not want to stop on every frame, you want to stop on the one where `hp` went negative.

**Errors, and the setting worth changing immediately.** The Debugger's Errors tab lists every error with its stack. By default the game **keeps running** after an error; **Debug > Break on Error** stops it at the moment of failure instead, with everything still inspectable. That is almost always what you want while developing, and it is off by default.

**Also in the Debug menu**, and all four are worth knowing:

| Option | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Visible Collision Shapes** | every collision shape and raycast, drawn in the running game |
| **Visible Navigation** | the navigation mesh |
| **Visible Avoidance** | avoidance agents |
| **Visible Paths** | `Path2D` curves |

**Visible Collision Shapes is indispensable** and stage 4 relies on it. A collision bug is invisible without it and obvious with it.

**The Monitors tab** draws live graphs — object count, node count, memory, draw calls. **The one to watch is node count**: if it climbs steadily while you play, something is being instanced and never freed, and stage 10's `print_orphan_nodes` lesson is about finding it.

**The limit to be honest about.** All of this needs the editor's debug connection, so it works when you press F5 and does not work in a release export. Debug exports keep it; stage 10 covers connecting a debugger to one.

**Practice.** Write a function with three local variables, set a breakpoint on its last line with **F9**, and run. When it stops, read all three values in the variable list and click up a stack frame. Then turn on **Debug > Break on Error**, write a deliberate error (call a method on `null`), and see the difference from last lesson. Then turn on **Debug > Visible Collision Shapes** and keep it on.
The remote Scene tree, while the game ru:
The most underused feature in the editor, and the one that makes a running Godot game legible.

**Where it is.** Press **F5**. Look at the **Scene dock** and notice two tabs have appeared at the top: **Remote** and **Local**.

| Tab | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| **Local** | the scene as you are editing it, saved on disk |
| **Remote** | **the live tree inside the running game** |

**Click Remote.** You are now looking at the actual node tree of the running process — every node that exists right now, including everything instanced at runtime, with `/root` at the top.

**And you can select a node in it and the Inspector shows its live values.** Not the saved values: the current ones, updating as the game runs. Position changing as the player moves. `hp` dropping as it takes damage.

**What this replaces.** Everything you would otherwise write `print()` for:

| Question | Without Remote | With Remote |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Where is the player actually?* | print position every frame | click it, read `position` |
| *Did that bullet get freed?* | print on free, count manually | look — is it in the tree? |
| *Is the state machine in the right state?* | print on every transition | click it, read `state` |
| *Why is nothing visible?* | guess | check `visible`, `modulate`, `z_index`, `position` |
| *Did the scene instance at all?* | print in `_ready` | look for it |

**And you can edit live.** Change a value in the Inspector while the game runs and it takes effect immediately — move a node, change a speed, toggle `visible`. **Nothing is saved**, which is the point: it is a sandbox for *what if this number were 300?* Find the right number by dragging, then write it down and set it properly.

**The three buttons at the top of the Remote tree:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Request scene tree** | refresh, for when it has gone stale |
| **Automatic refresh** | keep it live |
| **Copy node path** | gives you the exact `/root/...` path, useful in a `print()` |

**The three uses that are hard to get any other way:**

**1. Finding where a runtime-instanced node actually landed.** You spawned fifty sheep; the Local tree shows none of them because they do not exist on disk. The Remote tree shows all fifty, under whatever parent they were added to — which is how you discover they were added to the wrong one.

**2. Counting things.** Node leaks are visible: play for a minute, look at how many `Projectile` nodes are still in the tree. If it only goes up, something is not calling `queue_free()`.

**3. Reading another system's state without instrumenting it.** You did not write the thing and you do not know what it exposes. Click it; the Inspector lists every property it has.

**Where this pays off for you specifically.** `shepherds-we-shall-be/game/scenes/app/game.tscn` is the root of an 82-scene project, and its runtime tree is far larger than anything you can read in a file. **The Remote tree is how you find out what that game is actually made of** — press F5, click Remote, and expand it. That is a legitimate way to spend twenty minutes and it will teach you more about the project's structure than reading `.tscn` files would.

**Pair it with F7.** Pause the game, then explore the tree at leisure with nothing moving. Pause plus Remote tree plus the Inspector is the full picture of a frozen game.

**Practice.** Run a scene with **F5**, switch the Scene dock to **Remote**, and expand `/root`. Find your node, select it, and watch `position` update as you move it — and then change `modulate` in the Inspector while the game runs and watch it change on screen. Then press **F7** to pause and explore the tree. Then open `the-lost-sheep`, press F5, and spend ten minutes reading its remote tree.
The Asset Store, new in 4.7:
How to get other people's code and art into a project — and this is the one editor feature that changed in 4.7, so most tutorials describe something that no longer exists.

**What changed.** Godot 4.7 replaces the old **Asset Library** with the new **Asset Store**. The old library is **deprecated** and will become read-only; it is kept alive only because older engine versions still point at it.

**Practically, for you:** the **AssetLib** tab at the top of the editor is where you browse, and in 4.7 it is the new store behind it. What the store adds over the old library: multiple versions per asset, user reviews and ratings, proper tags, zoomable previews, and background threading so browsing does not freeze the editor.

**An honest warning.** There is an open bug in 4.7.2 where the in-editor store can fail with `Request failed, return code 500`. If that happens, the web version works, and an asset is only ever a zip — download it in a browser and unpack it into your project. **Nothing about Godot addons requires the store.**

**What an addon actually is.** A folder under `addons/`, containing a `plugin.cfg`. That is all. Installing one means putting the folder there; enabling it means **Project > Project Settings > Plugins** and ticking it.

```
my-project/
└── addons/
    └── SomeAddon/
        ├── plugin.cfg
        └── …
```

**`addons/` stays at the project root.** That is Godot's plugin path and it is not negotiable — your own `REPOSITORY_STRUCTURE.md` lists it as structural rule 4 for exactly that reason: *"`addons/` stays at root — Godot's plugin path."*

**The one addon your projects use.** `shepherds-we-shall-be/addons/AsepriteWizard/` — and it is the only one, which is worth noticing. It imports `.aseprite` files directly into Godot, turning Aseprite layers and tags into `SpriteFrames` or `AnimationPlayer` animations, so the art pipeline has no manual export step. Stage 6 covers it properly, and it connects this curriculum to the Aseprite one.

**Being sparing with addons is a real position**, and your projects take it: 672 script files and one addon. Every addon is code you did not write, that can break on an engine upgrade, and that someone has to understand when it does.

**What is genuinely worth getting, when you get there:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **AsepriteWizard** | if you draw in Aseprite, which you do |
| **A test framework** | GUT or GdUnit4 — though your projects deliberately use neither, and stage 10 explains why |
| **Dialogue addons** | if a game needs conversation trees |
| **Shader collections** | though **godotshaders.com** is better and needs no addon |

**Free art, which matters more than addons early on.** **Kenney.nl** publishes large CC0 asset packs — sprites, tiles, UI, audio — with no attribution required. The point is not to ship with them; it is that **a lesson should never stall for want of a sprite**. Your own projects keep stand-ins in `media/placeholder/` for the same reason.

**The licence question, briefly.** Everything in the store declares a licence. MIT and CC0 are safe. GPL in an addon is a real constraint on what you can ship. It takes ten seconds to check and it is worth checking.

**Practice.** Open the **AssetLib** tab and browse — if it errors, note the message and move on, because that is the known 4.7.2 bug rather than your machine. Then look at `shepherds-we-shall-be/addons/AsepriteWizard/` and find its `plugin.cfg`, and read it: four lines, and now you know what an addon is. Then open **Project Settings > Plugins** in that project and see it listed and enabled.
Editor settings worth changing on day on:
**Editor > Editor Settings** is enormous and almost all of it can wait. These are the ones that pay for themselves immediately.

**Editor settings are per-machine, not per-project.** They live in your user config, not in the repository, so changing them affects every project you open and commits nothing. That is the opposite of **Project Settings**, which are in `project.godot` and are shared.

**Interface:**

| Setting | Change it to | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Interface > Editor > Display Scale** | whatever is readable | the default guesses from your display and often guesses low |
| **Interface > Editor > Single Window Mode** | on | stops docks floating off as separate OS windows |
| **Interface > Theme > Preset** | taste | there is a Dark Rose and a Black preset if the default grey tires |

**Text Editor — the ones that matter:**

| Setting | Change it to | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Appearance > Show Line Numbers** | on | it is off-ish by default and you need them for stack traces |
| **Appearance > Minimap** | off | it costs width and tells you little in short scripts |
| **Behavior > Files > Autosave Interval Secs** | 60 | the editor can crash; autosave means it costs a minute |
| **Behavior > Files > Restore Scripts On Load** | on | reopens what you were reading |
| **Completion > Add Type Hints** | **on** | **the important one.** Godot's generated code and completions then carry types — matching this curriculum's standing decision that everything is statically typed. |
| **Completion > Use Single Quotes** | off | the engine and the docs use double quotes |
| **Indent > Type** | **Tabs** | Godot's own convention, and what every one of your 672 script files uses |

**`Add Type Hints` deserves the emphasis.** With it on, connecting a signal from the Node dock writes:

```gdscript
func _on_button_pressed() -> void:
```

With it off, you get `func _on_button_pressed():` and have to add `-> void` by hand every time. Over a project it is thousands of small corrections, and a codebase that is *mostly* typed is worse than one that is consistently typed, because you cannot trust it.

**Run:**

| Setting | Change it to | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Run > Window Placement > Rect** | **Custom Position** | stops the game window landing on top of the editor |
| **Run > Window Placement > Screen** | your other monitor | if you have one, this is the single best quality-of-life change in the list |
| **Run > Output > Always Clear Output On Play** | on | so what you are reading is from this run |

**Debugger:**

| Setting | Change it to |
| --- | --- |
| **Debugger > Auto Switch To Remote Scene Tree** | **on** — makes the previous lesson automatic |
| **Debugger > Profiler > Max Functions** | leave it |

**Network > Language Server**, if you ever edit GDScript outside Godot: the editor runs a language server on port 6005 and an external editor can attach to it. **Text Editor > External > Use External Editor** points Godot at it. Worth knowing exists; the built-in editor is good and this curriculum assumes it.

**The one to leave alone.** **Interface > Editor > Localize Settings** and the language options — the documentation, the class reference and every tutorial you will read are in English, and a localised editor makes them harder to follow, not easier.

**Finding anything.** The search box at the top of Editor Settings filters everything, and the **three-dots menu** beside it offers **Reset Setting** per item. Nothing here is dangerous and nothing here is permanent.

**Practice.** Turn on **Completion > Add Type Hints**, set **Indent > Type** to Tabs, turn on **Debugger > Auto Switch To Remote Scene Tree**, and set **Run > Window Placement** so the game does not cover the editor. Then connect a signal from the Node dock and confirm the generated function now ends in `-> void`.
The built-in docs: F1, Ctrl-click, and t:
Godot ships its entire class reference inside the editor, offline, matched to your exact version. This is the last lesson of stage 1 because it is the one that makes you independent of every other source.

**Three ways in:**

| How | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **F1** | **Search Help.** Type a class or method name. |
| **Ctrl-click** a class or method name in code | jumps straight to its documentation |
| **The Inspector's property tooltips** | hover any property for its description |

**Ctrl-click is the one that becomes a habit.** Reading a line of unfamiliar code, Ctrl-click the class name and the reference opens in a new tab beside your script. That is the fastest path from *what is a `CharacterBody2D`* to an answer, and it works on **anything** — your own classes included, where it jumps to your own source.

**What a class page gives you**, and reading it in this order is the skill:

| Section | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **Inherits** | the chain, e.g. `CharacterBody2D < PhysicsBody2D < CollisionObject2D < Node2D < CanvasItem < Node < Object` |
| **Description** | what it is for, in a paragraph |
| **Tutorials** | links to the relevant manual pages |
| **Properties** | every property, with type and default |
| **Methods** | every method, with signature and return type |
| **Signals** | every signal it can emit |
| **Enumerations** | its constants |
| **Constants** | likewise |

**Read the Inherits line first.** It tells you where to look for the property you want: `position` is not on `CharacterBody2D`'s page, it is on `Node2D`'s, because that is where it is declared. **A property you cannot find is almost always on a parent class**, and the chain tells you which.

**And the inherited members are listed too**, collapsed, at the bottom of each section. Expanding them is how you discover that a node you thought was simple has ninety properties.

**The method signatures carry everything you need:**

```
void move_and_slide()
bool is_on_floor() const
Vector2 get_real_velocity() const
void look_at(point: Vector2)
```

| Part | Means |
| --- | --- |
| the leading type | what it returns; `void` means nothing |
| `const` | it does not modify the node — safe to call anywhere |
| the parameter types | what you must pass |
| a parameter with `=` | optional, with that default |

**`move_and_slide()` taking no arguments is worth noticing now**, because every Godot 3 tutorial passes it a velocity and that is wrong in Godot 4 — it reads the `velocity` property instead, and it applies `delta` itself. Stage 4 teaches it properly; the point here is that **the reference is right and the tutorial is old**, and knowing how to check is the whole lesson.

**The online version is the same content**, at `docs.godotengine.org`, plus the manual — the hand-written tutorials that the class reference links to. Two things to know about it:

1. **Check the version selector.** The URL carries it: `/en/stable/` is currently 4.7, `/en/4.3/` is not. A great deal of wrong advice is correct advice for an older version.
2. **The manual and the class reference are different things.** The manual explains *how to do something*; the reference states *what exists*. You will want both, and F1 gives you the second instantly.

**Your own classes appear here too.** A script with `class_name` is registered engine-wide and gets a reference page built from its `##` documentation comments:

```gdscript
class_name PixelPerfectViewport
extends Node

## Sizes the internal viewport so whole pixels fill the window, instead of letterboxing.
```

**That is a real line from your own code**, and because it uses `##` rather than `#`, it becomes the class description in the editor's help. Press F1 in that project and search `PixelPerfectViewport` — your own code is in the reference, documented. Stage 3 teaches the annotation; stage 7 leans on it.

**Practice.** Press **F1** and search `Sprite2D`. Read its Inherits chain out loud, then find where `position` is declared and where `modulate` is. Then find `move_and_slide` on `CharacterBody2D` and confirm it takes no arguments. Then open `the-lost-sheep`, press F1, and search for one of its own `class_name` classes.
A node is an object in a tree:
The one idea the whole engine is built on. Everything else in Godot is a consequence of it, so it is worth getting exactly right before anything else.

**A node is an object that does one job.** It has a name, a type, a parent, children, properties, and some behaviour. That is all.

| Node | Its one job |
| --- | --- |
| `Sprite2D` | draw a texture |
| `AudioStreamPlayer` | play a sound |
| `Timer` | count down and announce it |
| `CollisionShape2D` | describe a shape for physics |
| `Label` | draw text |
| `Camera2D` | decide what the viewport shows |
| `Node2D` | have a position, and hold children |
| `Node` | hold children, and nothing else |

**Godot's answer to "how do I make a thing" is always: combine nodes.** A character is not a `Character` class you configure. It is a `CharacterBody2D` with a `Sprite2D` to draw it, a `CollisionShape2D` so it collides, an `AnimationPlayer` to animate it, and an `Area2D` to notice things near it. **Composition, in the engine's own structure.**

**That is the trade.** Other engines give you one object with a hundred properties; Godot gives you ten objects with ten each. The cost is more nodes; the gain is that every node is simple, replaceable and separately testable.

**What the tree gives a node**, and this is why parenthood is not just organisation:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Transform** | a child's `position` is **relative to its parent**. Move the parent, the children come. |
| **Lifetime** | free a parent and its children go too. No orphans. |
| **Visibility** | hide a parent and its children vanish. |
| **Draw order** | later siblings draw on top of earlier ones. |
| **Input order** | the tree decides who gets an event first, and the UI gets first refusal. |
| **Process order** | `_process` runs down the tree, parents before children. |

**So the tree is not a filing system.** Reparenting a node changes its coordinates, its lifetime and when it draws. That is a lot of behaviour to get for free from a drag in the Scene dock, and it is the reason the dock matters as much as it does.

**Every node inherits from `Node`**, and the chain carries capability:

```
Sprite2D < Node2D < CanvasItem < Node < Object
```

| Class | What it adds |
| --- | --- |
| `Object` | properties, methods, signals — the base of everything |
| `Node` | a name, a parent, children, the lifecycle, groups, the tree |
| `CanvasItem` | it can be drawn: `visible`, `modulate`, `z_index`, `material` |
| `Node2D` | it has a 2D transform: `position`, `rotation`, `scale` |
| `Sprite2D` | it draws a texture |

**Reading that chain answers "where is this property?"**, which stage 1's documentation lesson made the point about. `modulate` is on every drawable node because `CanvasItem` declares it.

**And the 3D and interface branches are siblings, not descendants:**

```
Node3D  < Node        — the 3D transform. Stage 11.
Control < CanvasItem  — the interface. Stage 9.
```

**`Control` is a `CanvasItem` but not a `Node2D`**, which is why interface nodes use anchors and sizes rather than `position` and `scale`. That one fact prevents a great deal of stage-9 confusion.

**The practical rule that follows from all of this**, and it is the engine's own advice: **if you are not sure what node to use, use the simplest one that does the job.** A `Node` for something with no position. A `Node2D` when it needs a position. Never a `Sprite2D` as a container just because it was there.

**Practice.** In `godot-practice`, build this tree: `Node2D` named `Thing`, with children `Sprite2D` and `Label`. Move `Thing` and watch both children move. Set `Thing`'s `visible` to off and watch both vanish. Then drag the `Label` above the `Sprite2D` in the dock and notice the draw order change. Then press **F1**, search `Node2D`, and read its Inherits line.
A scene is a saved tree:
The second half of the one idea: a scene is a tree of nodes saved to a file, and **it is also a node** the moment you put it inside another scene.

**What a scene is.** Any node, with its children, saved as a `.tscn`. There is no `Scene` class — a scene is a *file*, and what is in the file is a node and its descendants.

**So "scene" means two things depending on where you are standing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **On disk** | a `.tscn` file: a tree, saved |
| **In another scene** | a single node, which happens to expand into that tree |

**That double meaning is the whole design** and it is what makes Godot composable. A sheep is a scene while you edit it and a node while you place fifty of them in a field.

**The consequences, which are the reason this matters:**

**1. A scene is the unit of reuse.** Build a sheep once, place it anywhere, change the original and every copy changes. Stage 2's instancing lessons are about exactly this.

**2. A scene is the unit of work.** You open one scene at a time and it is small enough to hold in your head. `the-lost-sheep` is a whole game in **three** scene files — `title.tscn`, `ground.tscn`, `main.tscn` — because everything else is script and data.

**3. A scene can run on its own.** **F6** runs the open scene as if it were the game. A scene that cannot stand alone is usually a scene that knows too much about its surroundings.

**4. A scene is the unit of a file in git.** It is text, it diffs, and a conflict in one is readable.

**There is no "level" or "prefab" or "object" distinction.** A title screen, a sheep, a button, a whole game — all scenes, all the same mechanism. Other engines separate prefabs from levels; Godot does not, and once that lands it removes a whole category of decision.

**The main scene** is the one that runs on **F5**, named in `project.godot`:

```ini
run/main_scene="res://game/scenes/app/game.tscn"
```

**What loading a scene actually does.** The file is loaded as a `PackedScene` — a recipe, not a tree — and then **instantiated** into real nodes:

```gdscript
var packed := load("res://game/scenes/ground.tscn") as PackedScene
var ground := packed.instantiate()
add_child(ground)
```

**Those are three distinct steps and conflating them causes real bugs:**

| Step | What you have |
| --- | --- |
| `load(...)` | a `PackedScene` — the recipe. Cached, cheap to repeat. |
| `.instantiate()` | real nodes, **not yet in the tree**. No `_ready` has run. |
| `add_child(...)` | now it is in the tree. **Now** `_enter_tree` and `_ready` run. |

**A node that has been instantiated but not added is a common source of "why did nothing happen".** It exists, it is addressable, and none of its lifecycle has fired. Lesson 10 takes the lifecycle properly.

**Changing scenes wholesale:**

```gdscript
get_tree().change_scene_to_file("res://game/scenes/main.tscn")
```

which frees the current scene and loads that one as the new root child. There is also `change_scene_to_packed()` if you already hold the `PackedScene`.

**`.tscn` against `.scn`.** Both are scenes; `.tscn` is **text** and `.scn` is binary. **Use `.tscn` always** — it diffs, it merges, and you can read it, which is the next-but-two lesson. Binary is marginally faster to load and costs you git.

**Practice.** In `godot-practice`, save your `Thing` tree as `scenes/thing.tscn`. Create a new scene with a `Node2D` root, and drag `thing.tscn` from the FileSystem dock into it **three times**. Notice each one appears as a single node with a chain icon. Move them apart. Then press **F6** and confirm three things appear. Then open `the-lost-sheep` and confirm for yourself that the whole game is three `.tscn` files.
Choosing a root node, and what it decide:
The first decision in every new scene, made in two seconds and awkward to undo, so it is worth knowing the four answers.

**The question Godot asks** when you create a scene: *2D Scene*, *3D Scene*, *User Interface*, or *Other Node*. Those are shortcuts for four root types:

| Button | Root you get | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **2D Scene** | `Node2D` | the scene exists somewhere in 2D space |
| **3D Scene** | `Node3D` | the same, in 3D. Stage 11. |
| **User Interface** | `Control` | the scene is interface. Stage 9. |
| **Other Node** | anything | you want a specific type as the root |

**What the root decides**, and there are four things:

**1. Whether the scene has a position.** A `Node2D` root can be placed. A plain `Node` root cannot — it has no transform, so putting it at a position is meaningless. **That is a feature**: a scene that manages data or orchestrates other scenes *should* have no position, and using `Node` says so.

**2. What it can be a child of.** A `Control` inside a `Node2D` works but loses its layout behaviour unless the parent chain cooperates. A `Node2D` inside a `Control` draws, but the `Control` will not size itself around it. **Mixing the two branches is the commonest stage-9 mistake** and the root choice is where it starts.

**3. What the scene's own script extends.** The script on the root extends the root's class:

```gdscript
extends Node2D      # a placeable thing
extends Control     # an interface panel
extends Node        # a manager with no position
extends CharacterBody2D   # a thing that moves and collides
```

**4. How it behaves when instanced.** An instanced scene is a node of the root's type, so a `Node2D`-rooted scene can be moved by its parent and a `Node`-rooted one cannot.

**The four honest answers, in practice:**

| Root | For |
| --- | --- |
| **`Node`** | managers, orchestrators, data holders, autoloads, test harnesses — **anything with no position** |
| **`Node2D`** | anything in the world that is not a body: effects, markers, groups of sprites |
| **`CharacterBody2D` / `RigidBody2D` / `StaticBody2D` / `Area2D`** | things that collide. Stage 4. |
| **`Control`** | interface. Stage 9. |

**What your own projects choose**, which is a useful survey. From `the-lost-sheep/game/scenes/main.tscn`:

```
[node name="Main" type="Node2D"]
```

**`Node2D`, for the root of the whole game** — because the island is drawn in world space and the camera moves over it. And the three children in the same file:

```
[node name="Ground" parent="." instance=ExtResource("11_ground")]
[node name="WildView" type="Node2D" parent="."]
[node name="IslandView" type="Node2D" parent="."]
```

`Node2D` for each view, because each draws in world coordinates. The interface nodes in the same scene are `Control`s, kept separate — which is stage 9's whole subject.

**Changing a root after the fact.** Right-click the root > **Change Type**, which keeps the properties the two types share and silently drops the rest. It works and it is not free: a `Node2D` → `Node` change loses the position of everything that depended on it. **Decide once, at creation, by asking "does this thing have a place in the world?"**

**The rule worth memorising:** *the simplest node that does the job.* If the scene does not need a position, `Node`. If it does, `Node2D`. If it collides, a body. If it is interface, `Control`. Anything more specific than that is a decision you should be able to justify.

**Practice.** Create three scenes: one rooted at `Node` called `scenes/manager.tscn`, one at `Node2D` called `scenes/marker.tscn`, one at `Control` called `scenes/panel.tscn`. Try to set a `position` on the `Node` root and notice there is none to set. Then instance all three into one scene and notice which can be moved.
Your first scene: Node2D and Sprite2D:
The smallest useful scene, built deliberately, with every step named — because the habits set here are the ones repeated for the rest of the curriculum.

**Build it.**

1. **Scene > New Scene**, then **2D Scene** in the Create Root Node panel. You get a `Node2D` named `Node2D`.
2. **Rename the root** — **F2** — to something meaningful. `Sheep`.
3. **Ctrl-A**, type `Sprite2D`, Enter. It arrives as a child.
4. **Drag a texture onto it.** From the FileSystem dock, drag `icon.svg` onto the `Sprite2D`'s `texture` property in the Inspector — or straight into the viewport, which creates the node and assigns it in one move.
5. **Save it** — **Ctrl-S** — as `scenes/sheep.tscn`.

**Five steps, and three of them are habits worth naming.**

**Rename the root, always.** The root's name becomes the node's name when the scene is instanced. A field of `Node2D`, `Node2D2`, `Node2D3` is unreadable in the remote tree and in every error message. **Name it for what it is, not what it is made of.**

**Name children for their job, not their type.** `Sprite2D` is a fine name when there is one. When there are three, `Body`, `Shadow` and `Highlight` tell you something and `Sprite2D2` does not. **The name is what `$Path` and the Scene dock both use**, so it is API, not decoration.

**Save early, and into a folder.** `res://scenes/` or whatever layout you choose — but choose one. Stage 1's FileSystem lesson made the point: Godot imposes no layout, so a project either has a rule or becomes unnavigable.

**What you can now see, and should look at.** Select the `Sprite2D` and read its Inspector top to bottom:

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `texture` | the image |
| `centered` | **on by default** — the texture is centred on the node's origin |
| `offset` | shifts the texture relative to the origin |
| `flip_h` / `flip_v` | mirror it. Cheaper than a second texture. |
| `hframes` / `vframes` / `frame` | treat the texture as a grid and show one cell — **this is how a sprite sheet works** |
| `region_enabled` / `region_rect` | show an arbitrary rectangle of it instead |

**`centered` is the first real trap.** With it on, the node's origin is the middle of the sprite. For a character that stands on the ground you almost always want the origin at the **feet**, so either turn `centered` off and set `offset`, or leave it centred and offset by half the height. **Getting this wrong makes everything else — positioning, collision, sorting — slightly wrong in a way that is hard to see and easy to feel.**

**`hframes`/`vframes` is worth seeing now.** Set `hframes` to 4 on a four-frame sheet and `frame` cycles between them. That is the whole mechanism behind `AnimatedSprite2D` and behind the Aseprite import pipeline in stage 6.

**The two things not to do yet.** No script, and no `CharacterBody2D`. A scene with a sprite in it is a complete and legitimate thing, and stage 3 adds the script. Resisting the urge to attach a script to everything is a real discipline — a great many nodes need none.

**Where this is going.** `the-lost-sheep` has one scene for the ground, one for the title and one for everything else, and the sheep in it are drawn by a script rather than being scenes at all. **That is a legitimate choice and not the only one** — stage 4 and stage 8 compare drawing many similar things as scenes against drawing them directly, and which is right depends on how many there are.

**Practice.** Build `scenes/sheep.tscn` exactly as above. Then: turn `centered` off and watch the sprite jump so its top-left is at the origin. Set `offset` to put the origin back at the feet instead. Then set `hframes` to 2 and watch half the image show. Then **F6** and confirm it runs on its own.
Saving as .tscn, and reading the file:
