A `.tscn` is text you can read, and reading one is the fastest way to understand what a scene *is*. This lesson reads a real one from your own project.

**Open `the-lost-sheep/game/scenes/main.tscn` in a text editor.** It is 104 lines for the whole game's main scene. The first line:

```
[gd_scene load_steps=13 format=3]
```

| Part | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `gd_scene` | this file is a scene |
| `load_steps` | how many resources must load. A hint, so Godot can show a progress bar. |
| `format=3` | the file format version. 3 is Godot 4. |

**Then the external resources** — everything this scene refers to but does not contain:

```
[ext_resource type="Script" path="res://game/scripts/main.gd" id="1_main"]
[ext_resource type="Resource" path="res://game/data/island.tres" id="4_island"]
[ext_resource type="PackedScene" path="res://game/scenes/ground.tscn" id="11_ground"]
```

**Three kinds in those three lines**, and they are the three kinds you will meet: a **script**, a **data resource**, and **another scene**. Each gets a local `id` used below.

**Then the nodes:**

```
[node name="Main" type="Node2D"]
script = ExtResource("1_main")
```

**The root: a `Node2D` called `Main`, with `main.gd` attached.** Note that the script is just a property — `script = ...` — which is literally true. A script in Godot is a resource assigned to a node's `script` property, nothing more.

```
[node name="Ground" parent="." instance=ExtResource("11_ground")]
```

**That is an instanced scene.** No `type=`, because its type comes from the file; `instance=` points at the `PackedScene`. `parent="."` means the root. **This single line is the entire mechanism of scene reuse**, and the next lesson is about it.

```
[node name="WildView" type="Node2D" parent="."]
script = ExtResource("12_wild")
wild = ExtResource("13_wild")
```

**And there is the thing worth stopping on.** `wild = ExtResource("13_wild")` assigns a `.tres` data file to a property called `wild`. That property is not a Godot property — it is an `@export` in `wild_view.gd`. **Someone declared a variable in a script, it appeared in the Inspector, a data file was dragged onto it, and the scene recorded the wiring.** That is the standing decision about numbers living in resources, visible in the file. Stage 3 teaches `@export`; stage 7 builds the whole data layer on it.

```
label_parcels = false
```

**One more property, on `IslandView`** — a plain `@export`ed boolean, set to a non-default value and therefore saved. Everything at its default is **absent from the file**, which stage 1's Inspector lesson made the point about: a `.tscn` stores only what differs.

**So the rules of the format, in five lines:**

1. **A section per node**, in tree order, each with its `parent=` path.
2. **`type=`** for a new node, **`instance=`** for an instanced scene.
3. **Only non-default properties** are written.
4. **`ExtResource` / `SubResource`** reference things outside / inside the file.
5. **It is text**, so it diffs, merges and greps.

**Why this is worth your time rather than a curiosity.** Four real uses:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Reading a diff** | *what changed in this scene?* is answerable in git |
| **Fixing a broken reference** | a path that no longer exists is one line to correct |
| **Resolving a merge conflict** | two people adding nodes to one scene is readable |
| **Finding a property** | `grep` a value across every scene in the project |

**The one thing not to do: do not hand-edit a scene Godot has open.** It will overwrite you on save. Close it, edit, reopen.

**`[sub_resource]`, which you will meet shortly.** A resource stored *inside* the scene rather than in its own file — a `CollisionShape2D`'s shape, a one-off material. It gets an `id` and is referenced as `SubResource("...")`. Stage 4 and stage 7 both return to when to inline a resource and when to give it a file.

**Practice.** Open `the-lost-sheep/game/scenes/main.tscn` in a text editor and account for every line of the first 30. Find: the script on the root, the instanced scene, the two `.tres` files assigned to `@export` properties, and the one boolean override. Then open your own `scenes/sheep.tscn` and confirm it stores only `texture` and whatever else you changed.
Instancing a scene inside another scene:
How one scene becomes a node inside another, which is how every Godot project of any size is built.

**Three ways to do it.**

**1. Drag the `.tscn`** from the FileSystem dock into the viewport, or onto a node in the Scene dock.

**2. The chain-link button** at the top of the Scene dock — *Instantiate Child Scene* (**Ctrl-Shift-A**) — which asks you to pick a scene.

**3. In code**, which stage 3 uses constantly:

```gdscript
const SHEEP := preload("res://game/scenes/sheep.tscn")

func spawn(at: Vector2) -> void:
	var sheep := SHEEP.instantiate()
	sheep.position = at
	add_child(sheep)
```

**What you get.** A single node in the Scene dock, with a **chain-link icon**, named after the scene's root. Its children are there but shown greyed and not editable — they belong to the other file.

**And in the `.tscn`, one line**, as the last lesson showed:

```
[node name="Ground" parent="." instance=ExtResource("11_ground")]
```

**The point: the instance holds no copy.** It is a reference plus a short list of differences. Change `sheep.tscn` and every instance of it changes — in the editor, immediately, without re-placing anything.

**That is the whole argument for building with scenes**, and it is worth stating as a rule: **anything that exists more than once should be a scene.** A sheep, a tree, a bullet, a button, a damage number.

**`preload` against `load`**, since the code form needs one:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `preload("res://…")` | resolved **at parse time**. The file must exist. Costs nothing at runtime. Only takes a literal path. |
| `load("res://…")` | resolved **when the line runs**. Takes a variable. Can fail at runtime. |

**Use `preload` for a path you know**, in a `const` at the top of the script — which is both faster and tells you at parse time if the path is wrong. Use `load` when the path is computed.

**The three-step reminder from the scene lesson**, because the commonest instancing bug lives here:

```gdscript
var sheep := SHEEP.instantiate()   # exists, NOT in the tree, _ready has NOT run
sheep.position = at                # fine — properties work before the tree
add_child(sheep)                   # NOW _enter_tree and _ready run
```

**Setting a property before `add_child` is fine and often correct.** Calling a method that assumes `_ready` has run is not. If a scene's script sets things up in `_ready`, nothing it set up exists until you have added the node.

**`add_child` and its sibling:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `add_child(node)` | add at the end of the children |
| `add_sibling(node)` | add next to `self`, which is what a bullet usually wants |
| `move_child(node, index)` | reorder, which changes draw order |
| `remove_child(node)` | take it out of the tree **without freeing it** — it still exists and leaks if you forget it |

**`remove_child` without freeing is a real leak**, and lesson 16 covers the correct pair.

**Where instances come from in your own projects.** `the-lost-sheep` instances exactly one scene in `main.tscn` — the ground — and draws its sheep and buildings by script instead. `shepherds-we-shall-be` has **82 scenes** and instances heavily: `game/scenes/actors/{heroes,enemies,animals,npcs}/`, `combat/{attacks,projectiles,effects}/`, `interactables/`, `props/`. **The difference is how many of a thing there are and how different each one is**, and stage 8 makes that trade-off properly.

**One trap worth naming now.** An instanced scene's **root** is the node you see; you cannot add children to it in the parent scene without turning on Editable Children, and you cannot delete its children at all. That is deliberate — they are not yours — and the next two lessons are about the two escape hatches.

**Practice.** Instance `scenes/sheep.tscn` into a new scene four times and spread them out. Then open `sheep.tscn`, change its sprite's `modulate` to green, save, and go back — all four should be green. Then write a script that instances four more in a loop with `preload`, and confirm you get eight. Then try to add a child to one of the instanced nodes and see what the dock lets you do.
What an instance stores: the override li:
An instance is a reference plus a list of differences, and knowing exactly what is in that list explains every surprise instancing produces.

**The mechanism.** When you place `sheep.tscn` in another scene and then change its sprite's `modulate`, the parent scene does **not** copy the sheep. It records one line:

```
[node name="Sheep" parent="." instance=ExtResource("1_sheep")]
modulate = Color(0, 1, 0, 1)
```

**One reference, one override.** Everything else still comes from `sheep.tscn`, live.

**What can be overridden:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Any property of the instance's root** | position, modulate, and every `@export` |
| **Any property of its children** | yes — the Inspector lets you, and it is recorded with a path |
| **Nothing structural** | you cannot add, delete or reorder its children. Not without the next lesson. |

**Overriding a child's property** writes a path-qualified line:

```
[node name="Sheep/Body" index="0"]
modulate = Color(1, 0, 0, 1)
```

**Which is powerful and is the thing to be careful with**, because it is invisible unless you look: the sheep in this scene is red and the sheep file says nothing about red. **A scene full of child overrides is a scene nobody can reason about**, and the fix is almost always to make the difference a property of the scene itself — an `@export` — rather than reaching inside it.

**The revert arrow, again.** From stage 1: a property changed from its default shows a revert arrow. On an instance it means *changed from what the source scene says*, and clicking it hands the property back to the source. **That is how you find and undo an accidental override**, and it is worth doing a sweep of an instance's Inspector when something is inexplicably different.

**What happens when the source scene changes.** Godot re-reads it, and:

| Change in the source | Effect on instances |
| --- | --- |
| A property you have **not** overridden | **changes everywhere.** The point of the system. |
| A property you **have** overridden | your override wins. The source change is invisible here. |
| A child **added** | appears in every instance |
| A child **deleted** | disappears — and any override you had on it is dropped |
| A child **renamed** | your overrides on it are **lost**, because they were stored by path |

**That last row is the real trap.** Renaming a child in a source scene silently discards every override any instance had on it. There is no warning. **So: rename children early, before the scene is used in twenty places.**

**The right way to vary an instance.** Not by reaching into its children, but by giving the scene a knob:

```gdscript
extends Node2D

@export var tint: Color = Color.WHITE
@export var speed: float = 60.0

func _ready() -> void:
	$Body.modulate = tint
```

**Now the Inspector on the instance shows `tint` and `speed`**, the override is one line against the root, and the scene decides what it means. **That is the standing decision about numbers living in `@export`**, and this is the lesson where the reason becomes concrete.

**Your own projects do exactly this.** From `the-lost-sheep/game/scenes/main.tscn`:

```
[node name="IslandView" type="Node2D" parent="."]
script = ExtResource("2_view")
island = ExtResource("4_island")
label_parcels = false
```

**`island` and `label_parcels` are `@export`s on `island_view.gd`**, overridden on the node. No child of `IslandView` is touched from here. The scene exposes what can vary and hides the rest.

**Practice.** Instance `sheep.tscn` twice. On the first, override the root's `modulate` — note the revert arrow. On the second, override the **child sprite's** `modulate`, then open the parent `.tscn` in a text editor and compare the two lines. Then rename the child in `sheep.tscn`, save, and watch the second override vanish. Then do it properly: add `@export var tint: Color` to the sheep's script and set it per instance.
Editable children:
The escape hatch when an instance genuinely needs a different structure, and the reasons to reach for it rarely.

**The problem it solves.** An instanced scene's children are not yours — you cannot add to them, delete them or reorder them. Usually that is right. Occasionally you have a door scene and *this* door needs an extra light.

**Turning it on.** Right-click the instanced node > **Editable Children**.

**What changes:** the children stop being greyed out. You can now add nodes inside the instance, delete its children, and reorder them. The node keeps its chain-link icon, and it is still an instance.

**What gets recorded.** Structural changes go into the parent scene as ordinary node entries with a `parent=` path reaching inside the instance:

```
[node name="Light" type="PointLight2D" parent="Door"]
```

and deletions are recorded too. **So the parent scene now contains part of the door's structure**, which is exactly the coupling you were avoiding.

**The three consequences, and they are the reason to be sparing:**

**1. Source changes get harder to absorb.** Add a child to the source scene and it appears — but your local additions and deletions have to be reconciled with it, and Godot does the best it can. Renames still break paths.

**2. The instance is no longer "a door".** It is a door-plus-edits, and the only way to know what is different is to read the parent `.tscn`. Multiply that by thirty instances and the scene is unreadable.

**3. It is one-way in practice.** Turning Editable Children back off discards the structural edits. Godot asks first, and it is a real loss.

**When it is the right answer**, and these are genuine:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A one-off** | the boss room's door, which has a chain nothing else has |
| **Level assembly** | placing a scene and tying it to this level's specific markers |
| **Debugging** | adding a temporary visualiser inside an instance to see what it is doing |
| **Reparenting into it** | dropping an existing node inside an instanced container |

**When it is the wrong answer**, and these are the common misuses:

| Instead of… | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| Deleting a child you never want | remove it from the source scene, or gate it with an `@export var show_light: bool` |
| Adding the same child to every instance | add it to the **source** scene |
| Changing a child's values | `@export` the value on the root — the last lesson |
| Needing a *variant* | **scene inheritance** — the next lesson. This is what it is for. |

**That last row is the important one.** If three instances need the structure changed the same way, you do not want three sets of editable-children edits. You want an inherited scene, which records the difference **once**, in a file, with a name.

**The sibling feature: Load As Placeholder.** Right-click an instance > **Load As Placeholder** replaces it with a stand-in that loads nothing until asked. Useful for a huge scene you do not want loaded while editing the parent; irrelevant at the scale you are working at now, and worth knowing exists.

**And the reverse operation**, which is genuinely useful: right-click any node > **Save Branch as Scene** takes a subtree you have built in place and turns it into its own `.tscn`, replacing it with an instance. **That is how a scene usually comes into existence** — you build it where you need it, notice you need it twice, and extract it.

**Practice.** Instance `sheep.tscn`, turn on **Editable Children**, and add a `PointLight2D` inside it. Open the parent `.tscn` and find the line that records it. Then turn Editable Children back off and read the warning Godot gives you. Then do the same thing the other way: build a two-node group inside a scene, right-click it and **Save Branch as Scene**, and notice it becomes an instance.
Scene inheritance:
How to make a variant of a scene — the feature that does properly what editable children does badly, and the one most people never use.

**The idea.** A scene can **inherit** another scene the way a class inherits a class. The child scene starts as the parent's whole tree, and records only its differences — in its own file, with its own name.

**Creating one:** **Scene > New Inherited Scene…**, then pick the base. Or right-click a `.tscn` in the FileSystem dock > **New Inherited Scene**.

**What you get.** The full tree of the base, with every node shown in a different colour and marked as inherited. You can:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Override any property**, on the root or any child | yes |
| **Add new children** | yes, anywhere |
| **Replace a child's script** | yes |
| **Delete an inherited child** | **no** — but you can hide it or disable it |
| **Reorder inherited children** | no |

**What the file looks like.** The first line names the base:

```
[gd_scene load_steps=3 format=3]

[ext_resource type="PackedScene" path="res://game/scenes/sheep.tscn" id="1_base"]

[node name="BlackSheep" instance=ExtResource("1_base")]

[node name="Body" parent="." index="0"]
modulate = Color(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 1)
```

**One reference and one override** — the same mechanism as an instance, but **saved as a scene in its own right**, so it has a name, a file, and can itself be instanced fifty times.

**The difference from an instance, stated plainly:**

| | Instance | Inherited scene |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Lives in** | a parent scene | its own `.tscn` |
| **Reusable** | no — the edits belong to that one placement | **yes** — instance it anywhere |
| **Named** | by its node name | by its filename |
| **Can add children** | only with Editable Children | yes, natively |
| **Changes to base** | flow through | flow through |

**So the test is: do I need this difference more than once?** Once, in one place — an instance override. More than once, or anywhere else — an inherited scene.

**The canonical uses:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Enemy variants** | `enemy.tscn` → `enemy_fast.tscn`, `enemy_armoured.tscn` |
| **Button variants** | a base button with the theme and sounds; variants for primary, danger, icon-only |
| **Projectile variants** | one base with the collision and lifetime; variants for the art and damage |
| **A test fixture** | the real scene, inheriting, with a debug overlay added |

**Where it stops being the answer.** Three or four levels of inheritance becomes as hard to follow as deep class inheritance, and for the same reasons — a property's value is somewhere up a chain you have to walk. **One level is almost always enough.**

**And the alternative that is often better: composition plus data.** Instead of `enemy_fast.tscn` inheriting `enemy.tscn`, have **one** `enemy.tscn` with an `@export var stats: EnemyStats` and a `.tres` file per variant. The tree is identical for every enemy; only the data differs.

**That is what your own projects do**, and it is why `shepherds-we-shall-be/game/resources/definitions/` exists — a folder of `.tres` holding *"hero kits, skill trees, items, conversations, map defs"*. The structure is shared; the numbers are files. **Stage 7 builds this properly and makes the case.**

**So the honest ranking**, for a thing that comes in variants:

1. **One scene, data per variant** (`@export` a `Resource`) — if only values differ.
2. **An inherited scene** — if the *structure* differs and the difference is reusable.
3. **An instance override** — if it is genuinely a one-off.
4. **Editable children** — if you are debugging or assembling a level.

**Practice.** Make `scenes/sheep.tscn`, then **New Inherited Scene** from it, save as `scenes/black_sheep.tscn`, and darken the body's `modulate`. Instance both into a third scene and confirm they differ. Then change the base sheep's sprite and confirm **both** change. Then open `black_sheep.tscn` as text and find the one override line.
The node lifecycle: _init, _enter_tree,:
The order in which a node wakes up, which decides where your setup code can safely go — and getting it wrong is the single commonest beginner bug in Godot.

**The four callbacks, in order:**

| Callback | When | What is safe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `_init()` | the object is created, **before** it is in a tree | properties on itself. **No children, no tree, no `$`.** |
| `_enter_tree()` | it has been added to a tree | the tree, the parent. **Children may not be ready.** |
| `_ready()` | it **and all its children** are in the tree and ready | **everything.** This is where setup goes. |
| `_exit_tree()` | it is being removed from the tree | cleanup, disconnecting |

**And the one rule that follows: setup goes in `_ready()`.** Not `_init`, not `_enter_tree`. Ninety per cent of lifecycle bugs are code in the wrong one of these.

**Why `_init` cannot touch children.** At `_init` the node exists and nothing else does:

```gdscript
func _init() -> void:
	$Sprite2D.modulate = Color.RED   # ERROR: null instance
```

**There is no tree, so there is no `$`.** `$Sprite2D` resolves to `null` and you get *"Attempt to call function … on a null instance"* — the error stage 1's Output lesson said you would see most.

**Why `_enter_tree` is not enough either.** It fires when *this* node joins the tree, which happens **before** its children have been added and readied. So a parent's `_enter_tree` runs with its children still arriving.

**`_ready` is the one that waits.** It fires once, after this node and **every descendant** is in the tree. That is the guarantee, and it is why it is the right place for:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	$Sprite2D.modulate = tint
	$Timer.timeout.connect(_on_timeout)
	$HealthBar.set_max(max_hp)
```

**`@onready`, which is the same guarantee as a one-liner:**

```gdscript
@onready var sprite: Sprite2D = $Sprite2D
@onready var timer: Timer = $Timer
```

**`@onready` defers the assignment until just before `_ready()` runs.** Writing it without the annotation is the classic null:

```gdscript
var sprite := $Sprite2D          # null, every time — runs at _init
@onready var sprite := $Sprite2D # correct
```

**That is worth committing to memory**, because the broken form looks perfectly reasonable and fails silently until you use it.

**The other two worth knowing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `_notification(what)` | the low-level hook all of these are built on. Rarely needed directly. |
| `NOTIFICATION_WM_CLOSE_REQUEST` | the window's close button, caught via `_notification`. Stage 10. |

**`_init` with arguments**, which is the one legitimate reason to use it:

```gdscript
class_name Bullet
extends Area2D

var damage: int

func _init(dmg: int = 1) -> void:
	damage = dmg
```

**But a scene instanced from a `.tscn` cannot be given constructor arguments** — `instantiate()` takes none. So for scenes the pattern is: instantiate, set properties, add to tree:

```gdscript
var b := BULLET.instantiate()
b.damage = 5          # before add_child, which is fine
add_child(b)          # _enter_tree, then _ready
```

**The order across a whole scene**, which the next lesson takes in detail: Godot readies **children before parents**, deepest first. So by the time a parent's `_ready` runs, every child's `_ready` has already finished — which is exactly the guarantee that makes `_ready` safe.

**One practical consequence worth having now.** If a parent needs to tell a child something at startup, the parent's `_ready` is the place, and the child must not assume it has been told in its own `_ready` — because the child's ran first. **That asymmetry is the root of a lot of initialisation order confusion**, and stage 5's "call down, signal up" rule is partly an answer to it.

**Practice.** Put `print()` in `_init`, `_enter_tree`, `_ready` and `_exit_tree` on both a parent and a child node, run it, and write down the exact order you see. Then try `$Child` in `_init` and read the error. Then fix it with `@onready` and confirm it works. Keep the printed order — the next lesson explains it.
_ready order, and why children go first:
The order you just printed, explained — because it is the guarantee the whole lifecycle rests on, and because the exceptions are where real bugs live.

**The order, for a tree:**

```
Root
├── A
│   └── A1
└── B
```

| Phase | Order |
| --- | --- |
| `_enter_tree` | **Root, A, A1, B** — top down, as each joins |
| `_ready` | **A1, A, B, Root** — **bottom up**, depth first |
| `_exit_tree` | Root, A, A1, B — top down |

**`_ready` runs deepest-first.** By the time any node's `_ready` fires, every one of its descendants has already finished its own.

**Why it is built that way.** So that `_ready` can be the one place where everything is safe. A parent configuring its children needs the children to exist and be initialised; a child cannot wait for its parent without deadlock. **Children first is the only order that gives anyone a guarantee**, and the guarantee is worth more than symmetry.

**The three consequences you will actually meet:**

**1. A parent can configure children in `_ready`. A child cannot read its parent's `_ready` work.**

```gdscript
# Parent — fine. Children are ready.
func _ready() -> void:
	$HealthBar.maximum = max_hp

# Child — WRONG. The parent's _ready has not run yet.
func _ready() -> void:
	var hp = get_parent().max_hp   # may still be the default
```

**The fix is not to reach up.** It is for the parent to push down, or for the child to wait for a signal — which is stage 5's rule, and this is the mechanical reason for it.

**2. Nodes added at runtime ready immediately on `add_child`.**

```gdscript
var sheep := SHEEP.instantiate()
add_child(sheep)      # sheep's _ready runs HERE, synchronously
sheep.start()         # safe — _ready has finished
```

**That is a different order from scene load**, and it is usually what you want: the node is fully alive by the time `add_child` returns.

**3. Order among siblings is their order in the tree.** `A` before `B` because `A` is above `B` in the Scene dock. **So dragging a node in the dock changes initialisation order**, which is both useful and a trap — a dependency on sibling order is invisible and breaks when someone tidies the tree.

**The tools for when order genuinely matters:**

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `await ready` | wait for a node's `_ready` to have happened |
| `call_deferred("method")` | run it at the end of the current frame, after everything has settled |
| `await get_tree().process_frame` | wait one full frame |
| **Autoloads** | ready **before** the main scene. Lesson 17. |
| `process_priority` | order `_process` calls, not `_ready` |

**`call_deferred` is the workhorse** and worth understanding now, because it solves a whole class of problem:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	# Everything in the tree is ready, but the FIRST FRAME has not drawn.
	# Anything depending on sizes, layout or physics should wait.
	_position_the_hud.call_deferred()
```

**Sizes and layout are not final in `_ready`.** A `Control`'s `size` is still being computed; physics has not stepped. **If a value is zero in `_ready` and correct a moment later, `call_deferred` is almost always the answer** — and stage 9 hits this repeatedly with interface layout.

**A real case of exactly this from your own code.** `shepherds-we-shall-be/game/scripts/presentation/pixel_perfect_viewport.gd` is an autoload that must size the viewport to the window. It connects the signal in `_ready` — and then **polls every frame anyway**, with a comment explaining why:

> *The signal alone was not enough, and the failure was invisible from here: the window is 1280×720 when an autoload's `_ready()` runs, then becomes its real size, and the viewport stayed sized for the smaller one.*

**The window was lying in `_ready`.** The code asked a correct question of an object that had not finished becoming itself. That is this lesson's entire subject, found in production, and its fix — stop trusting a startup reading, keep checking — is a legitimate pattern when `call_deferred` is not enough.

**Practice.** Build the four-node tree above, print in `_ready` on each, and confirm the order is `A1, A, B, Root`. Then drag `B` above `A` and confirm the order changes. Then add a `Control` with a `size`, print its `size` in `_ready`, and print it again from a `call_deferred` method — and notice the difference.
$ paths and get_node:
How a node refers to another node, the four syntaxes for it, and the one rule that decides which to use.

**The shorthand:**

```gdscript
$Sprite2D              # a child called Sprite2D
$Body/Sprite2D         # a grandchild
$"../Sibling"          # up one, then down — note the quotes
$"Node With Spaces"    # quotes needed for anything not an identifier
```

**`$` is sugar for `get_node()`:**

```gdscript
$Sprite2D              # identical to…
get_node("Sprite2D")
```

**The four forms, and when each is right:**

| Form | Returns | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `$Path` / `get_node("Path")` | the node, **or an error** if missing | you are certain it is there |
| `get_node_or_null("Path")` | the node, or `null` | it legitimately may not be |
| `find_child("Name")` | searches **recursively** by name | you do not know where it is — slow, avoid |
| `%UniqueName` | the node, by its unique name | next lesson. **Usually the best answer.** |

**`get_node_or_null` plus a check is the honest form** when a node is optional:

```gdscript
var hud := get_node_or_null("HUD")
if hud != null:
	hud.show_message("…")
```

**The rule that matters more than the syntax: paths break, so keep them short and local.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `$Sprite2D` | **fine.** Your own child. You own its name. |
| `$Body/Sprite2D` | fine. Still inside your own scene. |
| `$"../Sibling"` | **suspect.** You now depend on your parent's structure. |
| `$"../../UI/HUD/Label"` | **wrong.** Four assumptions about a tree you do not own. |

**A path that leaves your own scene is a dependency on someone else's structure**, and it breaks the first time anyone reorganises. The standing decision in `godot.md` states it: **no `get_parent()`, no `$"../../Thing"`.** Stage 5 gives the positive form — call down, signal up — and the alternatives are: a signal upward, an `@export` reference set in the Inspector, a group, or an autoload.

**`@onready` is how a path becomes a variable**, from the lifecycle lesson:

```gdscript
@onready var sprite: Sprite2D = $Sprite2D
@onready var anim: AnimationPlayer = $AnimationPlayer
```

**Do this at the top of every script rather than writing `$Sprite2D` in ten methods.** Three reasons: it resolves once instead of every call, it gives you a **typed** variable so autocomplete works, and if the path is wrong you find out at startup rather than whenever that method first runs.

**The typing is worth stressing.** `$Sprite2D` returns `Node` as far as the editor knows, so `$Sprite2D.flip_h = true` gets no completion and no check. The annotated form is typed, so it does.

**Three ways to get the type right:**

```gdscript
@onready var sprite: Sprite2D = $Sprite2D      # annotate — clearest
var sprite := $Sprite2D as Sprite2D            # cast
@onready var sprite := $Sprite2D               # inferred as Node. Not enough.
```

**`NodePath` as a value**, which you will see in `.tscn` files and in `@export`:

```gdscript
@export var target_path: NodePath
@onready var target: Node2D = get_node(target_path)
```

**That is the Inspector-assigned alternative to a hard-coded path** — the scene says which node, rather than the script assuming. Better still is `@export var target: Node2D`, which Godot 4 supports directly and which gives you a drag-and-drop slot in the Inspector. **Prefer the typed export.**

**The error you will see, once more.** *"Attempt to call function 'x' in base 'null instance' on a null instance."* It means a path resolved to nothing. Three causes, in order of likelihood: the node was renamed, the path ran before `_ready`, or the node is in another scene entirely.

**Practice.** On your sheep scene: replace every inline `$Sprite2D` with an `@onready` typed variable at the top. Confirm autocomplete now offers `flip_h`. Then deliberately rename the child node and run it — read the error, then fix the path. Then add `@export var target: Node2D` and drag a node onto it in the Inspector.
% unique names:
The feature that solves the fragile-path problem inside a scene, added in Godot 4 and still underused — and the right answer most of the time.

**The problem.** A deep node inside your own scene:

```gdscript
@onready var label := $UI/Panel/VBoxContainer/HBoxContainer/NameLabel
```

**Four structural assumptions**, and any tidy-up of the layout breaks it. Interface trees are exactly where this happens, because containers get added and removed constantly.

**The fix: mark the node as unique, then address it by name alone.**

Right-click the node in the Scene dock > **Access as Unique Name** (**Ctrl-U**). A **`%`** appears beside it. Then:

```gdscript
@onready var label: Label = %NameLabel
```

**No path. Just the name.** Move the node anywhere in the scene and the reference still works.

**What it actually does.** It sets `unique_name_in_owner = true` on the node, and the scene's **owner** keeps a lookup from name to node. `%Name` asks the owner. That is why the next lesson is about `owner` — it is the thing that makes this work.

**The scope, which is the critical detail: unique names are unique within their scene, not globally.** Two different scenes can both have a `%NameLabel`, and `%NameLabel` from inside each resolves to its own. **An instanced scene's unique names are not visible to the parent scene** — they belong to the instance's own owner.

**That scoping is the feature, not a limitation.** It means a scene can expose internal landmarks to its own script without leaking them, and without a parent being able to reach in by name.

**When to use `%` over `$`:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `$Sprite2D` | a direct child. Short, obvious, stable. **Keep it.** |
| `%NameLabel` | anything two or more levels deep. **Use it.** |
| `%` for everything | no — a scene where every node is unique has no structure left to read |

**The honest rule: direct children with `$`, deep nodes with `%`, nothing outside your own scene at all.**

**The trap.** `%Name` fails if the node is not marked unique, and the error is the same null-instance message as a bad path. **Marking it is a separate step from writing the code**, and forgetting it is the one way this feature bites. The `%` in the Scene dock is the confirmation.

**Renaming a unique node** updates nothing in your scripts — same as any rename. But because the name is the whole reference, it is at least a single, greppable string.

**Where it earns its keep: interface.** Stage 9's lesson on containers will have you nesting `VBoxContainer` inside `MarginContainer` inside `PanelContainer`, and the tree will change several times as the layout settles. **Every `$` path through that is a maintenance cost; every `%` survives.** `the-lost-sheep/game/scripts/ui/` holds sixteen interface scripts — `build_bar.gd`, `top_bar.gd`, `resource_modal.gd`, `tutorial_panel.gd` — and interface is precisely where this feature pays.

**One alternative worth knowing**, for the case where the node is genuinely elsewhere: `@export var label: Label` and drag it in. The scene states the connection, the script assumes nothing, and it works across scene boundaries where `%` does not.

**So the full ranking for "how do I refer to that node":**

1. **`$Child`** — if it is a direct child.
2. **`%Unique`** — if it is deeper in your own scene.
3. **`@export var thing: Type`** — if it is outside your scene, or optional.
4. **A group** — if there are many, or you do not know where they are.
5. **An autoload** — if it is genuinely global. Lesson 18.
6. **`$"../../.."`** — never.

**Practice.** Build an interface scene: `Control` → `PanelContainer` → `VBoxContainer` → `Label` + `Button`. Reference the `Label` with a full `$` path and confirm it works. Then mark it **Access as Unique Name** (Ctrl-U), change the reference to `%Label`, and confirm it still works. Then wrap the `VBoxContainer` in a `MarginContainer` — the `$` path would now be broken, and the `%` is not.
owner, and what it means in a saved scen:
A property every node has, that almost nothing explains, and that quietly decides what gets written to a `.tscn` — and makes `%` unique names work.

**The definition.** `node.owner` is **the root of the scene the node was saved as part of.**

For a scene like this, saved as `sheep.tscn`:

```
Sheep          ← owner = null (it IS the owner)
├── Body       ← owner = Sheep
└── Shadow     ← owner = Sheep
```

**Every node's `owner` is `Sheep`, and `Sheep`'s own `owner` is `null`.**

**Why it exists: it is how Godot knows what to save.** When you save a scene, Godot writes the root and **every node whose `owner` is that root**. A node in the tree with a different owner, or no owner, is **not written**.

**That is the rule, and three consequences follow.**

**1. A node added in code is not saved, and that is correct.**

```gdscript
var sheep := SHEEP.instantiate()
add_child(sheep)        # sheep.owner is null
```

Its `owner` is `null`, so if you saved the parent scene from a `@tool` script, the sheep would not be written. Runtime children are runtime children.

**2. To add a node in code *and* have it saved, you must set the owner.** This only matters in `@tool` scripts and editor plugins, and it is the thing that makes them work:

```gdscript
@tool
extends Node2D

func _build() -> void:
	var marker := Marker2D.new()
	add_child(marker)
	marker.owner = get_tree().edited_scene_root   # NOW it will be saved
```

**Forgetting that line is the classic `@tool` bug**: the node appears in the editor, looks right, and vanishes on reload. Stage 7's `@tool` lesson returns to it.

**3. An instanced scene's children keep their own owner.** Instance `sheep.tscn` into `main.tscn` and the sheep's `Body` still has `owner == Sheep`, not `Main`. **So `main.tscn` does not write `Body`** — it writes one `instance=` line and lets `sheep.tscn` describe its own insides. That is the override-list mechanism from three lessons ago, explained from the other end.

**And this is why `%` unique names are scene-scoped.** `%Name` asks **the owner** for its lookup table. Inside `sheep.tscn`'s script, the owner is `Sheep`, so `%` sees the sheep's unique nodes. Inside `main.tscn`'s script the owner is `Main`, which has never heard of the sheep's internals. **The scoping is not a special rule — it falls straight out of `owner`.**

**The related properties, for completeness:**

| Property / method | What it gives |
| --- | --- |
| `owner` | the scene root this node was saved with |
| `get_parent()` | the node directly above. **Different thing.** |
| `get_tree()` | the `SceneTree` — the whole running tree |
| `get_tree().current_scene` | the scene that was loaded as the current one |
| `get_tree().root` | the `Window` at the very top |
| `is_inside_tree()` | whether it is in the tree at all |

**`owner` and `get_parent()` are routinely confused and are unrelated.** `Body`'s parent is `Sheep`; so is its owner — but for a grandchild the parent is the child and the owner is still the root.

**A real use of `is_inside_tree()` from your own code.** `pixel_perfect_viewport.gd` guards a static helper with it:

```gdscript
static func interface_frame(node: Node) -> Vector2:
	if node == null or not node.is_inside_tree():
		return Vector2(BASE)
```

**Because a node that is instantiated but not yet added has no tree to ask**, and the function is called from places where that is possible. Returning the design size rather than crashing is the right answer — and it is the three-step instantiate/add distinction from the scene lesson, defended in production code.

**Practice.** Add a script to your sheep's root and print `name`, `owner`, `get_parent()` for the root and for a child. Then instance the sheep into another scene and print the same from the parent scene's script for the instanced sheep's child — and confirm the owner is the sheep, not the parent. Then add a node in code and print its `owner`.
Adding and removing nodes in code:
The runtime half of the tree: making nodes, putting them in, taking them out — and the four methods that do it.

**Making a node.** Two kinds of thing to make:

```gdscript
# A bare node of a class
var timer := Timer.new()

# An instance of a scene
const SHEEP := preload("res://game/scenes/sheep.tscn")
var sheep := SHEEP.instantiate()
```

**`new()` for a class, `instantiate()` for a scene.** Both give you a node that exists and is **not in the tree**.

**Putting it in:**

| Method | Where it goes |
| --- | --- |
| `add_child(node)` | last child of `self` |
| `add_child(node, true)` | same, with a **readable auto-name** rather than `@Node2D@12` |
| `add_sibling(node)` | directly after `self`, under the same parent |
| `move_child(node, index)` | reposition among siblings — **changes draw order** |

**The second argument to `add_child` is worth knowing.** Without it, runtime nodes get internal names like `@Sprite2D@7`, which are unreadable in the remote tree. With `true`, you get `Sprite2D2`. **For anything you will want to find while debugging, pass it.**

**The order to do things in**, which the lifecycle lesson established and is worth restating as a recipe:

```gdscript
func spawn_sheep(at: Vector2) -> Node2D:
	var sheep := SHEEP.instantiate()
	sheep.position = at            # set properties FIRST — cheap, no tree needed
	sheep.tint = Color.WHITE
	add_child(sheep)               # _enter_tree and _ready run HERE, synchronously
	sheep.start()                  # safe now
	return sheep
```

**Properties before `add_child`, method calls after.** That single rule prevents most spawning bugs.

**Where to add it, which matters more than it looks.** `add_child` makes it a child of `self`, so a bullet fired by a gun becomes a child of the gun — and **moves with the gun**, because children inherit the parent's transform. Almost never what you want.

```gdscript
# WRONG — the bullet follows the player around
add_child(bullet)

# Right — the bullet belongs to the world
get_parent().add_child(bullet)

# Better — say explicitly where the world is
@export var projectile_container: Node2D
projectile_container.add_child(bullet)
```

**The third form is the one to prefer**, because it does not assume the parent is the world, and stage 5's structure rule is the reason. `shepherds-we-shall-be` has `game/scenes/combat/projectiles/` as its own area for exactly this.

**Taking it out — and the distinction that leaks memory:**

| Method | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `remove_child(node)` | out of the tree, **still exists**. You now own it. |
| `node.queue_free()` | out of the tree and **freed**, safely, at the end of the frame |
| `node.free()` | freed **immediately**. Dangerous. Next lesson. |

**`remove_child` without freeing is a leak.** The node is gone from the tree and still in memory, with nothing referencing it. It is the right call only when you intend to re-add it:

```gdscript
remove_child(card)
other_hand.add_child(card)   # moving it — correct use
```

**And since Godot 4 there is a method for exactly that:**

```gdscript
card.reparent(other_hand)              # keeps global position
card.reparent(other_hand, false)       # keeps local position
```

**`reparent` is the right way to move a node between parents** — it is the code form of stage 1's Ctrl-drag.

**Checking before you act**, because all of these error on a node that is already gone:

```gdscript
if is_instance_valid(node):
	node.queue_free()
```

**`is_instance_valid()` is the guard** for a reference you are not sure is still alive — a target that may have died, a node freed last frame. It is cheap and it prevents a whole class of crash.

**Finding what you have added:**

```gdscript
get_children()                  # an Array[Node]
get_child_count()
get_child(0)
has_node("Sheep")
for sheep in get_children():
	sheep.queue_free()
```

**Iterating `get_children()` while freeing is safe with `queue_free`** — because the freeing happens after the loop — and **unsafe with `free()`**, which mutates the array you are walking. Another reason for the next lesson's rule.

**Practice.** Write a script that spawns ten sheep in a row on `_ready`, each with a readable name via `add_child(sheep, true)`. Run it and read the names in the **Remote** tree. Then add a key press that frees them all with `queue_free()`. Then try adding the sheep as children of a moving node and watch them follow it — then fix it with an `@export` container.
queue_free, free, and why never free:
One of the standing decisions of this curriculum, stated with its reason: **use `queue_free()`, never `free()`.**

**What each does:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `queue_free()` | marks the node for deletion. It is freed **at the end of the current frame**, after everything has finished running. |
| `free()` | deletes it **right now**, on this line. |

**Why `free()` is dangerous.** Because something is almost always still using the node on that frame.

```gdscript
func _on_body_entered(body: Node2D) -> void:
	body.free()                 # the physics engine is mid-callback,
	                            # holding a reference to `body`
```

**You have deleted an object the engine is in the middle of using.** The result is a crash, or worse, a silent corruption — and the stack trace points somewhere unrelated, which is why these are expensive bugs.

**The same problem, closer to home:**

```gdscript
for child in get_children():
	child.free()            # mutating the array being iterated
```

**With `queue_free()` both are safe.** The node stays alive and functional for the rest of the frame, is removed from the tree, and is deleted when nothing is on the stack.

**What `queue_free()` guarantees:**

1. The node finishes the current frame.
2. `_exit_tree()` runs.
3. Its **children are freed too**, recursively.
4. Signal connections to and from it are dropped.
5. `is_instance_valid(node)` becomes `false`.

**Point 3 is worth stressing:** freeing a parent frees the whole subtree. You do not walk a tree freeing children — you free the root of it.

**The pattern for the frame between the call and the deletion**, which is a real gap:

```gdscript
func die() -> void:
	queue_free()
	# This still runs. The node is still alive.
	emit_signal("died")
	$Sprite2D.visible = false
```

**`queue_free()` does not return early and does not stop the function.** If the rest should not run, `return`.

**And `is_queued_for_deletion()`** tells you whether it has been called, which matters in a frame where several systems might all decide to kill the same thing:

```gdscript
if not is_queued_for_deletion():
	queue_free()
```

**The honest exceptions**, because *never* deserves a footnote. `free()` is correct for:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A non-`Node` `Object`** you created and nothing else holds | it is not in a tree; there is no frame to wait for |
| **A node never added to the tree** | `instantiate()`d and then abandoned — `free()` is fine, and `queue_free()` also works |
| **Inside `_exit_tree`-adjacent teardown** where you are certain | and *certain* is doing a lot of work in that sentence |

**For anything in the tree, during play: `queue_free()`.** That is the rule, and the exceptions are rare enough not to think about.

**`RefCounted` and what you do not have to free.** Not everything needs freeing:

| Type | Freeing |
| --- | --- |
| `Node` | **you free it** — `queue_free()` |
| `Resource` (and so `RefCounted`) | **automatic**, when the last reference goes |
| `Object` | you free it — `free()` |
| Built-ins (`Vector2`, `Array`, `Dictionary`, `String`) | automatic, by value |

**So a `Resource` — every `.tres`, every custom data class in stage 7 — manages itself.** You never free a resource. That asymmetry between `Node` and `Resource` is one of the few places Godot asks you to remember which kind of thing you are holding.

**Finding what you failed to free.** Two tools, both from stage 10 and worth naming now:

```gdscript
print(get_tree().get_node_count())   # climbing steadily? something leaks
print_orphan_nodes()                 # lists nodes alive and not in the tree
```

**`print_orphan_nodes()` is the direct answer to "did I `remove_child` and forget".** Call it on quit and it should print nothing.

**And the Monitors tab**, from stage 1's debugger lesson: watch **Object Count** and **Node Count** while you play. A sawtooth is healthy; a staircase is a leak.

**Practice.** Spawn fifty sheep, then free them all with `queue_free()` and confirm the Remote tree empties. Then try the same with `free()` inside a `for child in get_children()` loop and observe what goes wrong. Then call `print_orphan_nodes()` after doing `remove_child` without freeing, and read what it tells you.
Autoloads: always-there scripts and scen:
A node that exists before your game starts and outlives every scene change — Godot's answer to the global, with the mechanism explained before the next lesson argues about when to use one.

**What an autoload is.** A script or scene registered in **Project > Project Settings > Globals > Autoload**. Godot instantiates it once, at startup, and adds it as a child of the tree root — **above your main scene**.

```
root (Window)
├── ViewportSizer        ← autoload
├── HitStopController    ← autoload
└── Game                 ← your main scene
```

**Two consequences fall straight out of that position:**

1. **It is ready before your main scene.** Its `_ready` runs first, so a scene can rely on it existing.
2. **`change_scene_to_file()` does not touch it.** Scene changes replace the main-scene child; the autoloads are siblings and survive.

**Registering one.** Project Settings > Globals > Autoload, pick the `.gd` or `.tscn`, give it a **Node Name**, and tick **Enable**. In `project.godot` it looks like this — a real pair from your own project:

```ini
[autoload]

ViewportSizer="*res://game/scripts/presentation/pixel_perfect_viewport.gd"
HitStopController="*res://game/scripts/presentation/combat/hit_stop_service.gd"
```

**The leading `*` means enabled.** Remove it and the autoload is registered and off.

**Using one: the Node Name becomes a global identifier.**

```gdscript
ViewportSizer.interface_frame(self)
HitStopController.request(0.08)
```

**No `get_node`, no path, no reference.** The name is available in every script in the project.

**A script autoload against a scene autoload:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A `.gd` file** | Godot wraps it in a bare `Node` with that script. Fine for logic and state. |
| **A `.tscn` file** | the whole scene is instanced. Use this when the global needs **child nodes** — a music player with several `AudioStreamPlayer`s, a transition overlay with a `ColorRect` and an `AnimationPlayer`. |

**The `class_name` collision, which will catch you.** An autoload's Node Name occupies a global identifier, and so does `class_name`. **They cannot be the same**, and Godot refuses.

**Your own code hits this and documents it:**

```gdscript
class_name PixelPerfectViewport
extends Node

## Autoloaded as `ViewportSizer` rather than under its own class name, because Godot refuses
## a `class_name` that collides with a singleton. The class name is kept so the sizing rule
## can be tested as a pure function without a window.
```

**Two names for one script, deliberately.** `PixelPerfectViewport` is the class — so `PixelPerfectViewport.viewport_for(size)` can be called statically in a test with no autoload and no window. `ViewportSizer` is the singleton — so the running game has one instance of it. **That is the right way out of the collision** and it is worth copying: keep the `class_name` for testability, give the autoload a different Node Name.

**What an autoload is good at**, and all four are legitimate:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Something there must be exactly one of** | the audio bus manager, the save system, a scene-transition overlay |
| **Something that must survive scene changes** | the player's progress, settings, the music that keeps playing |
| **A service with no place in the world** | `HitStopController` — it affects presentation globally and has no position |
| **Something that must run before anything else** | `ViewportSizer`, which has to size the viewport before a scene draws |

**And the cost**, which the next lesson is about: every autoload is reachable from everywhere, so it is a dependency nothing declares. Two autoloads is a convenience; twenty is a global namespace with your game in it.

**Getting at it without the global name**, which is occasionally useful in a test:

```gdscript
get_node("/root/ViewportSizer")
get_tree().root.get_node_or_null("ViewportSizer")
```

**Practice.** Make `scripts/game_state.gd` with `extends Node` and a `var score := 0`. Register it as an autoload called `GameState`. Then from two different scenes, increment `GameState.score` and print it — and change scene between them to confirm the value survives. Then look at `shepherds-we-shall-be/project.godot` and find its two autoloads, and open `pixel_perfect_viewport.gd` to read the `class_name` comment.
When an autoload is right:
The judgement half of autoloads, because the mechanism is easy and the discipline is not — and a project with twenty of them is a project with no structure.

**The honest statement of the cost.** An autoload is reachable from every script, so:

- **Nothing declares the dependency.** A scene that uses `GameState` looks identical to one that does not.
- **Nothing constrains the coupling.** Any script can read and write any autoload's state.
- **It cannot be tested in isolation**, because the thing under test reaches out to a global.
- **It cannot be instanced twice**, so a split-screen or a preview window becomes a rewrite.

**None of that is an argument against autoloads.** It is an argument for having few, and for each one answering a question that nothing else can.

**The test: does this need to be global, or is it just convenient?**

| It is global | It is merely convenient |
| --- | --- |
| There must be **exactly one** in the running program | there happens to be one right now |
| It must **survive a scene change** | it lives as long as the current scene does |
| It has **no place in the world** | it could be a node in the scene |
| Everything needs it | three things need it |

**For the right column, the alternatives, in order of preference:**

| Instead of an autoload | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A thing the scene owns | a **child node** in the scene |
| A thing passed in | **`@export var service: Thing`**, dragged in the Inspector |
| A thing found by kind | a **group** — `get_first_node_in_group()` |
| Shared numbers | a **`Resource`** loaded where needed — stage 7 |
| Pure functions | a **`class_name` with `static` functions**. No instance, no autoload, no state. |

**That last row removes a great many would-be autoloads.** A maths helper, a formatter, a rule — none of it needs an instance:

```gdscript
class_name Pathing

static func cost(a: Vector2i, b: Vector2i) -> float:
	return absf(a.x - b.x) + absf(a.y - b.y)
```

```gdscript
var c := Pathing.cost(from, to)     # no autoload needed
```

**Your own projects' restraint is the data point.** 672 script files, and **two** autoloads — both in `shepherds-we-shall-be`, and `the-lost-sheep` has none at all. Both of the two pass the test:

| Autoload | Why it genuinely is global |
| --- | --- |
| **`ViewportSizer`** | must run **before any scene draws**, must survive every scene change, and has no position. A scene cannot size the window it is drawn into. |
| **`HitStopController`** | affects presentation **across every actor at once**; there must be exactly one; and it has no place in the world. |

**And `ViewportSizer` shows the discipline that makes an autoload acceptable**: its real logic is `static` and pure.

```gdscript
static func viewport_for(window_size: Vector2i) -> Vector2i:
static func scale_for_screen(screen_height: int) -> int:
static func letterbox_for(window_size: Vector2i) -> Vector2i:
```

with the comment saying why:

> *Pure, so it can be tested without a window.*

**The singleton holds no logic worth testing.** The rules are static functions anyone can call, and the autoload exists only to own the one instance that connects them to a real window. **That is the pattern to copy**: an autoload as a thin shell over testable functions, rather than a bag of state and behaviour.

**It also carries test seams**, deliberately:

```gdscript
static var screen_height_override: int = 0
static var window_size_override: Vector2i = Vector2i.ZERO
```

> *Stands in for the monitor's height, so a render or a test can see what a display it is not running on would get … Zero asks the monitor, which is all the game itself ever does.*

**A global that cannot be substituted is untestable; one with an override is not.** For a headless test suite that pins every window to 64×64, that is the difference between a tested rule and an untested one.

**The rule of thumb to leave with:** **if you are about to add a fourth autoload, you are probably solving a structure problem with a global.** Three is a lot. Two, each with a reason you can state in a sentence, is healthy.

**Practice.** List every global-feeling thing your `godot-practice` project might want. For each, decide which of the five alternatives fits, and only then whether it is an autoload. Then convert the `GameState` autoload from the last lesson into a `class_name` with `static` members and see which of its uses still work — that tells you whether it needed an instance at all.
Groups: finding nodes without paths:
The last of the four ways to find a node, and the right one when there are many of a thing or you do not know where it is.

**The mechanism**, from stage 1's Node dock lesson: a group is a name a node claims. Any node, any number of groups, no hierarchy.

**Joining and leaving:**

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	add_to_group("enemies")

func die() -> void:
	remove_from_group("enemies")
	queue_free()                 # freeing removes it from groups anyway
```

**Or in the editor** — the Node dock's **Groups** tab, which records it in the `.tscn`:

```
[node name="Wolf" type="CharacterBody2D" parent="."]
groups = ["enemies"]
```

**Prefer the editor form for a scene that is always in the group**, and the code form when membership is conditional.

**Asking the tree:**

| Call | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `get_tree().get_nodes_in_group("enemies")` | an `Array[Node]` of all of them |
| `get_tree().get_first_node_in_group("enemies")` | one, or `null` |
| `get_tree().get_node_count_in_group("enemies")` | how many |
| `is_in_group("enemies")` | whether **this** node is |
| `get_tree().call_group("enemies", "take_damage", 10)` | call a method on every one |
| `get_tree().notify_group("enemies", what)` | send a notification to every one |

**`get_first_node_in_group` for a singleton-ish thing** is the pattern that replaces an autoload most often:

```gdscript
var hud := get_tree().get_first_node_in_group("hud")
if hud != null:
	hud.show_message("…")
```

**One node, found by kind, with no path and no global.** The HUD can live anywhere, be absent in a test, and the caller neither knows nor cares.

**That is exactly what your own code does**, and it is worth reading as the canonical example. `pixel_perfect_viewport.gd`:

```gdscript
## A `PresentationShell` claims this group when one is running.
const SHELL_GROUP: StringName = &"presentation_shell"
```

and then:

```gdscript
if get_tree() != null and get_tree().get_first_node_in_group(SHELL_GROUP) != null:
	window.content_scale_size = window.size
	_applied_for = window.size
	return
```

**The autoload asks whether a shell exists at all, and behaves completely differently depending on the answer.** It holds no reference, knows no path, and works identically whether the shell is three levels deep or absent — which is what makes the same code serve the real game, the Foundation Lab and the headless test suite. The comment says so:

> *Without one, nothing changes: the Foundation Lab and every direct-instantiated scene keep the behaviour this class has always had.*

**Note `&"presentation_shell"` and the `const`.** Two things worth copying:

- **`&"..."` makes a `StringName`** — interned, compared by pointer. Group names, signal names and node paths are all `StringName` internally, so writing them that way avoids a conversion on every call.
- **Putting it in a `const`** means the name exists once. A group referred to by a bare string in six files is six chances to typo it, with no error when you do — **a misspelled group name silently matches nothing.** That is the one real hazard of groups and a `const` is the whole fix.

**What groups are good and bad at:**

| Good at | Bad at |
| --- | --- |
| *all of the X* — every enemy, every save point | asking *which* one, in order |
| *is there an X at all?* | a stable reference you hold for a long time |
| broadcasting — `call_group` | anything performance-critical per frame |
| decoupling across scene boundaries | expressing a relationship that matters |

**The performance note, honestly.** `get_nodes_in_group` walks and allocates an array. Calling it once in `_ready` is free; calling it every frame in `_process` for a hundred nodes is not. **Cache it, or hold the reference.**

**So the complete ranking**, now that all four exist:

1. **`$Child`** — a direct child.
2. **`%Unique`** — deeper in your own scene.
3. **`@export var thing: Type`** — across a scene boundary, declared.
4. **A group** — many of a thing, or *is there one?*
5. **An autoload** — genuinely global, and you have fewer than four.
6. **`$"../../.."`** — never.

**Practice.** Give your sheep scene `add_to_group("sheep")` in `_ready`. Spawn ten, then use `call_group` to make them all print their position. Then add one `Label` to a `"hud"` group and find it with `get_first_node_in_group` from a script that has no idea where it is. Then put both group names in `const` `StringName`s and use those instead of the literals.
Reading a real scene: main.tscn:
The last lesson of the stage, and the first real test of it: open a 104-line scene file from your own game and account for every part of it.

**Open `the-lost-sheep/game/scenes/main.tscn`** in a text editor, and open the same scene in Godot beside it. Everything in this stage is in that file.

**The header:**

```
[gd_scene load_steps=13 format=3]
```

Thirteen resources to load, Godot 4 format.

**The external resources — thirteen of them, in three kinds:**

| Kind | Example | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `type="Script"` | `main.gd`, `island_view.gd`, `build_bar.gd` | a script assigned to a node's `script` property |
| `type="Resource"` | `island.tres`, `wild.tres` | **data** — stage 7's whole subject |
| `type="PackedScene"` | `ground.tscn` | **another scene**, to be instanced |

**Eleven scripts, two data files, one scene.** That ratio tells you how the game is built: almost everything is script and data, with exactly one reusable sub-scene.

**The root:**

```
[node name="Main" type="Node2D"]
script = ExtResource("1_main")
```

A `Node2D`, because the island is drawn in world space — the root-choice lesson. `script =` is a property, because a script **is** a resource assigned to a property.

**The instanced scene:**

```
[node name="Ground" parent="." instance=ExtResource("11_ground")]
```

**No `type=`**, because the type comes from the file. No children listed, because `ground.tscn` describes its own insides — the `owner` lesson, from the other end. **No override lines**, so this instance is exactly what the file says.

**The nodes with data wired in:**

```
[node name="WildView" type="Node2D" parent="."]
script = ExtResource("12_wild")
wild = ExtResource("13_wild")

[node name="IslandView" type="Node2D" parent="."]
script = ExtResource("2_view")
island = ExtResource("4_island")
label_parcels = false
```

**`wild`, `island` and `label_parcels` are not Godot properties.** They are `@export` declarations in `wild_view.gd` and `island_view.gd`. Someone wrote a variable, it appeared in the Inspector, a `.tres` was dragged onto it, and **the scene recorded the wiring**. That is composition over inheritance, data over hardcoding, and the override list — all in four lines.

**And `label_parcels = false` is a default being overridden**, which is why it is in the file at all. Everything left at its default is absent.

**Now do the same in the editor.** Open the scene in Godot and check each of these against the file:

| In the editor | In the file |
| --- | --- |
| `Ground` has a chain-link icon | `instance=` |
| `Ground`'s children are greyed out | they belong to `ground.tscn` |
| `IslandView` shows `island` and `label_parcels` in the Inspector | the two property lines |
| `label_parcels` has a **revert arrow** | it differs from the default |
| `island` has one too | it differs from `null` |
| The UI nodes are `Control`s, not `Node2D`s | the two branches, kept apart |

**The questions to be able to answer by the end.** Work through them before moving on — this is the stage's real exercise:

1. **How many scenes does this game have?** Three. Why so few?
2. **What is instanced, and why is the ground the only one?**
3. **Where do the island's numbers live?** Not in the script.
4. **Which nodes have scripts, and which are plain?**
5. **Why is the root a `Node2D` and not a `Node`?**
6. **If you renamed `IslandView`, what would break?**
7. **Why is there no `[autoload]` in this project at all?**

**Then do it to the big one.** `shepherds-we-shall-be/game/scenes/app/game.tscn` is the root of an 82-scene project. You will not account for every line, and that is the point — **use the editor and the Remote tree instead**, as stage 1's lesson said: press F5, switch the Scene dock to **Remote**, and read the tree that actually exists.

**What you can now do that you could not at the start of this stage.** Open any `.tscn` in any of your three projects and say what it is made of, what it reuses, what it overrides, and where its numbers come from. **That is a real part of reading the codebase**, and it is two stages in.

**Practice.** Answer all seven questions above in writing. Then open `the-lost-sheep/game/scenes/ground.tscn` and do the same exercise on it unaided. Then open `game.tscn` in `shepherds-we-shall-be`, press **F5**, and spend fifteen minutes in the **Remote** tree seeing how much of its structure you can now name.
Attach a script: extends, class_name, an:
The first three lines of every GDScript file, and what each one decides.

**Attaching a script.** Select a node, click the **script icon** at the top of the Scene dock (or right-click > **Attach Script**). The dialog asks for a path and a template; take **Node: Default** and save it in your scripts folder. Godot writes:

```gdscript
extends Node2D

func _ready() -> void:
	pass

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	pass
```

**And deletes nothing when you detach it** — the file stays on disk. Detaching only clears the node's `script` property.

**`extends` — which class this script is.**

```gdscript
extends Node2D
```

**The script becomes a subclass of `Node2D`.** It inherits every property, method and signal, so `position`, `modulate` and `queue_free()` are all available unqualified. **It must match the node you attach it to** — or rather, the node must be of that class or a subclass. Attach an `extends Sprite2D` script to a `Node2D` and Godot refuses.

**`extends` can also name a file or another class:**

```gdscript
extends Node2D                               # a built-in class
extends "res://game/scripts/actor.gd"        # a file
extends Actor                                # a class_name — the best form
```

**`class_name` — registering the script engine-wide.**

```gdscript
class_name IslandView
extends Node2D
```

**What it buys you**, and it is a lot for one line:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A global type name** | `var v: IslandView` works in any script |
| **A node type** | `IslandView` appears in the **Create New Node** dialog |
| **Static access** | `IslandView.CELL`, `IslandView.some_static()` without an instance |
| **An F1 page** | built from the `##` comments, as stage 1's docs lesson showed |
| **`is` checks** | `if node is IslandView:` |

**The order is fixed: `class_name` before `extends`.** The other way round is a parse error.

**And it must be globally unique** — including against autoload names, which stage 2's autoload lesson showed `pixel_perfect_viewport.gd` working around deliberately.

**The file header, which is where your own code sets a standard worth copying.** `the-lost-sheep/game/scripts/island/island_view.gd` opens:

```gdscript
@tool
## Draws the island. Placeholder rectangles, and deliberately so.
##
## BRIEF.md: "Placeholders first, art later." …
##
## @tool, because Godot's place in this project is CONDITIONAL on the map being
## editable in the editor rather than in code. …
##
## IT IS A VIEW, and it is handed plain dictionaries rather than the settlement. …
class_name IslandView
extends Node2D
```

**Four things to notice.**

**1. `@tool` comes before everything**, including the doc comment. Annotations that apply to the whole script go at the very top. Stage 7 teaches what `@tool` does.

**2. `##` is a documentation comment**, not an ordinary one. `#` is a comment; `##` becomes the class description in the editor's F1 help. Lesson 28 covers it, and the point here is that **this file's explanation is in the engine's own documentation system**, not just in the source.

**3. The header says *why*, not *what*.** "Draws the island" is one line; the remaining forty explain the decision, who made it, when, and what it overruled. That is the convention across all 672 of your script files and it is the reason the codebase is readable at all.

**4. `class_name` and `extends` come last**, after the header. That reads oddly at first and is correct: the prose introduces the file, then the declaration states what it is.

**The order of a GDScript file**, which the official style guide sets and your projects follow:

| Order | What |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | `@tool`, `@icon`, `@static_unload` — script-wide annotations |
| 2 | `##` class documentation |
| 3 | `class_name` |
| 4 | `extends` |
| 5 | `signal` declarations |
| 6 | `enum` declarations |
| 7 | `const` declarations |
| 8 | `@export` variables |
| 9 | ordinary variables, then `@onready` variables |
| 10 | `_init`, `_enter_tree`, `_ready`, `_process`, then the rest |
| 11 | public methods |
| 12 | private methods (`_name`) |

**Following it is worth the small effort**, because every GDScript file you read — in the docs, in your projects, in anyone's example — is in that order, and a file that is not takes longer to read.

**Practice.** Attach a script to your sheep's root. Give it a `class_name Sheep` and confirm it appears in the Create New Node dialog and in F1. Then write a four-line `##` header saying what the scene is **for**, not what it contains. Then open `island_view.gd` and read its whole header — all forty lines — and note how much of it is reasoning.
Variables, static typing, and why you al:
The standing decision of this curriculum, stated with its reasons: **every variable is typed, without exception.**

**The three ways to declare one:**

```gdscript
var speed := 220.0            # inferred — the type comes from the value
var name: String = "Greg"     # explicit
var target: Node2D            # typed, no value — starts as null
var loose = 5                 # UNTYPED. Should feel wrong.
```

**`:=` infers; `: Type` states.** Both give you **static typing**. A bare `=` with no annotation does not.

**Why it matters, four reasons in order of how much they will affect you:**

**1. Autocomplete only works on typed variables.** This is the big one day to day.

```gdscript
var a := $Sprite2D            # inferred as Node2D — no Sprite2D completions
var b: Sprite2D = $Sprite2D   # typed — b.flip_h offered, and checked
```

**With an untyped variable the editor cannot know what you have**, so it offers nothing and checks nothing. Half the value of the editor evaporates.

**2. Typos become parse-time errors instead of 2 a.m. nulls.**

```gdscript
var hp: int = 100
hp = "full"       # ERROR at parse time
```

Untyped, that assignment is legal and the failure happens later, somewhere else, as a type confusion you have to trace back.

**3. Typed GDScript is measurably faster.** The compiler can skip variant dispatch and use direct instructions. Not a reason on its own, and a free bonus.

**4. The type is documentation that cannot drift.** `var target: Node2D` tells the next reader what it holds. A comment saying the same thing can be wrong.

**So: `var x = 5` with a bare `=` and no annotation should feel wrong to write.** That is the standing decision, and it holds for all 672 of your script files.

**When to prefer `:=` and when to prefer `: Type`:**

| Use `:=` | Use `: Type` |
| --- | --- |
| the value makes the type obvious — `var i := 0` | the value is `null` or ambiguous |
| a literal — `var s := "hi"`, `var v := Vector2.ZERO` | a node — `var s: Sprite2D = $Sprite2D` |
| a constructor — `var t := Timer.new()` | a declaration with no value — `var target: Node2D` |
| | an `@export`, always — the Inspector needs the type |

**The node case is the one to watch.** `$Sprite2D` is statically `Node`, so `var s := $Sprite2D` infers `Node` and you lose the sprite's API. **Annotate nodes explicitly**, or cast:

```gdscript
@onready var sprite: Sprite2D = $Sprite2D      # best
var sprite := $Sprite2D as Sprite2D            # equivalent
```

**`@onready`, from stage 2's lifecycle lesson**, because it is a variable rule as much as a lifecycle one:

```gdscript
@onready var sprite: Sprite2D = $Sprite2D
```

**`@onready` defers the assignment until just before `_ready()`.** Without it, `$Sprite2D` runs at `_init` when there is no tree, and you get `null` — silently, until you use it.

**Inference and `null`.** You cannot infer from nothing:

```gdscript
var target := null        # inferred as Variant. Useless.
var target: Node2D        # typed, starts null. Correct.
```

**Typed variables start at a sensible zero**, which is worth knowing:

| Type | Starts as |
| --- | --- |
| `int` | `0` |
| `float` | `0.0` |
| `bool` | `false` |
| `String` | `""` |
| `Array` | `[]` |
| `Dictionary` | `{}` |
| `Vector2` | `(0, 0)` |
| any class | `null` |

**`Variant`, the escape hatch.** An untyped variable is a `Variant` — it can hold anything. It exists, it is occasionally necessary (a dictionary's values, a signal's payload), and reaching for it should be a decision rather than a default.

**A real header from your own code**, showing the convention in place:

```gdscript
const CELL := IslandData.CELL
const PITCH := IslandData.PITCH
const GAP := 12.0
const LABEL := 56
const SMALL := 44
```

**Every one inferred with `:=`**, because every value makes its type obvious. And the comment above them explains the constraint they encode:

> *Everything drawn in world units has to grow with CELL or it vanishes when the camera pulls back.*

**Practice.** Open any script and add types to every variable in it. Then deliberately write `var sprite := $Sprite2D` and try to type `sprite.flip_h` — note the lack of completion. Fix it with an annotation and watch completion appear. Then write `var hp: int = 100` and try to assign a string to it, and read the parse error.
The built-in types, and which to reach f:
GDScript's value types, in one place — because choosing the right one is most of writing idiomatic Godot code, and the list is short enough to know.

**The scalars:**

| Type | What it is | Literal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bool` | true or false | `true`, `false` |
| `int` | 64-bit signed integer | `5`, `-3`, `0xFF`, `0b1010`, `1_000_000` |
| `float` | 64-bit double | `5.0`, `1e-3`, `.5` |
| `String` | a mutable text string | `"hello"`, `'hello'` |
| `StringName` | an interned, pointer-compared string | `&"hello"` |
| `NodePath` | a path to a node | `^"Sprite2D"` |

**The maths types** — and these are the ones that make Godot code read well:

| Type | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Vector2` / `Vector2i` | 2D float / integer vector |
| `Vector3` / `Vector3i` | 3D. Stage 11. |
| `Vector4` / `Vector4i` | rarely, in shaders |
| `Rect2` / `Rect2i` | position plus size |
| `Transform2D` | position, rotation and scale as one matrix |
| `Color` | r, g, b, a as floats 0–1 |
| `Basis`, `Quaternion`, `Transform3D`, `Plane`, `AABB` | 3D. Stage 11. |

**The containers:**

| Type | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Array` | an ordered list, any types — `[1, "two", 3.0]` |
| `Array[int]` | a **typed** array. Prefer it. |
| `Dictionary` | key → value — `{"hp": 100}` |
| `PackedInt32Array`, `PackedFloat32Array`, `PackedVector2Array`, `PackedByteArray`, `PackedStringArray`, `PackedColorArray` | compact, single-type arrays. Lesson 15. |

**The callable and signal types:**

| Type | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `Callable` | a reference to a function. Lesson 25. |
| `Signal` | a reference to a signal. Lesson 23. |
| `RID` | a low-level server handle. You will rarely touch one. |

**And the object types**, which behave differently from everything above:

| Type | Memory |
| --- | --- |
| `Object` | **you free it** |
| `Node` | you free it — `queue_free()` |
| `RefCounted` | **automatic** |
| `Resource` (a `RefCounted`) | automatic |

**The one distinction that matters more than any other: value types are copied, object types are shared.**

```gdscript
var a := Vector2(1, 2)
var b := a
b.x = 99
print(a.x)        # 1 — a was copied

var c := Node2D.new()
var e := c
e.name = "changed"
print(c.name)     # "changed" — same object
```

**Everything in the first three tables is a value.** Assigning copies it. `Vector2`, `Color`, `Rect2`, `Transform2D` — all copied.

**And the two exceptions that catch everyone: `Array` and `Dictionary` are passed by reference.**

```gdscript
var a := [1, 2, 3]
var b := a
b.append(4)
print(a)          # [1, 2, 3, 4] — SHARED
```

**They are value types that behave like references**, which is inconsistent and is simply how it is. To copy one:

```gdscript
var b := a.duplicate()        # shallow — nested arrays still shared
var b := a.duplicate(true)    # deep
```

**That is the single most common source of "why did my other array change".** A `Dictionary` handed to two systems is one dictionary.

**Which to reach for, for the cases that come up constantly:**

| You want | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A position, a size, a direction, a velocity | **`Vector2`** — not two floats |
| A tile or grid coordinate | **`Vector2i`** — integers, so no drift |
| A name used as a key or a group | **`StringName`** — `&"enemies"` |
| Text shown to a person | **`String`** |
| A fixed set of options | **`enum`** — lesson 7 |
| A list of one type | **`Array[Type]`** |
| Lots of numbers, every frame | a **`Packed…Array`** |
| Structured data with behaviour | a **`class_name` with `Resource`** — stage 7 |
| Structured data, quick and loose | a `Dictionary` — and regret it later |

**`Vector2` rather than two floats is the one to internalise.** `position`, `velocity`, `size` and `direction` are all vectors, and the engine's whole API expects them. Keeping `x` and `y` separate means converting at every call.
