**Practice.** Author `idle` (looping) and `attack` (not looping) on an actor. Confirm `animation_finished` fires for the attack and never for the idle. Then set the attack to loop and watch a state machine waiting on `animation_finished` hang. Then create a `RESET` animation with a key per animated property, scrub `attack` to the middle, save the scene, and confirm the `.tscn` holds the neutral values.
AnimatedSprite2D and SpriteFrames:
The dedicated sprite-animation node — simpler than an `AnimationPlayer` and limited to exactly one thing, which is often all you need.

**What it is.** A node that holds a **`SpriteFrames`** resource: a set of named animations, each a list of textures, each with an fps and a loop flag.

```
Actor (CharacterBody2D)
├── AnimatedSprite2D        ← holds a SpriteFrames
└── CollisionShape2D
```

**Building the `SpriteFrames`.** Select the node and the **SpriteFrames** panel opens at the bottom:

| Control | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Animations list** | add, remove, rename. `default` exists to start. |
| **Add frames from a sprite sheet** | the grid dialog — rows, columns, selection |
| **Add frames from files** | individual images |
| **Speed (FPS)** | per animation |
| **Loop** | per animation |
| **Frame duration** | per frame, as a multiplier — for holds |

**The per-frame duration multiplier is worth knowing.** A twelve-frame cycle where one frame holds twice as long is one number, rather than a duplicated frame.

**The API:**

```gdscript
@onready var spr: AnimatedSprite2D = $AnimatedSprite2D

spr.play(&"walk")
spr.play(&"walk", 1.5)              # custom speed scale
spr.play_backwards(&"walk")
spr.pause()
spr.stop()
spr.animation = &"walk"              # set without playing
spr.frame = 3
spr.frame_progress = 0.5
spr.speed_scale = 2.0
spr.flip_h = true
spr.sprite_frames.get_animation_names()
```

**The signals:**

```gdscript
spr.animation_finished.connect(_on_finished)
spr.animation_looped.connect(_on_looped)
spr.frame_changed.connect(_on_frame_changed)
```

**`frame_changed` is the one with a non-obvious use**: a footstep sound on frames 2 and 7 without an `AnimationPlayer` audio track:

```gdscript
func _on_frame_changed() -> void:
	if spr.animation == &"walk" and spr.frame in [2, 7]:
		footstep.play()
```

**And the same `play()`-every-frame trap** as `AnimationPlayer`, with the same fix:

```gdscript
if spr.animation != &"walk":
	spr.play(&"walk")
```

**`AnimatedSprite2D` against `AnimationPlayer`** — the decision:

| | `AnimatedSprite2D` | `AnimationPlayer` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Animates** | **frames only** | any property of any node |
| **Setup** | a panel, a sheet, done | tracks and keyframes |
| **Per-animation fps** | **yes, built in** | via animation length |
| **Several nodes at once** | no | **yes** |
| **Method calls, audio** | no | **yes** |
| **Shareable** | the `SpriteFrames` resource | an `AnimationLibrary` |
| **`AnimationTree`** | **cannot drive it directly** | yes |

**Row seven decides it for a complex character.** `AnimationTree` blends `AnimationPlayer` animations; it cannot blend `AnimatedSprite2D` frames. **So a character that will eventually need an `AnimationTree` should be on an `AnimationPlayer` from the start.**

**And row one decides it for everything else.** A coin spinning, a torch flickering, an explosion — nothing but frames, so `AnimatedSprite2D` and three clicks.

**The hybrid that is common and sensible:** an `AnimatedSprite2D` for the frames, **and** an `AnimationPlayer` whose tracks drive the `AnimatedSprite2D:animation` property plus everything else:

```
Actor
├── AnimatedSprite2D        ← the frames
├── AnimationPlayer         ← drives `AnimatedSprite2D:animation`, hitboxes, audio, offsets
└── CollisionShape2D
```

**That gets per-animation fps from `SpriteFrames` and method calls and audio from the player.** It is a legitimate arrangement and worth knowing exists.

**Sharing a `SpriteFrames`** — it is a `Resource`, so the sharing rules from stage 5 apply. **Two `AnimatedSprite2D`s assigned the same `SpriteFrames` share it**, which is what you want for ten identical coins and not what you want if one needs a different fps. **Make Unique, as always.**

**The `offset` and `centered` properties** are the same as `Sprite2D`'s, and the same trap from stage 2 applies: **`centered` on an odd-height sprite puts the origin on a half pixel.** For a character, origin at the feet.

**Practice.** Build a coin: an `AnimatedSprite2D` with a six-frame spin from a sheet, 12 fps, looping, autoplayed. Then build a character with `walk` and `attack`, and drive them from a state machine with the idempotent setter. Use `animation_finished` to leave the attack. Then add a footstep on `frame_changed`. Then assign the same `SpriteFrames` to a second coin and change one's fps to see the sharing.
Sprite sheets, hframes and the frame pro:
The three ways to get a sprite sheet into Godot, and the import settings that decide whether pixel art looks right.

**The three ways:**

| Method | Node | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`hframes`/`vframes`/`frame`** | `Sprite2D` | **a simple grid**, animated by an `AnimationPlayer` |
| **`region_enabled`/`region_rect`** | `Sprite2D` | an irregular atlas, or one frame of a packed sheet |
| **`SpriteFrames`** | `AnimatedSprite2D` | **a proper animation set** |

**The `hframes` approach**, from stage 2's first-scene lesson:

```gdscript
sprite.hframes = 8          # the sheet is 8 columns
sprite.vframes = 4          # and 4 rows
sprite.frame = 9            # frames count left-to-right, top-to-bottom
sprite.frame_coords = Vector2i(1, 1)       # the same frame, as a grid position
```

**`frame_coords` is the readable form** for a sheet where rows mean something — eight directions down the rows, frames across the columns:

```gdscript
sprite.frame_coords = Vector2i(frame_index, direction_index)
```

**That one line is an eight-direction animation system**, and it is why a sheet laid out as *directions × frames* is worth asking an artist for.

**Animating it with an `AnimationPlayer`:** a `Sprite2D:frame` track, set to **Discrete** — which Godot does automatically for an integer property, from the keyframes lesson.

**The import settings that matter for pixel art.** Select a `.png` in the FileSystem dock and the **Import** dock appears:

| Setting | For pixel art |
| --- | --- |
| **Filter** | **off** — nearest-neighbour. On, and the art is blurred. |
| **Mipmaps** | **off** |
| **Fix Alpha Border** | on — prevents dark edges from premultiplied alpha |
| **Compress > Mode** | **Lossless** |
| **Repeat** | off, unless tiling |

**Filter off is the important one**, and it is per-texture rather than project-wide — which is why `godot.md`'s original claim about a project-wide nearest-neighbour setting was wrong, as the plan's correction notes.

**Setting it for every future import.** Click **Preset > Set as Default for 'Texture'** in the Import dock, and new textures arrive with filtering off. **Do that once per project**, early, and you never think about it again.

**And the project-wide alternative:** Project Settings > Rendering > Textures > **Canvas Textures > Default Texture Filter** → **Nearest**. **That changes the default for everything**, which is simpler and is what many pixel-art projects do.

**Your own projects do neither**, because they do not need to: at a 960×540 viewport scaled by an integer factor, **every texel already lands on a whole screen pixel**, so the filter has nothing to interpolate. From `godot.md`'s corrected standing decisions — the viewport approach makes the filter question moot, and stage 9 explains it fully.

**The atlas question.** Two ways to store many sprites in one file:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A uniform grid** | `hframes`/`vframes` works; simple; wastes space on irregular art |
| **A packed atlas** | an `AtlasTexture` per sprite, or `region_rect`; tight; needs tooling |

**`AtlasTexture` is a `Resource`** pointing at a region of a bigger texture, and it can be used anywhere a texture can:

```gdscript
var a := AtlasTexture.new()
a.atlas = load("res://art/sheet.png")
a.region = Rect2(0, 0, 16, 16)
sprite.texture = a
```

**For hand-authored pixel art, a uniform grid is almost always the right answer** — it is simpler, it is readable, and the wasted space is irrelevant at these sizes.

**The common sheet layouts, and which to ask for:**

| Layout | Good for |
| --- | --- |
| **One row per animation, frames across** | simple characters |
| **One row per direction, frames across** | **eight-direction characters** — `frame_coords` |
| **One sheet per animation** | large frames, or many directions |
| **A packed atlas** | mixed-size props and UI |

**And the one practical request to make of an artist:** **consistent frame size, consistent origin.** A sheet where the character sits at a different height in each frame produces animation that bobs for no reason, and fixing it is per-frame offset work. **A fixed canvas with the feet on a marked line solves it at source** — which is exactly what your project's approved body-base references do.

**Reading the import of an `.aseprite` file** is the next lesson, and it bypasses most of this: the Aseprite Wizard addon reads layers and tags directly and builds the `SpriteFrames` or the animations for you.

**Practice.** Take an eight-column, four-row sheet and set `hframes`/`vframes` on a `Sprite2D`. Animate `frame` with an `AnimationPlayer` and confirm the track is Discrete. Then drive `frame_coords` from code with a direction index and a frame index. Then set the texture's Filter off and compare it at 4× zoom with Filter on. Then set the project-wide default texture filter to Nearest.
The Aseprite pipeline: Aseprite Wizard:
The addon that removes the export step between drawing and the game — which matters because you own Aseprite and because the Aseprite curriculum is next door.

**What it is.** **Aseprite Wizard**, by Vinicius Gerevini, version 9.8.0 — the one addon in `shepherds-we-shall-be/addons/`. Its description: *"Import Aseprite files to Godot in many different ways."*

**The problem it solves.** Without it, the loop is: draw in Aseprite → export a sheet → export a JSON of the frame data → import into Godot → build a `SpriteFrames` → repeat on every change. **Five steps, and three of them are clerical.**

**With it, the `.aseprite` file is the asset.** Godot reads it, reads its **layers** and its **tags**, and produces either a `SpriteFrames` or `AnimationPlayer` animations — and re-imports when the file changes.

**The three ways it can import**, which is what the description means:

| Mode | Produces |
| --- | --- |
| **As a `SpriteFrames`** | one resource, animations named from Aseprite **tags** — for `AnimatedSprite2D` |
| **Into an `AnimationPlayer`** | animations with frame tracks, named from tags |
| **As a static texture** | one layer, one frame — for props and tiles |

**The mechanism is Aseprite's own metadata:**

| In Aseprite | Becomes in Godot |
| --- | --- |
| A **tag** on a frame range | **an animation**, named after the tag |
| A tag's direction (forward/reverse/ping-pong) | the loop mode |
| **Layers** | separately importable — so a body and a cloak can be separate sprites |
| Layer visibility | respected, or overridable |
| Frame durations | per-frame timing |
| **Slices** | regions, for atlases |

**So the workflow becomes:** name your animations as **tags** in Aseprite, save, and Godot has them. **The naming convention in Aseprite is the naming convention in code**, which is the real win — one place to decide what an animation is called.

**Setting it up:**

1. The addon in `addons/AsepriteWizard/`, enabled in **Project Settings > Plugins**.
2. **Aseprite's own command-line tool must be on `PATH`**, or its path set in the addon's settings — the addon drives Aseprite itself to do the export.
3. Then either the **Import dock** on an `.aseprite` file, or the addon's **Wizard** dock for one-off imports.

**Point 2 is the one that catches people.** The addon is not a file-format reader — it shells out to Aseprite. **No Aseprite on the machine, no import**, which also means a build machine needs it.

**The practical conventions worth adopting:**

| Convention | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Tag names are animation names** | `idle`, `walk`, `attack` — `snake_case`, matching your state names |
| **One `.aseprite` per character** | tags inside it, rather than a file per animation |
| **Layers for separable parts** | body, cloak, weapon — importable separately |
| **A fixed canvas, feet on a guide** | so frames do not bob, from the last lesson |
| **Keep the `.aseprite` masters in the repo** | they are the source; the sheet is derived |

**That last one is what your project does.** `media/sprites/` holds *".aseprite masters by category"*, and `REPOSITORY_STRUCTURE.md` keeps them apart from everything derived. **The master is the truth; the imported resource is a build artefact.**

**And the honest state of the pipeline in your project**, which is worth knowing because it is mid-transition. From `body_base_run.gd`:

> *NOT THE SPRITE ROUTE. The frames are sprite-acus's output, read from disk out of a `.gdignore`d folder, as the idle preview reads its frames. Nothing is imported, so an exported build carries no frames and Eli stays grey there (`attach` gives nothing). His real run is `.aseprite` masters imported by Aseprite Wizard.*

**Three facts in that comment.**

**1. The current run animation is a placeholder** read from loose files, not imported.

**2. `.gdignore`** — a file in a folder tells Godot to ignore it entirely, so those frames are not imported, not in the `.godot` cache, and **not in an exported build**. That is a deliberate choice for placeholder art, and `.gdignore` is a genuinely useful thing to know about.

**3. The intended pipeline is `.aseprite` masters through Aseprite Wizard.** So the addon is the destination, and the loose-file reader is scaffolding.

**Which connects to the art decisions you have already made**: all art hand-drawn, Timon's approved eight-direction references, and 24-frame idle and 12-frame run cycles. **Those cycle lengths are tag ranges in an `.aseprite` file**, and the next lesson covers the eight-direction naming that makes them addressable.

**The alternative, if the addon is not wanted.** Aseprite can export a sheet plus a JSON, and Godot can read the JSON with `JSON.parse_string` and build a `SpriteFrames` in a `@tool` script. **That is a half-day of work to replace a free addon**, and it is worth knowing it is possible for a pipeline you need to control exactly.

**Practice.** If you have Aseprite: make a four-frame bounce, tag it `bounce`, save as `.aseprite` in the project, and import it as a `SpriteFrames`. Confirm the animation is named after the tag. Then add a second tag and re-import. Then put a `.gdignore` in a folder of loose frames and confirm Godot stops importing them. Then look at `shepherds-we-shall-be/media/sprites/` and `addons/AsepriteWizard/plugin.cfg`.
Eight directions, and the naming convent:
The convention your project's whole animation system rests on — eight authored directions, and the code that addresses them.

**Why eight.** A top-down character must face where it is going. Four directions reads as stiff; sixteen is twice the art for a difference nobody sees. **Eight — the cardinals plus the diagonals, 45° apart — is the standard, and it is what your approved body-base references use.**

**The ring, and the order matters:**

| Index | Direction | Angle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | `right` | 0° |
| 1 | `down_right` | 45° |
| 2 | `down` | 90° |
| 3 | `down_left` | 135° |
| 4 | `left` | 180° |
| 5 | `up_left` | 225° |
| 6 | `up` | 270° |
| 7 | `up_right` | 315° |

**Clockwise from right**, because `Vector2.angle()` returns 0 for right and increases clockwise in screen space — Y being down, from stage 4's coordinate lesson.

**Direction to index, which is the whole bridge:**

```gdscript
const DIRS: Array[StringName] = [
	&"right", &"down_right", &"down", &"down_left",
	&"left", &"up_left", &"up", &"up_right",
]

static func index_of(dir: Vector2) -> int:
	return posmod(roundi(dir.angle() / (TAU / 8.0)), 8)

static func name_of(dir: Vector2) -> StringName:
	return DIRS[index_of(dir)]
```

**Note `posmod`, not `%`** — from stage 3's numbers lesson. `roundi` on an angle near 180° can produce −4, and `-4 % 8` is `-4`, which indexes from the end of the array and gives you the wrong direction. **`posmod(-4, 8)` is 4.** That is a real bug and `posmod` is the whole fix.

**Using it:**

```gdscript
func _physics_process(_delta: float) -> void:
	if move_intent != Vector2.ZERO:
		facing = move_intent
	_set_animation(&"run_" + name_of(facing))
```

**The naming convention that makes it work: `action_direction`.**

```
idle_right      run_right
idle_down_right run_down_right
idle_down       run_down
…               …
```

**Sixteen animation names for two actions**, generated from two strings. **In Aseprite those are sixteen tags**, which the Wizard imports as sixteen animations — so the tag naming in the art file and the string concatenation in the code are the same convention.

**The alternative layout: one sheet per direction, `frame_coords`.** From the sprite-sheet lesson:

```gdscript
sprite.frame_coords = Vector2i(frame, index_of(facing))
```

**A sheet of directions × frames, and no animation names at all** — the direction is a row index. **Cheaper to set up, and it gives up per-animation fps and `animation_finished`.**

**The mirroring question, and why your project says no.** The usual economy is to draw four directions and mirror for the other four — `flip_h` on `right` gives you `left`, halving the art.

**Your project does not, and the reason is specific.** From `body_base_run.gd`:

> *Eight authored directions, no mirroring: the limb colours are tied to a side.*

**A colour-coded body base distinguishes left from right limbs**, so mirroring would swap them. **That is a real constraint from the art's own construction**, and it is the kind of thing that decides a pipeline. **Mirroring is a legitimate economy when the character is symmetrical and a bug when it is not** — a character with a sword in one hand, a scar on one cheek, or colour-coded limbs cannot be mirrored.

**The split-body technique**, which is what your project actually does with these eight directions and is worth understanding because it is unusual and clever. From the same header, quoting the instruction that produced it:

> *Master Roachi, 2026-09-18: "divide the top half of the body from the legs, so that the legs turn toward the direction of movement, and top half of the body goes toward aim but with a restriction on turn, so for example turning the top half 180 degrees would be impossible, only like 100 degrees max".*

**And the implementation:**

| Half | Faces | Constraint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The legs** | the **movement** direction, all eight | none |
| **The upper half** | the **aim** direction, all eight | **at most `MAX_TWIST_STEPS` either side of the legs** |

> *two steps, 90 degrees, the nearest the eight directions allow to his "about 100". Aiming straight behind turns it as far as it goes and no further.*

**Two steps of 45° is 90°**, which is the closest the eight-direction ring can get to the requested hundred. **The constraint is expressed in ring steps rather than in degrees**, because the ring is the unit the art comes in.

**And the two halves are joined by measured anchors:**

> *The two meet at the waist: every frame's waist is measured in the conversion (`conversion/run/split_halves.py`, `anchors.json`), and the upper half is moved so its waist lands on the legs' own. With no twist that move is nothing, and the frame is exactly the combined one.*

**Per-frame waist positions, measured by a script, stored in JSON**, so the upper half can be offset to align. **And the important property: with no twist, the offset is zero and the result is byte-identical to the unsplit frame.** That is the test that the split is correct — it degrades to the original.

**What to take from it.** Not the technique, which is specific. **The principle: when art and code share a convention — eight directions, named consistently, with measured anchors — the code can do things the art alone could not**, and the convention is what makes it possible.

**Practice.** Write `index_of` and `name_of` and print the direction name as you move a character around; confirm all eight appear and that the 180° boundary does not glitch. Then remove `posmod` and use `%`, and find the bug. Then build a `SpriteFrames` with eight directions of a two-frame idle and drive it by name. Then read `body_base_run.gd`'s header in full.
AnimationTree: the three node types:
A graph that blends and switches `AnimationPlayer` animations — powerful, more ceremony than most 2D games need, and worth knowing when it earns its place.

**What it is.** An `AnimationTree` node, pointed at an `AnimationPlayer`, holding a **graph** of blend nodes. It takes over playback: you stop calling `player.play()` and start setting parameters on the tree.

**Setting it up:**

```
Actor
├── AnimationPlayer        ← holds the animations
├── AnimationTree          ← anim_player = AnimationPlayer, active = true
└── Sprite2D
```

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `anim_player` | the path to the `AnimationPlayer` |
| `tree_root` | the root blend node — set this to begin |
| `active` | **must be true**, and it is not by default |
| `advance_expression_base_node` | for expression-driven transitions |

**`active = false` is the first thing to check** when an `AnimationTree` does nothing.

**The three kinds of node in the graph:**

**1. Leaves — they play something.**

| Node | Plays |
| --- | --- |
| `AnimationNodeAnimation` | **one animation** from the player |
| `AnimationNodeTimeScale` | wraps a child, scaling its speed |
| `AnimationNodeTimeSeek` | wraps a child, seeking it |

**2. Blends — they mix two or more.**

| Node | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `AnimationNodeBlend2` | mixes **two** inputs by a 0–1 amount |
| `AnimationNodeBlend3` | three inputs, −1 to 1 |
| `AnimationNodeAdd2` / `Add3` | **adds** one on top of another, rather than mixing |
| `AnimationNodeBlendSpace1D` | positions several animations along a **line** |
| `AnimationNodeBlendSpace2D` | positions them on a **plane** — lesson 15 |
| `AnimationNodeOneShot` | fires a one-off over a base — **an attack over a walk** |
| `AnimationNodeTransition` | switches between inputs, with cross-fades |

**3. The state machine — `AnimationNodeStateMachine`**, which is lesson 14 and is what most people actually want.

**Which of these a 2D game uses, honestly:**

| Node | Used? |
| --- | --- |
| **`StateMachine`** | **yes — almost always the root** |
| `Animation` leaves | yes, as its states |
| `OneShot` | occasionally — an attack layered over movement |
| `BlendSpace2D` | for eight-direction blending, sometimes |
| `Blend2`, `Add2`, `Transition` | rarely in 2D; common in 3D |
| `TimeScale` | occasionally — speed tied to velocity |

**`Add2` deserves a note** because it is how 3D games layer a lean onto a run, and in 2D with discrete sprite frames **additive blending is meaningless** — you cannot add frame 3 to frame 7. **So most of the blending machinery is for skeletal animation**, and a sprite-based 2D game uses the state machine and little else.

**That is the honest summary of this lesson: for pixel-art 2D, `AnimationTree` is mostly a state machine with a nice editor.**

**When it earns its place over `player.play()` plus an enum:**

| Reason | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| **Transitions with conditions** authored visually, not in code | real |
| **Cross-fade times per transition pair** | real for skeletal, moot for frames |
| **A designer can edit the graph** without touching code | real |
| **Automatic advance** on animation end | convenient |
| **Blend spaces** for directional movement | real, if blending |
| It looks impressive | not a reason |

**And the costs:**

| Cost | |
| --- | --- |
| **The logic moves into a graph**, which is data | harder to grep, harder to test |
| **Two state machines** — yours and the tree's — that can disagree | the real risk |
| **Debugging is visual**, which means it is not in the stack trace | |

**That second cost is the one to take seriously.** A gameplay state machine (stage 4) deciding `ATTACK` and an animation state machine deciding its own transitions is two authorities. **The rule that keeps it straight is the one from the playing-animations lesson: the gameplay machine decides *what*, the animation decides *when*.** If the animation tree is also deciding what, you have two sources of truth.

**The recommendation this curriculum makes.** Start with an `AnimationPlayer` and the idempotent `_set_animation()` setter. **Move to `AnimationTree` when the transitions themselves become the complexity** — when you have a dozen states with specific cross-fades and conditions, and the code expressing that is worse than a graph would be.

**Neither of your games uses one**, which is consistent with both being sprite-based and with `body_base_run.gd` driving frames directly. **That is not an argument against it; it is evidence that a 2D game can get a long way without it.**

**Practice.** Add an `AnimationTree` to an actor with three animations, set `anim_player`, set `active = true`, and set the `tree_root` to a `StateMachine`. Confirm that `player.play()` no longer has any effect. Then add a `OneShot` node with a walk as its base and an attack as its shot, and fire it. Then write down which of the eleven node types you would plausibly use in your own game.
The state machine in AnimationTree:
The one part of `AnimationTree` a 2D game genuinely wants — a visual graph of animations with transitions, edited in the editor.

**Creating it.** Set the `AnimationTree`'s `tree_root` to a **new `AnimationNodeStateMachine`**. The graph editor opens in the bottom panel.

**Building the graph:**

| Action | How |
| --- | --- |
| **Add a state** | right-click the canvas > **Add Animation**, pick one |
| **Connect two** | the connect tool, then drag from one to the other |
| **Set the start state** | connect from the green **Start** node |
| **An end state** | connect to the red **End** node |
| **Edit a transition** | click the arrow; its properties appear in the Inspector |
| **Travel preview** | the play buttons, to watch it move |

**The transition properties, which are where the behaviour lives:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Switch Mode** | **Immediate**, **Sync**, or **At End** |
| **Advance Mode** | **Disabled**, **Enabled**, or **Auto** |
| **Advance Condition** | a parameter name that must be true |
| **Advance Expression** | an expression, evaluated against a base node |
| **Xfade Time** | the cross-fade duration |
| **Priority** | which transition wins when several could fire |
| **Reset** | restart the target animation from 0 |

**Switch Mode is the one to get right:**

| Mode | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| **Immediate** | switch now, from the target's start |
| **Sync** | switch now, **keeping the current playback position** |
| **At End** | wait for the current animation to finish |

**`At End` is what makes an attack work.** A transition from `attack` to `idle` set to At End means the attack plays out rather than being cut off. **No `animation_finished` handler, no `await` — the graph does it.**

**And `Sync` is for same-length cycles** — walk to run, where you want the legs to stay in phase. **For discrete sprite frames it rarely matters; for skeletal animation it is the difference between smooth and a jolt.**

**Advance Mode:**

| Mode | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Disabled** | only `travel()` can take this path |
| **Enabled** | `travel()` can, and conditions are checked |
| **Auto** | **fires automatically** when its condition is met |

**`Auto` plus a condition is the declarative form:**

```gdscript
# A bool parameter, set from code
tree.set(&"parameters/conditions/is_moving", velocity != Vector2.ZERO)
```

**With a transition from `idle` to `walk` on Auto with condition `is_moving`, and the reverse on `!is_moving`** — the graph handles the whole idle/walk switch and the code sets one boolean.

**Driving it from code, the two ways:**

```gdscript
@onready var tree: AnimationTree = $AnimationTree
@onready var sm: AnimationNodeStateMachinePlayback = 	tree.get(&"parameters/playback")

# 1. Travel — find a path through the graph to this state
sm.travel(&"attack")

# 2. Start — jump straight there, ignoring transitions
sm.start(&"attack")
```

**`travel()` is the one to use.** It respects the transitions you authored — including their switch modes and cross-fades — and finds a route if the states are not directly connected. **`start()` ignores all of it**, which is occasionally what you want and usually not.

**Reading the state:**

```gdscript
sm.get_current_node()            # a StringName
sm.get_current_play_position()
sm.get_travel_path()
sm.is_playing()
```

**`get_current_node()` is how your gameplay code finds out what the animation is doing** — which should be rare, because the dependency is supposed to run the other way.

**Nested state machines.** A state can itself be a `StateMachine`, which gives you hierarchy — a `grounded` state containing `idle`, `walk` and `run`, with one transition out of the whole group to `airborne`. **That is genuinely useful and it is where the graph starts beating code**, because expressing nested states in an enum means two enums or a composite.

**The parameter paths**, which are the API surface and are strings:

```
parameters/playback
parameters/conditions/is_moving
parameters/StateName/blend_position
parameters/OneShotName/request
```

**They are strings, so they are not checked.** A typo is silent — `set()` on a non-existent parameter does nothing. **Put them in constants:**

```gdscript
const P_IS_MOVING := &"parameters/conditions/is_moving"
```

**Same discipline as group names and animation names**, and for the same reason.

**The debugging procedure when the graph does nothing:**

1. **`active = true`** on the tree.
2. **`anim_player`** points at the right node.
3. **A connection from Start** exists.
4. **Advance Mode** is not Disabled on the transition you expect.
5. **The condition parameter name** matches exactly.
6. **Watch it in the editor** — the graph highlights the current state while the game runs, which is the `AnimationTree` equivalent of the Remote tree.

**Step six is the good part.** The graph lights up as it plays, so you can see which state it is in and which transition fired. **That is a genuinely better debugging experience than printing an enum.**

**Practice.** Build a state machine with `idle`, `walk` and `attack`. Connect idle↔walk with Auto transitions on an `is_moving` condition, and walk→attack with `travel()` and attack→idle with Switch Mode **At End**. Drive `is_moving` from velocity. Confirm the attack plays out fully without any `animation_finished` handling. Then watch the graph highlight while you play.
BlendSpace1D and BlendSpace2D:
Positioning animations in a space and blending between them by coordinate — the right tool for directional movement, and a caveat for pixel art.

**`BlendSpace1D`** — animations along a line, selected by one number.

**The canonical use: speed.**

```
-1 ────────── 0 ────────── 1
walk_back    idle       walk_fwd
```

```gdscript
tree.set(&"parameters/Movement/blend_position", speed_ratio)
```

**Set the position and the tree blends between the two nearest animations.** At 0.5 you get half idle, half forward walk.

**Building one:** add an `AnimationNodeBlendSpace1D` to the graph, open it, and drag animations onto the line. Set each point's position. **The `min_space` and `max_space` properties set the range**, and `snap` quantises.

**`BlendSpace2D`** — animations on a plane, selected by a `Vector2`.

**The canonical use: eight-direction movement.**

```
        up
  up_left  up_right
left    ·      right
  down_left  down_right
       down
```

```gdscript
tree.set(&"parameters/Movement/blend_position", facing)
```

**Eight animations at the eight compass points, and `facing` as the coordinate.** The tree picks and blends.

**The blend modes, which matter:**

| Mode | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| **Interpolated** | blends between the nearest points — smooth |
| **Discrete** | **picks the nearest point only**, no blending |
| **Carry** | discrete, but keeps the playback position when switching |

**And here is the caveat for pixel art: use Discrete or Carry, never Interpolated.**

**Why.** Blending two sprite animations means cross-fading two sets of discrete frames, which produces a ghosted double image rather than an intermediate pose. **Skeletal animation blends; sprite frames do not.**

**`Carry` is the one you want for eight-direction sprite movement.** It picks the nearest direction and **keeps the cycle's phase**, so turning from `right` to `down_right` mid-stride continues the stride rather than restarting it. **That one setting is the difference between a walk that flows and one that stutters on every turn.**

**Setting up an eight-direction blend space:**

1. `AnimationNodeBlendSpace2D` in the graph.
2. Blend mode **Carry**.
3. Eight `walk_*` animations dropped at the eight points — `(1,0)`, `(0.7,0.7)`, `(0,1)` and so on.
4. `min_space` `(-1,-1)`, `max_space` `(1,1)`.
5. From code: `tree.set(&"parameters/Walk/blend_position", facing)`.

**And the comparison with doing it by name**, from the eight-direction lesson:

```gdscript
_set_animation(&"walk_" + name_of(facing))
```

| | Blend space | By name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Setup** | a graph node and eight drops | a constant array and one function |
| **Phase preserved on turn** | **yes, with Carry** | no — unless you seek manually |
| **Readable in code** | the parameter is a string | **the name is explicit** |
| **Testable** | poorly | **yes** |
| **Designer-editable** | **yes** | no |

**Row two is the real argument for the blend space.** Preserving the cycle phase across a direction change by hand means reading the old animation's position and seeking the new one to match:

```gdscript
var pos := anim.current_animation_position
anim.play(next)
anim.seek(pos, true)
```

**Three lines, and it works** — so the blend space's advantage is convenience rather than capability.

**Nesting a blend space inside a state machine**, which is the usual arrangement:

```
StateMachine
├── idle              (an Animation leaf, or its own blend space)
├── walk              (a BlendSpace2D, Carry, eight directions)
├── attack            (an Animation leaf)
└── hurt              (an Animation leaf)
```

**The state machine decides *which activity*; the blend space decides *which direction*.** That division is clean and it maps onto the gameplay state machine from stage 4 — states are states, direction is a parameter.

**The `blend_position` for a 1D space is a `float`; for 2D it is a `Vector2`.** Setting the wrong type silently does nothing, which is the string-parameter hazard again.

**One more node worth knowing here: `AnimationNodeTransition`.** A simple switch between inputs with a cross-fade, driven by an index:

```gdscript
tree.set(&"parameters/Transition/transition_request", &"state_b")
```

**Lighter than a state machine** when all you need is *pick one of these three*, with no graph of transitions.

**Practice.** Build a `BlendSpace2D` with eight walk directions at the compass points, blend mode **Carry**, nested inside a state machine's `walk` state. Drive `blend_position` from `facing` and walk in a circle — confirm the cycle does not restart on each turn. Then switch the blend mode to Interpolated and observe the ghosting. Then implement the same thing by name with a manual `seek` to preserve phase, and compare the two.
Driving an AnimationTree from code:
The API surface of a tree — which is entirely strings — and the discipline that keeps it from becoming unmaintainable.

**Everything is a parameter path:**

```gdscript
@onready var tree: AnimationTree = $AnimationTree

tree.set(&"parameters/conditions/is_moving", true)
tree.set(&"parameters/Walk/blend_position", facing)
tree.set(&"parameters/TimeScale/scale", 1.5)
tree.set(&"parameters/Attack/request", AnimationNodeOneShot.ONE_SHOT_REQUEST_FIRE)
var sm := tree.get(&"parameters/playback") as AnimationNodeStateMachinePlayback
```

**`set()` and `get()` with string paths**, which means:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **No completion** | the editor cannot know your graph |
| **No checking** | a typo does nothing, silently |
| **No refactoring help** | renaming a graph node breaks every path |

**So the first discipline is constants:**

```gdscript
const P_PLAYBACK := &"parameters/playback"
const P_IS_MOVING := &"parameters/conditions/is_moving"
const P_WALK_DIR := &"parameters/Walk/blend_position"
const P_ATTACK := &"parameters/Attack/request"
```

**One place per path.** Rename a graph node and you fix one line.

**The second discipline: a wrapper.** The tree's API is strings; your actor's should not be.

```gdscript
class_name ActorAnimator
extends Node

@export var tree: AnimationTree

var _sm: AnimationNodeStateMachinePlayback

func _ready() -> void:
	_sm = tree.get(P_PLAYBACK)

func set_moving(moving: bool) -> void:
	tree.set(P_IS_MOVING, moving)

func set_facing(dir: Vector2) -> void:
	tree.set(P_WALK_DIR, dir)

func attack() -> void:
	_sm.travel(&"attack")

func current() -> StringName:
	return _sm.get_current_node()
```

**Now the actor calls `animator.attack()`** and knows nothing about parameter paths. **Three benefits:** the actor is readable, the paths are in one file, and the animator can be swapped for a stub in a test.

**That is the told-not-asked pattern from stage 5** applied to animation: the actor tells the animator what is happening; the animator decides what to play.

**The parameter kinds, as a reference:**

| Path shape | Type | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `parameters/playback` | `AnimationNodeStateMachinePlayback` | **the state machine handle** |
| `parameters/conditions/NAME` | `bool` | advance conditions |
| `parameters/NODE/blend_position` | `float` or `Vector2` | blend spaces |
| `parameters/NODE/blend_amount` | `float` | `Blend2` / `Blend3` |
| `parameters/NODE/request` | enum | `OneShot` — fire, abort, fade out |
| `parameters/NODE/active` | `bool` | `OneShot` — is it running |
| `parameters/NODE/scale` | `float` | `TimeScale` |
| `parameters/NODE/current_state` | `StringName` | `Transition` |
| `parameters/NODE/transition_request` | `StringName` | `Transition` |

**`OneShot`'s request enum**, because it is the one with a non-obvious API:

```gdscript
tree.set(&"parameters/Attack/request", AnimationNodeOneShot.ONE_SHOT_REQUEST_FIRE)
tree.set(&"parameters/Attack/request", AnimationNodeOneShot.ONE_SHOT_REQUEST_ABORT)
tree.set(&"parameters/Attack/request", AnimationNodeOneShot.ONE_SHOT_REQUEST_FADE_OUT)
var running: bool = tree.get(&"parameters/Attack/active")
```

**A `OneShot` layers an animation over a base** — an attack over a walk — and `request` fires it. **For sprite frames this is of limited use** for the blending reason from the last lesson, and for a 3D or skeletal character it is the standard way to layer.

**The signals on `AnimationTree`:**

```gdscript
tree.animation_finished.connect(_on_finished)
tree.animation_started.connect(_on_started)
```

**And the one on the playback**, which there is not — **`AnimationNodeStateMachinePlayback` has no signals.** To know when a state changes, poll `get_current_node()` or drive the change from your own code. **That asymmetry is worth knowing**, because it is a reason to keep your gameplay state machine authoritative.

**The two-machines problem, stated once more.** With an `AnimationTree` you now have:

| Machine | Decides |
| --- | --- |
| **The gameplay state machine** (stage 4) | what the actor **is doing** |
| **The animation state machine** | what is **drawn** |

**They must agree, and nothing enforces it.** The discipline that works:

1. **The gameplay machine is authoritative.** It transitions on its own rules.
2. **On entering a state, it tells the animator** — `animator.attack()`.
3. **The animation machine never transitions on its own** except for presentation detail — a cross-fade, an At End return.
4. **Gameplay never reads `get_current_node()`** to decide anything.

**Rule four is the one that keeps it clean.** The moment gameplay asks the animation what state it is in, the dependency reverses and the two can deadlock.

**Practice.** Build an `ActorAnimator` wrapper with `set_moving`, `set_facing`, `attack` and `current`. Put every parameter path in a `const`. Drive it from your actor's state machine's `_enter`. Then rename a graph node and confirm you only had to change one line. Then try reading `get_current_node()` in gameplay code and write down what could go wrong.
Tween: the code-first animator:
Animation written in code, created on demand, with no node and no timeline — the right tool for anything you would describe in a sentence.

**Creating one.** `create_tween()` is a method on `Node`:

```gdscript
var t := create_tween()
t.tween_property(self, "position", Vector2(100, 0), 0.3)
```

**Two lines, and the node slides to `(100, 0)` over 0.3 seconds.**

**There is no `Tween` node in Godot 4.** Godot 3 had one and every old tutorial adds it; in Godot 4 a tween is an object created by a node, bound to that node's lifetime.

**The property path is a string**, and it supports sub-properties:

```gdscript
t.tween_property(self, "position", target, 0.3)
t.tween_property(self, "position:x", 100.0, 0.3)
t.tween_property(sprite, "modulate:a", 0.0, 0.5)
t.tween_property(sprite, "material:shader_parameter/flash", 1.0, 0.1)
```

**`"modulate:a"` for just the alpha** is the fade idiom, and it is shorter than building a `Color`.

**Relative, rather than absolute:**

```gdscript
t.tween_property(self, "position", Vector2(0, -20), 0.2).as_relative()
```

**`as_relative()` adds to the current value**, which is what a nudge or a recoil wants.

**From a specific value:**

```gdscript
t.tween_property(sprite, "modulate:a", 1.0, 0.3).from(0.0)
t.tween_property(self, "scale", Vector2.ONE, 0.2).from_current()
```

**`from(0.0)` sets the start**, so a fade-in does not need the node to be invisible first.

**The four things a tween can do:**

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `tween_property(object, path, final, duration)` | animate a property |
| `tween_interval(seconds)` | **wait** |
| `tween_callback(callable)` | **call a function** |
| `tween_method(callable, from, to, duration)` | **call a function with an interpolated value** |

**`tween_method` is the one people miss**, and it animates anything with a setter — including things that are not properties:

```gdscript
t.tween_method(_set_health_display, 100.0, 80.0, 0.4)

func _set_health_display(v: float) -> void:
	label.text = "%d" % roundi(v)
	bar.value = v
```

**A health number counting down** rather than snapping, in one line, with no property to animate.

**The lifetime rules, which are the main source of confusion.**

**1. A tween is bound to the node that created it.** Free the node and the tween dies — which is correct and prevents the stage-3 `await` problem.

**2. A tween starts immediately and runs once.** There is no `start()`; creating it and adding steps is enough.

**3. Creating a second tween does not stop the first.** Two tweens animating the same property fight, and the result is a mess.

```gdscript
# The fix — keep a reference and kill the old one
var _t: Tween

func bounce() -> void:
	if _t != null and _t.is_running():
		_t.kill()
	_t = create_tween()
	_t.tween_property(self, "scale", Vector2(1.2, 0.8), 0.1)
```

**That pattern — kill then create — is the single most important thing in this lesson.** A button that tweens on hover, hovered rapidly, creates a tween per hover without it.

**The control methods:**

```gdscript
t.kill()
t.pause()
t.play()
t.stop()
t.is_running()
t.is_valid()
t.set_speed_scale(2.0)
t.set_loops(3)             # or set_loops() for infinite
t.set_process_mode(Tween.TWEEN_PROCESS_PHYSICS)
t.set_pause_mode(Tween.TWEEN_PAUSE_PROCESS)   # keep running while paused
```

**`set_loops()` with no argument loops forever**, which is how you make a pulsing highlight in three lines.

**`set_process_mode(TWEEN_PROCESS_PHYSICS)`** for anything moving a physics body, for the same reason as stage 4's `_physics_process`.

**And `set_pause_mode(TWEEN_PAUSE_PROCESS)`** so a UI tween keeps running while the game is paused — the pause-menu case from stage 3's process lesson.

**The signal:**

```gdscript
t.finished.connect(_on_done)
await t.finished
```

**`await t.finished`** reads well for a sequence and carries the stage-3 caveat: guard with `is_inside_tree()` after it.

**When a tween is the right tool, as a list:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| A UI panel sliding, fading, scaling | **yes** |
| A squash on impact | **yes** |
| A camera shake's decay | yes |
| A number counting up | yes — `tween_method` |
| A door opening once | yes |
| A character's walk cycle | **no** — that is art on a timeline |
| Anything a designer should edit | no — `AnimationPlayer` |

**Practice.** Write four tweens: a slide using `tween_property`, a fade using `"modulate:a"` with `.from(0.0)`, a nudge using `.as_relative()`, and a counting number using `tween_method`. Then create two tweens on the same property without killing the first and watch them fight. Then add the kill-then-create pattern and confirm it is fixed.
Tween chaining, parallel and callbacks:
Sequencing a tween — which is where it stops being a one-liner and becomes a small animation language.

**The default is sequential.** Each step waits for the previous one:

```gdscript
var t := create_tween()
t.tween_property(self, "position:y", -30.0, 0.2)
t.tween_property(self, "position:y", 0.0, 0.2)
t.tween_callback(_land)
```

**Up, down, then call `_land()`.** Three steps, in order, 0.4 seconds total.

**Parallel, when steps should run together:**

```gdscript
var t := create_tween()
t.set_parallel(true)
t.tween_property(self, "position", target, 0.3)
t.tween_property(sprite, "modulate:a", 0.0, 0.3)
t.tween_property(self, "scale", Vector2.ZERO, 0.3)
```

**`set_parallel(true)` makes everything after it simultaneous.** Move, fade and shrink at once — a dying enemy in four lines.

**Or per-step, which is clearer when mixing:**

```gdscript
var t := create_tween()
t.tween_property(self, "position:y", -30.0, 0.2)        # first
t.parallel().tween_property(self, "rotation", TAU, 0.2) # with the first
t.tween_property(self, "position:y", 0.0, 0.2)          # then this
```

**`.parallel()` attaches that step to the previous one.** Reading it top to bottom tells you the timing, which `set_parallel(true)` for the whole tween does not.

**`chain()`, the explicit opposite:**

```gdscript
t.set_parallel(true)
t.tween_property(a, "modulate:a", 0.0, 0.2)
t.tween_property(b, "modulate:a", 0.0, 0.2)
t.chain().tween_callback(_both_faded)
```

**`chain()` waits for everything so far.** Fade two things together, then do something after both — which is otherwise awkward.

**Delays:**

```gdscript
t.tween_property(self, "scale", Vector2.ONE, 0.2).set_delay(0.1)
t.tween_interval(0.5)
```

**`set_delay` on a step; `tween_interval` as a step.** The first is for staggering parallel steps; the second for a gap in a sequence.

**Staggering, which is the nicest use of delays** — a list of items appearing one after another:

```gdscript
var t := create_tween().set_parallel(true)
for i in items.size():
	t.tween_property(items[i], "modulate:a", 1.0, 0.15)		.from(0.0).set_delay(i * 0.04)
```

**Forty milliseconds apart, all in one tween.** That is the standard way a menu list appears and it reads as considered rather than abrupt.

**Callbacks, the two forms:**

```gdscript
t.tween_callback(_spawn_dust)
t.tween_callback(queue_free)
t.tween_callback(_hit.bind(10))              # with an argument
t.tween_callback(func(): print("done"))       # a lambda
```

**`tween_callback(queue_free)` at the end of a death tween** is the idiom — animate out, then remove.

**A worked sequence, which is most of a UI transition:**

```gdscript
func show_panel() -> void:
	if _t != null and _t.is_running():
		_t.kill()
	modulate.a = 0.0
	scale = Vector2(0.9, 0.9)
	visible = true

	_t = create_tween().set_parallel(true)
	_t.tween_property(self, "modulate:a", 1.0, 0.15)
	_t.tween_property(self, "scale", Vector2.ONE, 0.2)		.set_trans(Tween.TRANS_BACK).set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)
	_t.chain().tween_callback(_on_shown)
```

**Six things from this stage in one function:** kill-then-create, setting the start state explicitly, parallel steps, `TRANS_BACK` with `EASE_OUT` from the easing lesson, `chain()` to wait, and a callback.

**Looping and `set_loops`:**

```gdscript
create_tween().set_loops()	.tween_property(self, "modulate:a", 0.4, 0.6)	.as_relative()
```

**An infinite pulse.** And to stop it, keep the reference and `kill()`.

**`tween_method` in a sequence**, which is how you animate something with no property:

```gdscript
t.tween_method(_set_shake, 8.0, 0.0, 0.4)

func _set_shake(amount: float) -> void:
	camera.offset = Vector2(randf_range(-amount, amount), randf_range(-amount, amount))
```

**A decaying screen shake in five lines**, with the decay curve available via `set_trans`. **That is stage 9's camera shake, and it is a tween.**

**The gotchas, collected:**

| Gotcha | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Two tweens on one property | **kill the old one** |
| A tween on a freed node | it dies with the node — fine |
| `await t.finished` and the node died | `is_inside_tree()` guard |
| A tween that should run while paused | `set_pause_mode(TWEEN_PAUSE_PROCESS)` |
| A tween moving a body | `set_process_mode(TWEEN_PROCESS_PHYSICS)` |
| Steps running together when they should not | you called `set_parallel(true)` earlier |
| A property path typo | **silent** — no error |

**That last one deserves care.** `tween_property(self, "possition", …)` does nothing and says nothing. **Check the spelling when a tween appears not to run.**

**Practice.** Write the `show_panel` function above and call it from a button. Then write a death sequence: flash white, shake, fade and shrink in parallel, then `queue_free`. Then stagger five labels appearing 40 ms apart in one tween. Then animate a decaying screen shake with `tween_method`. Then deliberately misspell a property path and confirm the silence.
Squash, stretch and the impact toolkit:
The small procedural effects that make a 2D game feel physical — each a few lines, each disproportionately effective.

**Squash and stretch.** The oldest animation principle there is: a thing deforms along its direction of motion.

```gdscript
func squash() -> void:
	if _t != null and _t.is_running():
		_t.kill()
	_t = create_tween()
	_t.tween_property(sprite, "scale", Vector2(1.3, 0.7), 0.06)
	_t.tween_property(sprite, "scale", Vector2.ONE, 0.12)		.set_trans(Tween.TRANS_BACK).set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)
```

**Wide and short on impact, then back with an overshoot.** Six hundredths of a second out, twelve back — **the return is always slower than the squash.**

**Conserve the area.** `(1.3, 0.7)` is roughly area-preserving; `(1.3, 1.3)` just makes it bigger and reads as a zoom rather than a squash.

**Scale the sprite, not the body**, from stage 4's transform lesson — scaling a `CollisionShape2D` is the thing to avoid.

**Where each belongs:**

| Effect | Scale |
| --- | --- |
| **Landing** | squash — `(1.2, 0.8)` |
| **Jumping** | stretch — `(0.8, 1.2)` |
| **Taking a hit** | squash, briefly and harder |
| **A button press** | squash to `(0.95, 0.95)` — uniform is fine for UI |
| **Spawning** | from `(0, 0)` with `TRANS_BACK` |

**The flash**, from stage 4's impact lesson, as a tween:

```gdscript
func flash() -> void:
	var t := create_tween()
	t.tween_property(sprite, "modulate", Color(6, 6, 6), 0.03)
	t.tween_property(sprite, "modulate", Color.WHITE, 0.08)
```

**`modulate` above 1.0 blows out to white.** Values of 4–8 give a hard flash; 2 gives a tint. **Use `self_modulate` if the node has children that should not flash.**

**Screen shake**, from the tween lesson, decaying:

```gdscript
func shake(amount: float = 6.0, time: float = 0.3) -> void:
	var t := create_tween()
	t.tween_method(_apply_shake, amount, 0.0, time)		.set_trans(Tween.TRANS_QUINT).set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)

func _apply_shake(a: float) -> void:
	camera.offset = Vector2(randf_range(-a, a), randf_range(-a, a))
```

**Two cautions.** **Keep it small** — 4 to 8 pixels at a 960×540 viewport is plenty, and more reads as a bug. And **snap the offset to whole pixels** for pixel art, or the shake un-snaps every sprite on screen:

```gdscript
	camera.offset = Vector2(randi_range(-a, a), randi_range(-a, a))
```

**Stage 9 returns to this**, because a fractional camera offset defeats the whole pixel-perfect arrangement from stage 4's quantising lesson.

**The recoil**, which is a relative nudge:

```gdscript
func recoil(dir: Vector2) -> void:
	var t := create_tween()
	t.tween_property(sprite, "position", -dir * 4.0, 0.04).as_relative()
	t.tween_property(sprite, "position", dir * 4.0, 0.1).as_relative()
```

**Four pixels, back and forward.** On the sprite, not the body, so collision is untouched.

**Hitstop**, from stage 4, which is the most effective of the lot and belongs to a service rather than a tween — and the trap from that lesson applies: **measure its duration in real time, not `delta`**, because `delta` is scaled by `time_scale`.

**Anticipation**, from the easing lesson, as two keyframes rather than a tween — it belongs on the timeline with the attack it precedes.

**The stacking order that reads best**, if you use several at once:

| Order | Effect | Timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Sound** | frame 0 — the single biggest contributor |
| 2 | **Hitstop** | frame 0, 30 ms |
| 3 | **Flash** | during the stop |
| 4 | **Squash** | as time resumes |
| 5 | **Knockback** | likewise |
| 6 | **Particles** | likewise |
| 7 | **Shake** | small, and only for heavy hits |

**And the honest advice: do not use all seven for every hit.** A light attack gets a sound and a flash; a heavy one gets the lot. **Uniform maximum feedback reads as noise**, and the contrast is what makes a heavy hit feel heavy.

**A reusable component**, since every actor wants these:

```gdscript
class_name ImpactFx
extends Node

@export var sprite: CanvasItem
@export var camera: Camera2D

var _t: Tween

func hit(heavy: bool) -> void:
	flash()
	squash()
	if heavy:
		shake(6.0, 0.25)
```

**Which is stage 5's component pattern** — a capability as a child node, with its targets as `@export`s, callable by whatever owns it.

**Practice.** Build an `ImpactFx` component with flash, squash, recoil and shake. Wire it to an actor and fire it on a key press. Tune each duration until it feels right, then write the numbers down. Then make the shake use `randi_range` for whole pixels and compare it with the fractional version at 2× zoom. Then do a light hit and a heavy hit with different subsets and judge the contrast.
Animating the interface:
UI animation, where a tween is almost always the right tool — with the durations and the three patterns that cover most of it.

**Why UI is different.** It is seen hundreds of times, it is usually in the player's way, and **it must never make them wait.** So the rules are stricter than for world animation: short, eased out, and interruptible.

**The durations, from the easing lesson, restated as law:**

| Element | Duration |
| --- | --- |
| Hover response | **0.05–0.1 s** |
| Press response | 0.03–0.06 s |
| A panel appearing | 0.15–0.25 s |
| A screen transition | 0.2–0.4 s |
| A tooltip | 0.1 s, after a 0.4 s delay |
| A list staggering in | 0.15 s each, 0.04 s apart |

**Anything the player must wait through, more than once, should be under 0.25 seconds.**

**Pattern 1: appear and disappear.**

```gdscript
func show_panel() -> void:
	_kill()
	visible = true
	modulate.a = 0.0
	scale = Vector2(0.95, 0.95)
	_t = create_tween().set_parallel(true)
	_t.tween_property(self, "modulate:a", 1.0, 0.15)
	_t.tween_property(self, "scale", Vector2.ONE, 0.2)		.set_trans(Tween.TRANS_BACK).set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)

func hide_panel() -> void:
	_kill()
	_t = create_tween().set_parallel(true)
	_t.tween_property(self, "modulate:a", 0.0, 0.1)
	_t.tween_property(self, "scale", Vector2(0.95, 0.95), 0.1)
	_t.chain().tween_callback(func(): visible = false)
```

**Three things to note.** **Out is faster than in** — 0.1 against 0.2, because leaving should not be waited for. **`visible = false` in a callback**, so the node stops costing anything once hidden. And **`scale` from 0.95, not 0** — a panel growing from nothing reads as a cartoon; a slight scale reads as a lift.

**The pivot matters.** A `Control` scales from its `pivot_offset`, which defaults to the top-left — so a panel scales out of its corner. **Set `pivot_offset` to half the size** for a centre scale:

```gdscript
pivot_offset = size * 0.5
```

**That is the commonest UI animation mistake**, and stage 9 covers `Control` sizing properly.

**Pattern 2: the hover and press response.**

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	mouse_entered.connect(func(): _to(Vector2(1.04, 1.04), 0.08))
	mouse_exited.connect(func(): _to(Vector2.ONE, 0.08))
	button_down.connect(func(): _to(Vector2(0.97, 0.97), 0.04))
	button_up.connect(func(): _to(Vector2(1.04, 1.04), 0.06))

func _to(s: Vector2, time: float) -> void:
	_kill()
	_t = create_tween()
	_t.tween_property(self, "scale", s, time).set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)
```

**Four signals, one helper, and the kill-then-create pattern** — which is essential here, because a mouse moved across ten buttons fires twenty signals.

**Pattern 3: the value change.** A number or bar that moves rather than snapping, from the tween lesson:

```gdscript
func set_health(current: int, maximum: int) -> void:
	_kill()
	var target := float(current) / maximum
	_t = create_tween()
	_t.tween_property(bar, "value", target, 0.25)		.set_trans(Tween.TRANS_CUBIC).set_ease(Tween.EASE_OUT)
```

**And the two-bar trick**, which is worth knowing: a second bar behind the first, tweened more slowly, shows the damage just taken as a trailing colour. **Two nodes, one extra tween, and it reads far better than a single bar.**

**What to animate with an `AnimationPlayer` instead.** Three cases:

| Case | Why |
| --- | --- |
| A complex multi-element sequence | a timeline is clearer than twenty tween lines |
| Something a designer should edit | the panel is the interface |
| Anything with audio keyed to it | audio tracks |

**A screen transition with six staggered elements and three sounds** belongs on a timeline. **A button's hover does not.**

**The pause problem.** A UI tween during a paused game stops, because tweens default to pausing:

```gdscript
_t.set_pause_mode(Tween.TWEEN_PAUSE_PROCESS)
```

**And the node itself needs `process_mode = PROCESS_MODE_WHEN_PAUSED`** or `ALWAYS`, from stage 3. **Both, or a pause menu animates into existence and then freezes.**

**Interruptibility, which is the thing that separates good UI animation from bad.** Every one of these patterns kills its predecessor. **A player clicking rapidly through menus should see the UI keep up, not queue** — and the kill-then-create pattern is what delivers that.

**The accessibility note, briefly and genuinely.** Some players need animation reduced. **A single `@export var animations_enabled: bool` consulted by a helper** — or a setting read from a `Resource` — lets every tween become instant:

```gdscript
func _to(s: Vector2, time: float) -> void:
	if not Settings.animations:
		scale = s
		return
	...
```

**Worth building in early**, because retrofitting it means touching every animation.

**Practice.** Build a panel with `show_panel` and `hide_panel`, with `pivot_offset` set to the centre. Confirm it scales from the middle, then remove the pivot line and see it scale from the corner. Then add hover and press responses to a button and move the mouse rapidly across several — confirm no queueing. Then animate a health bar with a trailing second bar. Then make a UI tween survive `get_tree().paused = true`.
Animating a shader parameter:
The bridge between this stage and stage 10 — animating a uniform, which is how most modern 2D effects are done.

**Why.** A flash by `modulate` whitens the whole sprite uniformly. A **shader** can whiten it, dissolve it, outline it, make it glow at the edges, or wash a colour across it from left to right — and all of those are one float you can animate.

**The setup, minimally.** A shader with a uniform:

```glsl
shader_type canvas_item;

uniform float flash : hint_range(0.0, 1.0) = 0.0;

void fragment() {
    vec4 c = texture(TEXTURE, UV);
    COLOR = vec4(mix(c.rgb, vec3(1.0), flash), c.a);
}
```

**Assign it as a `ShaderMaterial` on the sprite's `material`.** Stage 10 covers shaders properly; this lesson is about driving the uniform.

**Three ways to animate it.**

**1. From code, directly:**

```gdscript
var mat := sprite.material as ShaderMaterial
mat.set_shader_parameter(&"flash", 1.0)
```

**2. With a `Tween`, via `tween_method`:**

```gdscript
func flash() -> void:
	var mat := sprite.material as ShaderMaterial
	var t := create_tween()
	t.tween_method(
		func(v: float): mat.set_shader_parameter(&"flash", v),
		1.0, 0.0, 0.2)
```

**A lambda closing over the material** — from stage 3's callable lesson — is the idiomatic form.

**3. With a `Tween`, via the property path**, which is shorter and the one to prefer:

```gdscript
	t.tween_property(sprite, "material:shader_parameter/flash", 0.0, 0.2).from(1.0)
```

**`material:shader_parameter/NAME` is a real property path**, so `tween_property` works directly. **No lambda, no cast.**

**4. With an `AnimationPlayer`**, using the same path as a track:

```
Sprite2D:material:shader_parameter/flash
```

**Which means a hit animation can keyframe the shader alongside the sprite frames** — the flash, the frames, the hitbox and the sound on one timeline, from the track-types lesson.

**That is the argument for shader animation over `modulate`**: it is one more track on the animation you were already authoring.

**The trap: materials are shared.**

```gdscript
# Two sprites with the same ShaderMaterial resource
mat.set_shader_parameter(&"flash", 1.0)      # BOTH flash
```

**A `ShaderMaterial` is a `Resource`**, so the stage-5 sharing rules apply. Ten enemies instanced from one scene share one material, and flashing one flashes all ten.

**The fixes:**

```gdscript
# 1. Duplicate on ready — per-instance
func _ready() -> void:
	sprite.material = sprite.material.duplicate()

# 2. Make Unique in the Inspector, per scene
# 3. Use a per-instance uniform instead — see below
```

**Option 1 is the usual answer** and it costs one material per instance, which for a few dozen actors is nothing.

**Per-instance uniforms**, which are the better answer at scale:

```glsl
instance uniform float flash = 0.0;
```

```gdscript
sprite.set_instance_shader_parameter(&"flash", 1.0)
```

**`instance uniform` plus `set_instance_shader_parameter`** gives each node its own value with **one shared material** — so a hundred enemies can flash independently without a hundred materials. **That is the right tool for anything numerous**, and it is easy to miss because the API name is different.

**The uniforms worth animating, as a starter set:**

| Uniform | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `flash` | white-out on hit |
| `dissolve` | a threshold against a noise texture — a death fade |
| `outline_width` | a selection or hover outline |
| `tint` + `tint_amount` | a poison or freeze colour |
| `wave_amount` | a wobble, for water or confusion |
| `scroll` | a moving texture — a conveyor, a shield |
| `progress` | a radial or linear wipe — cooldowns |

**`dissolve` is the most satisfying** for the effort: a noise texture, a threshold uniform, and `discard` below it gives you a death that reads far better than a fade.

**Keeping it honest.** A shader parameter animated per frame on a hundred nodes is a hundred uniform updates, which is cheap — **the expense is the shader itself**, and stage 10 covers that. **Animating uniforms is not where the cost is.**

**And the pixel-art caveat.** An effect that samples neighbouring pixels — an outline, a blur — needs `TEXTURE_PIXEL_SIZE` and will look wrong if the sprite is scaled non-integrally. **At your projects' integer scaling it is fine**, which is one more thing the viewport arrangement buys.

**Practice.** Write the three-line flash shader, assign it to a sprite, and animate `flash` three ways: directly, with `tween_property` on the `material:shader_parameter/flash` path, and as an `AnimationPlayer` track. Then instance the sprite three times and confirm all three flash together; fix it with `duplicate()`. Then convert the uniform to an `instance uniform` and confirm independence with one shared material.
Frame-driven animation by hand:
The fifth way to animate — loading and swapping textures yourself — which is occasionally the right answer and is what one of your own systems does.

**The approach.** No `AnimationPlayer`, no `SpriteFrames`. A script holds a list of textures and sets `texture` or draws them, advancing on its own clock.

```gdscript
extends Node2D

const FRAMES_ROOT := "res://art/run_frames"
const FRAME_NAME := "run_%s_%02d.png"

@export var fps: float = 12.0

var _frames: Array[Texture2D] = []
var _time := 0.0
var _index := 0

func _ready() -> void:
	for i in 12:
		var path := "%s/%s" % [FRAMES_ROOT, FRAME_NAME % ["down", i]]
		_frames.append(load(path))

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	_time += delta
	var step := 1.0 / fps
	while _time >= step:
		_time -= step
		_index = (_index + 1) % _frames.size()
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_texture(_frames[_index], Vector2.ZERO)
```

**Why anyone would do this**, which is the point of the lesson — five legitimate reasons:

| Reason | |
| --- | --- |
| **The frames are not imported** | loose files, a `.gdignore`d folder, generated output |
| **Several layers must be combined per frame** | a split body, a paper-doll |
| **The frame choice is computed**, not authored | a direction from an angle, a blend from two sources |
| **Per-frame offsets come from data** | measured anchors |
| **A preview tool** that must work before the pipeline exists | |

**Rows two to four are what your own project needs**, and `presentation/world/body_base_run.gd` is the result. Its header:

> *Eli's run, until he has one of his own: Timon's colour-coded body-base run cycle, in two halves.*

**And the mechanism, which no built-in node can do:**

> *The legs play the run in the eight-way direction he is moving.*
> *The upper half (head, chest, arms) plays the same frame from the eight-way direction nearest the aim, at most `MAX_TWIST_STEPS` directions either side of the legs.*
> *The two meet at the waist: every frame's waist is measured in the conversion (`conversion/run/split_halves.py`, `anchors.json`), and the upper half is moved so its waist lands on the legs' own.*

**Two textures per frame, chosen by two different directions, offset by a per-frame measured anchor.** An `AnimatedSprite2D` plays one list; an `AnimationPlayer` keyframes properties. **Neither can pick two frames from two rings and align them by data** — so the hand-written version is not a shortcut, it is the only option.

**And the reason the frames are loaded rather than imported:**

> *NOT THE SPRITE ROUTE. The frames are sprite-acus's output, read from disk out of a `.gdignore`d folder, as the idle preview reads its frames. Nothing is imported, so an exported build carries no frames and Eli stays grey there (`attach` gives nothing).*

**`.gdignore` in a folder tells Godot to ignore it entirely** — not imported, not in the `.godot` cache, **not in an export**. So this animation exists in the editor and not in a shipped build, deliberately, because it is placeholder art. **That is a legitimate and unusual arrangement**, and knowing `.gdignore` exists is the transferable part.

**The costs of hand-rolling, honestly:**

| Cost | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **No editor preview** | unless you make it `@tool` |
| **`load()` at runtime** | slower than an imported resource, and it can fail |
| **No `animation_finished`** | you track completion yourself |
| **No `AnimationTree`** | none of stage 6's blending applies |
| **You own the timing** | including the frame-rate independence |

**The timing deserves attention.** The `while` loop in the example above — rather than `if` — is deliberate: at a low frame rate, `delta` may exceed one frame's step, and an `if` would drop frames while a `while` catches up. **That is the same class of correctness as stage 4's `delta` lesson.**

**Making it `@tool` so the editor shows it**, which is what your project does for its previews:

```gdscript
@tool
extends Node2D
```

**And then the `@tool` contagion rule from stage 3 applies** — this script may only call other `@tool` scripts, which is exactly the constraint `island_view.gd` documented. **Stage 7 covers `@tool` properly.**

**When not to hand-roll.** If the animation is *a list of frames played in order*, use `AnimatedSprite2D`. **The hand-written version exists for the cases where frame selection is a computation**, and using it for a simple cycle is throwing away the editor for nothing.

**Practice.** Write the frame-driven animator above against a folder of loose PNGs, with the `while` loop for the timing. Then cap the frame rate with `Engine.max_fps = 10` and confirm it keeps time rather than slowing. Then make it `@tool` and watch it animate in the editor. Then put a `.gdignore` in the frames folder and confirm the FileSystem dock stops showing them — and that `load()` still works.
Performance, and when animation costs:
What animation actually costs, measured rather than assumed — and the four things that are genuinely expensive.

**The honest starting point: animation is rarely the bottleneck in a 2D game.** Draw calls and physics usually are, from stage 4's scaling lesson. **Measure before optimising** — stage 10's profiler lesson.

**What each system costs, roughly:**

| System | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| **`AnimatedSprite2D`** | one texture swap per frame change. **Negligible.** |
| **`AnimationPlayer`** | proportional to **tracks × keys evaluated per frame**. Small. |
| **`AnimationTree`** | the graph is evaluated every frame, blending included. **Noticeably more.** |
| **`Tween`** | one property write per step. Negligible. |
| **Hand-rolled `_process`** | whatever you wrote |

**The four things that are actually expensive:**

**1. An `AnimationTree` per actor, at scale.** The graph is walked every frame whether anything changed or not. **Fifty actors with trees is fifty graph evaluations**, and for simple characters an `AnimationPlayer` with `play()` is far cheaper.

**2. Many `AnimationPlayer`s with many tracks.** A player evaluates every track every frame. An actor with twenty tracks across six animations costs more than one with four. **Splitting an animation into fewer, broader tracks helps; so does not animating things that do not change.**

**3. Unique materials per instance**, from the shader lesson. A hundred duplicated `ShaderMaterial`s is a hundred materials and a hundred draw-call breaks. **`instance uniform` plus a shared material is the fix** and it matters at scale.

**4. Texture swapping that breaks batching.** Stage 10's subject: sprites sharing a texture batch into one draw call; sprites with different textures do not. **An eight-direction character whose frames are in eight separate files cannot batch with itself** — a single atlas can.

**The optimisations worth knowing, in order of effect:**

| Optimisation | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Turn off animation for off-screen actors** | large |
| **One atlas per character, not a file per frame** | large, via batching |
| **`AnimationPlayer` instead of `AnimationTree`** for simple actors | moderate |
| **Fewer tracks** | small |
| **`instance uniform` instead of duplicated materials** | moderate at scale |
| **Lower fps on distant or background animation** | small, and free |

**The first is the big one**, and it is one node:

```gdscript
# A VisibleOnScreenEnabler2D child does this for you
```

**`VisibleOnScreenEnabler2D`** disables its parent's processing when it leaves the screen and re-enables it on return. **For a world full of animated props, that is most of the win in one node** — and it is the same family as the `VisibleOnScreenNotifier2D` from stage 4's projectile lesson.

**Manually, if you need the control:**

```gdscript
func _on_screen_exited() -> void:
	anim.active = false              # an AnimationTree
	set_process(false)

func _on_screen_entered() -> void:
	anim.active = true
	set_process(true)
```

**The `AnimationPlayer` equivalent** is to `stop()` or set `callback_mode_process` appropriately — though an idle `AnimationPlayer` costs little enough that this is rarely the first thing to reach for.

**Lowering the frame rate of animation that nobody is looking at closely:**

```gdscript
spr.speed_scale = 0.5      # half rate, half the texture swaps
```

**Or `Engine.max_fps`** for the whole game, which is a blunt but real tool for a pixel-art game: **a 2D game at 60 fps looks identical to one at 144 and costs less than half as much.**

**Measuring it**, which is the actual instruction of this lesson. From stage 1's debugger lesson and stage 10's profiler:

| Where | What to look at |
| --- | --- |
| **Debugger > Profiler** | the per-function cost. Look for `AnimationTree` and `_process`. |
| **Debugger > Monitors** | **Draw Calls**, Objects, Nodes |
| **Visual Profiler** | GPU time, if the shaders are suspect |

**And the sanity test: turn it off.** Set every `AnimationTree.active = false` and see whether the frame time moves. **If it does not, animation is not your problem**, and you have just saved yourself an afternoon.

**The honest conclusion.** For a 2D pixel-art game at 960×540:

- **`AnimatedSprite2D` and `AnimationPlayer` are free** at the scales you will work at.
- **`AnimationTree` is the one to be deliberate about**, and most 2D games do not need one.
- **The real costs are draw calls and physics bodies**, both from stage 4 and both revisited in stage 10.
- **`VisibleOnScreenEnabler2D` is the single best animation optimisation** and it is a node you drop in.

**Practice.** Instance fifty animated actors and read the profiler. Note the frame time. Then add an `AnimationTree` to each and read it again. Then add a `VisibleOnScreenEnabler2D` to each and move the camera so most are off-screen, and read it a third time. Then set `Engine.max_fps = 60` and compare.
Reading a real animation setup: body_bas:
The stage's closing exercise: an animation system from your own project that uses none of the built-in animation nodes, and the reasons it does not.

**Open `shepherds-we-shall-be/game/scripts/presentation/world/body_base_run.gd`** — 177 lines, and its sibling `body_base_idle.gd` at 118.

**Pass 1 — where it sits.** `presentation/world/`. From stage 5's layers: **presentation is display and sound**, and nothing depends on it. **So this file draws and nothing reads it** — which the class name confirms: `BodyBaseRun`, a view.

**Pass 2 — the header, which is a complete specification.** It gives you, in order:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What** | *"Eli's run, until he has one of his own: Timon's colour-coded body-base run cycle, in two halves."* |
| **Who asked, and when** | *Master Roachi, 2026-09-18*, quoted directly |
| **The mechanism** | legs follow movement; upper half follows aim, limited |
| **The constraint** | *"at most `MAX_TWIST_STEPS` directions either side of the legs — two steps, 90 degrees"* |
| **How the halves join** | measured waist anchors from `anchors.json` |
| **The degenerate case** | *"With no twist that move is nothing, and the frame is exactly the combined one."* |
| **Why no mirroring** | *"the limb colours are tied to a side"* |
| **What it is not** | *"NOT THE SPRITE ROUTE"*, and what the real pipeline will be |

**Eight things before any code.** That is the documentation convention from stage 3 doing its job — and the reason you can understand a 177-line animation system in two minutes.

**Pass 3 — the constants:**

```gdscript
const FRAMES_ROOT := "res://media/placeholder/animation/eli_run_frames"
const FRAME_NAME := "body-part-reference_run_%s_%02d.png"
## Ring order: each is one 45-degree step from its neighbours.
```

**Three things from earlier stages.** `:=` inference from stage 3. A `%s`/`%02d` format string from stage 3's string lesson — **the direction name and a zero-padded frame index**, which is exactly the naming convention from this stage's eight-direction lesson. And a comment establishing that the direction array is a **ring**, which the twist logic depends on.

**Pass 4 — the questions to answer.** This is the exercise:

1. **Why is this not an `AnimatedSprite2D`?** Three reasons from the frame-driven lesson apply. Name them.
2. **Why is it not an `AnimationPlayer`?**
3. **Why eight authored directions and no mirroring?** The header answers it in one clause.
4. **What is `MAX_TWIST_STEPS`, and why is it expressed in steps rather than degrees?**
5. **What happens when the aim is directly behind the movement direction?**
6. **Why do the frames not appear in an exported build?** (Find `.gdignore` in the explanation.)
7. **What is the test that the split is correct?** (The header states it.)
8. **Where will this code go when the real art arrives?**

**Question 7 is the best one.** The header says: *"With no twist that move is nothing, and the frame is exactly the combined one."* **The degenerate case reproduces the original frame exactly** — so the test of a complicated system is that it collapses to the simple one. That is a property worth looking for in any system you build.

**Pass 5 — compare it with its sibling.** `body_base_idle.gd` is 118 lines and has:

```gdscript
const FRAMES_ROOT := "res://media/placeholder/animation/body_base_idle_frames"
const FRAME_NAME := "body-part-reference_idle_%s_%02d.png"
```

**The same convention, a different cycle** — and from the header of the run file: *"Standing, Eli is the grey figure and this is hidden; there is no split idle."* **The idle has no twist because a standing figure has nothing to twist against.** The two files are deliberately asymmetric and the reason is in the prose.

**What this stage has given you.** Six systems — `AnimationPlayer`, `AnimatedSprite2D`, `AnimationTree`, `Tween`, shader uniforms, and hand-rolled frames — and the judgement to choose. **The judgement is most of it**, because every one of them works and five of them are wrong for any given job.

**And the choosing rule, one last time:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Frames in order | **`AnimatedSprite2D`** |
| Anything authored on a timeline | **`AnimationPlayer`** |
| Transitions that are themselves complex | **`AnimationTree`** |
| Procedural, one-off, short | **`Tween`** |
| An effect on the pixels | **a shader uniform** |
| Frame choice that is a computation | **by hand** |

**Practice.** Answer all eight questions in writing. Then open `body_base_idle.gd` and list every way it differs from the run, and why. Then find `MAX_TWIST_STEPS` in the code and confirm the ring arithmetic matches the eight-direction `posmod` lesson. Then pick one of your own animations and ask which of the six systems it should use — and whether it currently does.
