What a Resource is:
The second half of Godot's object model — and the answer to where a game's numbers should live.

**The definition.** A `Resource` is a **data object that can be saved to a file and shared between references.** It is not in the scene tree, it has no position, and it does not process.

**Everything you have already used is one:**

| Resource | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Texture2D` | an image |
| `AudioStream` | a sound |
| `PackedScene` | **a scene** — a `.tscn` is a resource |
| `Animation`, `AnimationLibrary`, `SpriteFrames` | from stage 6 |
| `Shape2D`, `CircleShape2D` | from stage 4 |
| `ShaderMaterial`, `Shader` | from stage 6 |
| `Font`, `Theme` | stage 9 |
| `Script` | **a `.gd` file is a resource**, assigned to a node's `script` property |
| `TileSet` | stage 8 |

**And you can write your own**, which is what this stage is for.

**The two families, stated plainly**, because getting this straight explains a great deal:

| | `Node` | `Resource` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Lives in** | the scene tree | a file, or inside another resource |
| **Has a position** | 2D/3D nodes do | **no** |
| **Processes** | `_process`, `_physics_process` | **no** |
| **Freed by** | **you** — `queue_free()` | **automatically**, when the last reference goes |
| **Assignment** | by reference | **by reference** |
| **Saved as** | `.tscn` | `.tres` or `.res` |
| **Cached** | no | **yes** — stage 7's cache lesson |
| **For** | things that **do** | things that **are** |

**That last row is the useful shorthand. A node acts; a resource describes.**

**Why this matters for a game's numbers.** The standing decision from stage 1 — *numbers live in `@export` or a `Resource`, never in the script body* — is now explicable in full:

| Where a number lives | Who can change it |
| --- | --- |
| **In the script body** | only someone editing code |
| **In an `@export`** | anyone with the scene open, per instance |
| **In a `Resource`** | **anyone with the `.tres` open, and a test, and a tool, and version control sees it as data** |

**The third gives you the most**, and it is why your own project has `game/scripts/definitions/` — twenty-four schema files — and `game/resources/definitions/` — the `.tres` data itself.

**And your project states the reason outright.** From `the-lost-sheep/game/scripts/island/parcel_data.gd`:

> *A Resource rather than a dictionary, because BRIEF.md makes Godot a CONDITIONAL recommendation — conditional on the map, characters and buildings being editable in the editor rather than in code. Everything the island is made of therefore has to be an Inspector-editable Resource with an @tool script drawing it live. This is the first test of that condition.*

**The choice of Godot as the engine was conditional on editor-editable content**, and a `Resource` with an `@export`ed field is what *editor-editable* means. **That is as strong a reason to use a resource as exists.**

**The three things a `Resource` gives you that a `Dictionary` does not:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Typed, named fields** | a typo is a parse error, not a silent new key |
| **The Inspector** | a designer-editable form, with the right widget per type |
| **A file** | version-controlled, diffable, loadable, testable |

**And what a `Dictionary` gives you that a `Resource` does not:** flexibility at a boundary, which stage 5's payload lesson showed `island_view.gd` using deliberately.

**`RefCounted`, since `Resource` extends it.** The hierarchy:

```
Object → RefCounted → Resource → Texture2D, PackedScene, your classes…
```

**`RefCounted` is the "freed automatically" part**, and you can extend it directly for a data object that does **not** need a file:

```gdscript
class_name ActorRuntimeState
extends RefCounted
```

**Which is exactly what your actor does** — `var runtime_state := ActorRuntimeState.new()` — for per-instance state that is not content and should not be a file. **`Resource` for content; `RefCounted` for runtime.** Lesson 13 takes that split properly.

**Practice.** List every `Resource` in one of your scenes by selecting nodes and reading the Inspector for properties whose value is a resource rather than a number. Then open a `.tres` from `the-lost-sheep/game/data/` in a text editor and look at it. Then read `parcel_data.gd`'s header and find the sentence explaining why it is a resource at all.
Writing a custom Resource class:
The mechanics, with a real one from your own project as the model — and it is four lines plus the fields.

**The minimum:**

```gdscript
class_name HeroStats
extends Resource

@export var max_hp: int = 100
@export var speed: float = 220.0
```

**`class_name`, `extends Resource`, and `@export`ed fields.** That is a complete, saveable, Inspector-editable data class.

**`class_name` is effectively required.** Without it the type has no global name, so you cannot write `@export var stats: HeroStats` anywhere, and the Inspector cannot offer to create one. **Every custom resource gets a `class_name`.**

**Creating one as a file.** Three ways:

| Way | How |
| --- | --- |
| **FileSystem dock** | right-click > **Create New > Resource…**, pick your class |
| **The Inspector** | on an `@export var stats: HeroStats` slot, the dropdown offers **New HeroStats** |
| **In code** | `HeroStats.new()`, then `ResourceSaver.save(...)` |

**The Inspector route is the one you will use**: a typed export slot offers to make one, and **Save As** turns it into a `.tres`.

**A real one, read in full.** `the-lost-sheep/game/scripts/island/parcel_data.gd` — 93 lines for one parcel of an island:

```gdscript
@tool
## … header …
class_name ParcelData
extends Resource

const PLAIN := "plain"
const RIVER := "river"
const TREES := "trees"
const ROCK := "rock"

## Every terrain a parcel may have. PLAIN is "nothing in particular", which is
## not a value any building asks for.
const TERRAINS: Array[String] = [PLAIN, RIVER, TREES, ROCK]

@export var id: int = -1
@export var cell: Vector2i = Vector2i.ZERO
@export_enum("plain", "river", "trees", "rock") var terrain: String = PLAIN
@export var buildable: bool = true
@export var only_types: Array[String] = []
```

**Six things worth taking from it.**

**1. `@tool` at the top, and the comment says it is not optional** — lesson 15's subject, and the reason is a real error message.

**2. Constants beside the exports**, naming the legal values — so the rest of the codebase writes `ParcelData.RIVER` rather than `"river"`.

**3. `@export_enum("plain", "river", …) var terrain: String`** — a **string** with a dropdown, not an `enum`. And the header explains why, which is the interesting part:

> *Those strings are not an enum on purpose — they are the very values `buildings.types.<type>.needs` carries in data/numbers.json, and an enum beside them would be a second copy to drift.*

**An enum would be a second representation of values that already exist in a JSON file.** Two copies drift; one does not. **That is a genuine argument against the enum that stage 3 recommended**, and it is the right call here — the external data file is the authority.

**4. `@export var only_types: Array[String] = []`**, with the reasoning for a list rather than a single value:

> *A list rather than a single type, because "the tower and nothing else" and "anything" are the two cases today and a third is cheap.*

**5. Methods on the resource**, which are pure and about its own data:

```gdscript
func takes_a(type: String) -> bool:
	if not buildable:
		return false
	return only_types.is_empty() or only_types.has(type)

func takes(needs: Variant) -> bool:
	return needs == null or str(needs) == terrain
```

**Two predicates, no side effects, no tree access.** From stage 5's layers lesson: a definition may hold pure functions about its own data and must not grow behaviour. **These qualify.**

**6. `_to_string()`**, which is worth adopting as a habit:

```gdscript
func _to_string() -> String:
	return "parcel %d at %s (%s)" % [id, cell, terrain]
```

**`print(parcel)` now says `parcel 7 at (3, 4) (river)`** rather than `<Resource#-9223...>`. **One function, and every debug print and every test failure message becomes readable.**

**What to put in a resource, and what not:**

| Put in | Keep out |
| --- | --- |
| `@export`ed fields | `_process`, `_ready` |
| Constants naming legal values | tree access — `get_node`, `get_tree` |
| **Pure predicates and computations** about its own data | anything stateful across frames |
| `_to_string()` | signals that drive gameplay (though lesson 14 allows one) |
| Validation | knowledge of nodes |

**The `_init` question.** A resource can have one, and it must have **default arguments for every parameter**, because Godot constructs resources with no arguments when loading a `.tres`:

```gdscript
func _init(i: int = -1, c: Vector2i = Vector2i.ZERO) -> void:
	id = i
	cell = c
```

**Without defaults, loading the `.tres` fails.** That is the one real constraint on a resource's constructor.

**Practice.** Write a `HeroStats` resource with five `@export`ed fields, a `const` naming a legal value, one pure predicate method, and a `_to_string()`. Create a `.tres` from it in the FileSystem dock, fill it in, and print it from a script. Then read `parcel_data.gd` in full and find all six features above.
@export in a Resource, and the Inspector:
How a resource becomes a designer-facing form — the annotations from stage 3, applied where they matter most.

**Everything from stage 3's `@export` lessons works in a resource**, and this is where it pays:

```gdscript
class_name HeroStats
extends Resource

@export_group("Vitals")
@export_range(1, 999) var max_hp: int = 100
@export_range(0, 999) var max_stamina: int = 50

@export_group("Movement")
@export_range(0.0, 500.0, 1.0, "suffix:px/s") var speed: float = 220.0
@export_range(0.0, 4000.0, 10.0) var acceleration: float = 2000.0

@export_group("Identity")
@export var display_name: String = ""
@export_multiline var description: String = ""
@export var portrait: Texture2D
@export var kit: Array[ActionDefinition] = []
```

**Four things that matter more in a resource than in a node:**

**1. Groups, because a resource is a form.** A `HeroStats` with thirty fields is a wall; the same in five named groups is navigable. **A designer will open this file more often than any script**, so the organisation is the interface.

**2. Ranges, because they are validation.** `@export_range(1, 999)` on `max_hp` means nobody sets zero and nobody sets a million. **A range on a designer-facing number is a cheap guard**, and it costs one annotation.

**3. Suffixes, because units are ambiguous.** `"suffix:px/s"` on a speed, `"suffix:s"` on a duration, `"suffix:%"` on a rate. **A number in a form with no unit is a question**, and the suffix answers it in the Inspector.

**4. Typed resource arrays**, which is where it becomes a data layer:

```gdscript
@export var kit: Array[ActionDefinition] = []
```

**The Inspector gives you a list you can add to, reorder, and drop `.tres` files into.** That is how a hero's action set is authored — and lesson 11 covers resource arrays properly.

**`@export_enum` on a String, which your own project uses deliberately:**

```gdscript
@export_enum("plain", "river", "trees", "rock") var terrain: String = PLAIN
```

**A dropdown that stores a string.** From the last lesson, the reason was that the strings already exist in an external JSON file and an enum would be a second copy. **So the dropdown gives the editor affordance without creating a second source of truth** — which is the best of both.

**Compare the three ways to express a closed set:**

| Form | Stored as | Dropdown | Typo-proof | Duplicates an external list |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@export var terrain: String` | string | no | **no** | no |
| `@export_enum("a","b") var t: String` | **string** | **yes** | yes, in the editor | **no** |
| `@export var t: Terrain` (an `enum`) | **int** | yes | **yes** | **yes, if the values exist elsewhere** |

**The middle row is the under-used one**, and it is right whenever the canonical list lives outside Godot.

**Setters, and the guard that differs from a node's.** A resource has no `is_node_ready()`, so the stage-3 guard does not apply — but a setter on a resource **runs while the `.tres` is loading**, field by field, in file order:

```gdscript
@export var max_hp: int = 100:
	set(value):
		max_hp = value
		current_hp = mini(current_hp, max_hp)     # `current_hp` may not be loaded yet
```

**Fields are assigned in the order they appear in the file**, so a setter that reads another field may read its default rather than its saved value. **Keep resource setters to clamping their own value**, and do cross-field work in a method called afterwards.

**`@export_storage`**, from stage 3, which is genuinely useful here: a field that is **saved but not shown**. For a cached or derived value a tool computes:

```gdscript
@export_storage var _baked_neighbours: Dictionary = {}
```

**The `@export_tool_button` annotation**, if your version has it, puts a button in the Inspector that calls a method — which is how a resource gets a *Regenerate* action without a separate tool:

```gdscript
@export_tool_button("Rebuild") var rebuild_action = _rebuild
```

**The documentation payoff.** `##` comments on exported fields appear **in the Inspector as tooltips** as well as in F1:

```gdscript
## Whether anything may be built here at all.
##
## OWNED IS NOT THE SAME AS BUILDABLE, and that is the point of this flag.
@export var buildable: bool = true
```

**That is from your own `parcel_data.gd`**, and hovering the field in the Inspector shows it. **For a designer-facing resource, documenting the fields is the difference between a form and a puzzle.**

**Practice.** Write a `HeroStats` with four groups, ranges on every number, a suffix on each unit, a `@export_multiline` description, a `Texture2D`, and a typed resource array. Document every field with `##`. Then create a `.tres`, open it, and hover the fields to read your own tooltips. Then add a `@export_enum` string and compare it with an `enum` version.
Saving a .tres, and reading one:
The file format, read as text — because a `.tres` is as legible as a `.tscn` and knowing it makes the whole system transparent.

**Open `the-lost-sheep/game/data/island.tres`.** The first line:

```
[gd_resource type="Resource" script_class="IslandData" format=3]
```

| Part | Means |
| --- | --- |
| `gd_resource` | this file is a resource |
| `type="Resource"` | the **engine** base class |
| `script_class="IslandData"` | **your** class, from `class_name` |
| `format=3` | Godot 4 |

**Note `type` and `script_class` are different.** The engine sees a `Resource` with a script attached; your `class_name` is recorded separately. **That is the same mechanism as a node's `script` property from stage 2.**

**Then the external references:**

```
[ext_resource type="Script" path="res://game/scripts/island/parcel_data.gd" id="1_mvtei"]
[ext_resource type="Script" path="res://game/scripts/island/island_data.gd" id="2_02u8y"]
```

**Two scripts**, each with a local id — exactly as a `.tscn` does.

**Then the sub-resources**, which is the part worth studying:

```
[sub_resource type="Resource" id="Resource_pqm5u"]
script = ExtResource("1_mvtei")
id = 0
cell = Vector2i(11, 17)

[sub_resource type="Resource" id="Resource_et6ox"]
script = ExtResource("1_mvtei")
```

**Each `sub_resource` is a `ParcelData`** — a whole resource stored **inside** this file rather than in its own. The first has `id = 0` and `cell = (11, 17)`; the second has **neither**, because both are at their defaults.

**Three facts fall out of that:**

**1. Only non-default values are written**, exactly as for scenes. The second parcel is one line plus its script.

**2. A resource can contain resources.** An `IslandData` holding an `Array[ParcelData]` of a hundred parcels is one file with a hundred `sub_resource` blocks — which lesson 10 covers.

**3. The script is a property.** `script = ExtResource("1_mvtei")` is how each sub-resource knows it is a `ParcelData`.

**Then the resource itself**, at the bott, with its fields and an array referencing the sub-resources by id.

**Why this is worth reading.** Four practical uses:

| Use | |
| --- | --- |
| **A diff** | changing one parcel's terrain is one line in git |
| **A grep** | find every parcel with `terrain = "river"` across the project |
| **A fix** | a broken `ext_resource` path is one line to correct |
| **A bulk edit** | a hundred parcels edited by a script, or by hand in an editor |

**The fourth is genuinely useful.** Hand-editing a hundred `sub_resource` blocks is unpleasant; **a Python script editing the text is ten lines**, and that is how a generated layout gets made. Your project does this — `tools/make_island.gd` generated the placeholder layout, and `island_data.gd`'s header says editing it in the Inspector is how the real one arrives.

**Saving from code:**

```gdscript
var stats := HeroStats.new()
stats.max_hp = 120
ResourceSaver.save(stats, "res://data/hero.tres")
```

**And the flags worth knowing:**

```gdscript
ResourceSaver.save(res, path, ResourceSaver.FLAG_COMPRESS)
ResourceSaver.save(res, path, ResourceSaver.FLAG_BUNDLE_RESOURCES)
```

**`FLAG_BUNDLE_RESOURCES` writes referenced resources into the file** rather than as `ext_resource` paths — a self-contained file, larger and portable.

**Saving to `res://` only works in the editor.** In an exported game `res://` is read-only, from stage 1's FileSystem lesson — so **a tool that generates data saves to `res://` and a game that saves progress saves to `user://`.** Lessons 18 to 21 cover the second.

**`.tres` against `.res`:**

| | `.tres` | `.res` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Format | **text** | binary |
| Diffs | **yes** | no |
| Greppable | **yes** | no |
| Hand-editable | **yes** | no |
| Load speed | slower | faster |
| Size | larger | smaller |

**Use `.tres` for everything you author.** The load-speed difference is irrelevant for a hundred parcels and the git difference is not. **`.res` is for generated or bulk data where nobody will ever read it.**

**And the `.uid` files**, which you will see beside every script in `shepherds-we-shall-be/game/scripts/definitions/`:

```
action_definition.gd
action_definition.gd.uid
```

**A stable unique id per file**, from stage 1's FileSystem lesson, so references survive a file being moved outside Godot. **Commit them; do not edit them.**

**Practice.** Create a `HeroStats` `.tres`, fill in three fields, and open it in a text editor. Change one value by hand, save, and reopen it in Godot. Then set a field back to its default and confirm the line vanishes from the file. Then open `island.tres` and count how many `sub_resource` blocks it has, and find one with no overridden fields.
Loading resources, and the cache:
The four ways to load, and the caching behaviour that explains why two loads give you one object — which is the source of a whole class of surprise.

**The four:**

```gdscript
const STATS := preload("res://data/hero.tres")          # at parse time
var s := load("res://data/hero.tres")                    # when the line runs
var s := ResourceLoader.load(path)                       # the same, with options
ResourceLoader.load_threaded_request(path)               # in the background
```

**`preload` against `load`**, from stage 2's instancing lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `preload` | resolved **at parse time**; a literal path only; the file must exist; free at runtime |
| `load` | resolved **when the line runs**; takes a variable; can fail |

**Use `preload` in a `const` for a path you know**, and `load` when the path is computed.

**The cache, which is the important part of this lesson.**

```gdscript
var a := load("res://data/hero.tres")
var b := load("res://data/hero.tres")
print(a == b)        # true — THE SAME OBJECT
```

**Godot caches loaded resources.** The second `load` returns the object the first one produced. **So two systems that both load the same `.tres` are holding one object, and a change by either is seen by both.**

**That is the single most surprising behaviour in the resource system**, and it is the same sharing problem stage 5's resource lesson and stage 6's material lesson both described, arriving from a third direction.

**The consequences:**

| Situation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Two actors `load` the same stats `.tres` | **one stats object**; damage one, damage both |
| Two sprites share a `ShaderMaterial` | **one material**; flash one, flash both |
| A test modifies a loaded resource | **the modification persists** for the next test in the same process |
| An `@export` slot with the same `.tres` in ten scenes | one object |

**Row three is worth flagging for stage 10's testing**: a test that mutates a cached resource poisons the next one. **Your project's test runner gives every test its own process**, which sidesteps this entirely — and that is one of the reasons it does.

**Controlling it:**

```gdscript
ResourceLoader.load(path, "", ResourceLoader.CACHE_MODE_IGNORE)   # a fresh copy
ResourceLoader.load(path, "", ResourceLoader.CACHE_MODE_REUSE)    # the default
ResourceLoader.load(path, "", ResourceLoader.CACHE_MODE_REPLACE)  # reload and replace
ResourceLoader.has_cached(path)
```

**`CACHE_MODE_IGNORE` gives you an independent object**, which is one of the three fixes. The others:

```gdscript
var mine := load(path).duplicate()        # a shallow copy
var mine := load(path).duplicate(true)    # deep — nested resources copied too
```

**`duplicate()` is the usual answer**, and the `true` matters when the resource contains other resources — which lesson 10 covers. **A shallow duplicate of an `IslandData` shares its hundred `ParcelData`s.**

**Checking before loading:**

```gdscript
if ResourceLoader.exists(path):
	var r := load(path)
```

**`ResourceLoader.exists()` rather than `FileAccess.file_exists()`** for a resource, because it understands remapped and imported paths in an exported build — where the `.png` you reference is actually a `.ctex` in the package.

**Threaded loading**, for anything large enough to hitch:

```gdscript
ResourceLoader.load_threaded_request(path)

func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	var status := ResourceLoader.load_threaded_get_status(path)
	if status == ResourceLoader.THREAD_LOAD_LOADED:
		var r := ResourceLoader.load_threaded_get(path)
```

**And with progress:**

```gdscript
var progress := []
ResourceLoader.load_threaded_get_status(path, progress)
print(progress[0])        # 0.0 to 1.0
```

**For a 2D pixel-art game this is rarely necessary** — the assets are small. **It is the answer for a large scene or a big audio file**, and it is how a loading screen is built.

**Freeing them.** You do not:

```gdscript
var r := load(path)
r = null                  # the reference goes; if it was the last, so does the resource
```

**`Resource` is `RefCounted`, so it is freed when nothing holds it** — from the first lesson of this stage. **Never call `free()` on a resource**, and the cache may keep holding it anyway.

**`take_over_path` and `ResourceUID`**, worth a mention: a resource created in code can claim a path so that future `load`s of that path return it. **Advanced, and occasionally the answer for a generated resource that should behave like a file.**

**Practice.** Load the same `.tres` twice into two variables and confirm they are the same object with `==`. Then change a field through one and read it through the other. Then fix it three ways: `duplicate()`, `CACHE_MODE_IGNORE`, and **Make Unique** in the Inspector. Then assign one `.tres` to three instances of a scene and watch them share state.
Sharing, duplicating, and Make Unique:
The one behaviour of resources that causes real bugs, in one lesson — with the three fixes and the rule for choosing between them.

**The behaviour.** A `Resource` is shared by every reference to it. **Always.** Whether it arrived by `load`, by `preload`, from an `@export` slot, or from the cache.

**The three places it bites:**

**1. Instances of a scene.**

```gdscript
@export var stats: HeroStats
```

**Ten sheep instanced from one scene, with `sheep_stats.tres` in the slot: one `HeroStats`.** Damage one sheep and all ten lose health.

**2. Sub-resources created in the Inspector.** Adding a `CircleShape2D` to a `CollisionShape2D` creates it **inside the scene**, so each instance has its own — **unless** the scene itself is instanced, in which case they share the one in the source scene.

**3. Materials.** From stage 6: one `ShaderMaterial` on a scene means every instance shares it.

**The three fixes.**

**Fix 1: `duplicate()`, in `_ready`.**

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	stats = stats.duplicate()
```

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Per-instance, automatically** | every instance gets its own |
| **Costs** | one object per instance |
| **Deep?** | `duplicate(true)` for nested resources |
| **Loses** | the connection to the file — edits to the `.tres` no longer reach it at runtime |

**This is the usual answer** for runtime state that starts from authored defaults.

**Fix 2: Make Unique, in the Inspector.** Right-click the resource property > **Make Unique**. It converts the shared reference into a copy stored in **this scene**.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Per-scene, at author time** | |
| **Visible** | the `.tscn` now holds a `sub_resource` instead of an `ext_resource` |
| **Right for** | a variant that genuinely differs — a boss's stats |
| **Wrong for** | per-instance runtime state — it is still shared between instances of **this** scene |

**Fix 3: split the definition from the state** — lesson 13, and the correct answer most of the time:

```gdscript
@export var definition: HeroDefinition      # shared, read-only, from a file
var runtime := ActorRuntimeState.new()      # per-instance, not a file
```

**Nothing is duplicated because nothing shared is ever written to.**

**Which to use, as a decision:**

| Situation | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Authored defaults, mutated at runtime | **`duplicate()` in `_ready`** |
| A genuine variant of a thing | **Make Unique**, or a separate `.tres` |
| **Shared state that should be shared** — a party inventory | **nothing. It is correct.** |
| A clean architecture from the start | **split definition from state** |
| Materials on many instances | **`instance uniform`** — stage 6 |

**Row three deserves emphasis: sharing is sometimes exactly right.** A party's shared gold, a world's time of day, a settlement's owned parcels — **one object that several things read and one writes** is the pattern stage 5's resource lesson recommended. **The bug is not sharing; it is sharing by accident.**

**How to tell which you have.** Ask: **should two instances of this scene see each other's changes?** If yes, share. If no, duplicate.

**The read-only guard**, which prevents the accident entirely:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	definition.make_read_only()
```

**Or better, at author time** — a resource marked read-only errors on write rather than silently sharing a mutation. **From stage 3's array lesson**, and it applies to resources too. **For a definition that should never be written, this is the cheapest possible guard.**

**Checking at runtime:**

```gdscript
print(stats.resource_path)        # "" for a duplicated or in-memory resource
print(stats.get_instance_id())    # different per object
print(a == b)                     # true if the same object
```

**`resource_path` being empty is the signal that a resource is not from a file** — which is how you confirm a `duplicate()` worked.

**`resource_local_to_scene`**, which is the fourth fix and the least known:

```gdscript
@export var stats: HeroStats     # with resource_local_to_scene = true on the resource
```

**A resource with `resource_local_to_scene = true` is duplicated automatically for each scene instance.** It is a property on the resource, set in the Inspector, and it does exactly what `duplicate()` in `_ready` does without the code. **Worth knowing; the explicit `duplicate()` is easier to notice when reading.**

**Practice.** Build a sheep scene with an `@export var stats: HeroStats` and a `.tres` assigned. Instance it three times, damage one, and confirm all three change. Fix it with `duplicate()` in `_ready` and confirm independence. Then undo that and set `resource_local_to_scene` on the resource instead. Then call `make_read_only()` on a definition and confirm writing to it errors.
Nested resources, and sub-resources:
A resource containing resources — which is how a data layer gets structure, and how one file holds a hundred objects.

**The declaration is ordinary:**

```gdscript
class_name IslandData
extends Resource

@export var parcels: Array[ParcelData] = []
@export var starting_parcel: ParcelData
```

**A typed array of resources, and a single one.** The Inspector gives you a list to add to and a slot to drop into.

**Where they are stored — two options, and the distinction matters.**

**Inside the parent's file, as a `sub_resource`:**

```
[sub_resource type="Resource" id="Resource_pqm5u"]
script = ExtResource("1_mvtei")
id = 0
cell = Vector2i(11, 17)
```

**Which is what `the-lost-sheep/game/data/island.tres` does** — a hundred `ParcelData`s living inside one `IslandData` file.

**Or in their own files, as an `ext_resource`:**

```
[ext_resource type="Resource" path="res://game/data/parcels/parcel_07.tres" id="3_abc"]
```

**The Inspector decides which you get:** creating a resource in a slot makes it a sub-resource; dragging a `.tres` in makes it external. **Save As on a sub-resource promotes it to a file.**

**Choosing between them:**

| Inline (`sub_resource`) | Separate file (`ext_resource`) |
| --- | --- |
| Belongs to exactly one parent | **shared between parents** |
| Many small parts of one thing | a thing in its own right |
| **One file to open, diff and move** | one file each |
| A hundred parcels of one island | a catalogue of items |
| Git diffs are one file | git diffs are precise |

**A hundred parcels inline is the right call** — they are parts of one island, nobody shares a parcel, and one file is easier to regenerate and to version than a hundred. **A hundred item definitions in separate files is also right**, because an item is referenced from many places.

**Your project does both**, which is the instructive part:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `the-lost-sheep/game/data/island.tres` | **inline** — a hundred `ParcelData` sub-resources |
| `shepherds-we-shall-be/game/resources/definitions/items_catalog.tres` | **a catalogue** — a resource whose job is to hold references |

**The catalogue pattern** is worth naming, because it is how you get both: one resource holding a typed array of **external** resources.

```gdscript
class_name ItemsCatalog
extends Resource

@export var items: Array[ItemDefinition] = []

func by_id(id: StringName) -> ItemDefinition:
	for i in items:
		if i.id == id:
			return i
	return null
```

**One file to load, many files to author.** And your project has several — `items_catalog.tres`, `authored_items_catalog.tres`, `prologue_catalog.tres`, `act_one_catalog.tres` — **one catalogue per act or per purpose**, which is how content is scoped.

**The `by_id` lookup is linear**, which is fine for dozens and not for thousands. **For many, build a dictionary once:**

```gdscript
var _by_id: Dictionary[StringName, ItemDefinition] = {}

func _build_index() -> void:
	_by_id.clear()
	for i in items:
		_by_id[i.id] = i
```

**Called from the thing that loads the catalogue**, not from `_init` — because `_init` runs before the exported array is populated, from the setter caveat in the `@export` lesson.

**The duplication trap, which nesting makes worse:**

```gdscript
var copy := island.duplicate()           # SHALLOW — the same hundred parcels
var copy := island.duplicate(true)       # deep — a hundred new parcels
```

**A shallow duplicate of a nested resource shares its children.** So duplicating an island to make a variant, and then editing a parcel, edits the original's parcel too. **`duplicate(true)` is the fix**, and it is not the default.

**Cycles, which Godot handles badly.** A resource referencing a resource that references the first will serialise, and loading it may not behave. **Avoid them**; if two resources must know about each other, give one an id and look the other up.

**Depth, honestly.** Two levels is comfortable — a catalogue of items, an island of parcels. **Three is a smell**; four means the data wants a different shape, often a flat array plus ids rather than a tree.

**Reading a nested `.tres`**, which is the practice: the sub-resources come first with their ids, and the main resource at the bottom references them:

```
[resource]
script = ExtResource("2_02u8y")
parcels = [SubResource("Resource_pqm5u"), SubResource("Resource_et6ox"), …]
```

**An array of `SubResource` references.** Everything is visible, and a diff that changes one parcel changes one block.

**Practice.** Write an `ItemDefinition` and an `ItemsCatalog` with a typed array of them. Create three item `.tres` files and add them to the catalogue — note they become `ext_resource`s. Then create a fourth **in** the catalogue's array slot and note it becomes a `sub_resource`. Then open `island.tres` and find the main `[resource]` block's `parcels` array. Then duplicate a nested resource shallowly, edit a child, and watch the original change.
Separating definition from runtime state:
The single most useful pattern in this stage — and the fix for the sharing problem that does not need a `duplicate()` anywhere.

**The problem, once more.** An actor's `@export var stats: HeroStats` holds both:

| Kind of value | Example | Should it be shared? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Authored** | `max_hp = 100`, `speed = 220` | **yes** — every sheep has the same maximum |
| **Runtime** | `hp = 73`, `is_stunned = true` | **no** — this sheep's condition |

**Putting both in one resource forces a choice between two wrong answers**: share it and every sheep has one health pool, or duplicate it and lose the connection to the authored file.

**The pattern: two objects.**

```gdscript
# The definition — a Resource, a file, shared, read-only
class_name HeroDefinition
extends Resource

@export_range(1, 999) var max_hp: int = 100
@export_range(0.0, 500.0) var speed: float = 220.0
@export var display_name: String = ""
@export var kit: Array[ActionDefinition] = []
```

```gdscript
# The runtime state — RefCounted, no file, per-instance
class_name ActorRuntimeState
extends RefCounted

var hp: int = 0
var stamina: float = 0.0
var stunned_for: float = 0.0
var facing: Vector2 = Vector2.DOWN
```

```gdscript
# The actor holds one of each
@export var definition: HeroDefinition
var runtime := ActorRuntimeState.new()

func _ready() -> void:
	runtime.hp = definition.max_hp
```

**Nothing is duplicated, because nothing shared is ever written to.**

**And `RefCounted` rather than `Resource` for the state** is the detail that makes it clean:

| | `Resource` | `RefCounted` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Saved to a file | **yes** | no |
| `@export`able | **yes** | no |
| In the Inspector | **yes** | no |
| Cached and shared | **yes** | **no** |
| `new()` per instance | possible | **the only way** |

**Runtime state should not be a file, should not be in the Inspector, and must not be cached.** `RefCounted` gives you exactly that — a plain object, constructed per actor, freed with it.

**Your own actor does precisely this.** From `production_actor.gd`:

```gdscript
var runtime_state := ActorRuntimeState.new()
## **THIS HERO'S STATS**, from their base and what they wear
## (`design/menu-runtime-contract.md` §3). Null until the scene
## hands them over, and then everything below reads them instead of the
## bare definition.
var stats: HeroStats = null
```

**Two objects, and three things to notice in those four lines.**

**1. `runtime_state` is constructed with `new()`** at declaration — per instance, no file, no sharing.

**2. `stats` is `null` until handed over**, which is the told-not-asked pattern from stage 5. The actor does not load its stats.

**3. `stats` is itself a composed thing** — *"from their base and what they wear"* — so it is not the raw definition but a computed combination of a base definition and equipment. **The comment says "everything below reads them instead of the bare definition"**, which means there are three layers:

| Layer | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **The definition** | authored, shared, in a `.tres` |
| **`HeroStats`** | the definition **plus equipment**, computed, per actor |
| **`ActorRuntimeState`** | current condition — hp, stamina, timers |

**Three layers rather than two**, because equipment changes the effective numbers without changing the authored ones. **That is the general shape when modifiers exist:**

```
definition (authored)  →  effective stats (computed)  →  current state (mutable)
```

**And the recomputation rule:** effective stats are recomputed when equipment changes, not every frame. **Caching a computed stat and recomputing on change is right; recomputing in `_process` is waste.**

**Where to put the computation.** On the thing that owns the composition, not on the definition:

```gdscript
# In orchestration — it knows about equipment
static func compose(base: HeroDefinition, worn: Array[ItemDefinition]) -> HeroStats:
	var s := HeroStats.new()
	s.max_hp = base.max_hp
	for item in worn:
		s.max_hp += item.hp_bonus
	return s
```

**A `static func` taking values and returning a new object** — stage 3's static lesson and stage 5's layers lesson agreeing: it is pure, it is testable, and it lives above the definitions it reads.

**The naming convention that makes this readable:**

| Suffix | Kind |
| --- | --- |
| `…Definition` | authored, shared, a `.tres` |
| `…Data` | likewise — `IslandData`, `ParcelData` |
| `…Stats` | computed effective values |
| `…RuntimeState`, `…State` | per-instance, mutable, `RefCounted` |
| `…Catalog` | a collection of definitions |

**Your project uses all five**, which is why `HeroDefinition`, `HeroStats` and `ActorRuntimeState` are distinguishable at a glance.

**Practice.** Split a combined stats resource into a `HeroDefinition` (`Resource`, exported) and an `ActorRuntimeState` (`RefCounted`, `new()`ed). Instance the actor three times with one shared definition and confirm the three have independent health. Then add an equipment layer: a `static func compose()` that produces effective stats from a definition and a list of items, and a recomputation when equipment changes.
Signals on a resource:
A resource that announces its own changes — which turns shared data into a communication channel, and the caveats that come with it.

**Declaring one is ordinary:**

```gdscript
class_name SettlementState
extends Resource

signal changed
signal gold_changed(total: int)

var gold: int = 0:
	set(value):
		gold = value
		gold_changed.emit(gold)
		changed.emit()
```

**And the listener needs no connection to the writer:**

```gdscript
@export var state: SettlementState

func _ready() -> void:
	state.gold_changed.connect(_refresh)
	_refresh(state.gold)
```

**From stage 5's resource lesson**: the writer writes, the reader reads, and the `.tres` in the Inspector is the only thing that knows both. **The signal is what makes the reader not have to poll.**

**Note the `_refresh(state.gold)` after connecting** — the connect-then-call-once rule from stage 5, because a signal reports changes and says nothing about the present.

**The setter pattern is the mechanism.** A plain field cannot announce; a field with a setter can:

```gdscript
var gold: int = 0:
	set(value):
		if gold == value:
			return               # do not emit for a no-op
		gold = value
		changed.emit()
```

**The equality guard is worth having.** Without it, setting gold to the same value emits, and a listener that rebuilds a panel rebuilds it for nothing.

**One signal or many?** Both, usually:

| Signal | For |
| --- | --- |
| `changed` | a coarse *something changed* — a view that redraws wholesale |
| `gold_changed(total)` | a specific listener that only cares about gold |

**Godot's own `Resource` already has a `changed` signal**, emitted when an exported property is modified in the editor — so **declaring your own `changed` shadows it.** Either use the built-in one by calling `emit_changed()`, or name yours differently:

```gdscript
emit_changed()                 # the built-in Resource.changed
```

**`emit_changed()` is the idiomatic form** and it is what the editor itself listens to, which means a `@tool` view can redraw when a designer edits the resource. **That is the mechanism behind lesson 15's live editing.**

**The caveats, and there are four.**

**1. A resource outlives scenes.** It is cached and reference-counted, so a connection from a node that is freed is dropped automatically — **but a connection from an autoload or another resource is not**, and will accumulate. For anything long-lived, disconnect in `_exit_tree`.

**2. A shared resource with signals is shared mutable state.** Three nodes writing to one resource with no coordination is exactly the problem stage 5's event-bus lesson warned about, in a different shape. **One writer, several readers** is the pattern that stays sane.

**3. Signals are not saved.** A `.tres` stores fields, not connections — which is correct, and it means every loader must connect for itself.

**4. The editor emits too.** With a `@tool` script, editing a field in the Inspector fires the setter and the signal **in the editor**, which is what you want for live preview and is surprising the first time a `print` appears while you are not running the game.

**When a resource with signals is the right tool:**

| Situation | |
| --- | --- |
| **Shared state many things read** | settlement gold, time of day, settings |
| **Readers that come and go** | a HUD rebuilt per screen cannot be wired by a parent that is gone |
| **State that must be saved** | it is already a resource |
| **A test that needs to set it up** | `new()`, set fields, assert |

**And when it is not:**

| Situation | Use instead |
| --- | --- |
| An **event** — *the enemy died* | a signal on the enemy |
| Per-instance state | `RefCounted`, no signals — lesson 13 |
| Something only one node reads | just call it |

**The distinction is state against events**, and it is the same one from stage 5's connection table: **a resource holds what is true; a signal on a node reports what happened.** A resource's signal is announcing *the truth changed*, which is a third thing and is legitimate.

**The settings object**, which is the clearest case:

```gdscript
class_name Settings
extends Resource

@export var master_volume: float = 1.0:
	set(v):
		master_volume = v
		emit_changed()
@export var animations_enabled: bool = true:
	set(v):
		animations_enabled = v
		emit_changed()
```

**Loaded once, `@export`ed into whatever needs it, saved to `user://`** — lesson 18 — **and every consumer reacts to `changed`.** No autoload, no bus, and it is testable.

**Practice.** Write a `SettlementState` resource with a `gold` setter that calls `emit_changed()` and a no-op guard. Assign the same `.tres` to a writer node and two reader nodes in separate scenes. Confirm both readers update with no connection between them and the writer. Then add the equality guard and confirm a redundant set emits nothing. Then make it `@tool` and edit gold in the Inspector, and watch the readers respond in the editor.
@tool, and running in the editor:
The annotation that makes a script run while you are editing — and the one your project's engine choice was conditional on.

**What it does.** `@tool` at the very top of a script makes it **execute in the editor**, not only in the running game.

```gdscript
@tool
extends Node2D

func _draw() -> void:
	draw_rect(Rect2(Vector2.ZERO, Vector2(32, 32)), Color.RED)
```

**That rectangle now appears in the editor viewport**, without pressing F5.

**Why it matters here.** Because a data layer you cannot see is a data layer you cannot author. **An `IslandData` with a hundred parcels is a hundred rows in the Inspector; the same data drawn as a map is editable.**

**And your project's engine choice depended on it.** From `the-lost-sheep/game/scripts/island/parcel_data.gd`:

> *A Resource rather than a dictionary, because BRIEF.md makes Godot a CONDITIONAL recommendation — conditional on the map, characters and buildings being editable in the editor rather than in code. Everything the island is made of therefore has to be an Inspector-editable Resource with an @tool script drawing it live. This is the first test of that condition.*

**And from `island_view.gd`:**

> *@tool, because Godot's place in this project is CONDITIONAL on the map being editable in the editor rather than in code. Change `island` in the Inspector, or edit the .tres, and the viewport redraws without running the game. That condition is the thing this file exists to prove.*

**So `@tool` is not a convenience in that project — it is the reason the engine was accepted.**

**What runs in the editor with `@tool`:**

| Callback | Runs in the editor |
| --- | --- |
| `_init` | **yes** |
| `_enter_tree`, `_ready`, `_exit_tree` | **yes** |
| `_draw` | **yes** |
| `_process`, `_physics_process` | **yes** — and this is the dangerous one |
| `_get_configuration_warnings` | yes — lesson 17 |
| `_notification` | yes |
| Setters on `@export`s | **yes** |

**`_process` running in the editor is the thing to be careful about.** It runs constantly while the editor is open, on every `@tool` node in every open scene. **Guard it:**

```gdscript
func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	if Engine.is_editor_hint():
		return
	...
```

**`Engine.is_editor_hint()` is the test**: true in the editor, false in the running game. **It is the other half of `@tool`** and almost every `@tool` script needs it somewhere:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	if Engine.is_editor_hint():
		_build_preview()
		return
	_start_the_game_properly()
```

**The three things `@tool` is genuinely for:**

| Use | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Previewing data** | `island_view.gd` drawing the map from a `.tres` |
| **Generating or validating content** | a script that builds a layout, or checks one |
| **Editor affordances** | configuration warnings, gizmos, buttons |

**And the three things it is not for:** gameplay, anything with side effects outside the project, and anything slow.

**The dangers, stated plainly.** A `@tool` script is **code running in your editor**, so:

| Danger | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| An infinite loop | **the editor hangs**, and you lose unsaved work |
| An exception in `_ready` | the scene may fail to open |
| Writing files | it writes them while you are editing |
| `queue_free()` on editor nodes | you can delete your own scene's contents |
| A slow `_process` | the editor becomes sluggish |

**The habit: save before testing a `@tool` script.** A hang means killing the editor.

**Adding nodes from a `@tool` script**, which needs the `owner` rule from stage 2:

```gdscript
@tool
extends Node2D

func _rebuild() -> void:
	for c in get_children():
		c.queue_free()
	var m := Marker2D.new()
	add_child(m)
	m.owner = get_tree().edited_scene_root        # ← or it will not be saved
```

**Without the `owner` line the node appears and vanishes on reload**, which is stage 2's owner lesson arriving with a practical consequence.

**A button in the Inspector**, which is the neatest way to trigger a tool action:

```gdscript
@export_tool_button("Rebuild") var rebuild_action = _rebuild
```

**Or, in versions without it, the older idiom:**

```gdscript
@export var rebuild: bool = false:
	set(_v):
		rebuild = false
		_rebuild()
```

**A checkbox that immediately unticks itself and does the work.** Ugly and effective.

**Practice.** Write a `@tool` script on a `Node2D` that draws a grid from an `@export var cell: int`. Change `cell` in the Inspector and watch the editor redraw. Then add a `_process` without a guard and notice the editor working constantly; add `Engine.is_editor_hint()` and fix it. Then add a node from a tool function, save, reload, and watch it vanish — then add the `owner` line.
The @tool contagion rule:
The constraint that shapes an entire architecture — `@tool` spreads, and your project has two files documenting the exact failure.

**The rule.** **A `@tool` script may only call into other `@tool` scripts.**

**Why.** In the editor, a script **without** `@tool` is not executed. Godot still loads the resource, but as a **placeholder** — an object of the right type with no working methods. **Calling anything on it fails.**

**The error, which your project found by hitting it.** From `the-lost-sheep/game/scripts/island/island_data.gd`:

> *@tool, and not optionally. island_view.gd is @tool and calls neighbours(), parcel() and by_cell() from _draw; without this the editor loads this script as a placeholder instance and every one of those calls fails with "Attempt to call a method on a placeholder instance". Found by opening the editor, 12 October 2026 — the checks could never have caught it, because they run the game rather than the editor.*

**Three things in that comment are worth separating.**

**1. The error message is specific**: *"Attempt to call a method on a placeholder instance."* **Recognising it tells you immediately that something in a `@tool` chain is missing its annotation.**

**2. The scope of the contagion**: `island_view.gd` is `@tool` and calls three methods on `IslandData`, so **`IslandData` must be `@tool` too** — and `ParcelData`, which `IslandData` holds, for the same reason. Its own header says so:

> *@tool, because island_view.gd is @tool and draws these in the editor. A non-tool script loads in the editor as a PLACEHOLDER whose methods cannot be called, so the view fails the moment it asks a parcel anything.*

**Three files, one annotation each, because one of them draws in the editor.**

**3. The tests could not catch it.** *"the checks could never have caught it, because they run the game rather than the editor."* **A `@tool` failure is invisible to a test suite** that launches the game, because in the game every script runs normally. **The only way to find it is to open the editor** — which is a real limit on automated verification and worth knowing about.

**The architectural consequence, which is the interesting part.** Contagion means *the view asks the model* would require marking the whole model `@tool`. So `island_view.gd` does not ask — it is **told**, in plain dictionaries:

> *IT IS A VIEW, and it is handed plain dictionaries rather than the settlement. York holds what is owned and what is built; this draws what it is told. The reason is the @tool rule above: a tool script may only call into tool scripts, so every object this one touches would have to become a tool script too. Passing values instead keeps that surface down to the island and its parcels.*

**The contagion was contained at a boundary by changing the data that crosses it.** Dictionaries, not objects — which stage 5's payload lesson used as its best example of choosing a loose type deliberately.

**So the rule produces a design principle: decide what the `@tool` surface is, and make its boundary values rather than objects.**

**The practical checklist for a `@tool` chain:**

| Check | |
| --- | --- |
| The script that draws or builds | `@tool` |
| Every `Resource` class whose **methods** it calls | `@tool` |
| Every class whose **methods** those call | `@tool` |
| Classes it only reads **fields** from | **not required** — field access works on a placeholder |
| Anything beyond the boundary | pass **values**, not objects |

**Row four is a useful subtlety: reading a property works, calling a method does not.** A placeholder holds the serialised values, so `parcel.terrain` is fine and `parcel.takes_a("farm")` is not. **Which means a data class with no methods needs no `@tool`** — and the moment you add a predicate to it, it does.

**That is a genuinely awkward property**, because adding a method to a resource can break the editor for a file that never changed. **The mitigation is to mark data classes `@tool` from the start** if anything `@tool` will ever touch them, which costs nothing at runtime.

**Does `@tool` cost anything in the game?** Essentially no. The annotation is ignored at runtime; the only cost is the `Engine.is_editor_hint()` guards you add. **So marking a data class `@tool` pre-emptively is close to free.**

**The diagnostic procedure**, when the editor reports a placeholder error:

1. **Read the message** — it names the method.
2. **Find the class that method belongs to.**
3. **Add `@tool` at the top.**
4. **Reload the scene** — Godot caches the placeholder, so the error persists until you reopen.
5. **Repeat** until the chain is complete.

**Step four is the one that wastes time.** The fix does not appear until the scene is reloaded, so it is easy to conclude the annotation did not work.

**Practice.** Build a `@tool` view that calls a method on a non-`@tool` resource, open the scene, and read the exact error. Add `@tool` to the resource, reload, and confirm it works. Then add a second resource one level deeper, call a method on it, and watch the chain fail again. Then convert one boundary to pass a `Dictionary` instead and confirm the contagion stops there.
Configuration warnings, and editor feedb:
Making your own nodes tell you when they are set up wrongly — the editor affordance that costs five lines and saves hours.

**The warning triangle**, from stage 1: a node with a configuration problem shows a yellow triangle in the Scene dock, and hovering it explains. **Godot's own nodes use it constantly** — a `CharacterBody2D` with no shape, an `Area2D` with nothing to collide with.

**Your own nodes can too:**

```gdscript
@tool
extends Node2D

@export var island: IslandData

func _get_configuration_warnings() -> PackedStringArray:
	var w: PackedStringArray = []
	if island == null:
		w.append("No IslandData assigned. Nothing will be drawn.")
	elif island.parcels.is_empty():
		w.append("The assigned IslandData has no parcels.")
	return w
```

**Three requirements:**

1. **The script must be `@tool`** — the editor has to run the method.
2. **Return a `PackedStringArray`** — empty means no warning.
3. **Call `update_configuration_warnings()`** when the condition changes, or the triangle is stale:

```gdscript
@export var island: IslandData:
	set(value):
		island = value
		update_configuration_warnings()
		queue_redraw()
```

**Without that call the warning only refreshes when the scene reloads**, which makes it look broken.

**What to warn about — the four kinds that earn their place:**

| Kind | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **A required reference is null** | *"No IslandData assigned."* |
| **A required child is missing** | *"This node needs a CollisionShape2D child."* |
| **A value is nonsensical** | *"cell must be greater than zero."* |
| **A combination is wrong** | *"only_types is set but buildable is false; nothing can be built here."* |

**The fourth is the valuable one.** Two fields that individually look fine and together mean nothing is exactly what a designer will produce, and a warning is the cheapest possible guard.

**Write the message as an instruction, not a complaint.** *"No IslandData assigned. Nothing will be drawn."* tells you what is wrong **and what happens because of it**. *"Invalid configuration"* tells you neither.

**The other editor affordances worth knowing.**

**`@icon`**, which gives your class its own icon in the Scene dock and the Create Node dialog:

```gdscript
@tool
@icon("res://editor/icons/island.svg")
class_name IslandView
extends Node2D
```

**A 16×16 SVG.** It costs nothing and it makes a tree of custom nodes readable at a glance, which matters once a project has twenty of them.

**`_to_string()`**, from the resource lesson, which improves every print and every error:

```gdscript
func _to_string() -> String:
	return "parcel %d at %s (%s)" % [id, cell, terrain]
```

**`_validate_property()`**, which hides or alters a property in the Inspector conditionally:

```gdscript
func _validate_property(property: Dictionary) -> void:
	if property.name == "only_types" and not buildable:
		property.usage = PROPERTY_USAGE_NO_EDITOR
```

**A field that is irrelevant given another field's value simply disappears.** That is a better answer than a warning for a genuinely inapplicable field, and it is the polish that makes a resource feel designed.

**`_get_property_list()`**, for properties that do not exist as variables — fully dynamic Inspector content. **Powerful, verbose, and rarely necessary.**

**Editor-only drawing**, which pairs with configuration warnings:

```gdscript
func _draw() -> void:
	if not Engine.is_editor_hint():
		return
	draw_rect(Rect2(Vector2.ZERO, Vector2(cell, cell)), Color(1, 1, 0, 0.3), false)
```

**A bounds box, a radius, a direction arrow — visible while authoring and absent in the game.** For a node whose effect is invisible — a spawn point, a trigger volume, a camera limit — **this is the difference between placeable and guesswork.**

**The combination worth building into every custom node you expect to place by hand:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `@tool` | so the editor runs it |
| `@icon` | so it is identifiable |
| `_get_configuration_warnings()` | so mistakes are visible |
| `_draw` gated on `is_editor_hint()` | so its extent is visible |
| `_to_string()` | so debugging it is readable |
| `##` on every `@export` | so the Inspector has tooltips |

**Six small things, perhaps thirty lines**, and the node becomes something a person can use rather than something only its author understands.

**Practice.** Take a custom node with a required `@export` and add `_get_configuration_warnings()` for the null case, with `update_configuration_warnings()` in the setter. Confirm the triangle appears and clears. Then add an editor-only `_draw` showing its extent. Then add an `@icon`. Then add `_validate_property` to hide one field when another is false.
A definitions folder: the pattern:
How a data layer is organised on disk — the convention your project uses, and the naming that makes it navigable.

**The split: schema in `scripts/`, data in `resources/`.**

```
game/
├── scripts/
│   └── definitions/            ← the CLASSES. 24 files.
│       ├── action_definition.gd
│       ├── attribute_definition.gd
│       ├── beacon_form_definition.gd
│       ├── combination_definition.gd
│       └── …
└── resources/
    └── definitions/            ← the DATA. .tres files.
        ├── items_catalog.tres
        ├── authored_items_catalog.tres
        ├── prologue_catalog.tres
        ├── act_one_catalog.tres
        └── …
```

**And `REPOSITORY_STRUCTURE.md` states the rule:**

> *What `game/resources/` is: Godot **Resource** data files (`.tres`), not artwork. Hero kits, skill trees, items, conversations, map defs, and similar editable data that scripts load. Code stays in `game/scripts/`; scenes in `game/scenes/`; data in `game/resources/`.*

**Three directories, three kinds of thing, one sentence.** That is the whole convention and it is worth copying.

**Why separate the class from the data.** Four reasons:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **They change at different rates** | a schema is edited rarely; data constantly |
| **They are edited by different means** | code in an editor, data in the Inspector |
| **Git diffs stay meaningful** | a schema change and a balance change are separate commits |
| **The layer rule** | `scripts/definitions/` is the definitions **layer**; the `.tres` files are its content |

**The naming convention**, from stage 5's services lesson and visible in the folder listing:

| Suffix | Kind |
| --- | --- |
| `…_definition.gd` | **a schema** — one kind of thing |
| `…_catalog.tres` | **a collection** of them, scoped |
| `…Data` | a schema for structure rather than a thing — `IslandData`, `ParcelData` |
| `…_rules_definition.gd` | a schema holding rules rather than values |

**`beacon_rules_definition.gd` beside `beacon_form_definition.gd`** is the pattern doing real work: the **form** of a beacon and the **rules** governing beacons are different schemas, because one is per-beacon content and the other is global policy. **Conflating them would mean every beacon carrying a copy of the rules.**

**The catalogue scoping, which is the part worth noticing.** Four catalogues:

| Catalogue | Scope |
| --- | --- |
| `items_catalog.tres` | the full set |
| `authored_items_catalog.tres` | the hand-made ones |
| `prologue_catalog.tres` | what exists in the prologue |
| `act_one_catalog.tres` | what exists in act one |
| `test_items_catalog.tres` | **what the tests use** |

**Content scoped per act means an act can be loaded without the rest** — and `test_items_catalog.tres` means tests do not depend on shipping content, so rebalancing an item cannot break a test. **That last one is a genuinely good idea and it is cheap.**

**The `.uid` files**, which you will see beside every script:

```
action_definition.gd
action_definition.gd.uid
```

**A stable id per file**, from stage 1, so a `.tres` referencing a script survives the script being moved outside Godot. **Commit them, do not edit them, do not delete them.**

**What goes in `definitions/` and what does not:**

| In | Out |
| --- | --- |
| `extends Resource` schemas | anything with `_process` |
| Constants naming legal values | tree access |
| Pure predicates about own data | gameplay behaviour |
| Loaders and parsers | presentation |
| Validation | anything about nodes |

**"Loaders and parsers" earns its place there** — `the-lost-sheep/game/scripts/numbers.gd` is a loader for the JSON authority and it belongs with the definitions, because it produces definitions and depends on nothing.

**For a smaller project.** `the-lost-sheep` has no `definitions/` folder at all — its data classes sit beside the things that use them:

```
game/scripts/island/
├── island_data.gd       ← schema
├── parcel_data.gd       ← schema
├── site_data.gd         ← schema
├── wild_data.gd         ← schema
├── island_view.gd       ← presentation
└── island_camera.gd
game/data/
├── island.tres
├── numbers.json
└── …
```

**Organised by subject, with the data in one `data/` folder.** At 69 scripts that is clearer than a layer split; at 535 it would not be. **The invariant that survives both is: data files live apart from code**, which both projects honour.

**Practice.** Create a `definitions/` folder with three `…Definition` schemas and a `…Catalog`. Put the `.tres` files in a separate `resources/definitions/`. Then make a second catalogue scoped to tests, with its own items, and write a test that uses it. Then look at `shepherds-we-shall-be/game/scripts/definitions/` and name what each of six files is for from its filename alone.
JSON as the authority:
When the canonical data lives outside Godot — a legitimate and sometimes necessary arrangement, with your own project as the worked example.

**The situation.** A `.tres` is excellent for data Godot owns. **It is a poor choice when something other than Godot must also read or prove the data** — a Python simulation, a web tool, a spreadsheet export, a server.

**Your project's case.** `the-lost-sheep/data/numbers.json` opens by declaring itself:

```json
"_": "The Lost Sheep: Black Pastures -- every number in the game, in one file.",
"_authority": "This file is the source of truth. design/the-numbers.md explains it; tools/simulate.py proves it; a Godot build loads it."
```

**Three consumers, named in the file**: a document explains it, a **Python simulation proves it**, and the Godot build loads it. **A `.tres` could not be read by the Python model**, so the authority has to be a format both understand.

**And it holds everything** — twenty-six sections: `clock`, `win`, `island`, `people`, `skills`, `mood`, `food`, `illness`, `buildings`, `signal`, `research`, `york_level`, `money`, `expeditions`, `wall`, `attacks`, `demand`, `tutorial`, `merging`, `warehouse`, `session`, `opening`, `interface`. **Every number in the game, in one file**, which is the claim the `_` key makes.

**The loader.** `game/scripts/numbers.gd`:

```gdscript
@tool
class_name Numbers
extends RefCounted

const PATH := "res://data/numbers.json"

static var _root: Dictionary = {}
static var _loaded := false
```

**Four decisions in those lines, each from an earlier lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `@tool` | **the contagion rule** — its header says *"because IslandData is @tool and reads the numbers"* |
| `extends RefCounted` | not a `Resource` and not a node — a static loader |
| `static var _root` | **loaded once, cached on the class** — stage 3's static lesson |
| `const PATH` | one place for the path |

**And a detail worth noticing from its header:**

> *…it reads the file itself — the project root is the repository root precisely so that `res://data/numbers.json` is the same bytes the simulation gates.*

**The Godot project root was placed at the repository root so that the engine and the Python model read the identical file.** That is a project-layout decision made to serve a data decision, and it is the kind of thing that is invisible unless written down.

**Reading JSON in Godot:**

```gdscript
static func load_numbers() -> String:
	if _loaded:
		return ""
	if not FileAccess.file_exists(PATH):
		return "missing %s" % PATH
	var text := FileAccess.get_file_as_string(PATH)
	var parsed: Variant = JSON.parse_string(text)
	if parsed == null or not parsed is Dictionary:
		return "could not parse %s" % PATH
	_root = parsed
	_loaded = true
	return ""
```

**`JSON.parse_string` returns `null` on failure** rather than raising, so the check is mandatory. **And returning a reason string rather than a bool** is the pattern that project uses — the caller gets something it can print.

**The alternative API, when you want the error position:**

```gdscript
var j := JSON.new()
var err := j.parse(text)
if err != OK:
	push_error("%s at line %d: %s" % [PATH, j.get_error_line(), j.get_error_message()])
```

**`get_error_line()` is worth it for a file a human edits.** *"Parse failed"* is unhelpful; *"line 412"* is not.

**Writing JSON:**

```gdscript
var text := JSON.stringify(data, "	")        # indented, readable
var f := FileAccess.open("user://save.json", FileAccess.WRITE)
f.store_string(text)
```

**The `"	"` indent argument** makes the output readable, which matters for anything a person will open.

**What JSON cannot hold**, and this is the cost:

| Not representable | Becomes |
| --- | --- |
| `Vector2`, `Vector2i`, `Color`, `Rect2` | you must encode them — `[x, y]` or `{"x":…}` |
| Integers against floats | **everything is a float** — `1` parses as `1.0` |
| `StringName` | a plain string |
| A resource reference | a path or an id string |
| A comment | **nothing — JSON has no comments** |

**The integer problem catches everyone.** `JSON.parse_string('{"n": 3}')` gives you `3.0`, so:

```gdscript
var n := int(data["n"])        # cast, every time
```

**And the no-comments problem** is why that file uses `_` and `_authority` keys — **leading-underscore keys as documentation**, which is a convention worth copying since JSON gives you nothing better.

**When to choose JSON over `.tres`:**

| Choose JSON | Choose `.tres` |
| --- | --- |
| **Something outside Godot must read it** | only Godot reads it |
| A human edits it in a text editor | a designer edits it in the Inspector |
| It is generated by another tool | it references Godot resources |
| It must be diffed by non-Godot tools | you want typed fields and validation |
| **It is the authority for a simulation** | it is content |

**And the honest cost of JSON**: no types, no Inspector, no validation, everything a float, and no resource references. **Which is why the next lesson is about validation** — a JSON authority needs a reader that refuses bad data, because the format will not refuse it for you.

**Practice.** Write a small `numbers.json` with three sections, and a `Numbers` static loader with a cached `static var` and a path `const`. Load it, cast an integer, and print it. Then break the JSON deliberately and use `JSON.new()` to report the line. Then try to store a `Vector2` in it and work out your own encoding.
Validating data, and failing loudly:
The discipline a loose data format demands — and the best single principle in your codebase about it.

**The principle, from `the-lost-sheep/game/scripts/numbers.gd`:**

> *NOTHING HERE MAY DEFAULT. A missing key raises rather than falling back to a plausible value, because a plausible value is how a game quietly stops being the one that was proved.*

**Read that second clause again.** A default is not a safety net — it is a silent substitution. **The game keeps running with a number nobody chose**, and since a Python simulation proves those numbers, the running game has quietly stopped being the thing that was proved.

**So the reader is built to refuse:**

> *`require()` is the reader for everything that must be there; `optional()` is for the one shape of field whose absence is itself the meaning, and its own note says why it is not a softer `require()`.*

**Two readers, and the distinction is semantic rather than convenient:**

| Reader | For |
| --- | --- |
| **`require(path)`** | everything. A missing key is a **bug**. |
| **`optional(path)`** | **one** shape of field, where **absence is a meaning** |

**Not "required and optional" as a convenience** — `optional` exists for the case where *not present* is itself data, and the comment on it says why it is not simply a `require` with a default. **That is the right way to think about it:** there is no third category of *missing but we'll cope*.

**The shape of such a reader:**

```gdscript
static func require(path: String) -> Variant:
	var node: Variant = _root
	for key in path.split("."):
		if not node is Dictionary or not node.has(key):
			push_error("numbers.json: missing %s" % path)
			assert(false, "numbers.json: missing %s" % path)
			return null
		node = node[key]
	return node
```

```gdscript
var ticks: int = int(Numbers.require("clock.ticks_per_day"))
```

**Four things in that:** a dotted path for nesting, a `push_error` that survives a release build, an `assert` that stops the editor immediately — from stage 3's errors lesson — and a named path in the message so the fix is obvious.

**Where to validate, and the answer is: once, at the boundary.**

| Place | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| **At load**, as the file is read | **yes** — the whole file, once |
| At each use | no — the same check, a thousand times |
| In a test | **yes, as well** — a test that loads and validates |
| Never | the default behaviour, and the thing to avoid |

**A whole-file check is the strongest form**, and your project has one: `check_island.gd`, which `island_data.gd`'s header describes:

> *What the two must agree on is the count, and `check_island.gd` asserts it rather than trusting it.*

**A script whose only job is to assert that two independent things agree** — the authored island's parcel count and the number the simulation assumes. **Not a test of behaviour; a test of consistency between two sources.** That is a category of check worth knowing about, and it catches the class of bug where both halves are internally correct and disagree with each other.

**The four kinds of validation, in order of value:**

| Kind | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Presence** | the key exists. `require()`. |
| **Type** | it is a number, not a string |
| **Range** | it is positive; it is a percentage |
| **Cross-consistency** | **two sources agree** — `check_island.gd` |

**The fourth is the one people skip and the one that finds real bugs**, because the first three are local and the fourth is not.

**For `.tres` data**, validation is partly free — typed fields mean a string cannot land in an `int`, and `@export_range` bounds it, from the `@export` lesson. **What remains is presence and cross-consistency:**

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	assert(definition != null, "%s has no definition assigned." % name)
```

**And for an editor-facing resource, `_get_configuration_warnings()`** from lesson 17 is better than an assert, because it tells you before you run.

**Failing loudly against failing safe**, which is a real tension:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Fail loudly** in development | an assert, so the mistake is unmissable |
| **Fail safely** in a shipped build | `push_error` and a defensible fallback, so the player is not stranded |

**`assert` gives you both for free**, from stage 3: it runs in the editor and a debug export and is **stripped from a release build**. So:

```gdscript
assert(ticks > 0, "clock.ticks_per_day must be positive")
if ticks <= 0:
	push_error("clock.ticks_per_day must be positive; using 1")
	ticks = 1
```

**Assert first, then handle.** The assert catches it during development; the handling keeps a shipped build alive. **And the fallback is logged**, so it is not silent — which is the whole objection to defaults answered.

**The test that proves the data loads**, which is the cheapest insurance there is:

```gdscript
extends SceneTree

func _initialize() -> void:
	var err := Numbers.load_numbers()
	if err != "":
		push_error(err)
		quit(1)
	_check(int(Numbers.require("clock.ticks_per_day")) > 0, "ticks must be positive")
	quit(0)
```

**A test that does nothing but load and validate the authority.** It runs in a second, it catches a malformed file before the game does, and stage 10's runner will run it with everything else.

**Practice.** Write `require()` with a dotted path, a `push_error`, an `assert` and a named path in the message. Delete a key from your JSON and confirm the failure names the path. Then add a whole-file validation pass that checks presence, type and range for every key you use. Then write a cross-consistency check between two independent sources and make them disagree.
Saving a game: the file, and the format:
Writing the player's progress to disk — the format decision, with your project's reasoning, and the mechanics.

**The format decision first, because it shapes everything.** Three options:

| Format | For |
| --- | --- |
| **JSON** | readable, diagnosable, portable, larger |
| **`.tres` via `ResourceSaver`** | typed, Godot-native, readable, resource references |
| **Binary via `FileAccess`** | small, fast, opaque |

**Your project chose JSON, and said why.** From `the-lost-sheep/game/scripts/saves.gd`:

> *WHY JSON RATHER THAN A BINARY BLOB. Every other piece of state in this project is readable — data/numbers.json, the replay fixtures — and a save you can open in an editor is a save you can diagnose from a description of what went wrong. It costs file size and nothing else, and none of it is secret.*

**Three arguments, each worth taking.**

**1. Consistency.** Every other piece of state in the project is readable, so a readable save is the least surprising choice.

**2. Diagnosability.** *"a save you can open in an editor is a save you can diagnose from a description of what went wrong."* **A player who says "my gold went negative" can send you the file**, and you can read it. With a binary blob you need a tool.

**3. The cost is named and dismissed.** *"It costs file size and nothing else, and none of it is secret."* **File size is irrelevant for a save**, and the anti-tamper argument does not apply to a single-player game. **Naming the cost and judging it is better than not considering it.**

**The anti-tamper point deserves a sentence.** A readable save can be edited by the player. **For a single-player game that is a feature**, or at worst harmless. For anything competitive or monetised it is not — and then you want a checksum, not obscurity.

**The mechanics, with `FileAccess`:**

```gdscript
const PATH := "user://save_1.json"

static func save(data: Dictionary) -> void:
	var f := FileAccess.open(PATH, FileAccess.WRITE)
	if f == null:
		push_error("could not open %s: %d" % [PATH, FileAccess.get_open_error()])
		return
	f.store_string(JSON.stringify(data, "	"))

static func load_save() -> Dictionary:
	if not FileAccess.file_exists(PATH):
		return {}
	var f := FileAccess.open(PATH, FileAccess.READ)
	if f == null:
		push_error("could not read %s" % PATH)
		return {}
	var parsed: Variant = JSON.parse_string(f.get_as_text())
	return parsed if parsed is Dictionary else {}
```

**Five things to note:**

**1. `user://`, not `res://`** — from stage 1: `res://` is read-only in an exported game, so a save written there works in the editor and fails when shipped. **The single commonest save bug.**

**2. `FileAccess.open` returns `null` on failure**, and `FileAccess.get_open_error()` says why. **Check it** — a full disk, a permissions problem, a path that does not exist.

**3. No `f.close()`.** `FileAccess` is `RefCounted`, so the file closes when the reference goes. **Calling `close()` is allowed and unnecessary**; letting it go out of scope is idiomatic.

**4. `JSON.stringify(data, "	")`** for a readable file, from the JSON lesson.

**5. The load returns `{}` rather than failing** when there is no save, because *no save* is a legitimate state. **That is the `optional` case from the validation lesson** — absence is a meaning.

**Multiple save slots**, which your project has:

> *MASTER ROACHI'S RULING, 13 October 2026: three profiles, each with a name, chosen on a profile screen reached from the title. The SELECTED profile is what Continue continues and what New game offers to overwrite.*

**Three profiles, one save each.** And the ruling changed an earlier decision:

> *This changes BRIEF.md's form table, which said "One save, cloud-synced between PC and mobile" — it is still one save per profile, there are simply three of them, and the sync question is unchanged for each.*

**Note how the change is recorded**: what the old document said, what the new ruling is, and **explicitly which parts are unchanged.** That last clause prevents someone concluding the sync decision was also overturned.

**The slot pattern:**

```gdscript
const SLOTS := 3

static func path_for(slot: int) -> String:
	return "user://profile_%d.json" % slot

static func exists(slot: int) -> bool:
	return FileAccess.file_exists(path_for(slot))
```

**And a small index file** holding which slot is selected, so Continue knows what to continue.

**Atomic saving**, which matters and is easy:

```gdscript
static func save_atomic(path: String, text: String) -> void:
	var tmp := path + ".tmp"
	var f := FileAccess.open(tmp, FileAccess.WRITE)
	if f == null:
		return
	f.store_string(text)
	f = null                                   # close it
	DirAccess.rename_absolute(
		ProjectSettings.globalize_path(tmp),
		ProjectSettings.globalize_path(path))
```

**Write to a temporary file, then rename over the real one.** A crash mid-write then leaves the old save intact rather than a half-written one. **For a game that autosaves, this is worth the six lines.**

**When to save.** Autosave at natural boundaries — a day ending, a screen changing — rather than on a timer, because a timer can fire mid-transaction. **And always offer a manual save** if the game is long.

**Practice.** Write a save and load pair using `user://`, `JSON.stringify` with indentation, and error checks on `FileAccess.open`. Save, then open the file in a text editor and read it. Then implement three slots with `path_for(slot)` and an index file recording the selection. Then make the write atomic and test it by killing the game mid-save.
What not to save, and migration:
The two hardest parts of saving — deciding what belongs in a save, and keeping old saves loadable — with your project's answer to the first.

**The principle: save what changed, not what is.**
