```gdscript
ground.set_pattern(at, pattern)
```

**`get_pattern` / `set_pattern` is the built-in stamp**, and it is what the editor's Patterns tab produces. **Prefer it to the manual loop.**

**Performance, honestly.** `set_cell` is cheap individually and not free in bulk:

| Operation | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| One `set_cell` | negligible |
| A thousand in one frame | **noticeable** — the quadrant must redraw |
| `get_used_cells()` | allocates an array of every cell |
| `get_cell_tile_data` per frame per actor | fine |
| `get_used_cells()` per frame | **no** — cache it |

**Generating a large map should happen once**, at load or in a tool, not per frame. **And if it must happen at runtime, spread it over frames** with the `await get_tree().process_frame` chunking from stage 3's `await` lesson.

**The signal for changes:**

```gdscript
ground.changed.connect(_on_map_changed)
```

**`changed` fires when cells are modified** — useful for a minimap or a navigation rebuild that must follow the map.

**And `update_internals()`**, which you occasionally need: after a bulk edit, call it to force collision and navigation to rebuild immediately rather than at the end of the frame.

**Practice.** Write a function that sets a cell under the mouse on click, and another that erases on right-click. Then write a breakable wall that erases its cell and confirm collision disappears. Then collect every `water` cell with `get_used_cells()` and custom data. Then copy a 3×3 region with `get_pattern` and stamp it elsewhere.
Scenes as tiles:
Painting scenes onto a grid rather than textures — the feature that bridges tiles and nodes, and when it is the right answer.

**What it is.** A `TileSet` can hold a **Scene Collection** source: instead of a texture region, each entry is a `PackedScene`. **Painting one instances the scene at that cell.**

**The setup:**

1. In the TileSet panel, **+ > Scene Collection**.
2. Drag `.tscn` files into it, or use its + button.
3. Paint from it like any other source.

**What you get.** A real node per painted cell, instanced as a child of the `TileMapLayer` — with its script, its signals, its collision, its animation and its `_ready`.

**So each one can do things**, which is the whole point:

| Tiles (texture) | Scenes as tiles |
| --- | --- |
| Drawn in a batch | **a node each** |
| No script | **a script each** |
| Shared collision body | **own body** |
| No signals | **signals** |
| No animation | **`AnimationPlayer`, `AnimatedSprite2D`** |
| Thousands, cheaply | **dozens** |

**When it is the right answer — four cases:**

| Case | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **A door, a chest, a lever** | it has state and must be interacted with |
| **A torch, a fountain** | it is animated |
| **A spawn point, a trigger** | it has behaviour and no art |
| **A tree that must sort** | a node sorts naturally — lesson 8's point |

**And when it is wrong:** anything numerous, anything purely decorative, anything that does not need behaviour. **A thousand grass tiles as scenes is a thousand nodes**, from stage 4's scaling lesson.

**The practical caveat: placement is on the grid.** A scene tile is positioned at the cell, so **anything that wants to sit between cells cannot** use this. For free placement, instance scenes normally and place them by hand.

**The second caveat: they are children of the layer.** So:

```gdscript
for child in ground.get_children():
	# every painted scene tile
```

**Which means you can find them**, and also that the `TileMapLayer`'s child list is no longer empty — worth knowing when a script iterates children expecting none.

**Reading which scene is at a cell:**

```gdscript
var source_id := ground.get_cell_source_id(cell)
var src := ground.tile_set.get_source(source_id)
if src is TileSetScenesCollectionSource:
	var alt := ground.get_cell_alternative_tile(cell)
	var scene := (src as TileSetScenesCollectionSource).get_scene_tile_scene(alt)
```

**Verbose, and rarely needed** — usually you want the instanced node, which is a child.

**The alternative that is often better: a marker layer.** Paint ordinary tiles on a hidden layer as *markers*, then instance scenes from code at load:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	for cell in markers.get_used_cells():
		var data := markers.get_cell_tile_data(cell)
		var scene: PackedScene = data.get_custom_data("scene")
		if scene == null:
			continue
		var n := scene.instantiate()
		objects.add_child(n)
		n.global_position = markers.to_global(markers.map_to_local(cell))
	markers.visible = false
```

**A `PackedScene` in custom data**, from lesson 6, and the instancing under your control.

| | Scene Collection | A marker layer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Setup | **built in** | ~15 lines |
| Editor preview | **yes, live** | no — markers only |
| Where the nodes end up | children of the layer | **wherever you choose** |
| Control over instancing | none | **full** — order, parent, parameters |
| Off-screen culling | harder | **yours to manage** |

**The marker approach wins when you need control over the parent** — projectiles and actors belonging to a container rather than to a tilemap, from stage 4's lesson — **or when instancing should be deferred**, which matters for a large world.

**The honest recommendation.** Use a Scene Collection for a handful of interactive props in a hand-painted level: it is immediate, it previews in the editor, and the count is small. **Use a marker layer when the world is generated, when the objects are numerous, or when their parent matters.**

**What your own project does: neither.** `the-lost-sheep` paints only ground tiles, and its buildings and people are **drawn** from the model — the `_draw` approach from stage 4's scaling lesson. **Because the buildings are not placed on a tile grid at all; they are placed on parcels**, which is a different grid with its own coordinates, from the coordinates lesson.

**That is worth noticing as a design point.** The tilemap is the picture of the ground; the model is parcels. **Scene tiles would have bound the buildings to the tile grid**, which is the wrong grid for them.

**Practice.** Build a Scene Collection with a door scene that has a script printing on `_ready`. Paint three doors and confirm three nodes appear as children of the layer, each printing. Then build the marker-layer alternative: a hidden layer with a `PackedScene` in custom data, instanced in `_ready` into a separate container. Compare how much control each gives you.
Navigation: the mesh and the agent:
Godot's built-in pathfinding — the four nodes, the setup, and the honest assessment of when to use it instead of a grid.

**The four pieces:**

| Node | Job |
| --- | --- |
| **`NavigationRegion2D`** | holds a **`NavigationPolygon`** — the walkable area |
| **`NavigationAgent2D`** | a child of the thing that moves; computes and follows a path |
| **`NavigationObstacle2D`** | a dynamic hole in the mesh |
| **`NavigationLink2D`** | a connection between unconnected regions — a ladder, a teleport |

**The simplest working setup:**

```
World
├── NavigationRegion2D          ← with a NavigationPolygon covering the floor
│   └── (the walkable area)
└── Enemy (CharacterBody2D)
    └── NavigationAgent2D
```

**And the movement:**

```gdscript
@onready var agent: NavigationAgent2D = $NavigationAgent2D

func _physics_process(_delta: float) -> void:
	if agent.is_navigation_finished():
		velocity = Vector2.ZERO
		move_and_slide()
		return
	var next := agent.get_next_path_position()
	velocity = global_position.direction_to(next) * speed
	move_and_slide()

func go_to(target: Vector2) -> void:
	agent.target_position = target
```

**Four lines of movement and one setter.** That is the whole API for the common case: set `target_position`, read `get_next_path_position()` each frame, move towards it.

**Note `move_and_slide()` is still called when finished**, from stage 4's reason: it keeps the collision state current.

**Building the navigation polygon.** Three ways:

| Way | How |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw it** | select the `NavigationRegion2D` and use the polygon tool |
| **Bake it** | the **Bake NavigationPolygon** button — Godot traces the collision geometry |
| **From a tilemap** | add a **navigation layer** to the `TileSet` and a nav polygon per walkable tile |

**The tilemap route is the one to use with a tilemap**, and it is the same two-step shape as collision from lesson 4: **add a Navigation Layer to the `TileSet` first**, then give each walkable tile a navigation polygon — usually a full-tile box, drawn once for a multi-selection.

**Then `navigation_enabled` on the `TileMapLayer`** and the layer contributes its walkable area automatically. **No `NavigationRegion2D` needed.**

**The agent's properties worth setting:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `path_desired_distance` | how close counts as reaching a waypoint |
| `target_desired_distance` | how close counts as arrived |
| `radius` | the agent's size, for avoidance |
| `avoidance_enabled` | **local avoidance between agents** |
| `max_speed` | for avoidance to work with |
| `navigation_layers` | which parts of the mesh it may use |
| `path_postprocessing` | Corridorfunnel (smooth) or Edgecentered |

**`avoidance_enabled` is the feature worth knowing about**: with it on, agents steer around each other using RVO, and you read `velocity` from the `velocity_computed` signal rather than setting it directly:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	agent.velocity_computed.connect(_on_velocity_computed)

func _physics_process(_delta: float) -> void:
	agent.set_velocity(desired_velocity)        # ask

func _on_velocity_computed(safe: Vector2) -> void:
	velocity = safe                              # receive
	move_and_slide()
```

**A two-step dance**, and it is the only way avoidance works. **Setting `velocity` directly with avoidance on does nothing.**

**The honest assessment: when to use navigation, and when a grid.**

| Use `NavigationAgent2D` | Use `AStarGrid2D` — next lesson |
| --- | --- |
| **Free movement** in open space | **grid movement**, cell to cell |
| Irregular walkable shapes | a tile grid |
| Agents avoiding each other | per-cell **costs** |
| You want it to work with no code | you want control over the path |
| 3D, or 2D with sloped geometry | turn-based or tactical movement |

**For a top-down game on a tile grid, `AStarGrid2D` is usually the better fit** — it understands cells, it gives you the whole path to inspect, and per-tile movement costs from lesson 6 drop straight in. **Navigation meshes are built for continuous space.**

**The three things that go wrong:**

| Problem | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| **No path at all** | the mesh is not baked, or `navigation_enabled` is off |
| **The agent walks through walls** | the mesh includes them — rebake, or fix the tile polygons |
| **It stutters at corners** | `path_desired_distance` too small, or postprocessing |
| **It will not start** | the agent is **outside** the mesh — `get_closest_point` first |
| **A rebuilt map does not update** | navigation rebuilds on the next frame; `await get_tree().physics_frame` |

**Row four is the common one.** An agent standing one pixel outside the navigation mesh has no path at all. **`NavigationServer2D.map_get_closest_point()`** gives you a valid start.

**Debugging it:** **Debug > Visible Navigation**, from stage 1 — it draws the mesh in the running game, and a mesh that looks wrong usually is.

**Neither of your projects uses navigation**, which is consistent: `the-lost-sheep`'s people move on a parcel grid, and `shepherds-we-shall-be`'s actors are steered by AI on open ground. **A tile-grid game and a free-movement action game both have simpler answers than a navigation mesh**, which is worth knowing before you reach for it.

**Practice.** Build a walled room from a tilemap with a navigation layer and per-tile nav polygons, and `navigation_enabled` on. Add an enemy with a `NavigationAgent2D` that paths to the mouse on click. Turn on **Debug > Visible Navigation** and confirm the mesh matches the floor. Then place the enemy inside a wall and watch it fail to path. Then enable avoidance with two agents and watch them steer round each other.
Pathfinding with AStarGrid2D:
The grid pathfinder — which for a tile-based game is simpler, more controllable and a better fit than a navigation mesh.

**What it is.** `AStarGrid2D` is A* over a rectangular grid of cells. **You tell it the size, mark cells solid, set costs, and ask for a path as a list of cells.**

**The setup:**

```gdscript
var astar := AStarGrid2D.new()

func _ready() -> void:
	astar.region = ground.get_used_rect()
	astar.cell_size = Vector2(16, 16)
	astar.diagonal_mode = AStarGrid2D.DIAGONAL_MODE_ONLY_IF_NO_OBSTACLES
	astar.default_compute_heuristic = AStarGrid2D.HEURISTIC_MANHATTAN
	astar.update()                                   # ← required after configuring

	for cell in walls.get_used_cells():
		astar.set_point_solid(cell, true)
```

**`astar.update()` is mandatory** after setting `region`, `cell_size` or the modes — and forgetting it is the commonest cause of *"it returns no path"*.

**And `region` from `get_used_rect()`** handles negative coordinates correctly, from the coordinates lesson.

**Asking for a path:**

```gdscript
var cells: Array[Vector2i] = astar.get_id_path(from_cell, to_cell)
var points: PackedVector2Array = astar.get_point_path(from_cell, to_cell)
```

| Method | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `get_id_path` | **the cells** — `Array[Vector2i]` |
| `get_point_path` | **world positions** — a `PackedVector2Array` |

**`get_id_path` is usually what you want**, because cells are what the game reasons about and you can convert when you move.

**The diagonal modes, which matter more than they look:**

| Mode | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `DIAGONAL_MODE_ALWAYS` | diagonals always allowed — **cuts corners through walls** |
| `DIAGONAL_MODE_NEVER` | orthogonal only — blocky, predictable |
| `DIAGONAL_MODE_AT_LEAST_ONE_WALKABLE` | a diagonal needs one free neighbour |
| `DIAGONAL_MODE_ONLY_IF_NO_OBSTACLES` | **a diagonal needs both free.** The sensible default. |

**`ALWAYS` lets an agent slip diagonally between two wall corners**, which looks like a bug because it is one. **`ONLY_IF_NO_OBSTACLES` is the right default.**

**The heuristics:**

| Heuristic | For |
| --- | --- |
| `HEURISTIC_MANHATTAN` | **orthogonal movement** |
| `HEURISTIC_EUCLIDEAN` | diagonal movement |
| `HEURISTIC_OCTILE` | diagonal, with correct diagonal cost |
| `HEURISTIC_CHEBYSHEV` | diagonals cost the same as orthogonals |

**Match the heuristic to the movement.** Manhattan with diagonals allowed overestimates and gives suboptimal paths; Euclidean with no diagonals wastes work.

**Per-cell costs, which is where this beats a navigation mesh:**

```gdscript
astar.set_point_weight_scale(cell, 3.0)        # three times as expensive
```

**And the custom-data layer from lesson 6 feeds it directly:**

```gdscript
for cell in ground.get_used_cells():
	var data := ground.get_cell_tile_data(cell)
	if data == null:
		continue
	if not data.get_custom_data("walkable"):
		astar.set_point_solid(cell, true)
	else:
		astar.set_point_weight_scale(cell, float(data.get_custom_data("move_cost")))
```

**Twelve lines, and the map's own data becomes the pathfinding graph.** Mud costs three, road costs one, water is solid. **No navigation mesh can express that** — it has no concept of a cell having a cost.

**Following a path:**

```gdscript
var _path: Array[Vector2i] = []

func go_to(cell: Vector2i) -> void:
	_path = astar.get_id_path(_current_cell(), cell)
	if not _path.is_empty():
		_path.remove_at(0)        # the first is where we already are

func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
	if _path.is_empty():
		return
	var target := ground.to_global(ground.map_to_local(_path[0]))
	global_position = global_position.move_toward(target, speed * delta)
	if global_position.distance_to(target) < 1.0:
		_path.remove_at(0)
```

**`move_toward` rather than `lerp`**, from stage 4: it arrives rather than approaching forever.

**And `remove_at(0)` on the first cell** — the path includes the starting cell, which you are already on.

**Keeping it current.** When the map changes, update the affected cells rather than rebuilding:

```gdscript
func _on_wall_broken(cell: Vector2i) -> void:
	astar.set_point_solid(cell, false)
```

**No `update()` needed for solidity or weights** — only for the region and the modes. **That makes incremental updates cheap**, which is the other advantage over baking a mesh.

**Performance, honestly.** A* on a 100×100 grid is sub-millisecond; on a 1000×1000 grid with a long path it is not. **Three mitigations:**

| Mitigation | |
| --- | --- |
| **Smaller cells only where needed** | one `AStarGrid2D` per region |
| **Cache paths** | a path from A to B is valid until the map changes |
| **Spread it over frames** | `await get_tree().process_frame` inside the loop |
| **Limit requests** | one pathfind per actor per second is usually plenty |

**The last is the big one**: an agent recomputing its path every frame is doing sixty times the necessary work. **Recompute on arrival, on blockage, or on a timer.**

**`AStar2D`, the non-grid version**, for graphs that are not grids — waypoints, a node network, a hex map with custom connections. **Same algorithm, you add points and connect them yourself.** Worth knowing it exists.

**Practice.** Build an `AStarGrid2D` over a tilemap, marking wall cells solid and reading `move_cost` from custom data. Path from the player to the clicked cell and draw the path with `_draw`. Then try each diagonal mode and watch a path cut a corner under `ALWAYS`. Then break a wall and update one cell's solidity. Then recompute every frame and then once a second, and compare the profiler.
A sparse grid without a tilemap:
When a `Dictionary` keyed by `Vector2i` is the better world representation — which for a model-driven game it often is.

**The case against a tilemap for the model.** A `TileMapLayer` is excellent at **drawing** a grid and poor at **being** one:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| Its data is a `PackedByteArray` blob | not readable, not diffable — lesson 1 |
| `TileData` is read-only at runtime | lesson 6 |
| It holds **which tile**, not **what is true** | one value per cell |
| Several properties per cell means several layers | or custom data, which is still authored |

**So for state that changes — who owns this parcel, what is built here, how much it has grown — a tilemap is the wrong container.** It is a picture.

**The alternative: a `Dictionary` keyed by `Vector2i`.**

```gdscript
var owned: Dictionary[Vector2i, bool] = {}
var buildings: Dictionary[Vector2i, BuildingState] = {}

func build(cell: Vector2i, kind: String) -> void:
	buildings[cell] = BuildingState.new(kind)

func building_at(cell: Vector2i) -> BuildingState:
	return buildings.get(cell)
```

**Why a `Dictionary` and not a 2D array**, from stage 3's dictionary lesson:

| | `Dictionary[Vector2i, T]` | `Array` of `Array` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sparse** | **only occupied cells stored** | every cell, occupied or not |
| **Negative coordinates** | **free** | needs an offset |
| **Unbounded** | **grows anywhere** | fixed size |
| **Lookup** | hashed, O(1) | indexed, O(1) |
| Iteration order | insertion | row-major |
| Memory for a mostly-empty world | **tiny** | the whole rectangle |

**Sparse is the decisive property.** A world where fifty of ten thousand cells have a building stores fifty entries. **And `Vector2i` as a key works directly** — no `y * width + x` arithmetic, no bounds, no negative-index bug.

**The pattern in full:**

```gdscript
class_name Settlement
extends RefCounted

var _owned: Dictionary[Vector2i, bool] = {}
var _built: Dictionary[Vector2i, StringName] = {}

func owns(cell: Vector2i) -> bool:
	return _owned.get(cell, false)

func claim(cell: Vector2i) -> void:
	_owned[cell] = true

func build(cell: Vector2i, kind: StringName) -> bool:
	if not owns(cell) or _built.has(cell):
		return false
	_built[cell] = kind
	return true

func neighbours_built(cell: Vector2i, kind: StringName) -> int:
	var n := 0
	for d in [Vector2i.LEFT, Vector2i.RIGHT, Vector2i.UP, Vector2i.DOWN]:
		if _built.get(cell + d) == kind:
			n += 1
	return n
```

**`extends RefCounted`**, from stage 7's definition-against-state lesson: this is runtime state, not content, so it is not a `Resource` and not a file.

**And it is trivially testable** — `Settlement.new()`, claim two cells, assert. No scene, no tilemap, no window.

**The division of labour this produces**, which is the shape your own project uses:

| Part | Where it lives |
| --- | --- |
| **The layout** — which cells exist, what terrain | a **`Resource`**, authored: `IslandData` |
| **The state** — who owns what, what is built | a **`Dictionary`** in a `RefCounted` model |
| **The picture** — the ground | a **`TileMapLayer`** |
| **The drawing** of parcels and buildings | **`_draw`** from the model — stage 4 |

**Four representations of one world, each good at one thing.** And `island_view.gd`'s header states the boundary:

> *York holds what is owned and what is built; this draws what it is told.*

**"What is owned and what is built" is the dictionary**; the view receives it as plain values and draws. **So the model is a sparse grid, the content is a resource, and the tilemap is scenery.**

**Saving it**, which is where the sparse grid pays again. From stage 7's save lesson: a save holds what changed. **A dictionary of occupied cells is already exactly that:**

```gdscript
func to_save() -> Dictionary:
	var out := {}
	for cell in _built:
		out["%d,%d" % [cell.x, cell.y]] = _built[cell]
	return out
```

**Note the string key.** JSON has no `Vector2i` and no non-string keys, from stage 7's JSON lesson — so a `Vector2i` key must be encoded. `"3,4"` is the simplest form, and parsing it back is a `split`.

**The alternative encoding, if you prefer:**

```gdscript
out["built"] = _built.keys().map(func(c): return [c.x, c.y])
```

**An array of pairs**, which avoids string parsing and is bulkier.

**When a tilemap *is* the right model.** Three cases:

| Case | |
| --- | --- |
| The world is **only** its appearance | a static level |
| Destructible terrain where the tile **is** the state | a dug-out cave |
| A very large world where memory matters | the blob is compact |

**Row two is legitimate**: for digging terrain, erasing the cell both changes the state and the picture and updates collision, all in one call. **Then the tilemap is the model and that is correct.**

**Practice.** Write a `Settlement` as above with two dictionaries and four methods, as a `RefCounted`. Test it with `new()` and no scene. Then write `to_save()` encoding `Vector2i` keys as strings, and a loader that parses them back. Then compare the memory of a sparse dictionary against a 200×200 array of arrays for fifty occupied cells.
Drawing a world instead of tiling it:
The approach your own game takes for everything except the ground — one node, `_draw`, and a model to draw from.

**The decision, from stage 4's scaling lesson, applied to a world.** For each kind of thing in the world, ask: **does it need to be a node?**

| Needs a node | Can be drawn |
| --- | --- |
| Collision | **no collision needed** |
| Its own script, state, signals | the model holds the state |
| Animation of its own | it changes with everything else |
| To be clicked, with an odd shape | **picking is arithmetic** on a grid |
| Independent movement | they move together, or not at all |

**For a parcel on a grid, every answer is "can be drawn"** — which is why `the-lost-sheep` draws seventy to a hundred of them with one node.

**The shape of a drawn world:**

```gdscript
@tool
class_name IslandView
extends Node2D

@export var island: IslandData
var _state: Array = []

func show_state(state: Array) -> void:
	_state = state
	queue_redraw()

func _draw() -> void:
	for p in _parcels_to_draw():
		_draw_parcel(p)

func _draw_parcel(p: Dictionary) -> void:
	var at := Vector2(p.cell) * PITCH
	# four corner marks, and whatever stands there
```

**And the real one's header describes exactly what it draws:**

> *A PARCEL IS FOUR CORNER MARKS AND ONE LITTLE OBJECT, and nothing else.*

**With the three states spelled out:**

| State | Drawn |
| --- | --- |
| **NOT FOUND** | **nothing at all** — *"the map stops advertising where the plots are"* |
| **FOUND** | four very thin corner marks, and a lock in the centre |
| **BOUGHT** | the lock replaced by a small pole with a sign reading *vacant* |

**Three states, one draw function, no nodes.** A hundred parcels as scenes with four children each would be five hundred nodes to draw something that changes as a unit.

**The drawing API worth knowing:**

```gdscript
draw_rect(rect, color, filled, width)
draw_circle(centre, radius, color)
draw_line(from, to, color, width)
draw_polyline(points, color, width)
draw_polygon(points, colors)
draw_texture(tex, position, modulate)
draw_texture_rect(tex, rect, tile)
draw_texture_rect_region(tex, rect, src_rect)
draw_string(font, pos, text, align, width, size, color)
draw_arc(centre, radius, from_angle, to_angle, points, color, width)
draw_set_transform(position, rotation, scale)
```

**`draw_texture_rect_region` is the important one for pixel art** — it draws a region of an atlas, so a drawn world can use the same sheet a tilemap would.

**And `draw_set_transform`** lets you draw a whole group offset and scaled without recomputing every point.

**The rules of `_draw`**, from stage 3's callbacks lesson:

| Rule | |
| --- | --- |
| **When it runs** | when the node needs redrawing, not every frame |
| **How to ask** | `queue_redraw()` |
| **Outside `_draw`** | drawing calls do **nothing** |
| **Coordinates** | **local** to the node |
| **Order** | call order — later calls draw on top |

**The picking problem**, which is the one real cost. A drawn world has no nodes to click, so you compute it:

```gdscript
func parcel_at(global_point: Vector2) -> int:
	var local := to_local(global_point)
	var cell := Vector2i((local / PITCH).floor())
	var p := island.by_cell(cell)
	return p.id if p != null else -1
```

**Arithmetic, and for a grid it is three lines.** For an irregular layout it would be harder — and then nodes or `intersect_point` from stage 4's queries lesson become the better answer.

**Hover, which needs per-frame work:**

```gdscript
func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	var hovered := parcel_at(get_global_mouse_position())
	if hovered != _hovered:
		_hovered = hovered
		queue_redraw()
```

**Only redraw when the hovered cell changes** — not every frame. **That guard is the difference between a drawn world costing nothing and costing a redraw sixty times a second.**

**And the real one animates on hover**, from the header: *"four very very thin corner borders that animate slightly on hover and a lock in the dead center that wiggles on hover and on click"*. **Which means a per-frame redraw while hovering**, and that is fine — one node, one redraw.

**The costs, honestly:**

| Cost | |
| --- | --- |
| **No per-item collision** | compute it, or use queries |
| **No per-item signals** | the view reports; the model decides |
| **No Inspector per item** | the data is in a `Resource` instead |
| **No per-item animation** | unless you animate in `_draw` |
| **You write the drawing** | rather than placing art |

**And the gains:**

| Gain | |
| --- | --- |
| **One node** instead of hundreds | |
| **One redraw** when the state changes | |
| The state lives in a model, not in the tree | |
| **It is `@tool`-able** and previews in the editor | |
| Changing how a parcel looks is one function | |

**That last one is the underrated gain.** Changing the appearance of a hundred parcels is editing `_draw_parcel`. Changing a hundred scenes is editing one scene — which is also fine — but changing the *rules* of how they look, by state, is code either way.

**Practice.** Draw a 10×10 grid of cells with `_draw`, each with a state from a dictionary, three states drawn differently. Add `parcel_at()` picking and print the cell under the mouse on click. Add hover with the change guard. Then build the same thing as a hundred instanced scenes and compare the node count, the frame time, and how long each took to write.
Chunking, and large worlds:
What to do when the world is bigger than memory or bigger than one scene — the three techniques, and the honest note that you probably do not need them.

**The honest note first.** A 2D pixel-art game at 960×540 can hold a very large world in one scene. **A 500×500 tile map is 250,000 cells, which a `TileMapLayer` stores compactly and draws only the visible part of.** Chunking is for worlds measured in millions of cells, or for streaming from disk.

**So: measure before chunking.** The profiler and the Monitors tab from stage 1 will tell you whether the world is the problem, and usually it is not.

**Technique 1: let the engine cull.** Mostly automatic:

| Mechanism | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`TileMapLayer` quadrants** | only visible quadrants are drawn — `rendering_quadrant_size` |
| **`VisibleOnScreenEnabler2D`** | disables a node's processing off-screen — stage 6's performance lesson |
| **`VisibleOnScreenNotifier2D`** | signals when something enters or leaves |

**For most worlds those three are the whole answer.** A tilemap of a hundred thousand cells with actors carrying `VisibleOnScreenEnabler2D` costs what is on screen.

**Technique 2: scene chunks, loaded and freed.** The world is divided into fixed regions, each a `.tscn`, instanced when the player is near and freed when not:

```gdscript
const CHUNK := 32          # cells per chunk side
var _loaded: Dictionary[Vector2i, Node] = {}

func _update_chunks(player_cell: Vector2i) -> void:
	var here := player_cell / CHUNK
	var wanted: Array[Vector2i] = []
	for dy in range(-1, 2):
		for dx in range(-1, 2):
			wanted.append(here + Vector2i(dx, dy))

	for key in wanted:
		if not _loaded.has(key):
			_load_chunk(key)
	for key in _loaded.keys():
		if key not in wanted:
			_loaded[key].queue_free()
			_loaded.erase(key)
```

**A 3×3 window around the player**, loading what enters and freeing what leaves. **And the sparse `Dictionary[Vector2i, …]` from the last lesson is exactly the right bookkeeping.**

**Three things that make it work:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Load off the main thread** | `ResourceLoader.load_threaded_request` from stage 7, or the frame hitches |
| **Free with `queue_free()`** | stage 2's rule, and the chunk's children go with it |
| **Keep the state outside the chunk** | a freed chunk must not take the game state with it |

**That third point is the one that catches people.** If a chunk's nodes own the state — which enemies are dead, which chests are open — freeing it loses that. **The state belongs in the model**, from the sparse-grid lesson, and the chunk is a view of it. **Told, not asked**, from stage 5.

**Technique 3: one tilemap, streamed data.** Keep a single `TileMapLayer` and write cells into it as the player moves, erasing behind:

```gdscript
func _reveal(area: Rect2i) -> void:
	for y in range(area.position.y, area.end.y):
		for x in range(area.position.x, area.end.x):
			var cell := Vector2i(x, y)
			ground.set_cell(cell, 0, _tile_for(cell))
```

**Where `_tile_for` reads from your data or generates it.** Lighter than scene chunks — no instancing, no node churn — and limited to things a tilemap can express.

**Which to use:**

| World | Technique |
| --- | --- |
| A few hundred screens, hand-made | **one scene. Nothing special.** |
| Large, hand-made, with props and actors per region | **scene chunks** |
| Large, generated, mostly tiles | **streamed cells** |
| Effectively infinite | streamed cells plus a generator |

**And the fourth option, which is often the real answer: separate levels.** A world made of discrete areas connected by doors needs no streaming at all — each area is a scene, and `change_scene_to_file()` from stage 2 moves between them. **Most games are this.**

**The coordinate care that chunking demands.** Two systems again, from the coordinates lesson:

| System | Unit |
| --- | --- |
| **World cell** | the global grid — `(347, 112)` |
| **Chunk** | `cell / CHUNK` — `(10, 3)` |
| **Cell within chunk** | `posmod(cell, CHUNK)` — `(27, 16)` |

**`posmod`, not `%`**, from stage 3's numbers lesson — because a negative world coordinate gives a negative remainder and the wrong local cell. **That is the bug chunking always produces at least once**, on the first chunk west of the origin.

**And integer division of a negative number truncates toward zero**, so `-1 / 32` is `0` rather than `-1`:

```gdscript
func chunk_of(cell: Vector2i) -> Vector2i:
	return Vector2i(floori(float(cell.x) / CHUNK), floori(float(cell.y) / CHUNK))
```

**`floori` on a float division**, not integer division. **Two bugs in one line, both from stage 3's numbers lesson**, and both guaranteed to appear in any chunking code written quickly.

**Practice.** Build a 3×3 chunk loader over a dictionary of chunk scenes, loading and freeing as a player moves. Confirm the state survives a chunk being freed by keeping it in a separate model. Then move the player west of the origin and watch `%` and integer division both produce the wrong chunk — then fix both with `posmod` and `floori`.
The world's edge, and camera limits:
Stopping the player and the camera at the boundary — a small subject with three mechanisms and one pixel-art caveat.

**The camera's limits.** `Camera2D` has four:

```gdscript
camera.limit_left = 0
camera.limit_top = 0
camera.limit_right = 1600
camera.limit_bottom = 900
camera.limit_smoothed = true
```

**The camera will not show beyond them**, so the world's edge never appears. **And `limit_smoothed` eases into the stop** rather than clamping hard, which matters if `position_smoothing_enabled` is on.

**Setting them from the tilemap**, which is the right way — one source of truth:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	var r := ground.get_used_rect()
	var cell := Vector2(ground.tile_set.tile_size)
	camera.limit_left = int(r.position.x * cell.x)
	camera.limit_top = int(r.position.y * cell.y)
	camera.limit_right = int(r.end.x * cell.x)
	camera.limit_bottom = int(r.end.y * cell.y)
```

**`get_used_rect()` handles negative coordinates**, from the coordinates lesson, which hand-written numbers do not.

**The pixel-art caveat, which is the important part of this lesson.** From stage 4's quantising lesson and stage 6's shake lesson: **a camera at a fractional position offsets every sprite on screen by that fraction**, and undoes all the whole-pixel work.

**Three sources of a fractional camera:**

| Source | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Following a body at a fractional position | **the body should be whole-pixel** — stage 4 |
| `position_smoothing_enabled` | it interpolates, so it is fractional by nature |
| Screen shake | **snap the offset** — stage 6 |

**And `limit_smoothed`** is a fourth, for the same reason.

**The fix, if the camera must be smoothed:**

```gdscript
func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	global_position = global_position.round()
```

**Round the camera every frame** — which stops the smoothing being sub-pixel while keeping its easing. **Or turn smoothing off entirely**, which is what a strict pixel-art game usually does: the camera jumps whole pixels, and at 60 fps that reads as smooth.

**Your own project's arrangement sidesteps part of this.** From `pixel_perfect_viewport.gd`, the game renders at a low viewport resolution and scales up by an integer factor — so **a whole game pixel is two screen pixels and the camera moves in game pixels.** Rounding the camera to a whole game pixel is therefore enough; there is no sub-screen-pixel residue to worry about.

**Stopping the player at the edge**, three ways:

**1. A wall.** The honest answer: `StaticBody2D`s or wall tiles around the perimeter. **Collision already works, nothing new to write, and the player cannot leave even by teleporting.**

**2. Clamping the position:**

```gdscript
func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
	move_and_slide()
	global_position = global_position.clamp(bounds.position, bounds.end)
```

**After `move_and_slide()`**, and it is blunt — it will teleport a body out of a wall it was overlapping.

**3. A bounds `Rect2`**, which is what your own actor has:

```gdscript
@export var constrain_to_movement_bounds: bool = true
@export var movement_bounds: Rect2 = Rect2(30.0, 82.0, 900.0, 426.0)
```

**An `@export`ed rectangle with a switch**, from `production_actor.gd` — the standing decision about numbers living in exports, applied to a boundary. **And the specific numbers are informative**: `Rect2(30, 82, 900, 426)` inside a 960×540 viewport, so thirty pixels of margin at the left and eighty-two at the top. **Not a symmetric border** — the top margin is larger because the HUD occupies it.

**That is a presentation constraint expressed in gameplay bounds**, which is a real coupling and is why it is an export rather than a constant: **the playable area depends on what the interface covers**, and stage 9 returns to it.

**The camera's other properties worth knowing:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `zoom` | **larger values zoom in**, which is the opposite of what people expect |
| `offset` | a shift, used for shake |
| `position_smoothing_enabled` / `_speed` | easing |
| `drag_horizontal_enabled` / `drag_*_margin` | a dead zone before the camera follows |
| `ignore_rotation` | keep the camera upright under a rotating parent |
| `process_callback` | **Physics** or Idle — Physics for following a body |

**`zoom` being inverted catches everyone**: `zoom = Vector2(2, 2)` makes everything twice as large. **And for pixel art, non-integer zoom destroys the grid** — so zoom in whole numbers or not at all, and prefer changing the viewport size, which is what your project's `ViewportSizer` does.

**`process_callback = Physics`** matters for the same reason as stage 4's `_physics_process`: a camera following a physics body in the idle frame lags behind it and the picture judders.

**The drag margins are worth knowing about**: with them the camera does not move until the player approaches the edge of a dead zone, which feels calmer than a camera glued to the character.

**Practice.** Set camera limits from `get_used_rect()` and confirm the world's edge never shows. Then turn on `position_smoothing_enabled`, zoom to 2×, and watch the sprites shimmer as the camera lands on half pixels; fix it by rounding the camera in `_process`. Then add a `movement_bounds` export to an actor and clamp to it after `move_and_slide()`. Then set `zoom` to 1.5 and look at the pixel grid.
Procedural generation, briefly:
Making a world with code — the three techniques worth knowing, and the discipline that separates a generator you can use from one you cannot.

**The discipline first, because it is the whole lesson: a generator must be deterministic and seeded.**

```gdscript
var rng := RandomNumberGenerator.new()

func generate(seed_value: int) -> void:
	rng.seed = seed_value
	...
```

**Not `randi()`**, which uses a global generator you do not control. **A seeded `RandomNumberGenerator` gives you:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Reproducibility** | the same seed gives the same world, every time |
| **Bug reports you can act on** | *"seed 4471 is broken"* is a fixable report |
| **Testability** | a test can generate seed 1 and assert |
| **Sharing** | a player can give a friend a seed |

**Without a seed, a generation bug is unreproducible**, and that is the difference between a generator you can develop and one you cannot.

**And your own project takes this further.** From memory of its design: the engine is checked against a Python model across **twenty seeds**, and `data/replay-fixture.json`, `replay-model.json` and `replay-engine.json` exist to diff one against the other. **A deterministic generator is what makes that possible at all** — two implementations can only be compared if both are reproducible.

**Technique 1: cellular smoothing.** Start random, then apply neighbour rules repeatedly. **This is the technique your own project uses for the coastline**, and `island_terrain.gd` documents its passes:

> *Three passes, in this order and for different reasons:*
>
> *SETTLE — a cell outvoted by three of its four neighbours becomes them. Takes lone steps out of a diagonal; cannot eat anything two cells wide, so inlets, spits and ponds survive.*
>
> *ROUGHEN — a boundary cell with at least two neighbours of the other ground flips to it, one in three, by a hash of its position.*

**Four things worth taking from that.**

**1. Named passes with stated purposes.** Not one loop doing everything — three passes, each with a reason, applied in a stated order.

**2. The rule's limits are named.** *"cannot eat anything two cells wide, so inlets, spits and ponds survive"* — the pass is chosen **because** of what it cannot do. A stronger smoothing would eat the features worth keeping.

**3. `by a hash of its position`** rather than a random call. **That is determinism without a sequence**: the same cell always gets the same answer regardless of iteration order, so the result does not depend on the order cells are visited. **A genuinely better technique than a seeded sequence for spatial noise**, and it means passes can be parallel or reordered.

**4. It exists to serve a human's note.** The reason for ROUGHEN is Master Roachi's *"i would also love to see less successive sharp corners"* and then *"yeah no pass over the diagonals again, we can adjust island shape a little to help"*. **The algorithm was written to a stated aesthetic complaint**, which is how generation should be driven.

**Technique 2: noise.** `FastNoiseLite` is built in:

```gdscript
var noise := FastNoiseLite.new()
noise.seed = seed_value
noise.noise_type = FastNoiseLite.TYPE_SIMPLEX_SMOOTH
noise.frequency = 0.02

func height_at(cell: Vector2i) -> float:
	return noise.get_noise_2d(cell.x, cell.y)      # −1 to 1
```

**And thresholding it gives you terrain:**

```gdscript
var h := height_at(cell)
var ground := "water" if h < -0.1 else ("rock" if h > 0.4 else "grass")
```

**`frequency` is the knob that matters** — lower is larger features. **And `get_noise_2d` is deterministic for a given seed and position**, so it is the same spatial-hash property as above.

**Technique 3: rules and templates.** Hand-authored pieces, assembled by code — rooms joined by corridors, prefabs stamped by `set_pattern` from lesson 10. **This produces the most controllable results** and is what most commercial roguelikes actually use.

**And the hybrid your project uses, which is the best of the three:** a hand-drawn **template** read as data, then processed.

> *the template is 400 x 300 and one pixel is one tile, so a diagonal coast is a one-pixel staircase*

**An artist draws the island as a 400×300 image; the generator reads it and smooths it.** The shape is authored, the detail is generated. **That is the generate-then-author pattern from stage 7, inverted — author-then-generate — and for a world whose shape matters it is the right way round.**

**The rule that makes any of this usable: generate, then let a human edit.** From stage 7's generator lesson and `island_data.gd`:

> *The layout in the repository is still a PLACEHOLDER, generated by tools/make_island.gd, and editing it in the Inspector is how the real one arrives.*

**A generator that must produce the final result is a generator you will fight.** One that produces a good start, saved as editable data, is a tool.

**The things that go wrong:**

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Unreproducible bugs | **seed it** |
| Results depend on iteration order | **hash the position** instead of a sequence |
| Unplayable results | **validate** — stage 7's checking lesson |
| Everything looks the same | more passes, or more hand-authored input |
| It takes seconds | chunk it over frames, or do it in a tool |
| A regenerate loses hand edits | generate from a template — stage 7 |

**Row three deserves a note.** A generator that can produce an unplayable world needs a check and a retry:

```gdscript
for attempt in 20:
	generate(seed_value + attempt)
	if _is_playable():
		return
push_error("no playable world in 20 attempts")
```

**Validate and retry** is the standard answer, and it needs the validation to be as carefully written as the generator.

**Practice.** Write a generator with a seeded `RandomNumberGenerator` and confirm the same seed gives the same world twice. Then rewrite the randomness as a hash of the cell position and confirm the result no longer depends on iteration order. Then add a SETTLE pass and watch lone diagonal steps disappear. Then read `island_terrain.gd`'s three passes and name what each is for.
Tools for painting a world:
The generator-as-tool pattern applied to a world — your project's nine tools, and the invocation that makes them usable.

**The nine, from `the-lost-sheep/tools/`:**

| Tool | Job |
| --- | --- |
| `make_island.gd` | generate the parcel layout |
| `make_island_from_template.gd` | **the same, from a drawn template** |
| `paint_the_ground.gd` | **write tilemap cells** |
| `make_water_tiles.gd` | produce the water tile art or set |
| `plant_the_island.gd` | place trees and scenery |
| `place_the_sites.gd` | place named sites |
| `make_names.gd` | generate the name list |
| `replay.gd` | drive a recorded session |
| `run_checks.sh` | run the lot |

**Nine single-purpose tools, each named as a verb.** Not one `world_tool.gd` with nine modes — and that is the convention worth copying, because a tool with one job can be read, run and trusted on its own.

**The invocation, which is the thing to know:**

```bash
godot --headless --script tools/paint_the_ground.gd
```

**From `paint_the_ground.gd`'s own header**, and it is the form from stage 1's running lesson: **no window, one script, exit.** Which means:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It can run in a shell script** | `run_checks.sh` runs them all |
| **It can run in CI** | no display needed |
| **It is scriptable** | arguments, pipes, a Makefile |
| **It does not need the editor open** | so it cannot fight the editor's state |

**And the script form for a headless tool** is `extends SceneTree` with `_initialize()`, the same as a test from stage 5's testing lesson — or `extends EditorScript` with `_run()` for one you trigger from the editor, from stage 7's generator lesson. **Two forms, two triggers:**

| Form | Triggered by |
| --- | --- |
| `extends SceneTree`, `_initialize()` | **`godot --headless --script …`** |
| `extends EditorScript`, `_run()` | **Ctrl-Shift-X** in the editor |
| A `@tool` node with a button | the Inspector |

**The headless form is the one to prefer for anything that writes files**, because it is repeatable from a shell and leaves no editor state involved.

**What `paint_the_ground.gd` actually does**, which is the pattern:

1. **Read the authored template** — the 400×300 image, one pixel per tile.
2. **Ask `island_terrain.gd`** for the settled shape — *"ONE PLACE, BECAUSE TWO TOOLS NEED THE SAME ANSWER"*.
3. **Compute each cell's corner mask** against its neighbours.
4. **Map the mask to a tile index** via the documented corner Wang set.
5. **Write the cells into `game/scenes/ground.tscn`.**

**And the output is a real scene**, not a separate data file:

> *It writes real cells into `game/scenes/ground.tscn`, which main.tscn instances and marks editable — so the ground opens for painting either on its own or inside the main scene.*

**Three decisions in that sentence.**

**1. It writes the scene the game uses**, so there is no import step and no second copy.

**2. The scene is instanced into `main.tscn`**, so it is reusable and its own file.

**3. It is marked Editable Children**, so the generated ground can be hand-painted **in context** — which is stage 8's painting lesson and stage 2's editable-children feature, used for the thing it is actually good at.

**Writing a scene from a tool**, which needs the `owner` rule from stage 2:

```gdscript
extends SceneTree

func _initialize() -> void:
	var packed := load("res://game/scenes/ground.tscn") as PackedScene
	var root := packed.instantiate()
	var layer := root as TileMapLayer

	layer.clear()
	for cell in _land_cells():
		layer.set_cell(cell, 0, _tile_for(_corner_mask(cell)))

	var out := PackedScene.new()
	out.pack(root)
	var err := ResourceSaver.save(out, "res://game/scenes/ground.tscn")
	print("wrote %d cells" % layer.get_used_cells().size())
	quit(0 if err == OK else 1)
```

**`PackedScene.pack(root)` then `ResourceSaver.save`** is how a tool writes a scene. **And `layer.clear()` first**, so the tool is re-runnable — stage 7's generator rule.

**`quit(0)` or `quit(1)`**, because a headless tool's **exit code** is how a shell script knows whether it worked. `run_checks.sh` depends on it.

**The reporting**, which stage 7's generator lesson insisted on: `print("wrote %d cells")`. **A tool that says nothing leaves you guessing.**

**The checking counterpart, `run_checks.sh`**, which runs the tools and the checks together. **A world pipeline with no check is a pipeline that will silently produce a broken world** — and `island_terrain.gd` names exactly the failure a check prevents:

> *if they disagree by one cell a parcel ends up in the sea.*

**Two tools, one shared function, and a check that they agree.** That is the whole discipline.

**Practice.** Write a headless tool that fills a `TileMapLayer` from a rule, packs it and saves the scene, printing the count and exiting with a code. Run it with `godot --headless --script`. Run it twice and confirm the cell count does not double. Then write a second tool that reads the same shape function and a check script that asserts they agree, and wire all three into a shell script that fails if any fails.
Reading a real world: the ground and the:
The stage's closing exercise: one tilemap, one drawn view, two grids, a template, four tools and a check — the whole of stage 8 in one subject.

**The files:**

| File | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `game/scenes/ground.tscn` | **one `TileMapLayer`**, `z_index = -10`, generated |
| `game/data/ground-tiles.tres` | the `TileSet` — a sixteen-tile corner Wang set |
| `game/scripts/island/island_terrain.gd` | **the shape**, settled from the template |
| `game/scripts/island/island_data.gd` | the **parcel** grid — a `Resource` |
| `game/scripts/island/parcel_data.gd` | one parcel |
| `game/scripts/island/island_view.gd` | **draws** the parcels |
| `game/scripts/island/sheet_cuts.gd` | cutting the art |
| `tools/paint_the_ground.gd` | writes the tilemap |
| `tools/make_island_from_template.gd` | places the parcels |
| `check_island.gd` | asserts the two agree |

**Pass 1 — the two grids, which is the key observation.**

| Grid | Unit | Holds | Drawn by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **The tile grid** | one tile | the **ground's appearance** | a `TileMapLayer` |
| **The parcel grid** | `IslandData.CELL` | **what can be owned and built** | `_draw` |

**Two grids over the same space, deliberately separate**, from the coordinates lesson: the tiles are the picture, the parcels are the model. **And the risk is named:**

> *ONE PLACE, BECAUSE TWO TOOLS NEED THE SAME ANSWER. `tools/paint_the_ground.gd` lays the tiles and `tools/make_island_from_template.gd` places the parcels, and if they disagree by one cell a parcel ends up in the sea. They both ask this.*

**One function, two callers, and a check that the result is consistent.** That is the answer to two coordinate systems, and it is the general answer.

**Pass 2 — why the ground is tiles and everything else is drawn.** Apply the decision table from the drawing lesson:

| Thing | Node? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The ground** | a `TileMapLayer` | genuinely a grid of repeated art, with autotiled edges |
| **The parcels** | **drawn** | no collision, no per-item script, they change together |
| **The buildings** | **drawn** | likewise; and they sit on parcels, not on tiles |
| **The people** | **drawn** | many, simple, moving together |
| **The interface** | `Control` nodes | stage 9 |

**One tilemap in the whole game.** And the reason the buildings are not scene tiles, from the scenes-as-tiles lesson: **they are placed on parcels, which is the wrong grid for a tilemap.**

**Pass 3 — the pipeline.**

```
Timon's 400×300 template image
        ↓
island_terrain.gd        ← SETTLE, ROUGHEN: one shape, asked by both tools
        ↓                               ↓
paint_the_ground.gd            make_island_from_template.gd
   (corner mask → tile)              (land cells → parcels)
        ↓                               ↓
ground.tscn                        island.tres
   (PackedByteArray blob)          (100 ParcelData sub-resources)
        ↓                               ↓
  instanced, Editable             @export on IslandView
        ↓                               ↓
        └──────── main.tscn ────────────┘
                     ↓
              check_island.gd  ← asserts the counts agree
```

**Author the shape, generate both representations from one function, check they agree, then hand-edit either.**

**Pass 4 — the questions.** Answer in writing:

1. **Why is there only one `TileMapLayer`?**
2. **Why is `z_index = -10` on it?** What convention is that?
3. **What is the sixteen-tile set, and how was the mapping determined?**
4. **Why do two tools call the same terrain function?** What breaks if they do not?
5. **Why is the ground a scene instanced into `main.tscn` rather than a layer inside it?**
6. **Why is it marked Editable Children?**
7. **Why are the parcels a `Resource` and the ground a `PackedByteArray`?** Which is reviewable?
8. **What does `check_island.gd` check, and why can no unit test replace it?**

**Question 7 is the one that connects the stage.** The parcels are 100 readable `sub_resource` blocks you can diff; the tilemap is an opaque blob. **Both are generated from the same template — and only one of them can be reviewed in a pull request.** That asymmetry is a real cost of tilemaps and it is why the model is not one.

**What this stage has given you.** `TileMapLayer` and its `TileSet`; collision and navigation as two-step setups; terrains and the corner Wang set; custom data as the tile's own authority; the three coordinate spaces; `AStarGrid2D` over a navigation mesh for grid games; a sparse `Dictionary[Vector2i, …]` as the model; `_draw` as the alternative to nodes; and tools that generate what a human then edits.

**And the judgement, which is the point: a world has several representations, and each should be good at one thing.**

**Practice.** Answer all eight questions. Then open `ground-tiles.tres` and confirm it is a sixteen-tile atlas source. Then find where `IslandData.CELL` is defined and where `island_view.gd` uses it. Then run `tools/run_checks.sh` and read what it does. Then draw your own 20×15 template, write the two tools against one shape function, and make them disagree deliberately to see the check fire.
Control, and why it is not Node2D:
The interface branch of the node tree — a sibling of `Node2D`, not a descendant, and the single fact that prevents most stage-9 confusion.

**The hierarchy, from stage 2's node lesson:**

```
CanvasItem
├── Node2D       → Sprite2D, CharacterBody2D, …   the WORLD
└── Control      → Label, Button, Panel, …        the INTERFACE
```

**`Control` is a `CanvasItem` and not a `Node2D`.** It can be drawn, modulated and hidden; **it does not have `position`, `rotation` and `scale` as its primary layout mechanism.**

**What a `Control` has instead:**

| Property | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `position` | **read-only in practice** — the layout computes it |
| `size` | its rectangle, **computed by the parent** |
| `anchor_left/top/right/bottom` | where its edges attach — 0 to 1 |
| `offset_left/top/right/bottom` | pixels from those anchors |
| `custom_minimum_size` | the smallest it will accept |
| `size_flags_horizontal/vertical` | **how it competes for space** |
| `pivot_offset` | where it rotates and scales from |
| `mouse_filter` | whether it takes mouse input |
| `focus_mode` | whether it can be focused |

**The mental shift: you do not place a `Control`, you describe where it should be.** Its parent — usually a container — computes the rectangle.

**That is the opposite of `Node2D`**, where you set `position` and the node is there. **Setting `position` on a `Control` inside a container is overwritten on the next layout pass**, which is the first thing people trip on.

**So the two rules:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Inside a container** | set `custom_minimum_size` and `size_flags`. Never `position`. |
| **Not inside a container** | set `anchors` and `offsets`. Never `position` directly. |

**The three consequences worth knowing now.**

**1. Mixing the branches loses behaviour.** A `Control` inside a `Node2D` draws, and no parent is computing its layout — so its anchors refer to its own rect and it will not resize with the window. **A `Node2D` inside a `Control` draws, and the `Control` will not size itself around it** because a `Node2D` reports no minimum size.

**Both work and both are usually mistakes**, and stage 2's root-node lesson flagged this as the commonest stage-9 error.

**2. The interface wants its own `CanvasLayer`.** A `Control` tree under the world is affected by the camera — it scrolls, it zooms. **Interface should not.** Lesson 11 covers `CanvasLayer`, and it is the standard answer.

**3. Input order favours the interface.** `Control` nodes get mouse and GUI events before `_unhandled_input`, which is stage 3's reason for the standing decision that gameplay uses `_unhandled_input`: **the UI gets first refusal, automatically.**

**The scene arrangement this produces:**

```
Game (Node2D)
├── World (Node2D)
│   ├── Ground (TileMapLayer)
│   ├── Actors (Node2D)
│   └── Camera2D
└── UI (CanvasLayer)
    └── Hud (Control)
        ├── TopBar (Control)
        └── BuildBar (Control)
```

**World under `Node2D`, interface under `CanvasLayer`, and they do not interleave.** That is the shape, and `the-lost-sheep/game/scenes/main.tscn` follows it — `Node2D` views for the island and the people, `Control` nodes for `top_bar`, `build_bar`, `resource_modal`, `tutorial_panel`.

**`Control`'s own drawing properties**, inherited from `CanvasItem`: `visible`, `modulate`, `self_modulate`, `z_index`, `material`. **So everything from stage 6's interface-animation lesson applies** — and `pivot_offset` is the one that lesson insisted on setting.

**What `Control` adds that `Node2D` does not have:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Automatic layout** | containers, anchors, size flags |
| **Theming** | lessons 7 and 8 |
| **Focus and keyboard navigation** | lesson 10 |
| **Tooltips** | `tooltip_text`, for free |
| **Mouse filtering** | pass, stop or ignore |
| **A minimum size protocol** | so containers can measure it |

**Practice.** Build a scene with a `Node2D` root, a `Sprite2D`, and a `CanvasLayer` holding a `Control` with a `Label`. Move the camera and confirm the label does not move. Then put the `Label` under the `Node2D` instead and watch it scroll with the world. Then put a `Control` inside a `VBoxContainer` and try to set its `position` — and watch the layout overwrite it.
Anchors and offsets:
How a `Control` describes where it sits when no container is managing it — four anchors, four offsets, and the presets that cover most cases.

**The model.** Each of a `Control`'s four edges has an **anchor** (a fraction of the parent, 0 to 1) and an **offset** (pixels from that anchor).

```
left   = parent_width  * anchor_left   + offset_left
top    = parent_height * anchor_top    + offset_top
right  = parent_width  * anchor_right  + offset_right
bottom = parent_height * anchor_bottom + offset_bottom
```

**Four numbers describe the position; four more describe the size.** And because the anchors are fractions, **the rectangle follows the parent as it resizes** — which is the whole point.

**The four useful configurations:**

| Anchors | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| All **0** | top-left corner. Offsets are absolute pixels; **fixed size**, pinned to the corner. |
| All **1** | bottom-right corner. |
| All **0.5** | centred. **Fixed size**, stays in the middle. |
| left/top **0**, right/bottom **1** | **full rect.** Offsets become margins; grows with the parent. |

**The last one is the one to internalise.** Anchors at 0,0,1,1 with offsets at 0 means *fill my parent*. With offsets of 16 all round, it means *fill my parent with a 16-pixel margin* — and that margin holds at every window size.

**The presets**, which is how you actually set them: the **Layout** menu in the toolbar (or the anchor preset button) offers:

| Preset | Anchors |
| --- | --- |
| **Top Left / Top Right / Bottom Left / Bottom Right** | a corner, fixed size |
| **Center Top / Center Left / Center / …** | an edge or the middle, fixed size |
| **Left Wide / Top Wide / Right Wide / Bottom Wide** | a full-height or full-width strip |
| **VCenter Wide / HCenter Wide** | a centred strip |
| **Full Rect** | fill the parent |

**Use the presets.** Setting eight numbers by hand is how people get lost; the presets set them correctly and you adjust the offsets afterwards.

**And the two modifier buttons beside them:** **Keep Ratio** and the *Anchors only* / *Anchors and Offsets* / *Offsets only* choice, which decides whether changing a preset moves the node or just re-describes where it already is.

**The six configurations you will use in practice:**

| What you want | Preset | Then |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A bar across the top | **Top Wide** | set `offset_bottom` to its height |
| A bar across the bottom | **Bottom Wide** | `offset_top` to minus its height |
| A side panel | **Left Wide** | `offset_right` to its width |
| A centred dialog | **Center** | set the size |
| A full-screen overlay | **Full Rect** | nothing |
| A corner badge | **Top Right** | offsets for the inset |

**Note how the top bar works:** Top Wide gives anchors `0, 0, 1, 0` — left and right follow the parent's width, top and bottom are both pinned to the top — **so `offset_bottom` is literally the bar's height in pixels**, and it stays that height at any window size while stretching across.

**`grow_horizontal` and `grow_vertical`**, which decide which way a node grows when its minimum size exceeds its rect: Begin, End or Both. **For a centred dialog, Both.**

**Setting it from code**, which is occasionally necessary:

```gdscript
set_anchors_preset(Control.PRESET_FULL_RECT)
set_anchors_and_offsets_preset(Control.PRESET_CENTER)
anchor_left = 0.0
offset_left = 16.0
```

**`set_anchors_and_offsets_preset` is the one that actually positions the node**; `set_anchors_preset` only changes the anchors and leaves the offsets, which usually moves it somewhere unexpected.

**Reading the result:**

```gdscript
print(size)              # the computed rectangle's size
print(position)           # its top-left, relative to the parent
print(global_position)
print(get_rect())         # a Rect2 of both
```

**And the lifecycle caveat from stage 2's ready-order lesson**, which bites hardest here: **`size` is not final in `_ready`.** The first layout pass has not run. Three fixes:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	await get_tree().process_frame            # wait a frame
	_use_the_size()

# or
	_use_the_size.call_deferred()

# or, best — react to it
	resized.connect(_use_the_size)
	item_rect_changed.connect(_use_the_size)
```

**`resized` is the right answer** for anything that must respond to its own size, because it fires again when the window changes — which a one-off deferred call does not.

**When anchors are the wrong tool: inside a container.** A container computes its children's rectangles and **ignores their anchors entirely.** So:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Not in a container** | anchors and offsets |
| **In a container** | `custom_minimum_size` and `size_flags` — the next two lessons |

**Practice.** Build a `Control` root with four children: a top bar via Top Wide, a bottom bar via Bottom Wide, a left panel via Left Wide, and a centred dialog via Center. Resize the window and confirm all four behave. Then print `size` in `_ready` and again from `resized`, and compare. Then put one of them in a `VBoxContainer` and watch its anchors stop mattering.
The container nodes:
Nodes whose job is to position their children — which is how any interface more complex than four rectangles is built.

**The principle.** A container computes its children's `position` and `size` every layout pass. **You stop describing positions and start describing relationships.**

**The containers, by what they do:**

| Container | Arranges children |
| --- | --- |
| **`VBoxContainer`** | **in a column** |
| **`HBoxContainer`** | **in a row** |
| **`GridContainer`** | in a grid, `columns` wide |
| **`FlowContainer`** (H and V) | wrapping, like text |
| **`MarginContainer`** | **one child, with margins** |
| **`PanelContainer`** | one child, with a styled background |
| **`CenterContainer`** | one child, centred, at its minimum size |
| **`AspectRatioContainer`** | one child, at a fixed ratio |
| **`ScrollContainer`** | one child, scrollable |
| **`SplitContainer`** (H and V) | two children, with a draggable divider |
| **`TabContainer`** | one child per tab |
| **`SubViewportContainer`** | a `SubViewport` — lesson 15 |
| **`Container`** | the base, for writing your own |

**The five you will use constantly are `VBox`, `HBox`, `Margin`, `Panel` and `Center`.**

**The nesting idiom**, which is the thing to learn:

```
PanelContainer                 ← the background and border
└── MarginContainer            ← the padding inside it
    └── VBoxContainer          ← the rows
        ├── Label
        ├── HBoxContainer      ← a row of buttons
        │   ├── Button
        │   └── Button
        └── Label
```

**Four containers to produce a padded panel with a column of rows.** That looks like a lot and each one has exactly one job:

| Node | Its one job |
| --- | --- |
| `PanelContainer` | **draw the background** |
| `MarginContainer` | **the padding** |
| `VBoxContainer` | **stack them** |
| `HBoxContainer` | **a row within the stack** |

**Separating them is what makes the layout changeable.** Changing the padding is one number on one node; changing the background is one theme override.

**Why not set a `Panel`'s own margins?** Because a plain `Panel` is not a container — it draws a background and does not position children. **`PanelContainer` does both**, and it sizes itself to its child plus the style's content margins.

**The two numbers every container child has:**

| Property | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **`custom_minimum_size`** | the smallest this child accepts |
| **`size_flags_horizontal/vertical`** | **how it competes for the leftover space** — the next lesson |

**That is the whole protocol.** A container asks each child for its minimum size, adds its own separation and margins, and distributes what is left according to the size flags.

**`MarginContainer`'s margins are theme constants**, not properties — which surprises people:

```gdscript
margin.add_theme_constant_override("margin_left", 16)
margin.add_theme_constant_override("margin_top", 8)
```

**Or in the Inspector under Theme Overrides > Constants.** Lesson 8 covers overrides; the point here is that the padding lives in the theme rather than on the node.

**Likewise `VBoxContainer`'s `separation`** — the gap between children — is a theme constant.

**`ScrollContainer`, which has one rule worth knowing:** its child must be allowed to exceed the container's size, so the child's `size_flags` should **not** include Expand on the scrolling axis, and the container's `horizontal_scroll_mode` / `vertical_scroll_mode` control the bars. **A `ScrollContainer` whose content never scrolls usually has a child that is being shrunk to fit.**

**`CenterContainer` against anchors.** Both centre a thing. **`CenterContainer` sizes the child to its minimum and centres it; the Center anchor preset keeps whatever size the child has.** For a dialog that should be as small as its content, the container; for one with a fixed size, the preset.

**Writing your own container**, which is occasionally right:

```gdscript
extends Container

func _notification(what: int) -> void:
	if what == NOTIFICATION_SORT_CHILDREN:
		for c in get_children():
			fit_child_in_rect(c as Control, Rect2(Vector2.ZERO, size))
```

**`NOTIFICATION_SORT_CHILDREN` and `fit_child_in_rect`** are the whole API. **Reach for it when no built-in container does what you want** — a radial menu, a custom stack — and not before.

**Practice.** Build the four-deep nesting above and confirm a padded panel with rows. Set the `MarginContainer`'s margins as theme constant overrides. Then put twenty labels in the `VBoxContainer` and wrap it in a `ScrollContainer` — and fix it if it does not scroll. Then replace the `PanelContainer` with a plain `Panel` and watch the layout break.
Size flags, and how space is divided:
The four flags that decide which child gets the leftover space — the least obvious part of Godot's layout system and the one that explains most unexpected results.

**The protocol.** A container measures every child's minimum size, subtracts them and its own separation from its own size, and **distributes the remainder according to the size flags.**

**The flags, per axis:**

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Fill** | occupy the space allotted. **On by default.** |
| **Expand** | **claim a share of the leftover space** |
| **Shrink Center** | sit in the middle of the allotted space |
| **Shrink Begin** / **Shrink End** | sit at one end |

**And `size_flags_stretch_ratio`**, a float deciding how much of the leftover an expanding child gets relative to its expanding siblings.

**The four combinations that matter:**

| Want | Flags |
| --- | --- |
| **Its natural size, no more** | Fill only — the default |
| **All the leftover space** | **Fill + Expand** |
| Natural size, centred in its slot | **Shrink Center** |
| Two children splitting the space | **Fill + Expand on both** |

**Fill + Expand is the one to know.** In an `HBoxContainer` with a label and a button, giving the label Expand pushes the button to the right — because the label takes all the slack.

**That is how a top bar is laid out:**

```
HBoxContainer
├── Label "Level 3"           Fill
├── Label "Greg"              Fill
├── TimeDial                  Fill
├── Control (spacer)          Fill + EXPAND      ← takes the slack
├── Button "Pause"            Fill
├── Button "1×"               Fill
└── Button "Settings"         Fill
```

**An empty `Control` with Expand as a spacer** is the standard trick: everything before it packs left, everything after packs right. **Two spacers centre a group.**

**`stretch_ratio` for proportional splits:**

```
HBoxContainer
├── Sidebar      Fill + Expand, ratio 1.0
└── Content      Fill + Expand, ratio 3.0
```

**One quarter and three quarters.** The ratios are relative, so 1 and 3 is the same as 10 and 30.

**The common failures, and each has one cause.**

**1. Everything is squashed to nothing.** No child has a `custom_minimum_size` and none has content with an intrinsic size. **Give them minimums.**

**2. One child takes everything.** It has Expand and the others do not. **Either give the others Expand or take it away from that one.**

**3. A child will not shrink below some size.** Its `custom_minimum_size`, or its content's minimum — a `Label` with long text reports a wide minimum. **Set `autowrap_mode` on the label, or a `custom_minimum_size` with a smaller width and `clip_text`.**

**4. A child ignores the container.** It is not a `Control` — a `Node2D` reports no minimum size and no container can arrange it. **From lesson 1: do not mix the branches.**

**5. Nothing scrolls in a `ScrollContainer`.** The child has Expand on the scrolling axis, so it is being fitted rather than overflowing. **Remove Expand on that axis.**

**That fifth one is the commonest `ScrollContainer` bug** and the fix is one checkbox.

**Setting them from code:**

```gdscript
size_flags_horizontal = Control.SIZE_EXPAND_FILL
size_flags_vertical = Control.SIZE_SHRINK_CENTER
size_flags_stretch_ratio = 2.0
```

**`SIZE_EXPAND_FILL` is the constant for Fill + Expand**, which is the combination you want nine times out of ten.

**The minimum-size protocol**, for completeness, because understanding it makes the rest obvious:

```gdscript
func _get_minimum_size() -> Vector2:
	return Vector2(100, 24)
```

**A custom `Control` can report its own minimum**, and `custom_minimum_size` is the override that takes the larger of the two. **A `Label` computes its minimum from its text and font; a `Button` from its text plus the style's margins.**

**And `update_minimum_size()`** must be called when a custom control's minimum changes, or containers will not re-measure it.

**The debugging procedure for a layout that is wrong:**

1. **Is every node a `Control`?**
2. **Does the container have a size at all?** Check its own anchors or its parent.
3. **Which children have Expand?** Usually too many or too few.
4. **What are the minimum sizes?** Print `get_combined_minimum_size()` for each.
5. **Are the theme constants what you think?** Separation and margins.

**`get_combined_minimum_size()` is the useful print** — it is what the container actually asked for, including the node's own `_get_minimum_size` and its `custom_minimum_size`.

**Practice.** Build an `HBoxContainer` with five children and give exactly one Expand; confirm it takes the slack. Then add a second Expand and set `stretch_ratio` to 1 and 3. Then build a top bar with a spacer in the middle so items pack to both ends. Then put a tall `VBoxContainer` in a `ScrollContainer` with vertical Expand on, see it not scroll, and fix it.
The common Control nodes:
The interface toolbox — what each node is for, and the three properties on each that matter.

**Text:**

| Node | For | Key properties |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`Label`** | static text | `text`, `autowrap_mode`, `horizontal_alignment`, `clip_text`, `uppercase` |
| **`RichTextLabel`** | **BBCode** — colours, bold, links, animation | `bbcode_enabled`, `text`, `fit_content`, `scroll_active` |
| **`LineEdit`** | one line of input | `text`, `placeholder_text`, `max_length`, `secret` |
| **`TextEdit`** | many lines of input | `text`, `wrap_mode` |

**`RichTextLabel` with `bbcode_enabled` is worth reaching for early.** `[color=red]12[/color]` in a damage number, `[b]` for emphasis, `[shake]` and `[wave]` for animated text — and it handles mixed fonts and inline images. **`fit_content = true` makes it report its height as a minimum size**, which is what you want inside a `VBoxContainer`.

**Buttons:**

| Node | For |
| --- | --- |
| **`Button`** | the ordinary one. `text`, `icon`, `disabled`, `toggle_mode`, `button_pressed` |
| **`TextureButton`** | art per state — normal, hover, pressed, disabled, focused |
| **`CheckBox`** / **`CheckButton`** | a boolean, two looks |
| **`OptionButton`** | a dropdown. `add_item`, `selected`, `get_selected_id` |
| **`MenuButton`** | a popup menu |
| **`LinkButton`** | text that looks like a link |

**All of them are `BaseButton`**, so all have `pressed`, `button_down`, `button_up`, `toggled`, and `disabled`. **`TextureButton` is the one for pixel art** — four textures, no theme work.

**Ranges:**

| Node | For |
| --- | --- |
| **`ProgressBar`** | a filled bar. `value`, `min_value`, `max_value`, `show_percentage` |
| **`HSlider`** / **`VSlider`** | a draggable value |
| **`SpinBox`** | a number field with arrows |
| **`TextureProgressBar`** | **a bar made of art** — radial, clipped, tinted |

**All are `Range`**, so all have `value`, `min_value`, `max_value`, `step`, and the `value_changed` signal. **`TextureProgressBar` is the pixel-art health bar** — `fill_mode` gives you left-to-right, radial, or clip-from-centre.

**Containers and panels:**

| Node | For |
| --- | --- |
| **`Panel`** | a background. **Not a container** — lesson 3's point. |
| **`PanelContainer`** | a background **that holds a child** |
| **`NinePatchRect`** | **a stretchable bordered box from one texture** |
| **`ColorRect`** | a flat colour. Cheap, and useful as a dimmer. |
| **`TextureRect`** | an image. `stretch_mode`, `expand_mode` |
| **`Separator`** (H and V) | a line |

**`NinePatchRect` is the one to know for pixel-art panels.** A 16×16 texture with its corners and edges marked by `patch_margin_*` stretches to any size without distorting the border. **It is how almost every pixel-art dialog box is made**, and the alternative — a `StyleBoxTexture` in a theme, lesson 7 — is the same mechanism wrapped in a theme.

**Popups and dialogs:**

| Node | For |
| --- | --- |
| **`PopupMenu`** | a list of items. `add_item`, `id_pressed` |
| **`PopupPanel`** | an arbitrary popup |
| **`AcceptDialog`** | a message with an OK |
| **`ConfirmationDialog`** | OK and Cancel |
| **`FileDialog`** | file picking — mostly for tools |
| **`Window`** | a real sub-window |

**Popups are `Window`s**, which means they are **not** laid out by their parent and they have their own coordinate space. **For an in-game menu, prefer a `Control` you show and hide** — a popup is an OS-level construct and it behaves like one.

**The rest worth knowing:**

| Node | For |
| --- | --- |
| **`ItemList`** | a scrollable list of selectable items |
| **`Tree`** | a hierarchical list. Powerful, fiddly. |
| **`TabBar`** | tabs without the container |
| **`ScrollContainer`** | lesson 3 |
| **`SubViewportContainer`** | lesson 15 |
| **`VideoStreamPlayer`** | video |
| **`Control`** | **a plain one, as a spacer** — lesson 4's trick |

**`mouse_filter`, which is on every `Control`** and causes a specific class of bug:

| Value | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| **Stop** | takes the event, stops it. **Default for most.** |
| **Pass** | takes it and lets it continue to the parent |
| **Ignore** | **does not take it at all** |

**A full-screen `Control` over the game with `mouse_filter = Stop` swallows every click**, and the game stops responding to the mouse for no visible reason. **Set decorative overlays to Ignore.** That is one of the most-hunted bugs in Godot UI work.

**What your own project uses**, from `the-lost-sheep/game/scripts/ui/`: sixteen scripts — `top_bar`, `build_bar`, `screen_bar`, `resource_modal`, `tutorial_panel`, `message_line`, `settings_rows` — each a `Control` subclass. **`class_name TopBar extends Control`**, so each panel is its own class with its own signals.

**Practice.** Build a panel using `NinePatchRect` with its patch margins set, containing a `RichTextLabel` with BBCode colour, a `TextureProgressBar`, and three `TextureButton`s. Then put a full-screen `ColorRect` over your game with `mouse_filter = Stop` and discover the clicks stop working; fix it with Ignore.
Themes: the resource:
How an interface gets a consistent look — one resource, inherited down the tree, rather than per-node styling.

**A `Theme` is a `Resource`** — so everything from stage 7 applies — holding named values for every `Control` class.

**The four kinds of entry:**

| Kind | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **Colors** | `Label/colors/font_color`, `Button/colors/font_hover_color` |
| **Constants** | `VBoxContainer/constants/separation`, `MarginContainer/constants/margin_left` |
| **Fonts** and **font sizes** | `Label/fonts/font`, `Label/font_sizes/font_size` |
| **Icons** | `CheckBox/icons/checked` |
| **Styles** | `Button/styles/normal` — a **`StyleBox`** |
