**And the inheritance: a `theme` set on any `Control` applies to it and every `Control` beneath it.** So one theme on the root of the interface styles the whole thing.

**Setting it up.** Create a `Theme` resource, assign it to the top `Control`, and **Save As** a `.tres` so it is shared and version-controlled.

**The theme editor** opens in the bottom panel when a `Theme` is selected: pick a class on the left, then add and edit its items. **The + button beside each category adds an override for that class.**

**`StyleBox`, which is the one that does the visual work.** Five kinds:

| StyleBox | For |
| --- | --- |
| **`StyleBoxFlat`** | **a rounded, bordered, filled rectangle** — defined numerically |
| **`StyleBoxTexture`** | **a nine-patch from a texture** — for pixel art |
| **`StyleBoxLine`** | a line, for separators |
| **`StyleBoxEmpty`** | nothing. For removing a background. |

**`StyleBoxFlat`'s properties** are the quickest way to a decent look: `bg_color`, `border_width_*`, `border_color`, `corner_radius_*`, `expand_margin_*`, `content_margin_*`, plus shadow and anti-aliasing.

**`StyleBoxTexture` is the pixel-art one**, and it is a nine-patch: a texture plus `texture_margin_*` marking the stretchable centre. **Same mechanism as `NinePatchRect` from the last lesson**, wrapped so a theme can apply it to every `Button` at once.

**`content_margin_*` on a `StyleBox` is the padding** — it is what makes a `Button` bigger than its text, and what a `PanelContainer` uses to inset its child. **Setting it in the style rather than on each node is the point of a theme.**

**The states a `Button` needs styled:**

| Style | When |
| --- | --- |
| `normal` | at rest |
| `hover` | mouse over |
| `pressed` | being clicked |
| `disabled` | greyed |
| `focus` | **keyboard focus** — lesson 9 |

**Styling only `normal` is the commonest half-done theme**, and the result is a button that gives no feedback. **Four styles minimum**, and `focus` matters for keyboard and gamepad navigation.

**Theme type variations**, which solve *"I want two kinds of button":*

```gdscript
button.theme_type_variation = &"DangerButton"
```

**In the theme, add a type called `DangerButton` with `Button` as its base**, and style the difference. **Now `theme_type_variation` on any button switches it** — and the base styles are inherited, so you only define what differs.

**That is the right answer for variants**, and far better than per-node overrides, which the next lesson covers.

**The default theme.** Godot ships one, and `ThemeDB` exposes it:

```gdscript
ThemeDB.get_default_theme()
ThemeDB.fallback_font
ThemeDB.fallback_font_size
```

**`ThemeDB.fallback_font` is useful for `draw_string`** from stage 8's drawing lesson, when you need a font and have not loaded one.

**And Project Settings > GUI > Theme > Custom** sets a project-wide default theme, which applies to every `Control` without one. **For a game with one look, set it there and you need not assign a theme per scene.**

**The practical order of work:**

1. **Make the theme early**, even if it is rough — retrofitting a look onto fifty nodes with overrides is painful.
2. **Style `normal`, `hover`, `pressed`, `disabled`, `focus`** for buttons.
3. **Set the fonts and font sizes** at the theme level.
4. **Set the container constants** — separation, margins.
5. **Add type variations** for the two or three variants you need.
6. **Only then** use per-node overrides, and only for genuine one-offs.

**The pixel-art caveat.** `StyleBoxFlat`'s rounded corners and anti-aliasing are **wrong for pixel art** — they produce smooth curves at odd scales. **Set `corner_radius` to 0 and `anti_aliasing` off**, or use `StyleBoxTexture` with drawn art, which is the better answer.

**Practice.** Create a `Theme`, save it as a `.tres`, and assign it to an interface root. Style `Button` in all five states with `StyleBoxFlat`, corner radius 0 and anti-aliasing off. Set `Label`'s font colour and `VBoxContainer`'s separation. Then add a `DangerButton` type variation in red and switch one button to it. Then set the theme as the project default and remove it from the node.
Theme overrides, and when to use them:
Per-node styling — the escape hatch from the theme, and the reason to reach for it rarely.

**What an override is.** A value set **on one node**, beating whatever the theme says. In the Inspector they are under **Theme Overrides**, grouped the same way as the theme's own categories.

```gdscript
label.add_theme_color_override("font_color", Color.RED)
label.add_theme_font_size_override("font_size", 24)
button.add_theme_stylebox_override("normal", my_style)
margin.add_theme_constant_override("margin_left", 16)
```

**And removing them:**

```gdscript
label.remove_theme_color_override("font_color")
label.has_theme_color_override("font_color")
```

**The lookup order**, which is worth knowing because it explains every surprise:

1. **The node's own override**
2. **Its `theme_type_variation`**, in the nearest theme that has it
3. **Its class**, in the nearest theme up the tree that has it
4. **Its parent classes**, in that theme
5. **The project default theme**
6. **Godot's built-in default**

**So an override always wins**, and a theme further up the tree is only consulted if nothing nearer answers.

**Reading the resolved value:**

```gdscript
var c := label.get_theme_color("font_color")
var f := label.get_theme_font("font")
var n := margin.get_theme_constant("margin_left")
```

**These give you what is actually in effect**, which is the thing to print when a node looks wrong.

**When an override is right — three cases:**

| Case | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **A genuine one-off** | one red label in the whole game |
| **A value that changes at runtime** | a label that turns red when a value is low |
| **A `MarginContainer`'s margins** | they are per-instance by nature |

**The second is the common legitimate one:**

```gdscript
func set_health(current: int, maximum: int) -> void:
	bar.value = float(current) / maximum
	var low := current < maximum / 4
	label.add_theme_color_override("font_color",
		Color.RED if low else Color.WHITE)
```

**A colour that depends on state cannot live in a theme**, so an override is correct. **And it is cheap** — overrides are a dictionary lookup, not a reflow.

**When an override is wrong — and this is most of the time:**

| Smell | Do instead |
| --- | --- |
| **Every button has the same override** | put it in the **theme** |
| Two kinds of button, each with overrides | a **`theme_type_variation`** |
| A whole panel's worth of overrides | a theme, or a variation for the panel's type |
| Font size set per label | theme-level font sizes, and variations for headings |

**The failure mode is a project where the theme is empty and every node carries overrides.** Then changing the look means editing fifty nodes, which is exactly what a theme exists to prevent. **And the overrides are invisible from the theme editor**, so nobody can see what the interface actually looks like without opening every scene.

**The test: if you would want to change it everywhere at once, it belongs in the theme.**

**`theme_type_variation` as the middle ground**, from the last lesson, because it is the thing people reach for overrides instead of:

```gdscript
heading.theme_type_variation = &"Heading"
caption.theme_type_variation = &"Caption"
danger.theme_type_variation = &"DangerButton"
```

**Three named looks, defined once in the theme, applied by one property.** That is the answer to *"I need three sizes of label"* — not three sets of font-size overrides.

**Overrides in the Inspector have a checkbox**, which is the thing to look for when diagnosing: **an unticked override is not applied**, and a ticked one with a default-looking value is still an override. **The checkbox is the only way to tell whether a node is overriding.**

**Finding them**, because they are easy to lose: a `.tscn` records them as properties, so grep works:

```bash
grep -rn 'theme_override' game/scenes/
```

**That is the audit for a project that has drifted into per-node styling**, and it is worth running once.

**One honest exception worth naming: a prototype.** While you are deciding what the interface looks like, overrides are faster than maintaining a theme. **The mistake is shipping them** — and the refactoring lesson from stage 5 applies: build it loosely, then move the values into the theme once they have settled.

**Practice.** Create a theme with a styled `Label`, then override one label's colour and confirm it wins. Print `get_theme_color("font_color")` on both. Then make three labels with overridden font sizes, and replace all three with a `Heading`, `Body` and `Caption` type variation. Then grep your scenes for `theme_override` and judge whether each one earns its place.
Fonts, and pixel-art text:
Text in a pixel-art game, which is a specific problem with a specific answer — and the three ways to get it wrong.

**The two kinds of font resource:**

| Resource | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **`FontFile`** | an imported `.ttf`, `.otf`, `.woff2`, or a **bitmap** `.fnt` / `.font` |
| **`FontVariation`** | a `FontFile` with modifications — weight, spacing, transform |
| **`SystemFont`** | whatever the OS has, by name |

**For pixel art, two routes:**

**Route 1: a pixel TTF at its design size.** Many pixel fonts are distributed as TTFs drawn on a grid — legible only at their intended size and exact multiples.

**The import settings that matter:**

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **Antialiasing** | **None** |
| **Hinting** | **None** |
| **Subpixel Positioning** | **Disabled** |
| **Multichannel Signed Distance Field** | **off** |
| **Generate Mipmaps** | off |

**All four of the first ones must be off**, and the symptom of missing one is text that looks slightly soft or jitters as it moves. **Then use the font only at its design size** — 8, 16, 24 — never at 13.

**Route 2: a bitmap font.** A texture of glyphs plus metrics, imported as a `FontFile`. **Exact by construction** — no rasterising, no hinting, no antialiasing to disable.

**And the third route, which is worth knowing: draw the text as sprites.** For a game with very little text — numbers on a HUD, a few labels — a `SpriteFrames` of digits indexed by value gives you perfect control. **Overkill for prose, right for a score.**

**The three ways to get it wrong:**

**1. Antialiasing left on.** The font is rasterised with grey edge pixels, which at a 2× integer scale become 2×2 grey blocks. **The text looks blurry and nothing else does**, which is the diagnostic.

**2. A non-integer font size.** A 16-pixel font at size 20 is resampled. **Use the design size or an exact multiple.**

**3. Text scaled by the viewport.** This is the subtle one. With the `viewport` stretch mode from lesson 11, **the interface is drawn at the low resolution and scaled up with everything else** — so a 16-pixel font becomes 32 screen pixels, crisply, which is usually what you want.

**But with `canvas_items` stretch mode, text is rendered at the full window resolution** and can be sharper than the art — which looks wrong in the opposite direction. **The choice of stretch mode decides what your text looks like**, and lesson 11 covers it.

**Your own project's arrangement** makes this straightforward: the game composes at 960×540 and scales by an integer factor, so **the interface is drawn in game pixels and scaled with the art.** Text and sprites share one grid, which is the consistent choice for pixel art.

**Setting a font in a theme**, which is where it belongs:

```
Theme
├── Label/fonts/font            → the FontFile
├── Label/font_sizes/font_size  → 16
├── Button/fonts/font           → the same
└── Button/font_sizes/font_size → 16
```

**One font, set once**, rather than per label. And **type variations** from lesson 6 for the sizes: `Heading` at 24, `Body` at 16, `Caption` at 8.

**The properties that affect text layout on a `Label`:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `horizontal_alignment` / `vertical_alignment` | within its rect |
| `autowrap_mode` | **Off, Arbitrary, Word, Word Smart** |
| `clip_text` | truncate rather than overflow |
| `text_overrun_behavior` | ellipsis, trim, or nothing |
| `uppercase` | force caps |
| `visible_characters` / `visible_ratio` | **a typewriter effect, for free** |
| `label_settings` | a `LabelSettings` resource as an alternative to theme overrides |

**`visible_characters` is the dialogue-reveal mechanism** — tween it from 0 to the length and the text types itself out. **One `tween_property` on `visible_ratio`**, from stage 6.

**`LabelSettings` is worth knowing about**: a small resource holding font, size, colour and outline, assignable to a `Label` directly. **It sits between a theme and per-node overrides** — shareable, but not inherited. **For a handful of distinctly-styled labels it is tidier than overrides.**

**Outlines and shadows**, which pixel art usually wants for legibility over a busy background:

| Theme item | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `font_outline_color` + `outline_size` | an outline. **Use 1 pixel for pixel art.** |
| `font_shadow_color` + `shadow_offset_x/y` | a hard shadow |

**A one-pixel dark outline is the standard pixel-art treatment** and it makes text readable over anything. **Set it in the theme, not per label.**

**`RichTextLabel` and fonts**, from the last lesson: it supports `[font]`, `[font_size]`, `[color]` and `[outline_size]` inline, so mixed styling needs no extra nodes.

**Practice.** Import a pixel TTF with antialiasing, hinting and subpixel positioning all off, and set it in a theme at its design size. Compare it with the same font at size 13 and with antialiasing on, at 2× zoom. Then add a one-pixel outline in the theme. Then tween `visible_ratio` on a `Label` from 0 to 1 for a typewriter effect.
The focus system, and keyboard navigatio:
Making an interface usable without a mouse — which is free if you let it be, and painful to retrofit.

**What focus is.** Exactly one `Control` in the tree can have keyboard focus. It receives key events first, draws its `focus` style, and **the `ui_*` actions move focus between controls.**

**And the `ui_*` actions are already bound**, from stage 4's input lesson: `ui_up`, `ui_down`, `ui_left`, `ui_right`, `ui_accept`, `ui_cancel`, `ui_focus_next`, `ui_focus_prev`. **Keyboard and gamepad both, out of the box.**

**So the default behaviour is: arrow keys and a gamepad stick move focus, Enter and the A button activate.** For free, if you do not break it.

**The properties:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `focus_mode` | **None**, **Click**, or **All** |
| `focus_neighbor_left/top/right/bottom` | explicit targets for directional moves |
| `focus_next` / `focus_previous` | explicit Tab order |
| `theme`'s `focus` style | **what focus looks like** |

**`focus_mode` defaults:**

| Node | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `Button`, `CheckBox`, `OptionButton`, `LineEdit`, `Slider` | **All** — focusable |
| `Label`, `Panel`, `TextureRect`, containers | **None** |

**Which is right**, and the thing to change is on a custom clickable control: **set `focus_mode = All`** or it cannot be reached by keyboard.

**The focus style is the part people forget.** From lesson 6: a theme that styles `normal`, `hover` and `pressed` but not `focus` gives you an interface where **keyboard users cannot see where they are.** That is not a polish issue; it makes the interface unusable without a mouse.

**Automatic neighbours.** Godot works out which control is left, right, up or down **geometrically**, so a sensible layout needs no configuration. **It gets it wrong when the layout is irregular**, and then:

```gdscript
button_a.focus_neighbor_right = button_b.get_path()
```

**Set the four neighbours explicitly** for anything the geometry cannot infer — a radial menu, a grid with gaps, a wrapping list.

**Setting focus from code:**

```gdscript
button.grab_focus()
button.release_focus()
get_viewport().gui_get_focus_owner()
```

**And the rule: when a screen appears, focus something.** A menu that opens with nothing focused leaves a gamepad user pressing buttons with no effect:

```gdscript
func show_menu() -> void:
	visible = true
	first_button.grab_focus()
```

**That one line is the difference between a menu that works on a controller and one that does not.**

**And when a screen closes, restore focus** to whatever opened it — otherwise focus is lost and the arrow keys do nothing.

**The signals:**

```gdscript
button.focus_entered.connect(_on_focused)
button.focus_exited.connect(_on_unfocused)
```

**`focus_entered` is how you show a description panel** for the currently highlighted item, which is the standard console-UI pattern.

**`ui_cancel`, which deserves its own note.** Every screen should handle it:

```gdscript
func _unhandled_input(event: InputEvent) -> void:
	if event.is_action_pressed(&"ui_cancel"):
		_close()
		get_viewport().set_input_as_handled()
```

**`set_input_as_handled()`** from stage 3, so the event does not also reach the game and open the pause menu behind it.

**Mouse and keyboard together.** The two interact badly if you let them:

| Problem | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| Hover and focus disagree, so two things look highlighted | style them the same, or grab focus on hover |
| Moving the mouse clears the keyboard position | `mouse_entered` → `grab_focus()` |
| A click leaves focus on something invisible | `release_focus()` when hiding |

**Grabbing focus on hover is the usual answer** — it makes the mouse and the keyboard share one notion of *the current item*:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	mouse_entered.connect(grab_focus)
```

**Modal screens**, and the thing that makes them behave: a `Control` covering the screen with `mouse_filter = Stop` blocks clicks beneath it — from lesson 5 — **and focus can still escape to the nodes behind.** Three fixes:

```gdscript
# 1. Disable the controls behind
# 2. Set their focus_mode to None while the modal is open
# 3. Use a real Popup, which captures focus by construction
```

**For an in-game menu, option 1 or 2.** A popup `Window` captures focus correctly and brings its own problems, from lesson 5.

**The accessibility point, briefly and genuinely.** Keyboard navigation is not only for gamepads — it is how some people use software at all. **Styling `focus` and focusing something on open costs two minutes** and is the difference between an interface everyone can use and one only a mouse can.

**Practice.** Build a menu of five buttons, style `focus` distinctly in the theme, and navigate it with the arrow keys and a gamepad. Confirm Enter activates. Then grab focus on the first button when the menu opens. Then connect `mouse_entered` to `grab_focus` and confirm the mouse and keyboard agree. Then handle `ui_cancel` with `set_input_as_handled()`.
CanvasLayer, and drawing above the world:
The node that lifts the interface out of the world — one property, and it solves three problems at once.

**The problem.** A `Control` tree under the world's `Node2D` is **in** the world: the camera moves it, the camera's zoom scales it, and its draw order competes with sprites.

**The answer: a `CanvasLayer`.**

```
Game (Node2D)
├── World (Node2D)
│   ├── Ground, Actors, …
│   └── Camera2D
└── UI (CanvasLayer)          layer = 1
    └── Hud (Control)
```

**What a `CanvasLayer` does, in three parts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It is not affected by `Camera2D`** | its children stay put as the world scrolls |
| **It has its own draw order** | `layer`, an integer, above or below other layers |
| **It has its own transform** | `offset`, `rotation`, `scale`, `transform` |

**Point one is the main reason**, and it is what makes an interface an interface.

**`layer`, which orders the layers:**

| `layer` | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| **−100** | a parallax background |
| **0** | the default layer — **the world** |
| **1** | the HUD |
| **10** | menus and modals |
| **100** | a transition fade, a debug overlay |

**Higher draws later.** And `layer` beats everything inside the layers — from stage 4's draw-order lesson, `CanvasLayer` is the highest-priority mechanism, above `z_index` and Y-sorting.

**So the arrangement that always works:** the world on layer 0, the HUD on 1, modals on 10, transitions on 100. **No `z_index` negotiation between the world and the interface ever again.**

**The transform properties**, which are occasionally exactly what you want:

```gdscript
ui_layer.offset = Vector2(0, -20)        # slide the whole HUD
ui_layer.scale = Vector2(2, 2)           # scale the whole interface
ui_layer.rotation = 0.1                  # tilt it
```

**Scaling the whole layer is one way to do interface scaling**, and it is a blunt one — lesson 13 covers the better arrangement. **But for a quick "make the UI bigger" setting, it is one property.**

**`follow_viewport_enabled`**, which is the odd one out: with it on, the layer **does** follow the camera, with an optional scale — so you can have a layer that moves with the world but draws above everything. **Useful for world-space markers that must not be occluded.**

**The things that go on their own layer:**

| Layer | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **The HUD** | must not scroll |
| **Menus** | must cover the HUD |
| **A transition fade** | must cover everything |
| **A debug overlay** | must cover everything, and be toggleable |
| **A parallax background** | must be behind the world — though `Parallax2D` handles this |

**And the one thing that should not: world-space UI.** A health bar above a character's head **should** move with the world, so it belongs in the world as a child of the character — lesson 18. **Putting it on a `CanvasLayer` and converting coordinates every frame is the hard way round.**

**`CanvasLayer` is not a `Control` and not a `Node2D`.** It extends `Node`, so it has no position of its own — only the layer-wide `offset`. **Its children are positioned normally within it**, and a `Control` child with Full Rect anchors fills the screen.

**What "the screen" means for a `CanvasLayer`**, which matters for lesson 11: its children's coordinate space is the **viewport**, so a Full Rect `Control` fills the viewport — which with the `viewport` stretch mode is 960×540 and with `canvas_items` is the window's real size. **That is the next lesson.**

**The transition pattern**, since it is the clearest use:

```gdscript
# A CanvasLayer at layer 100 with a ColorRect, Full Rect, mouse_filter = Ignore
func fade_out(time: float = 0.3) -> void:
	var t := create_tween()
	t.tween_property(fade, "modulate:a", 1.0, time)
	await t.finished
```

**`mouse_filter = Ignore` on the fade**, from lesson 5 — otherwise a transparent overlay swallows every click for the rest of the game.

**What your own project has.** `pixel_perfect_viewport.gd` refers to a **`PresentationShell`**, which claims a group and, when present, renders the world into a `SubViewport` while the interface draws in the window at its own resolution:

> *With a shell, the world is rendered into a `SubViewport` and the interface is drawn in the window at its own resolution — so the root viewport must be left at 1:1 and the shell does the scaling.*

**That is a step beyond a `CanvasLayer`** — lesson 14 reads it — and the reason is that a `CanvasLayer` shares the viewport's resolution, while a `SubViewport` lets the world and the interface have **different** ones.

**Practice.** Put your HUD on a `CanvasLayer` at layer 1 and confirm it stays put as the camera moves. Add a modal on layer 10 and confirm it covers the HUD. Add a fade `ColorRect` on layer 100 with `mouse_filter = Ignore`, and tween it. Then set the UI layer's `scale` to 2 and see the whole interface double.
The stretch problem:
What happens when the window is not the size you designed for — the single most-misunderstood area of Godot, and the settings that decide it.

**The setup.** Project Settings > Display > Window:

| Setting | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Viewport Width / Height** | **the resolution you design at** |
| **Window Width / Height Override** | the size the window actually opens at |
| **Stretch Mode** | how the viewport maps onto the window |
| **Stretch Aspect** | what happens when the ratios differ |
| **Scale** | an extra multiplier |
| **Scale Mode** | **fractional** or **integer** |

**The viewport size is a design decision, not a resolution.** 960×540 means *"I lay out at 960×540"*, and the window can be anything.

**Stretch Mode, the three values:**

| Mode | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`disabled`** | **no scaling.** The viewport is the window. A bigger window shows more. |
| **`canvas_items`** | **the world scales; the interface is drawn at the window's real resolution.** Text and vectors stay sharp. |
| **`viewport`** | **everything is rendered at the viewport size and the whole image is scaled up.** Pixels stay pixels. |

**For pixel art, `viewport`.** The game composes a 960×540 image and that image is enlarged — so one game pixel becomes a square block of screen pixels, sprites and text alike, and nothing is ever rendered at a resolution the art was not drawn for.

**For a high-resolution 2D game, `canvas_items`.** The art is drawn at the window's resolution, so text is crisp at any size and there is no upscaling blur.

**`disabled` is for a game that wants to use the extra space** — a strategy game where a bigger window means a bigger view. **And note that is also what `viewport` does in your own project**, by a different route, which is the next two lessons.

**Stretch Aspect, which decides what happens to a mismatched ratio:**

| Aspect | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| **`ignore`** | stretch to fill. **Distorts.** Almost never right. |
| **`keep`** | keep the ratio, **letterbox** the remainder with black bars |
| **`keep_width`** | keep the width, **show more or less vertically** |
| **`keep_height`** | keep the height, **show more or less horizontally** |
| **`expand`** | keep the pixel size, **show more in both directions** |

**`keep` is the safe default** — nothing distorts, nothing unexpected comes into view, and you pay for it in bars.

**`expand` is the one people want and the one that complicates the layout**, because the visible area is now variable: the interface must anchor to real edges rather than assume a size, which is why lesson 2's anchors matter and why lesson 21 covers the design frame.

**Scale Mode:**

| Mode | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`fractional`** | scale by any factor — 2.4×, 1.33× |
| **`integer`** | **scale by the largest whole factor that fits, and bar the rest** |

**`integer` is mandatory for pixel art**, because a fractional scale means some game pixels get 2 screen pixels and some get 3, which reads as a visible shimmer, worst of all while moving.

**And here is the honest trap, documented in your own project.** `scale_mode = "integer"` **scales by the largest whole factor that fits and bars the remainder** — and `stretch/aspect = "expand"` does **not** change that. Your own source records the test:

> *`window/stretch/scale_mode = "integer"` scales by the largest whole factor that FITS and bars the remainder, and `stretch/aspect = "expand"` does not change that — it was tried on 2026-09-02 and the bars stayed.*

**So "integer scaling, no bars" is not available from the project settings.** On a 1920×1080 window with a 960×540 viewport it happens to be exact, 2×, no bars. **On 1057 pixels of height — a maximised window with a title bar — 540 at 2× is 1080, which does not fit, so it drops to 1× and bars 537 pixels.** That is the whole problem, and lessons 12 and 13 are its answer.

**The settings your own project uses:**

```ini
window/size/viewport_width=960
window/size/viewport_height=540
window/size/window_width_override=1920
window/size/window_height_override=1080
window/stretch/mode="viewport"
window/stretch/scale_mode="integer"
```

**Design at 960×540, open at 1920×1080, render at the viewport and scale by whole pixels** — and then an autoload fixes what the settings cannot.

**The diagnostic, for when you do not know what you are looking at:**

```gdscript
print(get_window().size)                        # the window
print(get_viewport().get_visible_rect().size)   # what the game sees
print(get_window().content_scale_size)          # the viewport Godot is using
print(DisplayServer.screen_get_size())          # the display
```

**Those four numbers explain every stretch surprise**, and printing them is faster than reasoning about the settings.

**Practice.** Set a 320×180 viewport with `viewport` stretch and `integer` scale mode, and resize the window slowly while watching the bars appear and disappear. Switch to `fractional` and watch the shimmer in a moving sprite. Then switch to `canvas_items` and see the interface sharpen while the art stays blocky. Then print the four diagnostic numbers at each window size.
Integer scaling, and the whole-pixel rul:
The rule a pixel-art game must obey, why the obvious arrangement breaks it, and the reasoning that gets it right.

**The rule: every game pixel must occupy the same whole number of screen pixels.**

**Break it and you get two visible artefacts:**

| Artefact | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| **Shimmer** | a fractional scale — some rows 2 pixels, some 3, changing as things move |
| **Blur** | linear filtering across scaled edges |

**Blur is easy: nearest-neighbour filtering.** Project Settings > Rendering > Textures > **Canvas Textures > Default Texture Filter → Nearest**, or per-texture in the import settings. **Set it project-wide and forget it.**

**Shimmer is the hard one**, and it is what the rest of this lesson is about.

**The naive arrangement and why it fails.** Pick a viewport, set `scale_mode = integer`, and let Godot choose:

```
viewport 960×540, window 1920×1080  → 2×, exact, no bars         ✔
viewport 960×540, window 1920×1057  → 540×2 = 1080 > 1057
                                    → 1×, 960×540 drawn in 1920×1057
                                    → 537 pixels of black        ✘
```

**A maximised window is not 1080 tall** — the panel and title bar take some — so the common case is the broken one. **That is not a corner case; it is what happens when the player clicks maximise.**

**The two variables, which must be separated.** This is the insight, and your own source states it as the fix after four failed attempts:

> *scale = from the DISPLAY — how large a game pixel is drawn*
> *viewport = window / scale — how much world is on screen*

**Read that twice, because it inverts the obvious approach.**

| Variable | Derived from | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **scale** | **the display** | **how big a game pixel is** — the zoom |
| **viewport** | **window ÷ scale** | **how much world is visible** |

**The obvious approach derives the scale from the window**, which couples them: a bigger window buys bigger pixels instead of more world. **And that is backwards.** Your own source records what it felt like:

> *Master Roachi's words were "the window doesnt show more, everything just zooms", and that was exactly right.*

**Why each belongs where it does:**

**Zoom belongs to the display.** A denser screen should draw the same art physically larger, or the game is a postage stamp on a 4K panel. **So scale is a property of the monitor, computed once.**

**How much world is visible belongs to the window.** Make the window bigger and you should see more. **With the scale fixed, `viewport = window / scale` does exactly that, by construction.**

**And the letterbox disappears for free.** If the viewport is computed as `window / scale` by integer division, then `viewport × scale ≤ window` always, and the residue is **at most `scale − 1` pixels per axis** — one or two, invisible.

**The arithmetic, worked:**

| Display | scale | Window | Viewport | Covered | Residue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1080p | 2 | 1280×720 | 640×360 | 1280×720 | 0×0 |
| 1080p | 2 | 1920×1057 | 960×528 | 1920×1056 | 0×1 |
| 1440p | 2 | 2560×1400 | 1280×700 | 2560×1400 | 0×0 |
| 2160p | 3 | 3840×2120 | 1280×706 | 3840×2118 | 0×2 |

**Never a bar.** And a bigger window always shows more world, which is the behaviour a player expects.

**The cost, which is real and must be accepted deliberately.** A window **smaller** than the design frame is zoomed in — it shows less than 960×540 — because at a fixed whole-pixel scale a small window simply holds less. Your own source says so plainly:

> *The flip side is real and deliberate: a small window is zoomed in, because at a fixed whole-pixel scale a small window simply holds less. There is no integer scale that shows the composed 960×540 frame in a 1280×720 window.*

**There is no arrangement without that trade-off.** 960 × 2 = 1920 > 1280, and 960 × 1 = 960 wastes a third of the window. **Pick which one you want; you cannot have both.**

**The scale ladder, and why it is capped:**

```gdscript
static func scale_for_screen(screen_height: int) -> int:
	return clampi(int(floor(float(screen_height) / float(BASE.y))), 1, MAX_SCALE)
```

| Display height | `height / 540` | Scale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 540 | 1.0 | 1 |
| 1080 | 2.0 | 2 |
| 1440 | 2.67 | 2 |
| 2160 | 4.0 | **3, capped** |

**Why capped at 3?** Because at 4× a 2160p display gets `3840 / 4 = 960` — **exactly the composed frame — so a 4K player would see less world than a 1440p one.** The cap keeps the relationship monotonic: a bigger display never shows less.

**That is the kind of reasoning this lesson is really teaching.** The rule is arithmetic; the judgement is deciding what the player should experience and then deriving the arithmetic from it.

**The `content_scale_size` property**, which is how you apply a computed viewport at runtime:

```gdscript
get_window().content_scale_size = Vector2i(960, 528)
```

**That is the project setting's runtime equivalent**, and setting it is how the whole arrangement is implemented. **The next lesson reads the implementation.**

**Practice.** Write `scale_for_screen(height)` and `viewport_for(window)` as pure functions and test them against the table above. Then compute the residue for ten window sizes and confirm none exceeds `scale − 1`. Then do it the wrong way round — scale from the window — and confirm that enlarging the window reduces the visible world.
ViewportSizer: reading the real solution:
Your own `pixel_perfect_viewport.gd`, read end to end — a hundred and fifty lines that encode four failed attempts, and nearly every lesson so far.

**The declaration, and a Godot constraint worth knowing:**

```gdscript
class_name PixelPerfectViewport
extends Node
```

**Autoloaded as `ViewportSizer`, not under its class name**, and the comment says why:

> *Autoloaded as `ViewportSizer` rather than under its own class name, because Godot refuses a `class_name` that collides with a singleton. The class name is kept so the sizing rule can be tested as a pure function without a window.*

**Two facts in one sentence.** The engine constraint — **an autoload's name cannot collide with a `class_name`** — and the reason to keep the class name anyway: **`PixelPerfectViewport.viewport_for(...)` is callable from a test without the autoload running.**

**The constants:**

```gdscript
const BASE: Vector2i = Vector2i(960, 540)
const MAX_SCALE: int = 3
const INTERFACE_SLACK: float = 0.9
const SHELL_GROUP: StringName = &"presentation_shell"
```

**`BASE` is the design reference**, and the comment ties it to a design document: *"Every camera value in `P1_BRIEF.md` §7.3, and the 80 px adult standard's relationship to the screen, is composed against this."* **One number, cited.**

**`INTERFACE_SLACK` is the interesting one** — 0.9, meaning the interface may fall 10% short of the design size before it steps down a scale:

> *A maximised window on a 1080p display is 1057 tall, 528 at 2x: twelve units short is a HUD twelve units shorter, not an interface at half the size.*

**Twelve units short is better than half size.** That is a judgement, written down with the arithmetic that justifies it.

**The two instance methods:**

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	get_window().size_changed.connect(_apply)
	_apply()
```

**A signal and an immediate call** — the stage-5 pattern: connect, then run once so the initial state is correct.

**And then `_process`, which is the part worth studying:**

```gdscript
func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	if get_window().size != _applied_for:
		_apply()
```

**Polling, deliberately, with the reason recorded:**

> *The signal alone was not enough… the window is 1280×720 when an autoload's `_ready()` runs, then becomes its real size, and the viewport stayed sized for the smaller one. Godot then scaled 1280×720 by 1× into a 1920×1080 window and centred it — black on all four sides, which is exactly what Master Roachi saw while every measurement I could take reported "fills the window", because I was asking a window that had already stopped being that size.*

**Three things to take from that.**

**1. An autoload's `_ready()` sees a window that is not yet its real size.** A real Godot behaviour, and a real trap.

**2. The diagnostic was lying** — and it was lying because it was asking at the wrong time. **"Every measurement reported *fills the window*"** while the screen was black on four sides.

**3. The justification for the cost:** *"A Vector2i comparison per frame costs nothing and cannot miss a resize, a maximise, or a size the window adopts after startup."* **Polling against being told, chosen on evidence** — the same exception `top_bar.gd` makes, and lesson 20's subject.

**`_apply()`, in three parts.** First, the shell check:

```gdscript
if get_tree() != null and get_tree().get_first_node_in_group(SHELL_GROUP) != null:
	window.content_scale_size = window.size
	_applied_for = window.size
	return
```

**A group used as a capability flag**, from stage 5: *"A `PresentationShell` claims this group when one is running."* **If a shell is present, the root viewport is left at 1:1** and the shell scales the world into a `SubViewport` instead — lesson 14. **And the comment names the failure mode:** scaling here as well *"would compose the interface at the game's resolution and enlarge it, which is the thing the shell exists to stop."*

**Then the sizing:**

```gdscript
var chosen := viewport_for(window.size)
window.content_scale_size = chosen
if window.size == _applied_for:
	return
_applied_for = window.size
```

**Note the order: apply first, then the guard.** The size is set every frame — it is idempotent and free — but the **logging** below only runs when the window has actually changed.

**Then the log, which is the part most projects would not have:**

```gdscript
print("[presentation] window %dx%d | viewport %dx%d at %dx = %dx%d | %s" % [...])
```

**Unconditional, not behind a debug flag**, and the comment defends it:

> *Logged every time, not behind a debug flag. Whether the picture fills the screen is the kind of thing that is argued about from memory otherwise — on 2026-09-02 two fixes were shipped for letterboxing that could not be confirmed from a script harness, and the third needed Master Roachi to run it and report back. One line at startup settles it.*

**And the message is written for a human:** `"fills the window"` when the residue is two pixels or fewer, `"LETTERBOX 320x57"` when it is not — because *"a pixel or two of residue is invisible; only a real border is worth naming."*

**The static functions, which are the actual rule** and are pure so they can be tested:

| Function | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `viewport_for(window_size)` | **`window / scale`**, floored at 1 |
| `scale_for(_window_size)` | **`screen_scale()`** — note the unused parameter |
| `scale_for_screen(screen_height)` | **`clampi(floor(h / 540), 1, 3)`** |
| `screen_scale()` | the override, else `DisplayServer.screen_get_size()` |
| `letterbox_for(window_size)` | **`window − viewport × scale`** |
| `interface_scale_for(window_size)` | the world's scale, stepped down until 960×540 fits |
| `interface_frame_for(window_size)` | **the frame the interface lays out in** |
| `interface_frame(node)` | that frame, or the root viewport's without a shell |

**`scale_for(_window_size)` taking a parameter it ignores** is itself documentation: *"Deliberately independent of window size."* **The underscore says the parameter is there for the interface, not the logic** — a deliberate decision, left visible.

**The test seams:**

```gdscript
static var screen_height_override: int = 0
static var window_size_override: Vector2i = Vector2i.ZERO
```

**Both documented with why they exist**, and both the stage-10 testing pattern: *"the headless display server pins every window to 64 × 64, so a test cannot open a 2560 × 1440 one. Zero asks the window."* **Zero means "ask the real thing"**, so the production path is the default and the seam costs nothing.

**And the headless fallback inside `screen_scale()`:**

```gdscript
if screen.y <= 0:
	return 2  # Headless, or a display that will not answer. 1080p's answer.
```

**A sensible default rather than a crash**, and the comment says which case it is guessing.

**`interface_frame(node)`, which is what the rest of the game calls:**

```gdscript
static func interface_frame(node: Node) -> Vector2:
	if node == null or not node.is_inside_tree():
		return Vector2(BASE)
	var tree := node.get_tree()
	if tree.get_first_node_in_group(SHELL_GROUP) != null:
		return interface_frame_for(window_size_of(tree.root))
	return _held_to_the_design(tree.root.get_visible_rect().size)
```

**A null-and-not-in-tree guard returning the design size**, so a caller in `_init` gets a sane answer rather than a crash. **And the shell branch again** — with one, the window's frame; without one, the root viewport's.

**What it replaced**, and this is the lesson's conclusion: every interface node used to lay out against a constant, `ProductionHud.SCREEN`, *"which is right at 1080p and was wrong at every other size the P6 check tried."* **`act_one_title_card.gd` now calls `PixelPerfectViewport.interface_frame(self)` instead** — a function of the real window rather than a constant.

**Practice.** Read the file yourself, top to bottom, and for each comment decide whether it records a fact, a decision, or a failure. Then call `scale_for_screen` with 540, 1080, 1440 and 2160 and check the table. Then set `screen_height_override = 2160` and print `interface_frame_for(Vector2i(3840, 2120))`. Then find one constant in your own project that should be a function of the window.
SubViewport, and rendering the world sep:
Rendering into a texture — the node that lets the world and the interface have different resolutions, and the four things it is good for.

**What a `SubViewport` is.** A viewport that is **not** the window: it renders its children into a texture, which something else then displays.

**And it needs a display.** A `SubViewport` alone draws nowhere:

```
SubViewportContainer          ← displays it
└── SubViewport
    └── World (Node2D)
        ├── Ground, Actors
        └── Camera2D
```

**`SubViewportContainer` is a `Control`** that sizes its `SubViewport` to itself and draws the result. **Or display it manually with a `TextureRect` and `sub_viewport.get_texture()`**, which gives you more control at the cost of sizing it yourself.

**The properties that matter:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `size` | **the render resolution** — independent of everything |
| `render_target_update_mode` | **Disabled, Once, When Visible, When Parent Visible, Always** |
| `transparent_bg` | render with alpha, for compositing |
| `handle_input_locally` | whether it processes input itself |
| `canvas_item_default_texture_filter` | **per-viewport filtering** |
| `msaa_2d` / `msaa_3d` | anti-aliasing within it |
| `own_world_3d` | a separate 3D world, for previews |

**And on the container:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `stretch` | **resize the SubViewport to the container** — usually **off** for pixel art |
| `stretch_shrink` | an integer divisor — **`2` renders at half and displays at full** |
| `texture_filter` | how the result is scaled up. **Nearest for pixel art.** |

**`stretch_shrink` is the quick pixel-art route:** a container at 1920×1080 with `stretch` on and `stretch_shrink = 2` renders the world at 960×540 and displays it at 2×. **One property, integer scaling, no autoload.** Its limitation is that the factor is fixed in the scene rather than derived from the display.

**The four things a `SubViewport` is genuinely for:**

**1. The world and the interface at different resolutions.** This is your own project's `PresentationShell`:

> *With a shell, the world is rendered into a `SubViewport` and the interface is drawn in the window at its own resolution — so the root viewport must be left at 1:1 and the shell does the scaling.*

**Why that is better than the whole-window arrangement:** the world gets chunky 960×540 pixels, and the interface gets the window's full resolution — **so text is sharp and the art is blocky, each correctly.** With `stretch_mode = viewport` on the whole window, both are forced to the same grid.

**And it is why `ViewportSizer` checks for the shell group and bows out:** two things both scaling the same picture is one too many.

**2. A camera that shows a different place** — a minimap, a security monitor, a split screen. Each `SubViewport` gets its own `Camera2D`, and a `TextureRect` or container puts it where you want:

```
MiniMap (SubViewportContainer)
└── SubViewport           size = 200×200
    ├── (a RemoteTransform2D-driven view of the world)
    └── Camera2D          zoom = 0.1
```

**For 2D, a second view of the *same* world needs the nodes to be in the viewport** — which means either moving them or using `own_world_3d`'s 2D equivalent, and in practice a minimap is usually **drawn** rather than rendered, with `_draw` from stage 8.

**3. A screen-space post-processing pass.** Render the world into a `SubViewport`, then put a `ShaderMaterial` on the `SubViewportContainer`: the shader now sees the finished frame. **That is how a full-screen CRT, bloom or colour-grade effect is done** — stage 10's shader lesson.

**4. Rendering to a texture for use in the world** — a character portrait that is a live 3D model, a mirror, a camera feed on an in-world screen.

**`render_target_update_mode`, which is where the performance is:**

| Mode | Renders |
| --- | --- |
| **Disabled** | never |
| **Once** | one frame, then back to Disabled |
| **When Visible** | when something is displaying it — **the default, usually right** |
| **When Parent Visible** | when its parent is visible |
| **Always** | every frame, visible or not |

**`Always` on four `SubViewport`s means rendering the game five times.** **Once** is the mode for a portrait that never changes, and setting it back to `Once` after a change is the idiom:

```gdscript
portrait_viewport.render_target_update_mode = SubViewport.UPDATE_ONCE
```

**Input, which is the fiddly part.** A `SubViewportContainer` forwards mouse events into its `SubViewport`, **translating the coordinates** — so a click lands in the right place even though the viewport is a different size. **Without a container**, using a `TextureRect`, you get no translation and must do it yourself:

```gdscript
func _gui_input(event: InputEvent) -> void:
	if event is InputEventMouse:
		var local := event.position * (Vector2(sub_viewport.size) / size)
		sub_viewport.push_input(_shifted(event, local))
```

**Which is a good reason to use the container.**

**`get_viewport()` inside a `SubViewport` returns the `SubViewport`**, not the window — which is correct and occasionally surprising. **So `get_viewport().get_visible_rect().size` gives the render resolution**, and `get_window().size` gives the window. **Both are useful; mixing them up is a common bug**, and it is why `interface_frame(node)` in the last lesson distinguishes them.

**The filtering trap.** A `SubViewport` rendered at 960×540 and displayed at 1920×1080 is scaled by **the container's** `texture_filter`, not the project default. **Set it to Nearest on the container** or the whole point is lost to bilinear blur.

**When not to use one.** For a straightforward pixel-art game, `stretch_mode = viewport` plus a computed `content_scale_size` — the last two lessons — is simpler and does the same job. **Reach for a `SubViewport` when you need two resolutions, a post-processing pass, or a second view** — not by default.

**Practice.** Put your world in a `SubViewport` inside a `SubViewportContainer`, with `stretch` on and `stretch_shrink = 2`, and the container's filter Nearest. Confirm the world is chunky and a `Label` outside the container is sharp. Then set `render_target_update_mode` to Once and watch it freeze. Then put a `ShaderMaterial` on the container that inverts the colours, and see the whole frame invert.
Camera2D: following, smoothing, limits:
The camera — four properties that do ninety per cent of the work, and the ones people set wrongly.

**What `Camera2D` does.** It sets the viewport's transform: everything is drawn relative to it. **The camera does not move the world; it changes where the world is drawn.**

**`enabled` and the active camera.** Several `Camera2D`s can exist; the **last enabled one in the tree** wins, and `make_current()` switches:

```gdscript
cutscene_camera.make_current()
# later
player_camera.make_current()
```

**Two cameras and a `make_current()` call is the whole cutscene-camera mechanism** — no interpolation code, no saving and restoring the player camera's position.

**The core properties:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `zoom` | **larger zooms IN.** `Vector2(2, 2)` shows half as much. |
| `offset` | shifts the view without moving the node |
| `anchor_mode` | **Fixed Top Left** or **Drag Center** — centre is the default and usually right |
| `process_callback` | **Idle** or **Physics** — see below |
| `ignore_rotation` | keep the view upright even if the parent rotates |

**`zoom` is the one that catches everyone: bigger is closer.** It was the other way round in Godot 3. And for pixel art, **keep it at `Vector2.ONE`** — a zoomed camera resamples everything and undoes the whole whole-pixel arrangement from lesson 12. **Zoom by changing the viewport size, not the camera.**

**Following the player — the three ways, in order of preference:**

**1. Make the camera a child of the player.** Free, exact, no code. **Right for a game that wants a hard-locked camera.**

**2. Position smoothing**, which is the built-in soft follow:

```
position_smoothing_enabled = true
position_smoothing_speed = 5.0
```

**Still a child of the player**, but the camera lags behind and catches up. **One checkbox and one number for a camera that feels good** — and `5.0` is a sensible start, higher being tighter.

**3. A separate node, moved in code**, for anything the built-ins cannot express — a camera that frames two players, leads the player's motion, or follows a target that is not a node.

```gdscript
func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	var target := player.global_position + player.velocity * LEAD
	global_position = global_position.lerp(target, 1.0 - exp(-SPEED * delta))
```

**Note `1.0 - exp(-SPEED * delta)` rather than a bare `lerp(a, b, 0.1)`** — from stage 6: the bare form is frame-rate dependent, and this one is not.

**Drag margins, which are the underused feature:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `drag_horizontal_enabled` / `drag_vertical_enabled` | on or off per axis |
| `drag_left/right/top/bottom_margin` | **0 to 1 — a fraction of the screen** |
| `drag_horizontal_offset` / `drag_vertical_offset` | shift the dead zone |

**A drag margin is a dead zone: the camera does not move until the target leaves it.** `drag_bottom_margin = 0.3` means the player can move through the middle 70% without the camera following, which is **exactly right for a platformer** — small jumps do not move the view.

**Limits, which every camera in a bounded level wants:**

```
limit_left, limit_top, limit_right, limit_bottom
limit_smoothed = true
```

**The camera will not show beyond them**, so the level's edge is never visible. **And `limit_smoothed` matters**: without it the camera stops dead at the limit, which with smoothing on reads as a jolt.

**Setting limits from the level**, since hard-coding them is fragile:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	var bounds: Rect2 = level.bounds
	camera.limit_left = int(bounds.position.x)
	camera.limit_top = int(bounds.position.y)
	camera.limit_right = int(bounds.end.x)
	camera.limit_bottom = int(bounds.end.y)
```

**And the trap: limits are in global coordinates and are integers.** A camera whose parent is moving will fight its limits in a way that is hard to read, which is one reason a code-driven camera is a separate node.

**`process_callback`, which fixes the commonest camera bug.** A camera following a `CharacterBody2D` that moves in `_physics_process` will **jitter** if the camera updates in `_process`, because it is reading a position that updates at a different rate.

**Two fixes, and both are right in different cases:**

| Fix | When |
| --- | --- |
| `process_callback = Physics` | the camera follows a physics body |
| **Physics interpolation** | the whole game, from stage 4 |

**`process_callback = CAMERA2D_PROCESS_PHYSICS` is the one-property answer**, and it is what to reach for first when a camera stutters.

**The screen's edges, in world coordinates** — needed constantly, for culling, spawning and clamping:

```gdscript
func visible_world_rect() -> Rect2:
	var size := get_viewport_rect().size / zoom
	return Rect2(get_screen_center_position() - size * 0.5, size)
```

**`get_screen_center_position()` accounts for smoothing, limits and offset**, which `global_position` does not — so it is the one to use. **That distinction is the camera's single most useful piece of trivia.**

**And the coordinate conversions**, from stage 3:

```gdscript
get_global_mouse_position()                    # mouse in world space
camera.get_viewport_transform() * world_point  # world → screen
```

**What to keep at defaults.** `rotating` off, `zoom` at one, `anchor_mode` at Drag Center. **The three properties worth setting on nearly every camera** are `position_smoothing_enabled`, the four limits, and `process_callback` if it follows a physics body.

**Practice.** Give a player a child `Camera2D` with smoothing at 5.0, and compare it with smoothing off. Add drag margins of 0.2 and feel the dead zone. Set limits from the level's bounds with `limit_smoothed` on, and walk into a corner. Then make the camera stutter by following a `CharacterBody2D` from `_process`, and fix it with `process_callback = Physics`. Then write `visible_world_rect()` and draw it with `_draw` to confirm it matches.
Screen shake, properly:
The effect everybody adds badly — the four mistakes, the accessibility requirement, and your own project's version.

**The naive version, and what is wrong with it:**

```gdscript
# Do not do this
func shake() -> void:
	for i in 10:
		camera.position += Vector2(randf_range(-8, 8), randf_range(-8, 8))
		await get_tree().create_timer(0.02).timeout
```

**Four problems:**

| Problem | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| **It writes the camera's position** | fights the follow logic; the camera drifts |
| **No decay** | it stops dead rather than settling |
| **No cap** | two impacts at once shake twice as hard |
| **No way to turn it off** | **motion sickness, and no setting** |

**The fix for the first is the important one: shake is additive, not a position.**

**The shape that works.** Keep the camera's real position separate from what is presented, and add shake on top:

```gdscript
var _shake_amplitude: float = 0.0
var _shake_remaining: float = 0.0

func add_shake(amplitude: float, duration: float) -> void:
	_shake_amplitude = min(max(_shake_amplitude, amplitude), MAX_AMPLITUDE)
	_shake_remaining = min(max(_shake_remaining, duration), MAX_DURATION)
```

**Read `max` then `min` carefully, because that pair is the whole design:**

- **`max(current, new)`** — a bigger shake wins; a smaller one does not interrupt
- **`min(..., MAX)`** — **capped**, so a crowd of impacts cannot shake the screen off

**That is "repeated impacts refresh rather than stack"**, which is your own project's stated rule, and it is why a fight with ten hits does not become unplayable.

**The per-frame part:**

```gdscript
func _presented_position(delta: float) -> Vector2:
	var presented := _framed(_gameplay_position, delta)
	if _shake_remaining > 0.0:
		_shake_remaining = maxf(0.0, _shake_remaining - delta)
		var falloff := _shake_remaining / maxf(MAX_DURATION, 0.0001)
		var amplitude := _shake_amplitude * falloff * clampf(shake_scale, 0.0, 1.0)
		presented += Vector2(
			randf_range(-amplitude, amplitude),
			randf_range(-amplitude, amplitude)
		)
		if is_zero_approx(_shake_remaining):
			_shake_amplitude = 0.0
	return presented.round() if pixel_snap_position else presented
```

**Four things to notice.**

**1. `_gameplay_position` and the presented position are different variables.** The follow logic writes the first; this function produces the second. **So shake cannot corrupt the camera's idea of where it is** — which is the fix for problem one, and the reason your own project sets `position_smoothing_enabled = false` and does its own smoothing.

**2. `falloff` decays the amplitude over the remaining time**, so the shake settles instead of stopping. **And the division is guarded against zero** with `maxf(MAX_DURATION, 0.0001)`.

**3. `shake_scale`, which is the accessibility requirement** and is documented as such: *"Accessibility: scales shake to zero without touching gameplay framing."* **One float, exposed in the options screen, and a player who gets motion sick can set it to 0** — and the camera still follows, still frames conversations, still cuts. **Shake is the only thing that stops.**

**That is the right shape for an accessibility setting: a multiplier on the effect, not a branch around the feature.**

**4. `.round()` at the end** — the whole-pixel rule from lesson 12, applied to the final presented position. **A shake that puts the camera on a fractional position shimmers the entire scene**, and your own source states it as a requirement rather than a preference:

> *With integer scale mode a camera resting on a fractional position shimmers the entire scene, so this rounding is a requirement rather than a preference.*

**Random against noise.** `randf_range` per frame is white noise, which reads as a buzz. **For a weightier shake, sample a smooth noise function:**

```gdscript
var _noise := FastNoiseLite.new()
var _t: float = 0.0

func _offset(delta: float, amplitude: float) -> Vector2:
	_t += delta * 30.0
	return Vector2(_noise.get_noise_2d(_t, 0.0), _noise.get_noise_2d(0.0, _t)) * amplitude
```

**Noise gives a shake that moves coherently** — the camera travels rather than vibrating — and it is the difference between a hit that feels like an impact and one that feels like a glitch. **Both are legitimate; choose by what the hit should feel like.**

**Shake is not the only impact effect**, and usually not the best one:

| Effect | What it conveys |
| --- | --- |
| **Hit stop** — freeze for 2–4 frames | weight. **The strongest effect per line of code.** |
| **Flash** — `modulate` white for a frame | registration: *that landed* |
| **Knockback** | force |
| **Shake** | scale: something big happened |
| **Chromatic aberration or a vignette pulse** | drama |

**Hit stop is the one to reach for first**, and your own project has a `HitStopService` for exactly that reason — stage 6's lesson. **Shake is for the big moments; using it for every hit spends it.**

**What not to shake:** the interface. **Shake the camera and the HUD stays still**, because it is on a `CanvasLayer` from lesson 10 — which is correct, and is another reason that separation matters. **A shaking HUD reads as a bug.**

**Rotation shake**, which is worth knowing about and usually wrong: `camera.rotation += ...` shakes rotationally. **For pixel art it is forbidden** — a rotated camera resamples every sprite — and your own project sets `ignore_rotation = true` and says so.

**Practice.** Implement `add_shake(amplitude, duration)` with the max-then-min pair and a separate presented position. Confirm two simultaneous calls do not stack beyond the cap. Add a `shake_scale` and set it to 0, confirming the camera still follows. Then round the presented position and compare the static world's stability at 3× zoom. Then replace `randf_range` with `FastNoiseLite` and judge which fits a heavy impact.
Parallax, and backgrounds that move:
Depth from layers moving at different speeds — and the node that replaced the old one in Godot 4.3.

**The idea.** A background further away moves less as the camera pans. **Two or three layers at different rates reads as depth**, and it costs nothing.

**The current node is `Parallax2D`**, added in 4.3 and the one to use. **`ParallaxBackground` + `ParallaxLayer` still exist and still work**, but they are the older pair and have a real limitation: they only respond to the camera, and they do not work inside a `SubViewport` the way `Parallax2D` does.

**`Parallax2D` is a `Node2D`**, which is the first thing that makes it simpler — it goes anywhere in the world and its children are ordinary nodes.

**The properties:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`scroll_scale`** | **the rate.** `(0.5, 0.5)` moves at half the camera's speed |
| `repeat_size` | **the tile size** — non-zero makes it repeat |
| `repeat_times` | how many copies either side |
| `autoscroll` | pixels per second of constant motion, **independent of the camera** |
| `scroll_offset` | a manual offset |
| `screen_offset` | an offset in screen space |
| `limit_begin` / `limit_end` | bounds beyond which it stops scrolling |
| `follow_viewport` | whether it tracks the camera at all |

**`scroll_scale` is the one that matters**, and the mental model is the opposite of what people expect:

| `scroll_scale` | Behaviour | Reads as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **0** | does not move | **infinitely far — the sky** |
| **0.2** | moves a fifth as much | distant mountains |
| **0.5** | half | mid-distance hills |
| **1** | **moves with the world** | the same plane as the gameplay |
| **1.5** | moves faster | **foreground, in front of the action** |

**Above 1 is the underused one** — a foreground layer that overtakes the camera sells depth more strongly than three background layers, because it passes the player.

**The arrangement:**

```
World (Node2D)
├── Sky (Parallax2D)          scroll_scale = (0, 0)      z_index = -100
├── Mountains (Parallax2D)    scroll_scale = (0.2, 0.1)  z_index = -90
├── Hills (Parallax2D)        scroll_scale = (0.5, 0.3)  z_index = -80
├── Gameplay (Node2D)                                    z_index = 0
├── Grass (Parallax2D)        scroll_scale = (1.3, 1.0)  z_index = 10
└── Camera2D
```

**Note the vertical rates are lower than the horizontal ones.** That is deliberate: a background that moves as much vertically as horizontally looks like it is sliding, because the eye expects less vertical motion from a distant object. **Half the horizontal rate is a good starting point.**

**Repeating, which is what makes an endless background:**

```
repeat_size = Vector2(512, 0)      # the texture's width
repeat_times = 1
```

**`repeat_size` must match the texture's size exactly**, or the seam shows. **And the texture must tile** — its left edge continuing into its right — which is an art requirement, not a code one. **`repeat_times = 1` gives one copy each side**, enough for any screen narrower than twice the tile.

**`autoscroll`, which is the free win:**

```
autoscroll = Vector2(-20, 0)
```

**Clouds that drift without the camera moving.** Combined with `scroll_scale`, a cloud layer both drifts and parallaxes, and the two add. **This is how a static scene stops looking static.**

**Pixel art and parallax, which conflict in one specific way.** A layer at `scroll_scale = 0.37` will land on fractional positions, and in a pixel-art game that is a shimmer. **Three answers:**

| Answer | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| **Use rates that divide evenly** — 0.5, 0.25 | fewer choices |
| **Round the layer's position** | the motion becomes slightly steppy |
| **Accept it for distant layers only** | a distant blurry layer hides it |

**Rounding is usually right**, and at a low rate the stepping is invisible because the layer barely moves:

```gdscript
func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	scroll_offset = scroll_offset.round()
```

**The failure modes, all of which look like a bug:**

| Symptom | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| **The layer does not move** | `follow_viewport` off, or no active `Camera2D` |
| **A visible seam** | `repeat_size` does not match the texture |
| **The layer slides off** | `scroll_scale` above 1 with no `limit_end` |
| **It moves the wrong way** | **`scroll_scale` is a rate, not a direction** — use `autoscroll` for direction |
| **Shimmer** | a fractional rate on pixel art |

**When not to use parallax.** A top-down game has no horizon, so there is no "further away" — **parallax in a top-down game reads as the ground sliding.** Your own project is top-down and uses none: depth comes from Y-sorting and the terrain itself, from stage 8.

**And a side note on what replaces it there: a `Parallax2D` at `scroll_scale = 1` is pointless** — it is just a `Node2D`. **If every layer is at 1, delete the parallax nodes.**

**Practice.** Build three `Parallax2D` layers at 0, 0.3 and 0.6, with the vertical rate half the horizontal, and pan a camera across them. Set `repeat_size` to a tiling texture's width and confirm no seam. Add a foreground layer at 1.4 and see how much more it sells than the background ones. Add `autoscroll` to the sky. Then set a rate to 0.37 and look for the shimmer at 3× scale.
World-space UI: health bars and damage n:
Interface attached to things in the world — the three ways to do it, and the one your own project chose.

**The problem.** A health bar must sit above an enemy's head, so it must move with the enemy. **But it must be sharp, and it must not be scaled with the world's pixel grid** if the interface is drawn at a different resolution.

**The three approaches:**

| Approach | How |
| --- | --- |
| **1. A child node in the world** | a `ProgressBar` or `Sprite2D` under the enemy |
| **2. A `Control` on a `CanvasLayer`, repositioned each frame** | convert world → screen |
| **3. Drawn in one pass** | one `_draw` over every enemy |

**Approach 1 is the simplest and is right for a lot of games.** A `ProgressBar` as a child of the enemy at `position = Vector2(-20, -30)`:

```gdscript
func _on_health_changed(current: float, most: float) -> void:
	bar.value = current / most
	bar.visible = current < most
```

**No coordinate conversion, no per-frame work, and it moves for free.** Its costs: it is drawn in the world so it is scaled with the world, it inherits the enemy's `scale` and `modulate`, and it draws behind anything with a higher `z_index`.

**The `scale` inheritance is the one that bites** — an enemy scaled to 1.4 gets a bar scaled to 1.4, and text in it gets fuzzy. **`top_level = true` on the bar detaches it from the parent's transform**, and then you are back to positioning it yourself.

**Approach 2, the conversion.** The function you need:

```gdscript
var screen_point := enemy.get_global_transform_with_canvas().origin
```

**`get_global_transform_with_canvas()` is the one to remember.** It gives a node's transform **including the canvas transform** — which means the camera, the zoom, the stretch, all of it. **Its `origin` is where that node is on screen.** No manual camera arithmetic.

**The alternatives and why they are worse:**

| Expression | Problem |
| --- | --- |
| `node.global_position` | world space; ignores the camera |
| `camera.get_viewport_transform() * pos` | correct, but needs a camera reference |
| `get_viewport_transform() * global_position` | correct; the same thing, longer |

**So: `get_global_transform_with_canvas().origin`, and move on.**

**Approach 3 is what your own project does**, and it is worth reading because it solves a problem the other two do not.

**`enemy_health_bars.gd` is a `CanvasLayer`** with one `Control` child that draws every bar:

```gdscript
func _init() -> void:
	name = "EnemyHealthBars"
	# UNDER THE HUD'S 40, OVER LOOT LABELS' 35: a bar reads before the name on the ground under it.
	layer = 36

func _ready() -> void:
	_canvas = Control.new()
	_canvas.mouse_filter = Control.MOUSE_FILTER_IGNORE
	_canvas.draw.connect(_draw_bars)
	add_child(_canvas)

func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	if _canvas != null:
		_canvas.queue_redraw()
```

**Four things in those ten lines.**

**`layer = 36` with the ordering reasoned out in a comment** — under the HUD's 40, over the loot labels' 35, because *"a bar reads before the name on the ground under it."* **Layer numbers chosen against each other and written down**, which is the difference between a layer stack you can reason about and a pile of magic numbers.

**`mouse_filter = IGNORE`**, from lesson 5 — an invisible full-screen overlay that swallows clicks is the classic bug, and this is the one-line prevention.

**`draw.connect(_draw_bars)`** rather than a script on the `Control` — the `CanvasItem.draw` signal, so the whole system is one file with no second script.

**And `queue_redraw()` every frame**, because the enemies move.

**The draw itself:**

```gdscript
var head := enemy.get_global_transform_with_canvas().origin
var top := head + Vector2(-width * 0.5, -ABOVE_PX - height)
var back := Rect2(top, Vector2(width, height))
_canvas.draw_rect(back.grow(1.0), OUTLINE_COLOUR)
_canvas.draw_rect(back, BACK_COLOUR)
if fraction > 0.001:
	var fill := FILL_HIGH.lerp(FILL_LOW, 1.0 - fraction)
	_canvas.draw_rect(Rect2(back.position, Vector2(back.size.x * fraction, back.size.y)), fill)
```

**`back.grow(1.0)` for the outline** — a one-pixel border for free, from stage 8's `_draw`. **And `FILL_HIGH.lerp(FILL_LOW, 1.0 - fraction)`**, so the bar's colour tells you the health as well as its length — **never colour alone**, and never length alone either.

**Why this approach rather than a node per enemy.** Three reasons, and they are the ones that decide it:

**1. One node for every bar.** Fifty enemies cost one `Control`, not fifty `ProgressBar`s with their containers and themes.

**2. It is sharp.** The layer is lifted to the window's resolution by the presentation shell, so the bars are drawn at the display's resolution rather than the world's 960×540 — the point of lesson 14.

**3. It reads the world rather than being told.** No signal to connect per enemy, no cleanup when one dies. **The loop iterates a group and draws whoever is there**, which is the next lesson's subject.

**And how it decides who gets a bar**, which is the design content rather than the technique:

```gdscript
func shows(enemy: ProductionEnemy) -> bool:
	var most := enemy.enemy_definition.maximum_hp if enemy.enemy_definition != null else 0.0
	var damaged := most > 0.0 and enemy.current_hp < most - 0.01
	return damaged or _is_engaged(enemy)
```

**Damaged or engaged** — and the comment records that *"engaged"* had to be defined carefully, because every enemy has a target from its first frame, so `get_target_actor() != null` would light a bar on everything. **The real test is the enemy's own state machine.**

**Damage numbers**, which are the same shape with a lifetime:

```gdscript
var _numbers: Array[Dictionary] = []
```

**An array of plain dictionaries rather than nodes** — each with a position, a value, an age and a colour — ticked in `_process` and drawn in one pass. **No node allocation per hit**, which matters when a fight produces fifty.

**And `SCATTER_PX`, which is the design detail worth stealing:** each number is offset by a small random amount so *"a crowd stays readable rather than a stack of numbers on one spot."*

**Practice.** Draw health bars for every enemy in a group from one `Control` on a `CanvasLayer`, using `get_global_transform_with_canvas().origin`. Set `mouse_filter = IGNORE` and confirm clicks still reach the world. Give the bar a one-pixel outline with `grow(1.0)` and a colour that lerps with the fraction. Then add floating damage numbers as an array of dictionaries with a lifetime and a small random scatter.
The HUD, and what it must not know:
The largest interface in a game, and the one architectural rule that keeps it from becoming the worst file in the project.

**The rule: the HUD only reads.**

**Your own project states it, cites it, and tests it:**

> *`production-architecture.md` §7: presentation lives outside every production actor and gameplay never depends on it. `production_hud_test.gd` holds that two ways — it deletes the HUD mid-walk and plays on, AND scans this file for any assignment into actor, party or objective state, because the first check alone passes a HUD whose last write outlives it.*

**Read that second check again, because it is the clever part.** Deleting the HUD and continuing proves the game does not *need* it. **It does not prove the HUD never writes** — a HUD that sets a flag once at startup passes that test and has still corrupted the architecture. **So the test greps its own source for assignments into game state.**

**A test that reads the source file is unusual and here it is correct**, because the property being tested is a property of the code, not of a run.

**Why the rule matters.** A HUD that writes game state becomes load-bearing: delete it and the game breaks, so it can never be replaced, and every gameplay bug now has a presentation suspect. **Keeping it read-only means the interface is always disposable**, which is what lets it be rewritten.

**What the HUD is made of**, and the arrangement your own project uses, chosen by Master Roachi:

> *"two big orbs with the skills in between. The orbs are right resource, left hp, the rest of the party is shown top left... quest log goes on the right of the screen at the top, right under the minimap."*

| Region | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| **Bottom centre** | **two orbs with the skill bar between** — the numbers you watch without reading |
| **Top left** | the rest of the party, glanceable |
| **Top right** | the minimap |
| **Right, under the minimap** | the quest log |

**And the reasoning for it**, which is the part to learn: *"the leader's two numbers are the ones you watch without reading, and the rest of the party is glanceable rather than central."* **Two tiers of attention, and the layout follows them.**

**Never colour alone** — the accessibility rule, applied throughout:

> *Both orbs carry their numbers, the leader is named, Wounded and Down are words, reserved Unity is hatched as well as dimmed, and every quest line carries its count.*

**Every state has a second channel.** Colour **and** a number; dimming **and** hatching; a status **and** its word. **That is the whole rule, and it is cheap** — a label beside a bar, a pattern over a greyed region.

**And the enforcement, which is the same trick again:** *"The HUD records every string it draws so that claim can be checked rather than asserted."* **A test can then assert that the word "Wounded" appears when a hero is wounded** — rather than a human squinting at a screenshot.

**What is deliberately not on it:**

| Not shown | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **A threat meter** | canon says it is not player HUD |
| **A universal poise meter** | same |

**Both with a citation.** The lesson is not about those two numbers; it is that **"what the HUD does not show" is a decision that deserves recording** as much as what it does, because otherwise someone adds it back.

**Building for the game you will have, not the one you have.** The quoted reasoning is worth keeping:

> *Built to the shape Act I needs, not the shape the Prologue needs. The Prologue has no combat: nothing takes damage, no resource moves, no skill is used… So most of this sits inert for the whole of P3 — which is the point. One HUD that Act I adds to beats one that Act I replaces, and building it against the real state now means the numbers are already wired when something finally changes them.*

**That is a judgement, not a rule** — and it is the opposite of the usual advice. **It is right here because the HUD reads: wiring a number that never changes costs one line and no risk.** It would be wrong for a system that writes.

**Keeping a large HUD manageable — the three mechanisms:**

**1. Sub-scenes per region.** The orbs, the skill bar, the minimap, the quest log: each its own scene with its own script. **The HUD composes them and routes data down.**

**2. One update path.** Either every region polls, or every region is told — not a mixture. The next lesson is about choosing.

**3. No gameplay logic.** Computing *"is the hero wounded"* belongs in the hero; the HUD asks. **The test for a line of HUD code: if the answer would be the same with no HUD, it does not belong here.**

**The layout frame, which the next-but-one lesson covers properly.** Your own project's HUD had a real fault worth naming now:

> *The design resolution: the SMALLEST frame the HUD is laid out for, not the only one. It was the only one, and that was a real fault rather than a tuning problem… On a 1360 × 768 window it is 680 × 384 and the whole bottom bar, the minimap and the quest log were drawn off the edge.*

**A constant called `SCREEN` that was only right at one resolution.** The fix was `interface_frame(self)` from lesson 13 — **a function of the real window rather than a constant** — and the comment now says the constant is a *minimum*, not the size.

**Practice.** Write your HUD so it only reads, and prove it: delete the HUD node mid-game and confirm play continues. Then grep your HUD's source for assignments into game state and fix what you find. Then take one state the HUD shows with colour and add a second channel — a number, a word, a pattern. Then split one region of your HUD into its own scene.
Polling against being told, in interface:
The one place the told-not-asked rule from stage 5 is routinely and correctly broken — and how to tell when you are in that place.

**The rule, restated.** From stage 5: a system should be **told** when something changes, by a signal, rather than **asking** every frame. It is the right default — it scales, it makes the dependency visible, and it does no work when nothing happens.

**And an interface is where it is most often wrong.**

**Why.** A HUD displays a dozen values. Being told means a dozen signals, a dozen connections, a dozen emitters that each have to remember to emit. **Asking means one `_process` and a dozen assignments.**

**Your own `top_bar.gd` says so, in capitals:**

> *IT READS THE WORLD EVERY FRAME rather than being told when to change. The amounts move whenever a day passes, the dial's hand never stops, and the speed buttons have to agree with the clock even when something else changed it. Every refresh is setting a dozen strings, which costs nothing, and the alternative is a dozen places that each have to remember to say so.*

**Three separate arguments in that paragraph, and each one is a reason on its own.**

**1. Some of it changes continuously.** *"The dial's hand never stops."* **A clock face has no "changed" moment** — it is a function of time. A signal would have to fire every frame, which is polling with extra steps.

**2.
