Some of it changes from more than one place.** *"The speed buttons have to agree with the clock even when something else changed it."* **This is the strong argument.** If the clock's speed can be set by a button, a hotkey, a cutscene, a pause menu and a save load, then being told means **five** emitters that must each remember. **Miss one and the button lies.**

**3. The cost is nothing.** *"Every refresh is setting a dozen strings, which costs nothing."* **Twelve string assignments per frame is not a performance concern**, and saying so out loud is the right move — the objection to polling is almost always performance, and here it has been priced.

**And note the fourth argument, which is implicit: there is no correctness risk.** The HUD only reads, from the last lesson. **A reader that polls can be stale for one frame and nothing breaks.** A *writer* that polls can act on stale data and corrupt state — which is why the rule still holds everywhere else.

**So the test — and it is four questions:**

| Question | Polling is fine if… |
| --- | --- |
| **Does it only read?** | yes |
| **Can the value change from several places?** | yes |
| **Does it change continuously, or often?** | yes |
| **Is a one-frame delay harmless?** | yes |

**Four yeses: poll.** Any no, and especially the first, means be told.

**What polling looks like when it is done properly:**

```gdscript
func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	if _york != null:
		refresh()


func refresh() -> void:
	if _york == null or _clock == null:
		return
	_level.text = "LEVEL %d" % _york.york_level()
	_leader.text = _york.leader.to_upper()
	# …
```

**Two things to copy.**

**`refresh()` is a separate, callable function**, not inlined into `_process`. **So `watch()` can call it immediately** when the bar is given its world, and a test can call it without running a frame. **The per-frame call is one line; the logic is a named function.**

**And the null guards in both.** A HUD exists before it has a world to show, so `refresh()` returning early is the normal case, not an error.

**The state that must be derived, not remembered** — and this is the subtle payoff:

```gdscript
_pause.button_pressed = _clock.paused
for speed in _speeds:
	(_speeds[speed] as Button).button_pressed = \
		not _clock.paused and is_equal_approx(_clock.speed, float(speed))
```

**The buttons' appearance is computed from the clock every frame**, with the comment making the rule explicit: *"Its state is set from the clock on every refresh rather than left to the button, so the two cannot drift — whatever the click did to the button, the clock has the last word."*

**That is the real argument for polling an interface.** A `Button` with `toggle_mode` keeps its own state, and **two copies of one fact will drift.** Deriving the button from the clock every frame makes drift impossible — **not unlikely, impossible** — because there is only one copy.

**Compare the told version:** click the button, emit a signal, the clock changes, the clock emits back, the button updates. **Five steps, two sources of truth, and a bug the first time anything sets the clock without going through the button.**

**The polling that is wrong**, so the lesson is not taken too far:

| Polling | Why it is wrong |
| --- | --- |
| **An inventory screen rebuilding its grid every frame** | allocating fifty nodes per frame. **Rebuild on change.** |
| **A `_process` that queries a database or a file** | expensive, and not a string assignment |
| **Polling to decide whether to act** — spawn, damage, save | **a writer.** Be told. |
| **Polling a node that may be freed** | `is_instance_valid` every frame is a smell; connect to `tree_exiting` |

**The middle ground, and it is often the right answer: poll cheap, be told expensive.** The `top_bar` polls a dozen strings and is **told** when to open the warehouse. **Scalars and labels poll; structural changes are signalled.**

**And one honest caveat.** `_process` on an interface node runs even when the game is paused or the screen is hidden. **Set `process_mode` deliberately** — from stage 4 — and `visible`-gate it if the screen is one of several:

```gdscript
func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	if not visible:
		return
	refresh()
```

**Practice.** Write a HUD label that polls a value every frame and one that is told by a signal, and change the value from two different places. Confirm the polled one cannot drift. Then derive a toggle button's `button_pressed` from the real state every frame rather than from its own click. Then find one `_process` in your project that allocates nodes, and make it rebuild on change instead.
Responsive interface, and the design fra:
Laying out an interface that works at every window size — the mistake nearly every project makes once, and the two mechanisms that fix it.

**The mistake: a constant for the screen size.**

```gdscript
const SCREEN := Vector2(960, 540)   # the fault
# …
orb.position = SCREEN - Vector2(100, 100)
```

**It works perfectly at one resolution.** And your own project's HUD carries the correction, which names the failure exactly:

> *The design resolution: the SMALLEST frame the HUD is laid out for, not the only one. It was the only one, and that was a real fault rather than a tuning problem… On a 1360 × 768 window it is 680 × 384 and the whole bottom bar, the minimap and the quest log were drawn off the edge; on a 2560 × 1440 window it is 1280 × 720 and everything…*

**Two directions of failure.** Too small, and the interface is drawn off the edge. Too large, and it huddles in the corner with the rest of the screen empty. **Neither is a tuning problem; both are the same bug.**

**And why it bites harder in your own project than in most:** `ViewportSizer` takes the zoom from the **display** and the world from the **window**, so the space the interface is drawn into is `window / scale` — **960 × 540 only when the window happens to be exactly the design size times that scale.** The whole point of lesson 12 is that the frame is variable.

**Mechanism one: anchors.** From lesson 2 — and most of the problem disappears if the interface is built from containers and anchors rather than positions:

| Element | Anchor |
| --- | --- |
| A top bar | **Top Wide**, with `offset_bottom = HEIGHT` |
| A bottom bar | **Bottom Wide** |
| A minimap | **Top Right** |
| A centred menu | **Center**, or Full Rect with a `CenterContainer` |
| A quest log | **Top Right**, below the minimap |

**`top_bar.gd` is exactly this:**

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	mouse_filter = Control.MOUSE_FILTER_IGNORE
	set_anchors_and_offsets_preset(Control.PRESET_TOP_WIDE)
	offset_bottom = HEIGHT
```

**One preset and one offset, and the bar is correct at every width** — no constant, no resize handler, nothing to update. **`HEIGHT` is a constant and that is fine**, because the bar's height genuinely does not depend on the window.

**And the spacer trick from lesson 4, which is how the right-hand group stays on the right:**

```gdscript
# EVERYTHING AFTER THIS SITS ON THE RIGHT. The spec's order is left to right
# and the time controls are the end of it, so a spacer that eats the slack
# puts them against the right edge however wide the screen is.
var slack := Control.new()
slack.size_flags_horizontal = Control.SIZE_EXPAND_FILL
slack.mouse_filter = Control.MOUSE_FILTER_IGNORE
row.add_child(slack)
```

**An empty `Control` with Expand**, inside the `HBoxContainer`, between the left group and the right group. **"However wide the screen is"** — and no anchor arithmetic.

**Mechanism two: a design frame, for what anchors cannot express.** Some interfaces are genuinely positioned — a drawn HUD, an orb at a hand-placed offset, a title card. For those, **ask for the frame instead of assuming it:**

```gdscript
var frame := PixelPerfectViewport.interface_frame(self)
orb.position = Vector2(frame.x - 100.0, frame.y - 100.0)
```

**`interface_frame(node)` from lesson 13** — a function of the real window, with the shell and no-shell cases handled, the headless case handled, and a floor so an absurdly small window gets the design size and clips rather than collapsing.

**And the floor is the part worth copying:**

```gdscript
static func _held_to_the_design(frame: Vector2) -> Vector2:
	return Vector2(
		frame.x if frame.x >= BASE.x * INTERFACE_SLACK else float(BASE.x),
		frame.y if frame.y >= BASE.y * INTERFACE_SLACK else float(BASE.y)
	)
```

**Below 90% of the design size per axis, return the design size.** So the interface clips at the edges rather than shrinking to illegibility — **a deliberate choice between two bad outcomes**, and the right one, because a clipped HUD is usable and a 300-pixel-wide one is not.

**The design resolution is a minimum, not a size.** That is the sentence to take from this lesson. **Lay out for the smallest frame you support, and let the frame grow.**

**Reacting to a resize.** If you compute positions, you must recompute them:

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	get_window().size_changed.connect(_relayout)
	_relayout()
```

**Or use `resized` on the `Control` itself**, from lesson 2, which fires when its own rect changes and is the better signal when the control is inside a container.

**And the `_ready()` trap, restated because it is the one that wastes an afternoon:** a `Control`'s `size` is **not final** in `_ready()`. Containers sort their children after. **Read `size` in `resized` or after `await get_tree().process_frame`**, never in `_ready`.

**Testing it, which is the only way to know.** Three window sizes, deliberately:

| Size | What it catches |
| --- | --- |
| **The design size** | the baseline |
| **Something smaller** — 1360×768 | **things drawn off the edge** |
| **Something much larger** — 2560×1440 | **things huddled in a corner** |

**Your own project's P6 resolution check is exactly this**, and it found a real fault that no amount of looking at the game at 1080p would have. **Run the game at three sizes before calling an interface done.**

**And make it cheap to do:** `screen_height_override` and `window_size_override` from lesson 13 let a test ask *"what would a 4K display get?"* from a 1080p machine. **A test seam that makes the check one line is what makes it actually get run.**

**Text scaling and a UI scale setting**, briefly, since it is the same problem: a player on a large display may want a bigger interface. **The cheap answer is `CanvasLayer.scale`** from lesson 10; the proper one is a theme with scaled font sizes. **Either way, the layout must already be anchor-driven or scaling it will push things off the edge.**

**Practice.** Find a constant in your interface that stands for the screen size, and replace it with a function of the real window. Build a bar with `PRESET_TOP_WIDE` plus an expanding spacer, and resize the window from 800 to 2560 wide. Then run your interface at 1360×768 and at 2560×1440 and write down what breaks at each. Then add a floor so a tiny window clips rather than collapsing.
Reading a real interface:
`top_bar.gd` end to end — 256 lines of a working interface, and nearly every idea in this stage in one file.

**What it is.** The bar across the top of *The Lost Sheep*: level, leader, a time-of-day dial, population, eight resource chips, a pause button, three speed buttons, settings.

**The spec, in the user's own words, which the file records:**

> *Master Roachi's order, 13 October 2026, left to right: "current lvl, name of leader, halfcircle dial showing time of day, icon of food, current amount of food, icon of wood, current amount of wood and so on, pause button icon, left arrow for 1x speed, double left arrow icon for 2x speed, triple left arrow icon for 4x speed, settings button."*

**The order is the spec**, and the file's structure follows it top to bottom — which is itself a decision: **the code reads in the order the player reads the bar.**

**And an addition, dated and justified separately:**

> *POPULATION GOES AFTER THE DIAL, 14 October 2026, and it is an addition to that order rather than a change to it. BRIEF.md → Interface names four things that are always on screen — "population, currency, resources, and York's level" — and population was the one the bar did not have. It was in the block of text over the map instead, which is not the interface.*

**"Which is not the interface"** — a developer readout had been doing an interface's job. **Noticing that is design work, and the fix was moving one number.**

**The class:**

```gdscript
class_name TopBar
extends Control
```

**A `Control`, not a `CanvasLayer`** — it is placed inside whatever layer the screen owns, so the bar does not decide its own stacking. **A component, not a system.**

**The signals, which are the whole public interface going out:**

```gdscript
signal resource_hovered(resource: String)
signal resource_left()
signal warehouse_pressed()
signal pause_pressed()
signal speed_chosen(speed: float)
signal settings_pressed()
```

**Six signals and no references to anything that acts.** The bar does not pause the clock; it says `pause_pressed`. **Told-not-asked, outwards** — the bar reports, somebody else decides.

**And `speed_chosen(speed: float)` carries the value**, so one handler serves three buttons.

**`warehouse_pressed` has the best comment in the file**, and it is pure design:

> *THE WAREHOUSE HAD NO FRONT DOOR. It sits outside the parcel system — one of them, holding everything — so there is nothing on the map to click, and the only way to reach it was to click bare sea with nothing selected. main.gd's own note said "nobody would guess", and it was right.*
>
> *The chips are the answer because the chips ARE the warehouse: these eight numbers are what is in it. Hover explains one of them; clicking opens the store they are all kept in.*

**A discoverability bug, found in play, fixed by giving an existing element a second meaning** rather than adding a button. **That is interface design, and it is worth more than any node.**

**`_ready()`, three lines and all three deliberate:**

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	mouse_filter = Control.MOUSE_FILTER_IGNORE
	set_anchors_and_offsets_preset(Control.PRESET_TOP_WIDE)
	offset_bottom = HEIGHT
	_build_the_furniture()
```

**`MOUSE_FILTER_IGNORE` on the root** — lesson 5. The bar itself must not eat clicks; **only the things in it do.** The `PanelContainer` inside sets `STOP`, so the bar's visible area blocks and its invisible root does not.

**`PRESET_TOP_WIDE` plus `offset_bottom`** — lesson 21. Correct at every width, no constant for the screen.

**The container stack:**

```
TopBar (Control)            IGNORE, TOP_WIDE
└── Wall (PanelContainer)   STOP, FULL_RECT
    └── Row (HBoxContainer) separation 14, ALIGNMENT_BEGIN
        ├── Level, Leader (Label)
        ├── Dial (DayDial)
        ├── People (Label)
        ├── eight chips (HBoxContainer each)
        ├── Slack (Control)      SIZE_EXPAND_FILL
        ├── Pause, Speed1/2/4, Settings (Button)
```

**`PanelContainer` for the background, `HBoxContainer` for the row** — lesson 3's idiom. **`separation` as a theme constant override** rather than spacer nodes between every item.

**And `Slack`**, from lesson 4 and quoted in the last lesson: one empty `Control` with Expand, pushing everything after it to the right edge **however wide the screen is.**

**A chip, which is the most interesting node in the file:**

```gdscript
func _a_chip(resource: String) -> Control:
	var chip := HBoxContainer.new()
	chip.add_theme_constant_override("separation", 4)
	chip.mouse_filter = Control.MOUSE_FILTER_STOP
	chip.mouse_entered.connect(func() -> void: resource_hovered.emit(resource))
	chip.mouse_exited.connect(func() -> void: resource_left.emit())
	chip.gui_input.connect(func(event: InputEvent) -> void:
		if event is InputEventMouseButton and (event as InputEventMouseButton).pressed \
				and (event as InputEventMouseButton).button_index == MOUSE_BUTTON_LEFT:
			warehouse_pressed.emit())
```

**Four decisions in nine lines.**

**`mouse_filter = STOP` on a container**, which containers do not do by default — **and it is why `mouse_entered` fires at all.** The comment explains the choice: *"the whole chip takes the hover rather than the 26 pixels of the symbol — a modal you have to aim at is a modal nobody sees."*

**`gui_input` for the click rather than a `Button`**, with the reason recorded: *"A CONTAINER CANNOT BE PRESSED, so the click is taken off the raw input rather than off a button: wrapping the chip in a Button would put a button's own ground behind an icon and a number that are drawn to sit on the bar."* **A real constraint — a `Button`'s `StyleBox` would show — met by handling input directly.**

**Lambdas capturing `resource`**, so one function builds eight chips that each report their own name. **From stage 2's closures.**

**And `custom_minimum_size = Vector2(62.0, 0.0)` on the amount label** — lesson 2's rule for a control inside a container: **set the minimum size, not the size.** 62 pixels reserved so the row does not reflow as a number grows from 9 to 1000.

**The population line, which is the "never colour alone" rule in two statements:**

```gdscript
_people.text = "%d / %d" % [living, beds]
# CROWDED IS A STATE WORTH SEEING. More people than beds is the thing the
# opening is built around, and it is the one number here that can be bad.
_people.modulate = Color(0.95, 0.55, 0.45) if living > beds else Color(1, 1, 1)
```

**The colour is the second channel, not the only one.** *"A settlement of fourteen with eleven beds is three people sleeping outside and a mood falling three a day… and '14' does not say it where '14 / 11' does."* **The fact is in the text; the colour makes it noticeable.**

**`watch(york, clock)` as the wiring, which is the pattern to copy:**

```gdscript
func watch(york: York, clock: Clock) -> void:
	_york = york
	_clock = clock
	_dial.watch(clock)
	refresh()
```

**One function, one call site, and it cascades** — the bar passes the clock to its dial. **The bar is constructed by whoever owns it and then handed what to read**, rather than reaching for a singleton. **And it refreshes immediately**, so it is correct before the first frame.

**The polling, from lesson 20** — `_process` calls `refresh()`, and the state that could drift is derived rather than remembered:

```gdscript
_pause.button_pressed = _clock.paused
for speed in _speeds:
	(_speeds[speed] as Button).button_pressed = \
		not _clock.paused and is_equal_approx(_clock.speed, float(speed))
```

**`is_equal_approx` for the float comparison**, from stage 2. **And the three speed buttons are all unlit while paused**, which is a small correctness detail that falls out of deriving them.

**`what_it_says()`, which is the testing seam:**

```gdscript
## What the bar is currently saying, for the checks -- they cannot read a screen.
func what_it_says() -> Dictionary:
	return {
		"level": _level.text,
		"leader": _leader.text,
		"people": _people.text,
		"crowded": _people.modulate != Color(1, 1, 1),
		"held": held,
		"paused": _pause.button_pressed,
		"speed": _which_speed_is_lit(),
		"dial": _dial.what_it_shows(),
	}
```

**This is how an interface becomes testable**, and it is the thing almost no project has. **"They cannot read a screen"** — so the interface reports what it is saying, in words, and a test asserts on that. **Including `"crowded"`, which is the colour**, reported as a boolean so even the colour channel can be checked.

**And it composes** — `_dial.what_it_shows()` — so the whole bar's state is one call. **Stage 10's testing lesson builds on this.**

**What the file admits it has not built:**

> *WHAT IS NOT BUILT YET, said plainly rather than faked: the leader's name comes from `York.leader`, which the NEW GAME screen will set from the save profile; and the settings button opens a list of what will be in settings, because a button wired to nothing is read as broken and a button wired to a pretend screen is worse.*

**Two gaps, named, with the reasoning for how each is handled.** *"A button wired to nothing is read as broken and a button wired to a pretend screen is worse"* — **so it opens a real list of what is coming.** The honest third option.

**What to take from the whole file:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Anchors and containers, not positions** | correct at every size |
| **One expanding spacer** | for the right-hand group |
| **`mouse_filter` set deliberately on every node** | IGNORE on the root, STOP on the chips |
| **`custom_minimum_size` inside containers** | never `size` |
| **Signals out, no references to systems** | the bar reports; others act |
| **Polled, because it only reads** | and derived state cannot drift |
| **`watch()` to wire, `refresh()` to update** | one call site each |
| **`what_it_says()`** | so a test can read the interface |
| **Every non-obvious choice carries its reason** | and most of the reasons are from play |

**Practice.** Read `top_bar.gd` yourself, and for each `mouse_filter` assignment work out what breaks without it. Then build your own bar with a `PanelContainer → HBoxContainer`, a spacer, and `custom_minimum_size` on anything whose contents vary. Give it signals rather than references. Derive its toggle buttons from the real state. Then add a `what_it_says()` and write one test that asserts on it.
The renderers: Forward+, Mobile, Compati:
The choice made when the project was created, what each option actually gives you, and how to change it safely.

**Godot 4 has three rendering backends**, picked in the project-creation dialogue and changeable later in Project Settings > Rendering > Renderer > Rendering Method.

| Renderer | API | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Forward+** | Vulkan | **desktop.** Every feature. |
| **Mobile** | Vulkan | phones and tablets, and desktop too |
| **Compatibility** | **OpenGL 3.3 / ES 3.0 / WebGL 2** | **old hardware, and the web** |

**What Forward+ gives you that the others do not:**

| Feature | Forward+ | Mobile | Compatibility |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **SDFGI** (global illumination) | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ |
| **Volumetric fog** | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ |
| **SSAO, SSIL, SSR** | ✔ | ✘ | ✘ |
| **Many lights efficiently** | ✔ (clustered) | limited | limited |
| **Compute shaders** | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ |
| **HDR 2D** | ✔ | ✔ | ✘ |
| **Web export** | ✘ | ✘ | **✔** |
| **Runs on 2014 hardware** | ✘ | partly | **✔** |

**For a 2D game, almost none of that matters.** The 2D feature set is nearly identical across all three, and the differences that remain are:

| 2D difference | Which |
| --- | --- |
| **Compute-shader-based effects** | not in Compatibility |
| **`SCREEN_TEXTURE` and mipmaps on it** | more limited in Compatibility |
| **HDR 2D and glow** | not in Compatibility |
| **Startup time, and memory** | **Compatibility is lighter** |

**Which is why your own project chose Compatibility**, and why that is a defensible choice for a pixel-art game: nothing in it needs Vulkan, it starts faster, it runs on more machines, and **web export is available if it is ever wanted.**

**The cost of changing renderer later.** It is one setting, and then:

| Needs checking | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Every shader** | some built-ins are unavailable in Compatibility |
| **Glow and HDR** | Compatibility has no HDR 2D |
| **Any compute shader** | unavailable |
| **The export presets** | the driver fallback settings differ |

**So changing is cheap in 2D and expensive in 3D.** Changing *to* Compatibility is the risky direction; changing *from* it is almost always safe.

**The fallback setting worth knowing:**

```ini
rendering/renderer/rendering_method = "gl_compatibility"
rendering/renderer/rendering_method.mobile = "gl_compatibility"
```

**Per-platform overrides** — the `.mobile` and `.web` suffixes, from stage 7's project-settings lesson. **So a Forward+ desktop game can ship a Compatibility web build** without a second project.

**And the driver fallback:**

```
rendering/rendering_device/driver          → vulkan
rendering/rendering_device/fallback_to_opengl3 → on
```

**With that on, a Vulkan build that cannot create a device falls back to OpenGL** rather than failing to launch — which is the difference between a bad review and no review. **Leave it on.**

**What to actually do.** For a 2D game: **Compatibility, unless you have a reason.** For a 3D game: **Forward+**, and Mobile only if you are shipping to phones. **And check the renderer in the running build, not the editor:**

```gdscript
print(RenderingServer.get_video_adapter_name())
print(RenderingServer.get_rendering_device() != null)  # false on Compatibility
print(OS.get_video_adapter_driver_info())
```

**The editor can run one renderer while the export uses another**, which is a real and confusing source of *"it works in the editor"* — and printing it at startup settles it, the same argument as the presentation log from stage 9.

**Two settings that are not the renderer but are mistaken for it:**

| Setting | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **V-Sync Mode** | **Disabled, Enabled, Adaptive, Mailbox** — tearing against latency |
| **Max FPS** (`Engine.max_fps`) | a frame cap. **Set it for a 2D game**; 500 fps heats the machine for nothing. |

**`Engine.max_fps = 60` for a pixel-art game is a kindness to laptops**, and a setting worth exposing.

**Practice.** Print the adapter name and driver info at startup. Switch your project between Compatibility and Forward+ and check that every shader still compiles. Set `fallback_to_opengl3` on. Then set `Engine.max_fps` to 60 and watch the GPU usage drop.
The canvas_item shader: vertex, fragment:
Writing a 2D shader — the language, the three functions, and the built-ins that do nearly everything.

**What a shader is, in Godot's terms.** A `Shader` resource holding code in **Godot Shading Language**, a GLSL dialect. Applied to a node through a **`ShaderMaterial`**.

**The first line decides everything:**

```glsl
shader_type canvas_item;
```

**Four types:** `canvas_item` (2D), `spatial` (3D), `particles`, `sky`, and `fog`. **For 2D, `canvas_item`.**

**The three functions you may define:**

| Function | Runs | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`vertex()`** | per vertex (**four, for a sprite**) | moving, scaling, distorting |
| **`fragment()`** | **per pixel** | colour — where most work happens |
| **`light()`** | per pixel per light | custom 2D lighting |

**And a fourth, which is not per-pixel:**

```glsl
void fragment() { … }
```

...plus `shader_parameter` uniforms, which are the next lesson.

**The minimal useful shader:**

```glsl
shader_type canvas_item;

void fragment() {
	COLOR = texture(TEXTURE, UV);
}
```

**That is the default behaviour written out** — sample the node's texture at this pixel's UV and output it. **Every 2D shader is a variation on that line.**

**The built-ins you will use constantly:**

| Built-in | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **`COLOR`** | **in: the vertex colour × modulate; out: the final pixel** |
| **`TEXTURE`** | the node's texture |
| **`UV`** | **this pixel's texture coordinate, 0–1** |
| `TEXTURE_PIXEL_SIZE` | **one texel in UV units** — `1.0 / texture size` |
| `SCREEN_UV` | this pixel's position on screen, 0–1 |
| `TIME` | seconds since start |
| `VERTEX` | in `vertex()`: the local position |
| `MODULATE` | the node's `modulate`, separately |
| `AT_LIGHT_PASS` | whether this is a light pass |

**`TEXTURE_PIXEL_SIZE` is the one people miss**, and it is what makes neighbour sampling work:

```glsl
vec4 left = texture(TEXTURE, UV - vec2(TEXTURE_PIXEL_SIZE.x, 0.0));
```

**One texel left**, correctly, at any texture size. **Hard-coding `0.001` instead is the commonest shader bug** and it breaks the moment the texture changes size.

**The types, briefly**, since the language is small:

| Type | |
| --- | --- |
| `float`, `int`, `bool` | scalars |
| `vec2`, `vec3`, `vec4` | **`.xyzw`, `.rgba`, `.stpq` — interchangeable** |
| `mat2`, `mat3`, `mat4` | matrices |
| `sampler2D` | a texture |

**Swizzling is the thing to get comfortable with:** `col.rgb`, `col.a`, `col.bgr`, `col.rrr`, `UV.yx`. **All legal, all free.**

**The functions worth knowing by name:**

| Function | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `mix(a, b, t)` | **lerp** |
| `clamp(x, lo, hi)`, `min`, `max` | bounds |
| `step(edge, x)` | 0 or 1. **A branchless if.** |
| `smoothstep(lo, hi, x)` | a smooth 0→1 ramp |
| `fract(x)`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `mod` | **`fract` and `floor` are the tiling pair** |
| `length`, `distance`, `normalize`, `dot` | vector maths |
| `sin`, `cos`, `atan`, `pow`, `abs`, `sign` | the usual |
| `texture(tex, uv)` | **sample** |

**`step` instead of `if` is the habit to build.** `step(0.5, x)` is 0 below and 1 above, and multiplying by it is a branchless conditional — **which matters because a GPU runs both branches of an `if` anyway.**

**`vertex()`, which is small but useful:**

```glsl
void vertex() {
	VERTEX.y += sin(TIME * 2.0 + VERTEX.x * 0.1) * 3.0;
}
```

**A wave, applied to the four corners of a sprite** — which is the catch: **a sprite has four vertices**, so a per-vertex effect on a sprite can only move its corners. **For a smooth distortion, distort the UV in `fragment()` instead:**

```glsl
void fragment() {
	vec2 uv = UV;
	uv.x += sin(TIME * 3.0 + UV.y * 20.0) * 0.01;
	COLOR = texture(TEXTURE, uv);
}
```

**That is the wobble every water surface and heat haze is made of**, and it is three lines.

**The pixel-art caveat, which is important.** Any shader that samples at a shifted UV will land **between** texels, and the texture's filter decides what happens. **With Nearest filtering you get a hard jump; with Linear you get a blur** — and in a pixel-art game, the hard jump is correct. **So snap the UV to the texel grid when you need to:**

```glsl
vec2 snapped = (floor(uv / TEXTURE_PIXEL_SIZE) + 0.5) * TEXTURE_PIXEL_SIZE;
```

**Where a `canvas_item` shader goes:**

| Target | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| A `Sprite2D`'s `material` | that sprite |
| A `CanvasItem` parent's `material` with `use_parent_material` on children | a group |
| A full-screen `ColorRect` | **a post-processing pass** |
| A `SubViewportContainer` | **the whole composed frame** — stage 9 |

**`render_mode`, on the second line**, for the ones you will actually use:

```glsl
render_mode blend_mix;      // the default
render_mode blend_add;      // additive — fire, magic, light
render_mode unshaded;       // ignore 2D lights
```

**`blend_add` plus `unshaded` is the glow-effect pair**, and it is most of what a particle shader needs.

**Practice.** Write a shader that outputs `COLOR = texture(TEXTURE, UV)` and confirm nothing changes. Then tint it with `COLOR.rgb *= vec3(1.0, 0.5, 0.5)`. Then wobble the UV with `sin(TIME + UV.y * 20.0)`. Then sample the texel to the left with `TEXTURE_PIXEL_SIZE` and blend it in. Then replace an `if` with `step` and confirm the result is identical.
Shader uniforms, ShaderMaterial, and set:
Getting values from GDScript into a shader — the hints that make the Inspector useful, and the two traps with shared materials.

**A uniform is a shader's input:**

```glsl
shader_type canvas_item;

uniform float strength : hint_range(0.0, 1.0) = 0.0;
uniform vec4 tint : source_color = vec4(1.0);
uniform sampler2D mask : filter_nearest, repeat_disable;
uniform bool enabled = true;
```

**Each appears in the Inspector** under Shader Parameters on the `ShaderMaterial`, and each is settable from code.

**The hints, which are the difference between a usable Inspector and a bad one:**

| Hint | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **`hint_range(min, max)`** | a slider |
| `hint_range(min, max, step)` | a stepped slider |
| **`source_color`** | **a colour picker, and correct sRGB handling** |
| `hint_default_white` / `_black` / `_transparent` | a default texture |
| `hint_normal` | marks a normal map |
| `filter_nearest` / `filter_linear` | **the sampler's filter, per uniform** |
| `filter_nearest_mipmap` etc. | with mipmaps |
| `repeat_enable` / `repeat_disable` | wrapping |
| `instance_index(n)` | **a per-instance uniform** |

**`source_color` is not cosmetic.** Without it, a colour from the picker is passed through unconverted and the result is wrong in a linear-space renderer. **Every `vec4` or `vec3` that represents a colour gets `source_color`.**

**And `filter_nearest` on a sampler uniform is how a pixel-art shader stays sharp** when it samples a texture you passed in — the project default does not apply to uniform samplers.

**Setting them from code:**

```gdscript
var mat: ShaderMaterial = sprite.material
mat.set_shader_parameter("strength", 0.7)
mat.set_shader_parameter("tint", Color.RED)
mat.set_shader_parameter("mask", my_texture)

var current: float = mat.get_shader_parameter("strength")
```

**A string, not a property.** So typos are silent — **setting `"strenght"` does nothing and reports nothing.** Two defences:

```gdscript
const STRENGTH := &"strength"   # one place to misspell it
```

**And checking it in a test**, which is the honest fix: `get_shader_parameter` returns `null` for a name the shader does not have.

**Tweening a uniform**, which is what most effects are:

```gdscript
var t := create_tween()
t.tween_method(
	func(v: float) -> void: mat.set_shader_parameter("strength", v),
	0.0, 1.0, 0.25
)
```

**`tween_method` with a lambda**, from stage 6, because `tween_property` cannot reach a shader parameter by path. **Actually it can:**

```gdscript
t.tween_property(mat, "shader_parameter/strength", 1.0, 0.25)
```

**`shader_parameter/<name>` is a real property path**, which is tidier and also works in an `AnimationPlayer` track — so a flash can be authored in the animation editor rather than coded.

**Trap one: a shared material.** A `ShaderMaterial` assigned to a scene's `Sprite2D` is **shared by every instance of that scene.** Set a parameter on one enemy and **every** enemy flashes.

**Three fixes:**

| Fix | When |
| --- | --- |
| **`material = material.duplicate()` in `_ready()`** | the usual answer |
| **A per-instance uniform** | when the shader is on many nodes |
| **Keep it shared, deliberately** | when the effect is global — a day/night tint |

**The duplicate:**

```gdscript
func _ready() -> void:
	material = material.duplicate() as ShaderMaterial
```

**One line, and it costs one material per instance** — negligible for dozens, worth thinking about for thousands. **And note it must be `duplicate()`, not a new `ShaderMaterial`**, or you lose the shader and the authored defaults.

**Per-instance uniforms, which are the efficient version:**

```glsl
instance uniform vec4 team_colour : source_color = vec4(1.0);
```

```gdscript
sprite.set_instance_shader_parameter("team_colour", Color.BLUE)
```

**One material, per-node values, no duplication.** Its limits: a small number of slots, and **only scalar and vector types** — no textures. **For a team colour or a per-enemy flash amount, it is exactly right.**

**Trap two: a uniform with no default.** `uniform float strength;` is zero-initialised, which for a *multiplier* means the effect is fully on or fully off depending on how it is used. **Always give a default that means "no effect":**

```glsl
uniform float strength : hint_range(0.0, 1.0) = 0.0;
uniform vec4 tint : source_color = vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0);
```

**So a material with nothing set behaves like no shader at all**, which makes the shader safe to add before it is wired.

**Global uniforms**, for a value every shader needs — a time of day, a global tint:

```glsl
global uniform float daylight;
```

```gdscript
RenderingServer.global_shader_parameter_set("daylight", 0.3)
```

**Declared in Project Settings > Shader Globals first**, then set once and read by every shader. **Right for a genuinely global value, overkill for anything else.**

**Reading a shader's parameters at runtime**, which is the diagnostic:

```gdscript
for p in mat.shader.get_shader_uniform_list():
	print(p["name"], " = ", mat.get_shader_parameter(p["name"]))
```

**That prints every uniform and its current value**, which answers *"is my parameter actually getting through"* in one line.

**Practice.** Write a shader with `strength : hint_range(0.0, 1.0) = 0.0` and a `tint : source_color` and confirm the Inspector shows a slider and a picker. Tween `shader_parameter/strength` with `tween_property`. Then put the material on two instances of one scene and watch them flash together; fix it with `duplicate()`. Then convert the per-instance value to an `instance uniform`. Then misspell a parameter name and confirm nothing happens — then print the uniform list to catch it.
Reading a real shader: wind:
`sway.gdshader` from *The Lost Sheep* — sixty lines that turn one sine wave into weather, and a case study in how feedback becomes code.

**What it does.** Leans trees, plants and grass in the wind. **A vertex shader on a `canvas_item`**, which is unusual and is the first thing to understand.

**The feedback that shaped it**, recorded at the top:

> *MASTER ROACHI, 14 October 2026: "add trees, rocks, plants and animate them", and then, seeing it: "the shader looks okay, but it affects everything in the exact same way at all times".*

**"The exact same way at all times."** Two faults in one sentence, and the file splits them:

> *It did. One sine, one amplitude, one rate: every tree on the island leaning the same distance at the same moment for ever. Three things fix it and none of them needs a material per tree.*

**"None of them needs a material per tree"** is the constraint that makes the solution interesting. **One shared material, and every tree still different** — which rules out passing a per-tree parameter and forces the variation to come from something the shader already knows.

**The three fixes, as the file names them:**

| Fix | What it addresses |
| --- | --- |
| **WHERE IT STANDS** | the phase comes from the sprite's world position, **so a gust crosses the island** |
| **HOW FAST IT IS** | each thing's rate is **hashed from that same position** |
| **WHETHER IT BLOWS** | a slow envelope, so the wind **rises, holds and drops away** |

**The hash, which is the key technique:**

```glsl
float own_number(vec2 at) {
	return fract(sin(dot(at, vec2(12.9898, 78.233))) * 43758.5453);
}
```

**This is the standard GLSL pseudo-random function**, and it is worth recognising on sight. **It is not random** — it is a deterministic function of position that *looks* random. Which is exactly what is wanted: **the same tree gets the same number every frame, every run, and two trees a pixel apart get unrelated numbers.**

**And it needs no uniform, no texture, no per-instance data.** The position is already available.

**Where the position comes from:**

```glsl
vec2 standing = MODEL_MATRIX[3].xy;
```

**`MODEL_MATRIX[3].xy` is the node's world position** — the translation column of its transform. **That is the built-in worth remembering**, because it is how a vertex shader knows where its node is in the world rather than just where the vertex is within the node.

**And `floor(standing)` is passed to the hash**, so sub-pixel differences do not produce a different number.

**The lean, assembled:**

```glsl
float crown = 1.0 - UV.y;
float mine = own_number(floor(standing));

float rate = speed * (0.72 + 0.56 * mine);

float weather = mix(1.0 - lulls, 1.0,
	0.5 + 0.5 * sin(TIME * gusts + standing.x * 0.0009));

float lean = sin(TIME * rate + (standing.x + standing.y * 0.6) * ripple
	+ mine * 6.283)
	* sway * strength * weather * crown * crown;
```

**Read each factor:**

| Factor | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `sin(TIME * rate + position * ripple + mine * 6.283)` | **the oscillation**, phase-shifted by position *and* by its own number |
| `sway` | **how far**, in art pixels |
| `strength` | **per-material**, set from the drawing |
| `weather` | **the gust envelope**, 0.38–1.0 |
| `crown * crown` | **the vertical falloff** |

**`mine * 6.283` is the phase offset** — `6.283` being 2π, so each thing's own number maps to a full cycle of phase. **Two pines side by side are never in step**, which was fault one.

**`crown = 1.0 - UV.y`, squared**, with the reason recorded:

> *crown IS SQUARED on purpose. Linear, the whole trunk leans; squared, the base barely moves and the canopy does the work.*

**`UV.y` is 0 at the top of the sprite and 1 at the bottom**, so `1.0 - UV.y` is 1 at the top. **Squaring biases the motion to the top**, which is how a tree actually bends. **A one-character change with a visible result**, and the comment explains the choice rather than the syntax.

**The `weather` envelope**, which was fault two:

```glsl
uniform float gusts = 0.17;   // cycles per second
uniform float lulls = 0.62;   // how far it drops between gusts
```

**A second, much slower sine, used as a multiplier**, and the comment names the failure it fixes: *"At 0.0 it never rests, which is what was wrong. A wood that never rests reads as a screen wobbling rather than as weather."*

**That is the whole insight: motion without rest does not read as motion.** It reads as a broken screen. **Stillness is what makes the movement legible** — which generalises to animation, camera work and audio.

**And the `zoom` uniform, which is the pixel-art problem again:**

> *Master Roachi, 14 October 2026: "the shader looks a little jumpy when zoomed out too far." It was. The lean is in WORLD units, and the art is pixel art sampled nearest-neighbour — so a crown drifting a third of a screen pixel does not drift, it SNAPS between texel columns, and a wood full of that reads as a shimmer.*

**The fix:**

```glsl
VERTEX.x += round(lean * zoom) / max(zoom, 0.01);
```

**Convert the lean to screen pixels, round, convert back.** So the silhouette lands on the pixel grid at every zoom — **the whole-pixel rule from stage 9, applied inside a shader.**

**And `max(zoom, 0.01)` guards the division**, the same defensive habit as `maxf(MAX_DURATION, 0.0001)` in the camera.

**Note the zoom has to be pushed in from outside:** *"THE CAMERA'S ZOOM, PUSHED IN BY WildView EVERY TIME IT CHANGES."* **A shader cannot see the camera**, so the one thing it needs that it cannot derive is passed as a uniform. **Everything else comes from built-ins.**

**And `strength` comes from the art**, not the code: *"see WildView, which buckets the pieces so a full pine leans, a grass tuft shivers, and a fallen log and a rock do not move at all."* **A rock with `strength = 0` uses the same material and does not move** — which is why one material serves everything rooted in the ground.

**What to take from the file:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Vertex shaders are not only for 3D** | `MODEL_MATRIX[3].xy` gives world position in 2D |
| **A position hash gives per-instance variation** | with one shared material |
| **An envelope over an oscillation** | is the difference between weather and a wobble |
| **Round to whole screen pixels** | even inside a shader |
| **Pass in only what cannot be derived** | here, the zoom |
| **Every uniform has a comment with its units** | "in cycles a second", "in world units — which are art pixels" |

**And the process:** the first version was *"okay"*, the feedback named two faults in one sentence, and each got its own named fix in the comments. **The code records what it looked like before.**

**Practice.** Write a vertex shader that leans a sprite with `1.0 - UV.y` squared as the falloff. Add `own_number(floor(MODEL_MATRIX[3].xy))` and use it to offset the phase and vary the rate — then place ten copies and confirm none are in step. Add a slow `gusts` envelope and set `lulls` to 0, then to 0.6, and judge the difference. Then round the offset to whole screen pixels with a `zoom` uniform.
2D lights: PointLight2D and occluders:
Lighting a 2D scene — the three nodes, how the shadow system works, and what it costs.

**2D lighting in Godot is additive on top of what is drawn.** A `CanvasItem` has a `light_mask`, a light has a `range_layer_min/max`, and where they overlap the light brightens the sprite.

**The nodes:**

| Node | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **`PointLight2D`** | **a light from a texture**, positioned. Despite the name, its shape is its texture. |
| **`DirectionalLight2D`** | a light from a direction — **the sun** |
| **`LightOccluder2D`** | **a shape that casts shadows** |
| **`CanvasModulate`** | **tints every canvas item in the viewport** — the next lesson |

**`PointLight2D`'s key insight: the texture is the light.** There is no radius property. **A radial gradient texture gives a round light; a cone texture gives a spotlight; a window-shaped texture gives light through a window.**

**So the first thing to make is a gradient texture**, and it needs no art:

```gdscript
static func _radial(radius: int) -> Texture2D:
	var gradient := Gradient.new()
	gradient.offsets = PackedFloat32Array([0.0, 1.0])
	gradient.colors = PackedColorArray([Color.WHITE, Color(1, 1, 1, 0)])
	var tex := GradientTexture2D.new()
	tex.gradient = gradient
	tex.fill = GradientTexture2D.FILL_RADIAL
	tex.fill_from = Vector2(0.5, 0.5)
	tex.fill_to = Vector2(1.0, 0.5)
	tex.width = radius * 2
	tex.height = radius * 2
	return tex
```

**`GradientTexture2D` with `FILL_RADIAL`** — from stage 7's resources lesson, generated at runtime, **and shared between every light** rather than one per lamp.

**The properties:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`enabled`** | **off means the renderer skips it entirely** |
| **`energy`** | brightness. **Above 1 overexposes.** |
| **`color`** | the light's colour |
| `texture_scale` | scales the texture, so one texture serves many sizes |
| `offset` | shifts the texture relative to the node |
| **`blend_mode`** | **Add, Subtract, Mix** |
| `shadow_enabled` | **cast shadows** — the expensive one |
| `shadow_filter` | None, PCF5, PCF13 |
| `shadow_color`, `shadow_filter_smooth` | how shadows look |
| `range_layer_min/max`, `range_z_min/max` | **which layers and z-ranges it lights** |
| `range_item_cull_mask` | which `light_mask`s it affects |

**`blend_mode = Subtract` is the one people do not expect:** a light that *darkens*. **For a shadow pool, a dark aura, or an area of gloom**, it is exactly right and there is no other node for it.

**Shadows, and how they work.** A `LightOccluder2D` holds an `OccluderPolygon2D`:

| Property | Note |
| --- | --- |
| `occluder` | the `OccluderPolygon2D` |
| `occluder_light_mask` | which lights it blocks |
| `OccluderPolygon2D.closed` | **closed casts from all sides; open casts from one** |
| `OccluderPolygon2D.cull_mode` | Disabled, Clockwise, Counter-Clockwise |

**The polygon's winding order decides which side casts**, which is the confusing part. **`cull_mode = Disabled` casts from both sides** and is what to use when the shadow looks inverted.

**And the cost, which is the thing to know before designing around shadows:** every shadow-casting light must consider every occluder in range. **One light with fifty occluders is fine. Fifty lights with fifty occluders is not.**

**Which is why your own project's rule is what it is.** `night_light.gd` divides its lights into two families, and the shadow decision is explicit:

> ***Flame** — the firepit, the braziers, the lanterns. Warm, restless, and the only ones that cast shadows: a shadow needs a source the eye can point at, and fifty shadow-casting windows would be both wrong and slow.*

**"A shadow needs a source the eye can point at"** is the design reason, and **"fifty shadow-casting windows would be both wrong and slow"** is the performance one. **They agree**, which is the comfortable case — and the lesson is that the aesthetic argument came first.

**The other family is the design content worth stealing:**

> ***Window** — the lit windows of the homes. Cool, steady, small, and electric, which is why they are the ones that answer `WorldClock.surge()`… They flare, and then they fail, and stay out. York runs north by firelight.*

**Two light families, differing in colour, steadiness, size and *what they respond to*.** The flames flicker and persist; the windows are steady and fail. **Lighting carrying narrative**, which is what distinguishes a lit scene from a decorated one.

**Flicker, which is four lines and transforms a flame:**

```gdscript
const FLICKER_DEPTH: float = 0.13
const FLICKER_HZ: float = 2.7

func _process(_delta: float) -> void:
	var t := Time.get_ticks_msec() / 1000.0
	energy = _base * (1.0 + sin(t * TAU * FLICKER_HZ) * FLICKER_DEPTH)
```

**Note the depth is a *fraction of its own energy*, not an absolute** — so a bright lantern and a dim candle flicker proportionally. **And 0.13 is small**; a flicker you can clearly see is too much.

**Disabling what is not needed**, which is the performance rule:

> *OFF BY DAY, AND IT COSTS NOTHING TO BE. Every light here reads the clock and scales itself by how far the fall has got, so dusk brings York up rather than switching it on. At full day they are `enabled = false` and the renderer skips them entirely.*

**Two things there.** `enabled = false` is **free**, not cheap — the renderer skips it. **And scaling by the transition's progress rather than switching at a threshold** means dusk is a fade, not a pop.

**The light mask system, briefly, because it is how you keep lights off the wrong things:**

```gdscript
sprite.light_mask = 0b0010          # only lit by lights on layer 2
light.range_item_cull_mask = 0b0010 # only lights layer-2 items
```

**The common use: keep the lights off the ground, or off the interface.** Though for the interface the better answer is stage 9's `CanvasLayer` — a light does not reach another canvas layer at all.

**What to do in Compatibility.** 2D lights work, shadows work, and the limits are on **how many lights affect one item at once**. **Keep overlapping lights to a handful** and it behaves.

**Practice.** Generate a radial `GradientTexture2D` and share it between five `PointLight2D`s. Add a `CanvasModulate` at 0.3 brightness and confirm the lights read. Flicker one by a fraction of its own energy at under 3 Hz. Add a `LightOccluder2D` and fix the inverted shadow with `cull_mode = Disabled`. Then set `blend_mode = Subtract` on one light and see it darken. Then set `enabled = false` and confirm the frame cost drops.
CanvasModulate, and night:
Making it dark — one node, one trap that ruins it, and the arrangement that makes a dark scene legible.

**What `CanvasModulate` does.** It multiplies **every canvas item in its viewport** by a colour. One node, no per-sprite work.

```gdscript
var tint := CanvasModulate.new()
tint.color = Color(0.30, 0.36, 0.62)
add_child(tint)
```

**And that is night**, with the lights from the last lesson on top.

**The trap, and it is the one that ruins the effect: it tints the interface too.** A darkened HUD is not night; **it is a bug**, and it is what every first attempt looks like.

**Your own project states both the problem and why it is safe there:**

> *A `CanvasModulate`, and it is safe to put one here. It tints every canvas item in its viewport, which would be a disaster if the HUD were in the same one — a darkened interface is not night, it is a bug. It is not: `PresentationShell` renders the world into its own `SubViewport` and lifts every UI layer out to the window at native resolution, so the tint stops at the edge of the world.*

**"The tint stops at the edge of the world."** That is the payoff of the `SubViewport` arrangement from stage 9 — **and the comment notes this was the first thing to depend on it**, which is a nice illustration that architecture earns its keep later.

**The three ways to keep the tint off the interface:**

| Way | How |
| --- | --- |
| **A `SubViewport` for the world** | the tint is inside it. **The clean answer.** |
| **`light_mask`** | exclude the interface's items — fiddly |
| **A `CanvasLayer` for the interface** | **a `CanvasModulate` does affect other canvas layers in the same viewport**, so this alone is not enough |

**That third row is the one to be careful about.** A `CanvasLayer` protects you from the *camera* and from *draw order*, but **not** from a `CanvasModulate` — it is per-viewport, not per-layer. **So the HUD on `CanvasLayer` 40 still goes dark.**

**The workaround without a `SubViewport`:** put the `CanvasModulate` **inside** a `CanvasLayer` of its own. A `CanvasModulate` affects only the canvas it is in — so one on the world's layer tints the world and leaves layer 40 alone. **That works, and it is worth knowing when a shell is not available.**

**Why a dark night is hard.** Multiplying toward black gives you a black screen, and your own project's note says exactly that:

> *`WorldClock.NIGHT_LIGHT` was held deliberately high because a greybox world multiplied toward black is a black screen — its own note says so, and so does `night_falls_on_york_test.DARKEST_ALLOWED`: "When York has its own lights this floor should come down." A night is legible because it has lamps in it, not because the dark is weak.*

**"A night is legible because it has lamps in it, not because the dark is weak."** That is the whole design rule. **The sequence is:**

1. **Add the lights first.**
2. **Then bring the tint down.**

**Doing it the other way round gives you a black screen, so you weaken the tint, and then the night never feels like night.**

**And there is a test enforcing the floor** — `DARKEST_ALLOWED` — with a comment saying when it should change. **A numeric bound on how dark the scene may get, with its own expiry condition written down.**

**The actual value:**

```gdscript
const NIGHT_LIGHT := Color(0.30, 0.36, 0.62, 1.0)
```

**Note it is not grey.** 0.30 red, 0.36 green, **0.62 blue** — **moonlight is blue**, and a neutral grey night looks like a brightness slider rather than nightfall. **Tint the darkness, do not just reduce it.**

**The transition, which is where the craft is:**

```gdscript
const FALL_SECONDS: float = 6.0
```

**With the reasoning recorded, including its uncertainty:**

> *PROVISIONAL. Nothing in `scope-and-campaign.md` gives a duration, and this is the kind of number that wants a playtest rather than a decision. Long enough not to read as a switch being thrown — criterion 9 — and short enough that the player is not left holding the stick.*

**Two bounds, named from both ends.** And **"PROVISIONAL"** marking a number that is a guess, so it is not later mistaken for a decision.

**Implementing the fade** — and the key point is that one value drives everything:

```gdscript
var _fallen: float = 0.0   # 0 at day, 1 at night

func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	if _over_seconds > 0.0:
		_fallen = clampf(_fallen + delta / _over_seconds, 0.0, 1.0)
	_light.color = Color.WHITE.lerp(NIGHT_LIGHT, _fallen)
```

**And every light reads the same `_fallen`**, scaling its energy by it. **One number, and the whole scene transitions coherently** — tint, lamps, window lights, all in step. **The alternative is a dozen tweens that drift apart.**

**An effect riding on top**, which is the structural detail worth copying:

```gdscript
const SURGE_LIGHT := Color(1.35, 1.28, 1.05, 1.0)
const SURGE_SECONDS: float = 1.1
```

> *So this rides ON TOP of whatever part it is, rather than being a part of its own. Night does not end because the lights flared.*

**A momentary flare composed over the current tint, not a third state.** **Note the colour is above 1** — 1.35, 1.28 — which **overexposes**, and that is how a flash reads as a flash rather than a tint change.

**That is the same shape as additive camera shake** from stage 9: a base value plus a decaying effect, kept in separate variables. **Two channels composed, never one channel fought over.**

**`DirectionalLight2D`, briefly**, since it pairs with this: a light from a direction, with no position, which is the sun or the moon. **Its `height` property controls how normal maps respond to it** — the next lesson — and it is the natural companion to a `CanvasModulate` for an outdoor scene.

**Practice.** Add a `CanvasModulate` at `Color(0.3, 0.36, 0.62)` and watch your HUD go dark. Fix it by putting the modulate inside the world's own `CanvasLayer`. Then add three lights and bring the tint down further until it is as dark as it can be while the road is still visible. Drive the tint and every light's energy from one `_fallen` float over six seconds. Then add a 1.1-second flare at `Color(1.35, 1.28, 1.05)` composed on top, and confirm the night resumes afterwards.
Normal maps, and lighting pixel art:
Making flat sprites catch the light — how it works, when it is worth it, and the honest answer for pixel art.

**What a normal map is.** A texture where each pixel's **colour encodes a surface direction** rather than a colour:

| Channel | Axis |
| --- | --- |
| **Red** | X — left to right |
| **Green** | Y — **up or down, depending on convention** |
| **Blue** | Z — toward the viewer |

**A flat surface facing the viewer is `(0.5, 0.5, 1.0)`**, which is the characteristic lavender-blue of a normal map. **Deviations from that lean the surface.**

**In Godot 2D:**

```
Sprite2D
└── Texture: the art
    CanvasTexture
    ├── diffuse_texture  → the art
    ├── normal_texture   → the normal map
    └── specular_texture → optional shininess
```

**`CanvasTexture` is the resource that holds all three**, which is the thing to know — you do not set a normal map on the `Sprite2D`; you give the `Sprite2D` a `CanvasTexture` whose diffuse is the art.

**Its properties:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `diffuse_texture` | the colour |
| `normal_texture` | the directions |
| `specular_texture` | per-pixel shininess |
| `specular_color` | the highlight colour |
| **`specular_shininess`** | **0–1, how tight the highlight is** |
| `texture_filter`, `texture_repeat` | per-texture overrides |

**And the import flag:** a texture used as a normal map should be imported with **Normal Map** as its compression mode hint, and `hint_normal` if it is a shader uniform. **Otherwise the compression artefacts show up as lighting noise.**

**What it gives you.** A `PointLight2D` moving past a sprite with a normal map makes the sprite's surface detail **light and shade correctly** — a brick wall gets depth, a character's face catches the light from the right side, a coin looks round. **It is the single biggest visual upgrade available to a 2D lit scene.**

**And the light's `height` property is what makes it work:**

```gdscript
light.height = 20.0
```

**How far the light is "above" the canvas.** At 0 the light is in the plane and the normals barely respond; higher gives a more top-down fall of light. **It is the one property to tune after adding a normal map**, and the default is often wrong for the look you want.

**Where normal maps come from:**

| Source | Note |
| --- | --- |
| **Drawn by hand** | in Aseprite or Krita, with a normal-map brush. **Laborious and exact.** |
| **Generated from the art** | **Laigter** (free, open source) or **Sprite Illuminator** (paid) |
| **Baked from 3D** | if the art was rendered from a model |
| **Derived in a shader** | from the sprite's own luminance — **cheap and approximate** |

**Laigter is the free answer** and it is genuinely good: it takes a sprite and produces a normal map, with controls for how it reads height. **For a project with a lot of art, it is the only practical route.**

**Now the honest part, which is why this lesson is short.**

**Normal maps and pixel art are an uncomfortable fit**, for three reasons:

**1. The resolution is too low.** A 16×16 sprite has 256 pixels. **A normal map over 256 pixels cannot express much surface detail**, and what it does express is a single-pixel gradient that reads as noise rather than form.

**2. The look fights the art.** Pixel art's shading is **drawn**, deliberately, with a chosen palette and hand-placed highlights. **Dynamic lighting overrides that** — the artist's careful highlight is now wherever the light happens to be. **For many pixel-art styles that is a loss, not a gain.**

**3. The effort is enormous.** A normal map per frame of every animation, per direction. **Your own project has an 8-direction, 24-frame idle and a 12-frame run per character** — that is 288 sprites per character, each needing a normal map. **Not happening by hand.**

**So what does your own project do?** Nothing of the sort. **Night is `CanvasModulate` plus `PointLight2D`s**, from the last two lessons, with flat unlit sprites brightened by the lamps. **And it looks right**, because that is how the art is drawn.

**When a normal map *is* worth it in 2D:**

| Case | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **High-resolution 2D art** | enough pixels to carry detail |
| **A game whose look is dynamic lighting** | the lighting *is* the aesthetic |
| **A few hero assets** | a boss, a title screen, an interactive object |
| **Tiles and walls** | one normal map, used ten thousand times. **The best ratio.** |

**That last one is the genuinely good deal.** A tileset has few unique tiles and enormous reuse, so one afternoon of normal maps gives every wall in the game depth. **If you do one thing with normal maps, do the tiles.**

**The cheap shader alternative**, which gets most of the look for none of the art:

```glsl
shader_type canvas_item;

void light() {
	float l = dot(LIGHT_DIRECTION.xy, normalize(UV - vec2(0.5)));
	LIGHT = vec4(LIGHT_COLOR.rgb * COLOR.rgb * (0.6 + 0.4 * l), COLOR.a);
}
```

**A fake normal derived from the UV**, so the sprite lights as though it were a sphere. **Wrong, and often convincing enough** for a round object — a coin, an orb, a barrel.

**And the `light()` function is the thing to notice**, from the shader lesson: a `canvas_item` shader can take over 2D lighting entirely. **`LIGHT_DIRECTION`, `LIGHT_COLOR`, `NORMAL` and `LIGHT` are its built-ins**, and writing `light()` is how you get a custom lighting model — cel shading, a two-tone ramp, a palette-constrained light.

**That is often the better answer for pixel art than normal maps:** rather than lighting the sprite realistically, **quantise the light into two or three steps so it stays within the palette.**

```glsl
void light() {
	float l = step(0.5, LIGHT_COLOR.r * LIGHT_ENERGY);
	LIGHT = vec4(COLOR.rgb * mix(vec3(1.0), LIGHT_COLOR.rgb, l), COLOR.a);
}
```

**Practice.** Make a normal map for one tile with Laigter and give the tile a `CanvasTexture`. Move a `PointLight2D` past it and tune the light's `height` from 0 to 50. Then try the same on a 16×16 character sprite and judge honestly whether it helped. Then write a `light()` function that quantises the light to two steps, and compare it with the default.
GPUParticles2D and the process material:
The particle system — one node, one resource with eighty properties, and the dozen that matter.

**Two nodes, and the choice is simple:**

| Node | Where it runs | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`GPUParticles2D`** | **the GPU** | **the default.** Thousands of particles, free. |
| `CPUParticles2D` | the CPU | when the GPU one is unavailable or you need per-particle logic |

**Use `GPUParticles2D`.** `CPUParticles2D` exists for old hardware and for the rare case where you need to read a particle's position — **and there is a converter in the editor's toolbar** to go from one to the other.

**The node's own properties:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`amount`** | **how many particles exist at once** |
| **`lifetime`** | how long each lives, in seconds |
| **`one_shot`** | **a burst rather than a stream** |
| `preprocess` | start mid-way through, **so rain is already falling** |
| `speed_scale` | time multiplier |
| `explosiveness` | **0 = evenly spread, 1 = all at once** |
| `randomness` | jitter on the emission timing |
| `fixed_fps`, `interpolate` | **set `fixed_fps = 0` to run at the real frame rate** |
| `local_coords` | **off means particles stay where they were born** |
| `draw_order` | Index, Lifetime, Reverse Lifetime |
| `emitting` | **the on switch** |
| `visibility_rect` | culling bounds — **generate it from the toolbar** |

**Three of those decide the feel.**

**`amount` × `lifetime` gives the rate.** 100 particles with a 2-second lifetime is 50 per second. **To make something denser, raise `amount`; to make it last longer, raise `lifetime`** — and raising both multiplies.

**`explosiveness = 1` plus `one_shot = true` is an explosion.** `explosiveness = 0` is a stream. **Everything between is a puff.**

**`local_coords = false` is the one people get wrong.** With it **on** (the default in some versions), the particles move with the emitter — so a trail from a moving object drags along behind it instead of staying put. **For a dust trail, smoke, or sparks, turn it off.**

**Then the material, which is where the work is.** `process_material` takes a **`ParticleProcessMaterial`**, and its properties are grouped:

| Group | The ones that matter |
| --- | --- |
| **Emission Shape** | **Point, Sphere, Sphere Surface, Box, Points, Directed Points, Ring** |
| **Direction** | `direction`, **`spread`** (degrees), `flatness` |
| **Gravity** | **`gravity`** — a `Vector3`; set `y` positive for falling |
| **Initial Velocity** | `min`/`max` |
| **Angular Velocity** | spin |
| **Orbit Velocity** | circular motion |
| **Linear Accel / Radial Accel / Tangential Accel** | push, outward, sideways |
| **Damping** | slow down over life |
| **Scale** | `scale_min`/`max`, **`scale_curve`** |
| **Color** | `color`, **`color_ramp`**, `color_initial_ramp` |
| **Animation** | for sprite-sheet particles |
| **Turbulence** | noise-driven drift |

**The two curve properties do most of the visual work.**

**`scale_curve` takes a `CurveTexture`** — a `Curve` resource from stage 7 — and scales each particle over its life. **A curve that rises then falls gives you a puff that grows and shrinks**, which is what smoke does.

**`color_ramp` takes a `GradientTexture1D`**, and **the alpha in that gradient is the fade.** A ramp from opaque to transparent is how a particle disappears — **not `lifetime` alone, which makes it vanish abruptly.**

**Those two together — a scale curve and a colour ramp fading to zero alpha — are the difference between particles and confetti.**

**Four recipes:**

**Dust from footsteps:**
```
amount 8, lifetime 0.6, one_shot, explosiveness 0.9, local_coords off
emission: Sphere, radius 4
direction (0, -1), spread 40, initial velocity 10–25
gravity (0, 30)
scale curve: rises to 1 then holds; colour ramp: fades to alpha 0
```

**A hit spark:**
```
amount 12, lifetime 0.25, one_shot, explosiveness 1.0
emission: Point, spread 180, initial velocity 80–160
damping 100
colour ramp: white → the hit colour → transparent
```

**Rain:**
```
amount 400, lifetime 1.2, preprocess 1.2, local_coords off
emission: Box, a wide thin box above the screen
gravity (0, 900), initial velocity 0
```

**`preprocess 1.2` is the detail** — without it the first second has no rain in the lower half of the screen.

**Smoke:**
```
amount 20, lifetime 3.0, explosiveness 0
emission: Sphere radius 8, direction (0, -1), spread 20
initial velocity 10–20, damping 5, turbulence on, low strength
scale curve rising; colour ramp fading to 0
```

**The pixel-art problem**, which is real: particles are drawn as textured quads at **arbitrary positions and scales**, so in a pixel-art game they land between pixels and scale fractionally. **Three mitigations:**

| Mitigation | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Use a 1×1 or 2×2 texture and no scaling** | particles are single pixels — **often the best look** |
| **Keep `scale` at integer values** | no fractional scaling |
| **Accept it** | at small sizes and short lifetimes it is barely visible |

**Single-pixel particles with a colour ramp are genuinely the right answer for a lot of pixel art** — sparks, blood, embers — and they cost nothing.

**The performance facts:**

| Fact | Note |
| --- | --- |
| **`amount` is allocated up front** | `amount = 10000` costs memory whether or not it emits |
| **`emitting = false` still processes** | set it false *and* the node stops emitting, but existing particles finish |
| **`visibility_rect` enables culling** | **generate it from the toolbar** or offscreen emitters keep rendering |
| **One emitter with 500 is cheaper than 50 with 10** | the per-emitter cost dominates |

**That last row is the design guidance: prefer one shared emitter.** A `GPUParticles2D` with `emission_shape = Points` and a `PointsTexture` can emit from many places at once — one node, many sources.

**Restarting a one-shot:**

```gdscript
particles.restart()
```

**Not `emitting = true`**, which does nothing if it is already true. **`restart()` is the one to call** for a burst that fires repeatedly.

**Practice.** Build a footstep dust puff with `one_shot`, `explosiveness 0.9` and `local_coords` off, and confirm the dust stays where it was made as the player walks on. Add a `scale_curve` that rises then falls and a `color_ramp` fading to alpha 0 — then remove each and see what it was doing. Then build rain with `preprocess` and watch the first second with and without it. Then make a spark emitter with a 2×2 white texture and no scaling.
Particles by hand, and when to prefer th:
Doing it yourself in `_draw` — when that is better than the particle system, and the pattern that makes it easy.

**The case for hand-rolled particles.** `GPUParticles2D` is excellent and the right default. **It cannot do four things:**

| Cannot | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Be read from code** | the particles live on the GPU. You cannot ask where one is. |
| **Interact** | no collision with your world, no reacting to game state |
| **Be tested** | a headless run has no GPU particles to assert on |
| **Carry data** | a damage number needs a *value*, not just a position |

**And the fourth is the common one.** Your own project's `DamageNumbers` is exactly this case: each particle is a **number**, and it must show the right one.

**The pattern, which is the whole lesson:**

```gdscript
extends CanvasLayer

const RISE_PX: float = 30.0
const SECONDS: float = 0.8
const SCATTER_PX: float = 10.0

var _numbers: Array[Dictionary] = []
var _canvas: Control
var _rng := RandomNumberGenerator.new()


func _ready() -> void:
	_canvas = Control.new()
	_canvas.mouse_filter = Control.MOUSE_FILTER_IGNORE
	_canvas.draw.connect(_draw_numbers)
	add_child(_canvas)
	_rng.randomize()


func add(at: Vector2, amount: int, crit: bool) -> void:
	_numbers.append({
		"at": at + Vector2(_rng.randf_range(-SCATTER_PX, SCATTER_PX), 0.0),
		"text": str(amount),
		"crit": crit,
		"age": 0.0,
	})


func _process(delta: float) -> void:
	var i := _numbers.size() - 1
	while i >= 0:
		_numbers[i]["age"] += delta
		if _numbers[i]["age"] >= SECONDS:
			_numbers.remove_at(i)
		i -= 1
	_canvas.queue_redraw()


func _draw_numbers() -> void:
	var font := ThemeDB.fallback_font
	for number: Dictionary in _numbers:
		var t: float = number["age"] / SECONDS
		var at: Vector2 = number["at"] - Vector2(0.0, RISE_PX * t)
		var colour: Color = CRIT_COLOUR if number["crit"] else ENEMY_COLOUR
		colour.a = 1.0 - t
		_canvas.draw_string(font, at, number["text"],
			HORIZONTAL_ALIGNMENT_CENTER, -1.0,
			CRIT_FONT_SIZE if number["crit"] else FONT_SIZE, colour)
```

**Six things in that, each worth noting.**

**1. An `Array[Dictionary]`, not nodes.** Fifty numbers is fifty dictionary entries — **no `Label`s, no scene instantiation, no `queue_free`.** For short-lived visual things, this is dramatically cheaper and simpler than a node per particle.

**2. `age` normalised to `t` in 0–1**, and everything derived from `t`: the rise, the alpha, the scale. **One number drives the whole animation**, which is the same discipline as the night fade from the `CanvasModulate` lesson.

**3. The backwards `while` loop for removal.** Iterating forwards and removing shifts the indices under you. **Backwards is the standard fix**, and this is the case where a `for i in range()` is wrong.

**4. One `_draw` for all of them.** From stage 8 — fifty `draw_string` calls in one `_draw` is one node's worth of work.

**5. `SCATTER_PX`**, the design detail: *"small, short-lived and slightly scattered so a crowd stays readable rather than a stack of numbers on one spot."* **Without it, ten hits in one place draw ten numbers on top of each other and you can read none.**

**6. It carries data.** `amount` and `crit` are per-particle facts that change what is drawn. **No particle system can do this.**

**And it is testable**, which the `GPUParticles2D` version is not:

```gdscript
func what_is_showing() -> Array:
	return _numbers.map(func(n: Dictionary) -> String: return n["text"])
```

**The same `what_it_says()` idea as stage 9's interface** — the system reports its own state, and a headless check asserts on it.

**When to use which:**

| Use `GPUParticles2D` | Use hand-rolled |
| --- | --- |
| Smoke, rain, sparks, dust, fire | **damage numbers, floating text** |
| Thousands of identical things | **anything carrying data** |
| Anything purely decorative | **anything that must be tested** |
| Anything with no logic | **anything that reacts to the game** |
| Anything you will tune visually | **anything that collides or interacts** |

**And a middle option worth knowing: a pooled scene.** For particles that genuinely need to be nodes — a bouncing coin with physics, a projectile with an `Area2D` — **pre-instantiate twenty and reuse them**:

```gdscript
var _pool: Array[Node2D] = []

func _ready() -> void:
	for i in 20:
		var one := COIN.instantiate() as Node2D
		one.process_mode = Node.PROCESS_MODE_DISABLED
		one.visible = false
		add_child(one)
		_pool.append(one)

func spawn(at: Vector2) -> void:
	for one in _pool:
		if not one.visible:
			one.global_position = at
			one.visible = true
			one.process_mode = Node.PROCESS_MODE_INHERIT
			return
```

**Pooling is the answer when the particle must be a node**, and the two things it avoids are instantiation cost and `queue_free` churn. **From stage 5's node-lifecycle lesson.**

**The honest caveat on pooling: do not do it until you have measured.** Instantiating a small scene is fast, and a pool is state you have to manage — a pooled object that remembers something from its last life is a genuinely nasty bug. **The profiler lesson is two lessons away; use it before pooling.**

**Draw-based effects beyond particles.** Once you are comfortable drawing a list of things, a lot becomes easy:

| Effect | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| **Floating text** | the pattern above |
| **A hit-direction indicator** | an arc drawn at an angle, fading |
| **Debug trails** | append a position per frame, draw a polyline |
| **Impact rings** | `draw_arc` with a growing radius and fading alpha |
| **Lightning** | a `draw_polyline` of jittered points, regenerated per frame |

**All of them are: a list, an age, and a `_draw`.** One pattern, and it is worth having written once by hand.

**Practice.** Build the damage-number system above and fire twenty numbers at one point — then remove `SCATTER_PX` and see why it is there. Confirm the backwards removal loop is necessary by making it forwards and watching numbers survive. Add a `what_is_showing()` and assert on it from a headless check. Then draw an expanding fading ring with `draw_arc` using the same list-and-age pattern.
Audio: AudioStreamPlayer and positional:
The three player nodes, the one that pans, and the details that make game audio not sound amateur.

**The three nodes:**

| Node | Position | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`AudioStreamPlayer`** | **none — flat** | music, interface, ambience, narration |
| **`AudioStreamPlayer2D`** | **2D, pans and attenuates** | things happening in the world |
| `AudioStreamPlayer3D` | 3D, with doppler | 3D games |

**The rule is simple and your own project states it twice.** For a bed of ambience:

> *FLAT, NOT POSITIONAL. A bed is the air around the player rather than a thing standing somewhere, so it plays on plain `AudioStreamPlayer`s. The pens (`amb.fold`) stay positional, because they ARE a thing standing somewhere and walking away from them should quieten them.*

**"Is it a thing standing somewhere?"** That is the whole test. **The air of a place is flat; an object in the place pans.**

**The shared properties:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`stream`** | the `AudioStream` |
| **`volume_db`** | **decibels. 0 is unchanged, −6 is half as loud, −80 is silence.** |
| **`pitch_scale`** | 1 is normal. **Changes speed too.** |
| **`bus`** | which bus it plays on |
| `autoplay` | play on entering the tree |
| `playing`, `stream_paused` | state |
| `max_polyphony` | **how many instances of this player may overlap** |
| `process_mode` | **whether it runs while paused** |
| `mix_target` | stereo, surround, centre |

**`volume_db` is decibels, not a 0–1 scale**, and that is the single most common mistake. **The conversion:**

```gdscript
volume_db = linear_to_db(0.5)   # -6.02
var linear := db_to_linear(-12.0)  # 0.251
```

**Use `linear_to_db` whenever a slider or a fraction becomes a volume.** A slider mapped directly to `volume_db` feels wrong because decibels are logarithmic — **the middle of a −80 to 0 slider is 0.01% of the power.**

**`AudioStreamPlayer2D`'s own properties:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`max_distance`** | **beyond this, silence** |
| **`attenuation`** | the falloff curve exponent |
| `panning_strength` | how hard it pans |
| `area_mask` | which `Area2D` audio buses it respects |

**And it needs a listener.** By default the **`Camera2D`** is the listener, which is usually right. **An `AudioListener2D` node overrides it** — useful when the camera is not where the player is.

**Your own project sets the range deliberately:**

```gdscript
## How far a sound in the world carries. About a screen and a half: a bleat from the next field is
## part of the place, one from across the Highfold is not.
const HEARD_WITHIN_PX: float = 1400.0
```

**"About a screen and a half"** — the distance expressed in terms of what the player can see, not an arbitrary number. **That is the right way to pick a `max_distance`.**

**And the art requirement that goes with positional audio:**

> *The audio authority makes every world sound mono for exactly this.*

**A stereo file cannot pan.** It already has a left and a right, and Godot will play it as-is. **Every positional sound must be mono**, which is a mastering requirement, not a code one — **and it is the reason a sound that will not pan does not pan.**

**Variation, which is the difference between a game and a buzzer.** The same sound played twenty times in ten seconds becomes unbearable. **Two fixes, and use both:**

**1. Pitch jitter**, which your own `ImpactAudioPlayer` does:

```gdscript
@export_range(0.1, 4.0, 0.01) var minimum_pitch_scale: float = 0.96
@export_range(0.1, 4.0, 0.01) var maximum_pitch_scale: float = 1.04

func request_impact(at: Vector2) -> void:
	global_position = at
	stream = impact_stream
	volume_db = impact_volume_db
	pitch_scale = randf_range(minimum_pitch_scale, maximum_pitch_scale)
	play()
```

**0.96 to 1.04 — four per cent.** Small enough that nobody notices the pitch, large enough that twenty hits do not sound identical. **A wider range reads as a broken tape.**

**2. Variations of the file.** Five recordings of a footstep, chosen at random — **and your own project makes this free with a naming convention:**

> *A file's name IS its cue — the cue ID with dots as underscores, plus a variation number. `sfx.eli.step.grass` → `sfx_eli_step_grass_01.wav` … `_05.wav`. So nothing has to be registered: a file placed in one of the `ROOTS` folders is playable by its cue on the next run, and a cue with no file yet is simply silent.*

**Three good ideas there.** **A convention instead of a registry** — no file to update when audio is added. **A cue with no file is silent, not an error** — so the game can be built before the audio exists and *"asking would cost nothing."* **And variations are discovered**, not listed.
